# Build: Agent Log

The shared machinery behind BoardUI's Task List and Web Search: a line of agent work drawing itself down the page. `useRevealTicker` paces how many units are visible, `LogRow` blurs each row in as its height opens, softening the clipping edge with an animated mask, and draws its own piece of a curved tree guide so the line reads as one pen stroke. `WorkingRow` is the loose "still going" indicator at the bottom, and `ShimmerText` marks a line in progress. It says nothing about what a row contains; that is the consumer's job.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

Streaming agent-log parts: a reveal ticker, rows that blur in under a soft clipping edge, and a curved tree guide that draws itself.

- Category: display
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: motion@^12.43.0

## How it works

1. `useRevealTicker({ total, stepInterval = 850, startDelay = 320, delayFor, revealed, run, onComplete })` returns how many units to show. Uncontrolled, it schedules one `setTimeout` per step (`startDelay` before the first, `stepInterval` after, or `delayFor(index)` per unit) and clears it on cleanup. Passing `revealed` disables the timer so real events drive the log. `onComplete` fires once per completion, guarded by a ref.
2. `LogRow` is a `motion.li` animating from `UNIT_INITIAL` (`opacity 0, height 0, y 4, blur(6px)`) to `UNIT_ANIMATE` (`opacity 1, height auto, y 0, blur(0px)`). Height runs 0.38s and the rest 0.42s, all on `SOFT_EASE` [0.22, 1, 0.36, 1], so the row has made space just before the text sharpens.
3. Growing from height 0 behind `overflow-hidden` would cut a hard line through the text, so `useRevealMask` applies a `mask-image` gradient whose solid part ends `--bui-reveal-fade` pixels short of the bottom. Motion animates that custom property from 22px to 0 over 0.44s; on `onAnimationComplete` the mask is removed so nothing is composited at rest.
4. `RowConnector` draws the row's piece of the guide: an SVG branch (down the trunk, a 6px quadratic corner at y = 14, out 12px) animating `pathLength` 0 → 1, and, unless the row is last, a 1px trunk below it scaling from its top edge.
5. The pieces run in sequence like one pen: the tail (trunk) of the row above draws for 0.12s, then the new row's branch draws for 0.14s after a 0.12s delay (no delay for the first row). Both are `linear` so the stroke keeps one pace through each junction.
6. `WorkingRow` uses the same blur-in to show `AgentThinking variant="stars"` with a label, off the guide. `GuideBridge` fills the gap between a parent row's glyph and a nested list's trunk. `useLogMotion` reads `prefers-reduced-motion` once for the whole log.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `SOFT_EASE = [0.22, 1, 0.36, 1]`
  Steeply front-loaded, so text has settled by about 0.2s of its 0.42s blur-in.
- `UNIT_TRANSITION = height 0.38s; opacity, filter, y 0.42s; --bui-reveal-fade 0.44s`
  The container settles first, then the words arrive, which reads as smooth rather than as a jump.
- `--bui-reveal-fade = 22px → 0px`
  Longer than a 20px text line, so a growing row is always faintest exactly where it is being clipped.
- `branch geometry = BRANCH_Y 14, BRANCH_RADIUS 6, BRANCH_WIDTH 12`
  The elbow sits at half of the 20px line plus the 4px top padding, fixed from the top, so a wrapped label still branches at its first line.
- `guide timing = tail 0.12s, branch 0.14s after 0.12s, linear`
  Lengths over one pen speed of about 160px/s, so the handoff between pieces is invisible.
- `ticker defaults = startDelay 320ms, stepInterval 850ms`
  A short wait before the first row, then a steady pace that `delayFor` can override per unit.

## API

```ts
function useRevealTicker(options: { total: number; run?: boolean; stepInterval?: number; startDelay?: number; revealed?: number; delayFor?: (index: number) => number; onComplete?: () => void }): number
function LogRow(props: { first: boolean; last: boolean; reduce: boolean; className?: string; children: ReactNode }): JSX.Element
function WorkingRow(props: { label: string; reduce: boolean; className?: string }): JSX.Element
function ShimmerText(props: { children: string }): JSX.Element
function GuideBridge(props: { height: number; offset?: number; reduce: boolean }): JSX.Element
function RowConnector(props: { first: boolean; last: boolean; reduce: boolean }): JSX.Element
function useLogMotion(): boolean
function useRevealMask(reduce: boolean): { style?: CSSProperties; onAnimationComplete: () => void }
```

- `total: number`
  useRevealTicker: how many units the log has.
- `stepInterval / startDelay: number` — default `850 / 320`
  useRevealTicker: wait between units and before the first, in ms.
- `delayFor: (index: number) => number`
  useRevealTicker: per-unit wait; overrides both defaults.
- `revealed: number`
  useRevealTicker: controlled count; disables the internal timer.
- `run: boolean` — default `true`
  useRevealTicker: pause and resume the timer.
- `onComplete: () => void`
  useRevealTicker: fires once when the last unit lands.
- `first / last: boolean`
  LogRow: position in the list; controls the branch delay and whether a trunk is drawn.
- `reduce: boolean`
  LogRow, WorkingRow, GuideBridge: skip the entrance and draw animations (from useLogMotion).
- `label: string`
  WorkingRow: text next to the stars indicator.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
/**
 * Each unit blurs in as it lands: 6px of blur and a 4px lift resolving over
 * 0.42s, the same language the AI Chat thread uses for a streaming line. The
 * height runs a touch shorter on the soft curve so the row has finished making
 * space slightly before the text finishes sharpening — the container settles
 * first, then the words arrive, which is what reads as smooth rather than as a
 * jump.
 *
 * Growing a row from height 0 means `overflow-hidden` cuts a hard line through
 * the text while it emerges. `--bui-reveal-fade` softens that edge: the row is
 * masked with a gradient whose solid portion ends that many pixels short of the
 * bottom, and the reveal animates it to 0, at which point the mask is a no-op
 * and nothing pops. The fade is longer than a text line, so a row is always
 * faintest exactly where it is being clipped.
 */
const REVEAL_FADE_VAR = "--bui-reveal-fade";

// The transparent stop sits just past the box: with both stops at exactly 100%
// the gradient is degenerate and browsers soften the final pixel row, which
// shows up as breaks in the guide where one row meets the next.
const REVEAL_GRADIENT = `linear-gradient(to bottom, #000 calc(100% - var(${REVEAL_FADE_VAR}, 0px)), transparent calc(100% + 1px))`;

const REVEAL_MASK: CSSProperties = {
  WebkitMaskImage: REVEAL_GRADIENT,
  maskImage: REVEAL_GRADIENT,
};

export const UNIT_INITIAL = {
  opacity: 0,
  height: 0,
  y: 4,
  filter: "blur(6px)",
  [REVEAL_FADE_VAR]: "22px",
};

export const UNIT_ANIMATE = {
  opacity: 1,
  height: "auto",
  y: 0,
  filter: "blur(0px)",
  [REVEAL_FADE_VAR]: "0px",
};

export const UNIT_TRANSITION = {
  height: { duration: 0.38, ease: SOFT_EASE },
  opacity: { duration: 0.42, ease: SOFT_EASE },
  filter: { duration: 0.42, ease: SOFT_EASE },
  y: { duration: 0.42, ease: SOFT_EASE },
  [REVEAL_FADE_VAR]: { duration: 0.44, ease: SOFT_EASE },
};

/**
 * The soft edge only earns its keep while a unit is growing. Once the reveal
 * finishes, drop the mask entirely: no compositing layer at rest, and the guide
 * meets pixel-exactly at every row boundary.
 */
export function useRevealMask(reduce: boolean) {
  const [revealing, setRevealing] = useState(!reduce);
  return {
    style: revealing ? REVEAL_MASK : undefined,
    onAnimationComplete: () => setRevealing(false),
  };
}
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** `useRevealTicker` clears its pending `setTimeout` whenever the count, options or component change, and on unmount. Motion stops its animations when rows unmount. No global listeners are added.

**Reduced motion.** With `reduce` true, every `initial` is `false`: rows mount at full height and opacity with no blur, the mask is never applied, and the branch and trunk appear fully drawn. The ticker still paces rows, since that is content arriving rather than decoration. `ShimmerText` drops its sweep through the theme's reduced-motion rule.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Give each row content a 4px top padding and a 20px line (the demo uses `py-1` with body text). The branch elbow is fixed at 14px and will not meet the label otherwise.
- Pass `last` correctly: only the final visible row omits its trunk. When a new row arrives the previous one gains its trunk, which is what draws the tail first.
- Keep `delayFor` and `onComplete` stable or cheap. `delayFor` is an effect dependency, so an inline function restarts the pending timer on every render.
- Change the parent's `key` to replay a log. Toggling `run` only pauses and resumes from the current count.
- Do not render a log with motion on the hydration pass if the server cannot know the reduced-motion preference. `initial` differs between the two, so start revealing after mount.

## Notes

- Real agent steps do not take equal time. Drive the log with `revealed` from real events as soon as you have them, or use `delayFor` to dwell on the slow steps.
- `ShimmerText` uses the theme's `.agent-progress-loading-text`: a 3.4s linear gradient sweep through `background-clip: text`, replaced by plain secondary text under reduced motion.
- `agent-log` imports `AgentThinking` for the working row, so installing it brings that item in.

## Definition of done

A log of five steps with the default ticker shows its first row about 320ms after mount, then one row roughly every 850ms (or per `delayFor`). Each row opens its height and sharpens from a 6px blur while lifting 4px, with no hard line cutting the text as it grows. The guide draws as one continuous stroke: the previous row's trunk extends down, then the new row's curved branch draws out to its label. The last row has no trunk hanging below its corner. `onComplete` fires exactly once. With reduced motion, rows appear instantly with the guide already drawn.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Agent Progress

A compact block that runs an ordered list of steps. Each step runs for stepDuration with its own ring filling, then checks off with a strike-through while the next one lights up; the header ring tracks the whole run and counts the steps left. The block can be minimized without losing its place, and after the last check it holds for completionDelay before calling onFinished.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

A minimizable step list for multi-step agent work: an overall ring, a timed ring on the running step, check-offs and a completion hand-off.

- Category: display
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: motion@^12.43.0, @remixicon/react@^4.9.0

## How it works

1. useStepClock stamps performance.now() when a step becomes active and samples the elapsed fraction in a requestAnimationFrame loop; at 1 it calls advance(step + 1), which changes the effect key and starts the next clock.
2. The fraction is stored with the step it belongs to, so a new step reads 0 on its first render without a synchronous reset in the effect.
3. Rings are a 16-unit SVG circle with stroke-dasharray equal to its circumference; dashoffset = C·(1 − fraction). The header ring uses (done + fraction) / total.
4. Rows enter with a 60ms stagger (opacity, 6px rise, 2px blur) through motion; finished steps swap their ring for a check that springs in.
5. Minimizing collapses the list with a grid-template-rows 0fr transition and makes it inert; the clock keeps running, so reopening shows the current step.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `stepDuration = 2400ms`
  Long enough to read a step label and watch its ring fill, short enough that five steps finish in about 12s.
- `completionDelay = 1000ms`
  Lets the last check and "All steps done" register before the caller swaps in the reply.
- `STAGGER_S = 0.06`
  Rows arrive as a quick cascade; slower reads as lag on a five-step list.
- `REDUCED_TICKS = 4`
  Under reduced motion the rings step in quarters instead of moving every frame.

## API

```ts
<AgentProgress steps={["Analyze the request", "Generate the component"]} stepDuration={2400} completionDelay={1000} onFinished={() => reply()} />
```

- `steps: readonly string[]`
  Ordered step labels.
- `step / defaultStep / onStepChange: number / number / (step: number) => void` — default `0`
  Index of the running step, controlled or uncontrolled. steps.length means done.
- `stepDuration: number` — default `2400`
  Milliseconds each step runs.
- `completionDelay: number` — default `1000`
  Milliseconds to hold the done state before onFinished.
- `onFinished: () => void`
  Fires once after the final step and the completion delay.
- `minimized / defaultMinimized / onMinimizedChange: boolean / boolean / (minimized: boolean) => void` — default `false`
  Collapses the list to the header.
- `remainingLabel: (remaining: number) => string` — default `"{n} steps left"`
  Header copy while running.
- `doneLabel: string` — default `"All steps done"`
  Header copy once finished.
- `className: string`
  Classes on the block.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
/** done / running / pending for row i while step `active` runs. */
export function stepState(index: number, active: number): AgentStepState {
  if (index < active) return "done";
  return index === active ? "running" : "pending";
}

/**
 * Drives one step: measures elapsed time from the moment `step` became active
 * and reports the fraction. A frame loop paints the rings smoothly; under
 * reduced motion a 4-tick interval moves them in quarters. When the fraction
 * reaches 1 the step is handed to `advance`, which re-keys this effect.
 */
function useStepClock(
  step: number,
  total: number,
  duration: number,
  reduced: boolean,
  advance: (next: number) => void,
) {
  const [tick, setTick] = useState({ step: -1, fraction: 0 });
  const advanceRef = useRef(advance);
  useEffect(() => {
    advanceRef.current = advance;
  });

  useEffect(() => {
    if (step < 0 || step >= total) return;
    const started = performance.now();
    const span = Math.max(1, duration);
    let raf = 0;
    let interval: ReturnType<typeof setInterval> | undefined;
    const sample = () => {
      const fraction = Math.min(1, (performance.now() - started) / span);
      setTick({ step, fraction });
      if (fraction >= 1) advanceRef.current(step + 1);
      return fraction >= 1;
    };
    if (reduced) {
      interval = setInterval(() => {
        if (sample() && interval) clearInterval(interval);
      }, span / REDUCED_TICKS);
    } else {
      const loop = () => {
        if (!sample()) raf = requestAnimationFrame(loop);
      };
      raf = requestAnimationFrame(loop);
    }
    return () => {
      cancelAnimationFrame(raf);
      if (interval) clearInterval(interval);
    };
  }, [step, total, duration, reduced]);

  return tick.step === step ? tick.fraction : 0;
}
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** The clock effect cancels its requestAnimationFrame or interval whenever the step, duration or motion preference changes and on unmount; the completion timeout is cleared the same way.

**Reduced motion.** Rows appear without the stagger, checks appear without the spring, the list opens and closes instantly, the label shimmer stops, and the rings advance in four discrete quarters per step instead of every frame. Steps still advance on time.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Restarting at the same step index does not restart the clock; remount with a new key to replay the stagger and the timer from zero.
- In controlled mode the clock only advances through onStepChange; if the parent ignores it, the running ring stops full.
- onFinished is read through a ref, so an inline callback does not restart the completion timer.

## Notes

- Pass step + onStepChange to skip ahead or sync with real agent events; steps.length means every step is done.
- The running label uses the theme agent-progress-loading-text shimmer, which already falls back to plain text under reduced motion.

## Definition of done

The header reads "5 steps left" then counts down as each step checks off; Skip step jumps to the next row; minimize hides the list and the count keeps moving; after the last step the header reads "All steps done" and onFinished fires about a second later; Restart replays from the first step.

and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Agent Thinking

The status line an agent shows while it works on a reply. Four indicators share one layout: a 3×3 dot grid with a diagonal wavefront (`wave`), the same grid with a bright head orbiting it (`spin`), five sparkles twinkling in a stagger (`stars`) and a comet lapping a figure-eight (`infinity`). Each sits next to a label with a travelling text shimmer and an optional elapsed-seconds counter, inside a `role="status"` row whose colour comes from one of four tones.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

The "thinking" line above a chat composer: dot wave, dot spin, stars or infinity, with a shimmering label and an elapsed timer.

- Category: display
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: none beyond React

## How it works

1. The dot variants are driven from JavaScript. Each of the nine cells gets a scalar in [0, 1) along the direction of travel: for `wave` it is `(col + row) / 4` compressed by 3/4, so the front leaves the grid before the phase wraps; for `spin` it is the cell's `atan2` angle around the centre, which is naturally cyclic.
2. A `setInterval` every 80ms advances the phase by 1/8 (one lap per 640ms) and recomputes opacities as a comet: `behind = (phase - s + 1) % 1`, `lit = max(0, 1 - behind / 0.3) ** 1.5`, mapped onto 0.12–1. A 220ms CSS opacity transition on every cell blends the 80ms steps into a glide.
3. `stars` is pure CSS: five 4-point sparkle paths placed at fixed percentages and scales, each running the `bui-agent-thinking-star` keyframes (scale 0 → 1 → 0.8 → 0 with fade) over 1.4s, with `animation-delay` staggered by `i × 1.4 × 0.7 / 5`s.
4. `infinity` draws the figure-eight twice: a 15%-opacity track, and a copy with `pathLength={100}` and `strokeDasharray="11 89"` whose `stroke-dashoffset` animates to -100 every 1.2s, so an 11%-long dash laps the loop at constant speed.
5. The root sets `color` and `--bui-agent-thinking-tone` to the tone colour. The indicators paint with `currentColor`; the label's `.bui-agent-thinking-label` paints a 300%-wide gradient (tone at 55% → 100% → 55%) through `background-clip: text` and slides it with the theme's `ai-chat-text-shimmer` keyframes over 2.6s.
6. `ElapsedTimer` records `performance.now()` on mount and re-renders every 100ms with `elapsed.toFixed(1)` seconds in a tabular mono caption.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `DOTS_GRID / DOTS_SIZE / DOTS_GAP = 3 / 4px / 2px`
  Three 4px cells and two 2px gaps make a 16px square indicator beside the label.
- `DOTS_TICK_MS / DOTS_PHASE_STEP = 80ms / 1/8`
  Eight steps per lap gives a 640ms cycle: lively without reading as a flicker.
- `DOTS_FADE_MS = 220ms`
  Longer than the 80ms tick, so each cell is always mid-transition and the stepped updates read as continuous motion.
- `DOTS_TRAIL / DOTS_MIN_OPACITY = 0.3 / 0.12`
  The tail covers 30% of the lap with a power-1.5 falloff; unlit cells keep 12% so the grid shape never disappears.
- `DOTS_SEED = [0.55, 0.3, 0.15, 0.85, 0.55, 0.3, 1, 0.85, 0.55]`
  A fixed first frame shared by server and client, and the resting state under reduced motion.
- `STAR_PERIOD_S / STAR_SIZE / STAR_COUNT = 1.4s / 14px / 5`
  The box is 21px (1.5 × size); the largest sparkle is 14px and the others are scaled 0.4–0.55 around it.
- `INFINITY_TRAIL / INFINITY_STROKE / INFINITY_DURATION_S = 11 of 100 / 2.75 / 1.2s`
  An 11% dash is long enough to read as a comet but short enough to stay on one lobe of the eight at a time.
- `TONE_COLORS = subtle text-tertiary, default text-secondary, primary text-primary, accent blue-500`
  Every variant defaults to `default` except `stars`, which defaults to `subtle`.

## API

```ts
type AgentThinkingVariant = "wave" | "spin" | "stars" | "infinity"
type AgentThinkingTone = "subtle" | "default" | "primary" | "accent"
function AgentThinking(props: { variant?: AgentThinkingVariant; label?: string; tone?: AgentThinkingTone; shimmer?: boolean; showTimer?: boolean; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `variant: "wave" | "spin" | "stars" | "infinity"` — default `"wave"`
  Which indicator sits before the label.
- `label: string` — default `"Thinking"`
  Status text, e.g. "Searching the docs".
- `tone: "subtle" | "default" | "primary" | "accent"`
  Colour of the indicator and label. Defaults to `default`, or `subtle` for `stars`.
- `shimmer: boolean` — default `true`
  Animated highlight travelling across the label.
- `showTimer: boolean` — default `true`
  Elapsed seconds since mount, shown after the label.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the root flex row.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
/**
 * How far along the pattern's travel direction each cell sits, in [0, 1).
 * The wave scalar is compressed below 1 so the phase wrap reads as the front
 * leaving the grid and re-entering; the spin angle is naturally cyclic.
 */
function dotScalar(variant: "wave" | "spin", col: number, row: number) {
  const m = DOTS_GRID - 1;
  if (variant === "wave") {
    return ((col + row) / (2 * m)) * (DOTS_GRID / (DOTS_GRID + 1));
  }
  const center = m / 2;
  return (Math.atan2(row - center, col - center) / (2 * Math.PI) + 1) % 1;
}

function dotOpacities(variant: "wave" | "spin", phase: number) {
  return Array.from({ length: DOTS_GRID * DOTS_GRID }, (_, i) => {
    const s = dotScalar(variant, i % DOTS_GRID, Math.floor(i / DOTS_GRID));
    // Comet: bright head at the phase front, tail fading behind it.
    const behind = (phase - s + 1) % 1;
    const lit = Math.max(0, 1 - behind / DOTS_TRAIL) ** 1.5;
    return DOTS_MIN_OPACITY + (1 - DOTS_MIN_OPACITY) * lit;
  });
}
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** The dot interval and the timer interval are each cleared by their effect cleanup on unmount; the dot interval is also restarted when `variant` changes. The stars and the infinity comet are CSS animations and stop with the element. No global listeners are added.

**Reduced motion.** The dot variants check `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` on mount and, if it matches, never start their interval, so the grid rests on `DOTS_SEED`. The theme's reduced-motion block removes the label gradient and shows it in the plain tone, stops the comet (leaving the dash still), and shows the stars at 70% opacity instead of frozen at scale 0. The elapsed timer keeps counting, since it is information rather than decoration.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Only the dot variants check `prefers-reduced-motion` in JavaScript, and only on mount. Changing the OS setting while one is mounted does not stop its interval until it remounts or its `variant` changes.
- The timer starts when the component mounts. To restart it for a new request, remount with a new `key`; changing `label` or `variant` keeps counting.
- The root is `role="status"` (a polite live region) and the timer text inside it changes every 100ms. If screen readers in your audience re-announce it, pass `showTimer={false}` or show the time elsewhere.
- The label span carries `aria-label={label}` without a role, so assistive technology reads its text content in practice. Do not rely on the attribute to change what is announced.
- The shimmer paints the label with `color: transparent` and a gradient. A parent that sets `background` on text or overrides `color` with `!important` will hide or flatten it.

## Notes

- The infinity SVG has about 4px of empty viewBox on each side, so it uses `margin: 0 -4px` to keep the label at the same 10px gap as the other variants.
- In light mode the stars are softened to 75% of the tone through `color-mix`; in `.dark` they use the full tone.
- BoardUI's own preview stacks all four variants with timers off, because four clocks in one card is noise.

## Definition of done

With `variant="wave"` a bright band sweeps the 3×3 grid from top-left to bottom-right about every 0.64s, with a fading tail and no cell ever fully invisible. `spin` shows a head circling the grid clockwise. `stars` shows five sparkles popping in and out in a stagger; `infinity` shows a short dash lapping a faint figure-eight every 1.2s. The label shimmers left to right in the same tone as the indicator, and the timer counts up in tenths of a second from 0.0s. Remounting resets it. Under reduced motion nothing moves except the timer.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Agents Bar Card

The agents card of an AI profile. A grey card shows "Agents", the number of agents that ran this month and a bordered month switcher, then a row of thin purple bars, one per agent. Agents that did not run sit on the baseline as short grey stubs. A readout row above the bars shows an avatar, name and value: the busiest agent by default, the hovered or focused one while you explore.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

One purple bar per agent for a month, grey stubs for idle ones; hover or arrow keys highlight a bar and show its avatar, name and value.

- Category: display
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: @remixicon/react@^4.9.0

## How it works

1. The bars are plain flex columns, no chart library. Each column fills the 160px chart height as its hit area, and the bar inside is sized as a percentage of the month's maximum with a 6px floor, so small values stay visible. Idle agents render a fixed 3px stub in `chart-neutral`; busy ones use `chart-agents-bar`, and the active one switches to `chart-agents-bar-active`.
2. Height changes are a 300ms CSS transition, so paging months makes the bars grow and shrink in place; the highlight colour follows the pointer in 120ms. `motion-reduce:transition-none` turns both off.
3. The bar row is a single `role="slider"` over the agent index: one tab stop instead of thirty. ArrowLeft and ArrowRight step, Home and End jump, Escape clears; `aria-valuetext` reads "Nova: 1,250 runs". Pointer enter on a column sets the same active index, and leaving the row or blurring it clears it, so mouse and keyboard highlight identically.
4. The readout uses the kit Avatar (24px, tinted by the agent's colour), the name, the value and a rank caption ("#3 of 30"); with nothing active it shows the busiest agent labelled "Most active". It is `aria-hidden` because the slider already announces the same text.
5. The month switcher is a bordered pill of two ghost icon Buttons around the month name, disabled at either end; the name is `aria-live` so a screen reader hears the new month. The card works controlled (`month`) or uncontrolled (`defaultMonth`, the last month by default).

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `chart height = 160px (h-40), bars from a 6px floor to 100% of the month max`
  Tall enough to rank thirty agents by eye; the floor keeps a 1% agent from vanishing into the baseline.
- `gaps = 3px below sm, 6px from sm, 3px top radius`
  Thirty bars still fit a 360px phone at about 7px each, and open up into the reference rhythm on wider cards.
- `idle stub = 3px chart-neutral`
  Shows the agent exists but did nothing, rather than leaving a gap that reads as missing data.
- `transition = 300ms ease-out on height, 120ms on colour`
  Long enough to follow which agents rose or fell between months; the highlight is quicker so it keeps up with a sweeping pointer.

## API

```ts
function AgentsBarCard(props: AgentsBarCardProps): JSX.Element
interface AgentsBarCardProps extends Omit<HTMLAttributes<HTMLElement>, "children"> { title?: string; months: AgentMonth[]; month?: string; defaultMonth?: string; onMonthChange?: (id: string) => void; unit?: string; formatValue?: (value: number) => string; startLabel?: string; endLabel?: string; ref?: Ref<HTMLElement> }
interface AgentMonth { id: string; label: string; agents: AgentUsage[] }
interface AgentUsage { id: string; name: string; initials?: string; color?: "neutral" | "blue" | "lime" | "pink"; value: number }
```

- `title: string` — default `"Agents"`
  Caption above the headline and part of the chart label.
- `months: AgentMonth[]`
  Months in order, each with its label and per-agent values.
- `month: string`
  Controlled month id.
- `defaultMonth: string` — default `last month`
  Initial month when uncontrolled.
- `onMonthChange: (id: string) => void`
  Called when the switcher pages to another month.
- `unit: string` — default `"runs"`
  Word after values.
- `formatValue: (value: number) => string` — default `en-US grouping`
  Formats values in the readout and label.
- `startLabel: string`
  Caption under the first bar.
- `endLabel: string`
  Caption under the last bar.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
const max = agents.reduce((m, a) => Math.max(m, a.value), 0);
const activeCount = agents.filter((a) => a.value > 0).length;
const topIndex = agents.reduce((best, a, i) => (a.value > (agents[best]?.value ?? -1) ? i : best), 0);
const shownIndex = activeIndex ?? topIndex;
const shown = agents[shownIndex];
const rank = shown ? agents.filter((a) => a.value > shown.value).length + 1 : 0;

const goMonth = (step: -1 | 1) => {
  const next = months[monthIndex + step];
  if (!next) return;
  setActiveIndex(null);
  if (month === undefined) setInnerMonth(next.id);
  onMonthChange?.(next.id);
};

// One tab stop for every bar: arrows step, Home/End jump, Escape clears.
const onKeyDown = (e: KeyboardEvent<HTMLDivElement>) => {
  const last = agents.length - 1;
  if (last < 0) return;
  let next: number | null | undefined;
  if (e.key === "ArrowLeft") next = activeIndex === null ? last : Math.max(0, activeIndex - 1);
  else if (e.key === "ArrowRight") next = activeIndex === null ? 0 : Math.min(last, activeIndex + 1);
  else if (e.key === "Home") next = 0;
  else if (e.key === "End") next = last;
  else if (e.key === "Escape") next = null;
  if (next === undefined) return;
  e.preventDefault();
  setActiveIndex(next);
};
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** No timers, observers or global listeners. Pointer and keyboard handlers live on the chart element and go away with it.

**Reduced motion.** With prefers-reduced-motion the bars jump to their new heights and colours without the 300ms and 120ms transitions. Nothing else moves.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Making every bar a button. Thirty tab stops to cross one chart is hostile to keyboard users; one slider with arrow keys is the same information in one stop.
- Highlighting on hover only. Keyboard users then never see the readout; the active index is shared by pointer and keys.
- Scaling bars to a fixed maximum across months. A quiet month then looks empty; each month scales to its own busiest agent, and the readout gives the absolute numbers.
- Dropping idle agents from the row. Bars then shift position between months and the same agent lands in a different place; keep every agent and stub the idle ones.

## Notes

- Order agents by creation date (as the demo does, with "Oldest" and "Newest" captions) so a bar keeps its place month to month.
- Use `unit` and `formatValue` for tokens or minutes instead of runs.

## Definition of done

The card shows "Agents", "22 agents", a "December" switcher and thirty bars with eight grey stubs; the readout shows Cipher, 1,400 runs, "Most active". Hovering a bar turns it the darker purple and the readout shows that agent and its rank. Focusing the chart and pressing Home selects Atlas (620 runs). The previous button goes to November and October and is disabled there. At 360px all thirty bars still fit.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: AI Chat

A full AI coding chat for a 1280 × 800 frame. The left card holds the account menu, quick search and chats grouped by repository; the middle pane is the open chat with a glowing composer and a status bar for branch, project, mode and context; the right pane lists uncommitted changes with their code. Sending a message runs a simulated agent with timers only: a step checklist ticks through, a thinking indicator counts up, then the reply streams in and the run leaves a new file in the changes panel.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

A coding-agent workspace: chat history sidebar, a thread with a live step checklist and streamed replies, and a changes panel with diffs.

- Category: block
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: @remixicon/react@^4.9.0, react-aria-components@^1.22.1

## How it works

1. All state lives in `AiChat`: chats, the open chat, the view, files, terminal lines, mode, branch, project, context use and the single active run. The sidebar, thread and changes panel are controlled components in their own files.
2. A run is `{ steps, step, phase, full, shown }`. One effect keyed on the run arms one timeout: in the working phase it advances `step` every 1300ms, holds 600ms on the finished list, then switches to streaming; in streaming it appends three characters every 24ms. Cleanup clears the timeout, so Stop, deleting the chat or unmounting never leaves a callback.
3. The run lives in the page, not the thread, so it keeps going while another chat is open. The sidebar shows a working dot on that chat and the composer of other chats will not send until it ends.
4. `AgentProgress` gets the parent's `step` as a controlled prop with no `onStepChange`, so its own clock only animates the bar between steps while the page decides when a step is done.
5. Mode changes the run: Agent runs three steps and writes a file, Ask skips the checklist and only thinks, Plan returns a plan without touching files. Turning off "Run lint and a production build" in Customize drops the lint step and its terminal lines.
6. The changes panel is real: selecting a file shows its tokenised code, Revert removes one file, Discard all asks first, and Commit empties the list and reports the commit. The Browser tab keeps a back and forward history over three local routes.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `STEP_MS = 1300ms`
  Long enough to read each checklist line as it completes; the reference's five steps take about seven seconds.
- `stream tick = 3 characters every 24ms`
  About 125 characters a second reads as typing without making a two-sentence reply wait long.
- `CONTEXT_LIMIT = 200,000 tokens, opening at 114,000`
  Opens at 57% like the reference ring and climbs with each finished run.
- `panel width = 400px, 560px when widened`
  At 1280px the narrow panel leaves about 600px for the chat column next to the 248px sidebar.

## API

```ts
function AiChat(props: AiChatProps): JSX.Element
interface AiChatProps { folders?: AiChatFolder[]; threads?: AiChatThread[]; files?: AiChatFile[]; defaultThreadId?: string; autoStart?: boolean; className?: string }
```

- `folders: AiChatFolder[]` — default `AI_CHAT_FOLDERS`
  Repositories shown as folders in the sidebar.
- `threads: AiChatThread[]` — default `AI_CHAT_THREADS`
  Seed chats; each names its folder and holds its turns.
- `files: AiChatFile[]` — default `AI_CHAT_FILES`
  Uncommitted files listed in the changes panel at load.
- `defaultThreadId: string` — default `"coding"`
  Chat open on first render.
- `autoStart: boolean` — default `true`
  If the opening chat ends with a user message, run the agent on it at load.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the root, which is h-full w-full.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
// The agent timeline: one timer at a time walks the steps, holds on the
// finished checklist, then streams the reply a few characters per tick.
// Every state change re-arms the effect, and cleanup clears the old timer,
// so stopping, deleting or unmounting never leaves a callback behind.
useEffect(() => {
  if (!run) return;
  let timer: ReturnType<typeof setTimeout>;
  if (run.phase === "working") {
    const total = run.steps.length;
    const done = run.step >= total;
    timer = setTimeout(
      () => {
        if (done) {
          setRun({ ...run, phase: "streaming" });
          return;
        }
        log(`✓ ${run.steps[run.step] ?? ""}`);
        setRun({ ...run, step: run.step + 1 });
      },
      total === 0 ? THINK_MS : done ? DONE_HOLD_MS : STEP_MS,
    );
  } else {
    timer = setTimeout(
      () => {
        const shown = reduced ? run.full : run.full.slice(0, run.shown.length + CHUNK);
        if (shown.length >= run.full.length) finish(run);
        else setRun({ ...run, shown });
      },
      reduced ? 0 : TICK_MS,
    );
  }
  return () => clearTimeout(timer);
  // finish/log only call state setters, so the run and motion setting are the real inputs.
  // eslint-disable-next-line react-hooks/exhaustive-deps
}, [run, reduced]);
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** The run timeout is cleared on every run change and on unmount. The dictation timer, the share copied-state timer and the browser loading timer each clear on unmount.

**Reduced motion.** Under reduced motion the reply appears at once instead of streaming, the composer glow stops pulsing, the thinking label drops its shimmer, and hover and panel-width transitions use motion-reduce:transition-none. The step checklist still advances so the run stays readable.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Running the timeline in the thread component. Switching chats would unmount it and lose the run; the page owns it and passes it down only to the chat it belongs to.
- Letting `AgentProgress` advance itself while the page also advances. Two clocks drift apart; pass a controlled `step` and leave `onStepChange` unset.
- Sending on Enter during IME composition. The composer checks `isComposing` so confirming a Japanese or Chinese candidate does not send a half-typed message.

## Notes

- The "coding scenario" chat opens mid-run with the reference's five steps, so the first reply streams in about eight seconds after load.
- Support and Upgrade are local stand-ins: Support copies an address and Upgrade switches the plan name on the sidebar card.

## Definition of done

At 1280 × 800 a sidebar, a chat and a changes panel fill the frame. The coding scenario chat ticks through five steps, then a reply streams in and a fourth file appears under Uncommitted changes. Typing a message and pressing Enter adds a bubble and starts a new run; Stop ends it. Selecting another chat, Automations or Customize switches the middle pane. The sidebar collapses to a rail, the panel hides, widens and switches to Browser.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: AI Image Generation

A full image-generation workspace for a 1280 × 800 frame. The left card lists repositories and their threads, the grey middle pane holds the selected thread and a pill composer, and the right pane is the gallery. Sending a prompt adds a user bubble and a generating tile that counts up with the halftone loader, reveals its picture, then turns into a finished card with copy, like, dislike, regenerate and download actions while the picture is filed at the top of the gallery. Automations and Customize are real views inside the block, and Customize settings change how the next image is made.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

Three-pane image studio: repo sidebar, prompt thread with a pill composer and live generating tiles, and a masonry gallery with styles.

- Category: block
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: @remixicon/react@^4.9.0, react-aria-components@^1.22.1

## How it works

1. All state lives in `AiImageGeneration`: repositories, a `Record<sessionId, ThreadEntry[]>` of threads, the gallery list, the running jobs, the composer draft and styles, and the Customize defaults. The sidebar, thread, composer and panels are controlled components in their own files.
2. Running generations are a `Record<entryId, Job>` with a `progress` and a per-tick `step`. One `setInterval` at 100ms exists only while at least one job does. It reads the jobs from a ref, advances each, removes those that reach 100, prepends their pictures to the gallery when Save to gallery is on, and raises an "Image ready" toast. Each tile gets its progress and seconds left as props, so `ImageGeneratingLoader` runs controlled.
3. A job's step is `100 × 100ms / duration`. The duration is `generationMs`, halved for the Fable 5 Mini model and halved again in Draft mode, so the model picker and the mode picker change real behaviour.
4. Pictures come from `itemFromPrompt`: an FNV-1a hash of the entry id and prompt picks one of twelve inline-SVG artworks and one of six palettes, the title is the prompt with its leading verb stripped, the ratio comes from the Customize aspect setting and the style line is the chosen styles or the model name. The same prompt and id always draw the same picture.
5. The composer is a form: Enter or the round send button submits, and the button is disabled while the field is empty. The + menu and the Styles tab toggle the same style list, which shows as removable chips and is cleared after sending. Dictate is a pressed toggle that, after 1.8s, writes a phrase into the field.
6. Thread actions are real: Share copies a label to the clipboard, the more menu duplicates the finished entries into a new thread, clears the thread or deletes it (hidden for the last thread), and Stop generating removes a running tile. Clearing or deleting also cancels that thread's jobs.
7. The sidebar collapse button hides the sidebar and the thread header shows a button to bring it back; the gallery's panel button does the same on the right. Below 1024px both panes become drawers over a backdrop, opened from the thread header and closed by the backdrop, Escape or their own close buttons.
8. Quick Search opens the kit Command palette (also on ⌘L) with actions and every thread; Settings opens the kit Settings modal.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `frame = 12px padding and gaps; sidebar 240px; gallery 372px, 500px when widened`
  At 1280px this leaves about 620px for the thread, enough for a 640px message column to sit centered with room for a 200px loader card.
- `tick = 100ms`
  Ten updates a second keeps the percentage and the halftone reveal smooth without re-rendering the page every frame.
- `generationMs = 7000ms default`
  Long enough to watch the loader stages and the reveal, short enough that a demo visitor sees the result land in the gallery.
- `context = 114k of 200k tokens, +3200 plus 4 per character per prompt`
  Opens at 57% like the reference ring and climbs visibly with each send.

## API

```ts
function AiImageGeneration(props: AiImageGenerationProps): JSX.Element
interface AiImageGenerationProps { generationMs?: number; defaultSessionId?: string; className?: string }
```

- `generationMs: number` — default `7000`
  Milliseconds one generation takes with the default model and mode.
- `defaultSessionId: string` — default `"image-generation"`
  Thread selected on first render.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the root, which is h-full w-full.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
// One interval drives every running generation. It only exists while a job
// does, reads the latest jobs from a ref, and files finished pictures in
// the gallery (unless Customize turned that off) before announcing them.
const running = Object.keys(jobs).length > 0;
useEffect(() => {
  if (!running) return;
  const id = window.setInterval(() => {
    const next: Record<string, Job> = {};
    const done: Job[] = [];
    for (const [key, job] of Object.entries(jobsRef.current)) {
      const progress = Math.min(100, job.progress + job.step);
      if (progress >= 100) done.push(job);
      else next[key] = { ...job, progress };
    }
    jobsRef.current = next;
    setJobs(next);
    if (done.length === 0) return;
    if (saveRef.current) {
      setGallery((prev) => [...done.map((job) => job.item), ...prev.filter((item) => !done.some((job) => job.item.id === item.id))]);
    }
    for (const job of done) {
      toast("Image ready", {
        id: `ready-${job.item.id}`,
        description: saveRef.current ? `“${job.item.title}” was added to the gallery.` : `“${job.item.title}” is in the thread.`,
        status: "success",
      });
    }
  }, TICK_MS);
  return () => window.clearInterval(id);
}, [running]);
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** The generation interval is cleared when the last job ends and on unmount. The copied-state, dictation and focus effects clear their timers, and the Escape listener for the drawers is removed when they close.

**Reduced motion.** Hover and press transitions use motion-reduce:transition-none and the dictation pulse is motion-reduce:animate-none. The generating loader drops its ripple under reduced motion while progress keeps counting, the gallery stops zooming on hover, and the kit palette, modal and toasts follow their own reduced-motion rules.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Doing side effects inside a `setJobs` updater. React may call updaters twice in development, which would double the gallery insert and the toast. The interval computes the next jobs from a ref, then sets state and fires effects once.
- Keying a running tile by its array index. Regenerate, Stop and Clear change the list while the timer runs; every entry has its own id and jobs are keyed by it.
- Unmounting the Automations view when switching away. Its rows are local state, so it stays mounted and is hidden with `display: none` instead.

## Notes

- The opening thread starts with one generation in flight, so the first image lands in the gallery about seven seconds after load.
- Downloads, Support and Upgrade are local stand-ins that report through toasts; wire them to a real endpoint in an app.

## Definition of done

At 1280 × 800 a sidebar, a grey thread pane and a gallery fill the frame. The "image generation" thread shows a user prompt and a loader that counts to 100% and then becomes a finished card while the picture appears first in the gallery with an "Image ready" toast. Typing a prompt and pressing Enter adds a bubble and a new loader. Picking a style chip, a model, Draft mode or a new aspect changes the next image. Selecting another thread, Automations or Customize switches the middle pane. The sidebar and gallery hide and come back. Below 1024px both become drawers.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: AI Profile

A full AI usage profile for a 1280 × 800 frame. A workspace sidebar sits on the left; the main pane holds a cover header with the owner's name, handle, badge, inline stats, Share and Edit, and four tabs. Overview shows a contributions headline with four selectable lifetime tiles and a Weekly / Monthly / Yearly activity heatmap. Agents ranks the month's active agents, Images is a masonry gallery and Activity is a timeline. Under the header an Agents bar chart steps through months and a Tokens area chart switches between 7, 30 and 90 days. Every sidebar entry opens a real view.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

AI usage profile page: cover header with tabs, stat tiles, an activity heatmap, and agent and token charts beside a workspace sidebar.

- Category: block
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: @remixicon/react@^4.9.0, react-aria-components@^1.22.1

## How it works

1. All page state lives in `AiProfile`: the view, the profile tab, the sidebar and drawer flags, the open overlays, the editable profile, the agent month, the token period, the selected tile, the unread count and the team. The sidebar, panels, workspace pages and edit form are controlled components in their own files.
2. The agent month is shared. `AgentsBarCard` steps it through `onMonthChange`, and the same month drives the Agents tab count, the Agents panel ranking and the header's agents stat, so they always describe one month.
3. The heatmap is a CSS grid with `grid-flow-col` and inline row and column templates, so one component draws the 7 × 38 weekly grid, the 4 × 12 monthly grid and the 3 × 12 yearly grid from column-major values. Each cell's level is `ceil(value / max × 4)`, capped at 4, with 0 for idle cells. One `pointerover` handler on the grid reads the cell's `data-cell` index and the readout under the grid names that cell and its runs.
4. All series come from a seeded mulberry32 generator and hard-coded day labels, so the server and client render the same numbers and the demo never reads the clock.
5. Edit opens a kit Modal with a form. Name and handle are validated (the handle must be 2 to 24 letters, numbers, dots or underscores, with a leading @ stripped), and Save writes the name, handle, bio and cover tone back to the header and the sidebar account button.
6. The sidebar collapse button hides the sidebar and a Show sidebar button brings it back. Below 1024px the sidebar becomes a drawer over a backdrop, opened from the menu button and closed by the backdrop, Escape, a nav choice or the collapse button.
7. Quick Search opens the kit Command palette (also on ⌘L) with every page and the profile actions; Settings opens the kit Settings modal. Share, Support, team switches and gallery downloads report through toasts.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `frame = 12px padding and gaps; sidebar 248px; content column up to 720px`
  At 1280px the profile column sits centred in the main pane with room for the two charts side by side.
- `heat levels = 5 steps: empty, then violet at 20%, 40%, 70% and 100%`
  Quartiles of the busiest cell keep the grid readable whatever the range's scale.
- `agents shown = top 6, then Show all`
  Six rows fit the tab panel without pushing the charts below the fold.

not finished.

**Cleanup.** The only listener the page adds is the Escape handler for the drawer, which exists while the drawer is open and is removed when it closes or the page unmounts. The kit overlays and toasts clean up their own timers.

**Reduced motion.** Hover and selection transitions use motion-reduce:transition-none. The token chart turns its Recharts animation off under reduced motion, the agent bars stop easing their height, and the kit tabs, modal, palette and toasts follow their own reduced-motion rules.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Giving the Agents chart and the Agents tab their own month state. They drift apart as soon as the chart steps; the month lives in the page and both read it.
- Seeding the series from `Math.random()` or the clock. The server and client then render different grids and hydration fails; the data uses a fixed-seed generator and fixed labels.
- Attaching a listener to every heatmap cell. The weekly grid alone has 266 cells; one delegated `pointerover` on the grid reads a `data-cell` index instead.

## Notes

- The workspace pages (Home, Project board, Marketing and so on) are light stand-ins with seeded rows; Home's Mark all read clears the sidebar badge.
- Share copies a profile link to the clipboard when the browser allows it. Support and downloads are local stand-ins that report through toasts.

At 1280 × 800 a sidebar and a profile column fill the frame. The cover shows Mara Ellison, @maraellison, a PRO badge, Share and Edit. # Build: Analytic Disc Picking

A slow ring of camera-facing discs that answers "what is under the pointer" without a raycaster. Because every disc is parallel to the image plane, the pick reduces to intersecting the pointer ray with one plane per disc and comparing the hit against the radius — four arithmetic operations, no traversal, no allocation, and exact rather than approximate. It is also the only correct answer here: the billboard happens in the vertex shader, so `Raycaster` intersects a square that is not on screen.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

Hit-test camera-facing discs by intersecting the pointer ray with their plane. Exact, allocation-free, and correct for shader billboards.

- Category: primitive
- Runtime cost: webgl
- Dependencies: three@^0.185.1

## How it works

1. The vertex shader billboards in view space: `vec4 mv = modelViewMatrix * vec4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0); mv.xy += position.xy * uScale;` takes only the translation out of the model-view matrix and adds the quad offset afterwards. The mesh's rotation and scale never reach a vertex, so the disc is always exactly parallel to the image plane and its view-space radius is exactly `uRadius * uScale`.
2. Because the disc is parallel to the image plane, its plane normal is the camera's view direction for every disc in the scene. `camera.getWorldDirection(viewDir)` is called once per frame and `plane.setFromNormalAndCoplanarPoint(viewDir, disc.position)` then differs only in its constant.
3. `raycaster.setFromCamera(ndc, camera)` builds the pointer ray and nothing else is used from the Raycaster — `intersectObjects` is never called. Constructing the ray is the cheap half of raycasting; the traversal, the per-object matrix inverse, and the per-triangle intersection are the half being skipped.
4. `ray.intersectPlane(plane, hit)` returns `Vector3 | null`, and the null case is a free depth rejection: `Ray.distanceToPlane` returns null for `t < 0`, so anything behind the camera drops out before any distance work.
5. The winner is the nearest hit along the ray whose distance from the disc centre is within the radius, both compared squared. Depth is tested FIRST — `if (along >= bestAlong) continue;` — so a disc that cannot beat the incumbent never runs its own radius test.
6. The pick radius is `uRadius * uScale`, the same two numbers the vertex shader multiplies. Hover eases `uScale` from 1 to 1.14, and the pick reads the eased value in the same frame, so a disc is never clickable over area it has not grown into and never stops being clickable over area it still occupies.
7. Every scratch object — ray, plane, hit vector, view direction, NDC vector — is allocated once into the stage object and reused. A pick loop that allocates a `Vector3` per disc per frame produces 780 garbage vectors a second at 60 Hz on a ring of thirteen.
8. Rendering is gated on a dirty flag. The flag is set by the spin, by pointer movement, by a hover easing that is still in flight, and by resize. Under `prefers-reduced-motion` the spin never sets it, so the renderer idles at zero draw calls until the pointer moves.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `FOV = 42`
  Camera vertical field of view in degrees. Wide enough that the near discs are visibly larger than the far ones — which is what makes an analytic test worth having — and narrow enough that the ring does not distort into an oval at preview aspect ratios.
- `CAM_Z / ringRadius = 5.6 / 2.15`
  A ratio of about 2.6. Closer and the front disc overruns the frame at preview width; further and the perspective flattens until a cheap screen-space approximation would have been good enough, which defeats the demonstration.
- `discRadius = 0.46`
  World units, and simultaneously the pick radius. A single source for both is the entire point: two constants that mean "how big is this disc" is how a hit region drifts away from the pixels it is supposed to cover.
- `WAVE = 0.34`
  Vertical amplitude of the sin(2a) offset. Enough that the ring reads as a ribbon rather than a flat carousel; past ~0.6 the discs at the crossings overlap and the nearest-along-the-ray tie-break starts doing visible work the user has no way to predict.
- `HOVER_SMOOTHING = 0.0006`
  Fraction of the hover gap remaining after one second, as `damp` defines it — about 12% of the gap per frame at 60 Hz, settling in roughly 0.2 s. A per-frame constant instead would converge twice as fast on a 120 Hz display and the growth would feel like a different component.
- `HOVER_GROWTH = 0.14`
  A hovered disc grows 14%. Large enough to read at the back of the ring where a disc is a third of its front size, small enough that the grown disc does not swallow its neighbours and make the pick ambiguous.
- `FEATHER = 0.035`
  Rim gradient width in units of the radius — roughly 1.5 px at preview scale. This is why the renderer is built with `antialias: false`: MSAA would pay for an entire extra sample buffer to solve a problem one smoothstep already solved.

## API

```ts
function AnalyticDiscPicking(props: { count?: number; period?: number; discRadius?: number; ringRadius?: number; color?: string; accent?: string; seed?: number | string; compare?: boolean; onPick?: (index: number) => void; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `count: number` — default `13`
  Discs around the ring.
- `period: number` — default `30`
  Seconds for one revolution.
- `discRadius: number` — default `0.46`
  Disc radius in world units. Also the pick radius — the two cannot drift apart.
- `ringRadius: number` — default `2.15`
  Ring radius in world units.
- `color: string` — default `'#7d848e'`
  Base plate colour. Any value `THREE.Color` accepts.
- `accent: string` — default `'#e8e4dc'`
  Colour of the picked disc.
- `seed: number | string` — default `'analytic-disc-picking'`
  Seeds the per-disc plate pattern. Same seed, same ring every reload.
- `compare: boolean` — default `false`
  Also run a real `Raycaster` each frame and report what it thinks was hit.
- `onPick: (index: number) => void`
  Fired when a disc is clicked, with its index.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the host element via `cn`.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
useRaf((dt) => {
  const s = stage.current;
  if (!s) return;

  // The ring phase is integrated from dt, not read from a wall clock, so
  // freezing it for reduced motion is a matter of not adding anything.
  if (!reduced) {
    spin.current = (spin.current + (TAU / period) * dt) % TAU;
    dirty.current = true;
  }

  // -- place the discs -----------------------------------------------------
  for (const disc of s.discs) {
    const a = disc.phase + spin.current;
    disc.mesh.position.set(
      Math.sin(a) * ringRadius,
      Math.sin(a * 2) * WAVE,
      Math.cos(a) * ringRadius,
    );
    // `cos(a)` is +1 at the front of the ring and -1 at the back. Remapped
    // to 0..1 it is the depth fade, and it costs nothing extra here.
    disc.uniforms.uDepth.value = Math.cos(a) * 0.5 + 0.5;
  }
  // No `updateMatrixWorld` here on purpose. The discs are direct children of
  // the scene at identity, so `mesh.position` IS the world position, and the
  // camera's matrix was made current in `resize`. The only consumer of the
  // full matrix graph is `render`, which updates it itself.

  // -- the analytic pick ---------------------------------------------------
  let best = -1;
  const p = pointer.current;
  if (p) {
    s.ndc.set(p.x, p.y);
    // The Raycaster is used for its RAY and nothing else. Building an
    // NDC-to-world ray by hand means duplicating `unproject`; the expensive
    // half of raycasting is `intersectObjects`, which is never called.
    s.raycaster.setFromCamera(s.ndc, s.camera);
    const ray = s.raycaster.ray;
    // Every disc is parallel to the image plane, so they all share one
    // normal — the camera's view direction, already unit length. Only the
    // plane's constant differs from disc to disc.
    s.camera.getWorldDirection(s.viewDir);

    let bestAlong = Infinity;
    for (let i = 0; i < s.discs.length; i += 1) {
      const disc = s.discs[i];
      if (!disc) continue;

      s.plane.setFromNormalAndCoplanarPoint(s.viewDir, disc.mesh.position);
      // `intersectPlane` returns null when the plane is behind the ray
      // origin, which rejects anything behind the camera for free. Note that
      // `Ray.distanceToPlane` returns null too but is TYPED `number` in
      // @types/three — the honest signature is on this method.
      if (ray.intersectPlane(s.plane, s.hit) === null) continue;

      // Nearest along the ray wins. Checked first so a disc that cannot
      // beat the incumbent skips its own radius test.
      const along = s.hit.distanceToSquared(ray.origin);
      if (along >= bestAlong) continue;

      // The drawn radius, hover growth included. `uScale` was eased last
      // frame and is applied by the vertex shader this frame, so the region
      // tested is the region rasterised.
      const r = disc.uniforms.uRadius.value * disc.uniforms.uScale.value;
      if (s.hit.distanceToSquared(disc.mesh.position) > r * r) continue;

      bestAlong = along;
      best = i;
    }
  }

  // -- ease the hover, which the next frame's pick will read ---------------
  for (let i = 0; i < s.discs.length; i += 1) {
    const disc = s.discs[i];
    if (!disc) continue;
    const target = i === best ? 1 : 0;
    const next = damp(disc.hover, target, HOVER_SMOOTHING, dt);
    if (Math.abs(next - disc.hover) > 0.0005) dirty.current = true;
    disc.hover = next;
    disc.uniforms.uHover.value = next;
    disc.uniforms.uScale.value = 1 + HOVER_GROWTH * next;
    disc.uniforms.uPicked.value = i === pickedRef.current ? 1 : 0;
  }

  if (best !== hovered.current) {
    hovered.current = best;
    setHover(best);
    dirty.current = true;
  }

  // -- what a real raycaster would have said -------------------------------
  if (compare) {
    let g = -1;
    if (p) {
      // The raycaster reads `matrixWorld`, which `render` would not refresh
      // until the end of this frame. The analytic path needed no such call —
      // it reads `position` directly — so this traversal is a cost the
      // comparison introduces, not one it inherits.
      s.scene.updateMatrixWorld();
      // Reused array, cleared by hand: `intersectObjects` pushes into the
      // target and sorts it, but never empties it.
      s.intersects.length = 0;
      s.raycaster.intersectObjects(s.meshes, false, s.intersects);
      const first = s.intersects[0];
      if (first) g = s.meshes.indexOf(first.object as THREE.Mesh);
    }
    if (g !== ghost) setGhost(g);
  }

  if (dirty.current) {
    dirty.current = false;
    s.renderer.render(s.scene, s.camera);
  }
}, ready && !unsupported);
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** The effect removes every disc from the scene and disposes its `ShaderMaterial`, disposes the one shared `PlaneGeometry`, then calls `disposeRenderer` — which stops the animation loop, disposes the renderer, calls `forceContextLoss()`, and zeroes the drawing buffer — and finally removes the canvas it appended. The canvas is created by the renderer inside the effect and never handed to React, so a StrictMode double-invoke rebuilds a fresh context rather than reusing a killed one. The frame loop unsubscribes with `useRaf`; the shared rAF parks once nothing is subscribed. The `ResizeObserver` unobserves with its hook.

**Reduced motion.** The ring holds still: the phase is integrated from delta time, so freezing it is a matter of adding nothing. The dirty flag is then only set by the pointer, which means the renderer draws zero frames until the pointer moves. Picking, hover growth and selection are unaffected — the technique is about where things are, not about them moving.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Reaching for `THREE.Raycaster` against a shader billboard. The vertex shader runs on the GPU; the `BufferGeometry` in main memory is an unrotated square lying in world XY. The raycast intersects that square and reports hits on a shape nobody can see — turn on `compare` and the two readouts disagree the moment the camera is not staring down the world Z axis.
- Using `Ray.distanceToPlane` and testing its result for null. It does return null at runtime for a plane behind the ray origin, but `@types/three` declares it as `number`, so the null check is a type error and removing the null check is a crash. `intersectPlane` has the honest `Vector3 | null` signature; use it.
- Approximating the disc as a screen-space circle whose NDC radius is `halfDiagonal / (tanHalfFov * camDist)`. That is only correct for a sphere. For a flat disc it over-reports near the edges of frame, where perspective stretches the footprint, so the hover boundary is visibly not the disc boundary. The plane intersection is exact for the same cost.
- Deriving the pick radius from a second constant. Hover growth then applies to the pixels but not the hit region, and the disc becomes clickable on a ring of its own body it has already grown past.
- Leaving `frustumCulled` on. The culler tests the geometry bounding sphere at the mesh transform, but the vertices are moved by the shader, so a disc vanishes the instant the untransformed square leaves the frustum.
- Allocating in the pick loop. `new THREE.Vector3()` per disc per frame is invisible in a profile and unmistakable in a GC trace; reuse a scratch object on the stage.
- Enabling depth test on the discs. They are square quads with the corners discarded, so the depth buffer records the quad, not the disc, and neighbouring rims punch holes in each other. Painter's-algorithm sorting is correct here because the billboard leaves the object position — the key three sorts on — untouched.
- Handing three's renderer a React-rendered `<canvas ref>`. StrictMode double-invokes the effect, the first cleanup calls `forceContextLoss()`, and the second run is given the same permanently dead element. Let the renderer make its own canvas inside the effect and remove it in cleanup.

## Notes

- The same reduction works for any primitive with a closed-form ray test: a sphere is `ray.intersectSphere`, an axis-aligned card is `ray.intersectBox`, a ground plane is one `intersectPlane`. Raycasting against triangles is the fallback for arbitrary meshes, not the default for known shapes.
- A square quad plus `discard` beats a `CircleGeometry` fan on both counts — two triangles instead of thirty-two, and a rim anti-aliased by a smoothstep instead of a polygon approximated by segments.
- The `compare` prop exists to be switched on once. Leave it on in production and you pay for the traversal you set out to avoid, plus an `intersectObjects` call whose result you throw away.

## Definition of done

Hover a disc at the front of the ring and it brightens and grows, and the readout says `plane hit NN`. Follow one disc as it travels to the back: it stays pickable over exactly its drawn silhouette, smaller but never offset. Set `compare` and hover a disc anywhere off the centre of frame — the `raycast` readout says something different, usually nothing, because it is testing an unrotated square in world XY. Click and the disc under the pointer takes the accent colour. With reduced motion the ring is static and every one of those behaviours still works.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.
