# Build: Calendar Toolbar

The header row of the calendar template, assembled from kit pieces: the month as a heading with a Today button on the left, and the month stepper, a Day / Week / Month segmented control, a search field and the primary New event button on the right. Month, view and search are each independently controlled or uncontrolled. The row wraps into a second line, then stacks, as its container narrows.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

Calendar page header: month title, Today, month stepper, Day/Week/Month segments, event search and a New event button.

- Category: navigation
- Runtime cost: css
- Dependencies: @internationalized/date@^3.12.4, @remixicon/react@^4.9.0

## How it works

1. Month state is a `CalendarDate` normalised with `startOfMonth`. `month` controls it; otherwise `defaultMonth`, then `today`, then the local current date seed internal state. Both the stepper and the Today button write through one `setMonth` that updates internal state and calls `onMonthChange`.
2. The heading defaults to `DateFormatter(locale, { month: "long", year: "numeric", timeZone: "UTC" })` of the month and carries `aria-live="polite"`, so stepping the month is announced. Passing `title={null}` removes it; any other node replaces it.
3. Today sets the month to `startOfMonth(today)` and calls `onToday(today)` so the parent can also select or scroll to the day. `today` is a prop so server-rendered pages can pin it and avoid a hydration mismatch.
4. The view switch is the kit `SegmentedControl` with `selectedKeys={[view]}`. `onSelectionChange` reads the single key out of the Set, ignores anything that is not a known view, then updates internal state and calls `onViewChange`. `views` picks and orders the segments.
5. The search is the kit `SearchField` passed `value`/`defaultValue`/`onChange` straight through, so Escape clears it. Layout is two flex groups in a `flex-wrap` row: from `sm` up the right group is `flex-1 justify-end flex-wrap`. Below `sm` both groups take `w-full` (title and Today pushed apart), and the stepper and search also take `w-full`, so on a phone they each get their own line.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `control height = 36px everywhere`
  Button medium, MonthStepper medium, SearchField medium and the solid SegmentedControl (4px track padding + 28px segment) all land on 36px, so the row reads as one baseline without per-control fixes.
- `stepper width = w-60 (240px) from sm up`
  Narrower than the stepper's 320px default so all five controls fit in one 1100px row, still wide enough that "September 2026" does not truncate.
- `search width = w-52 (208px) from sm up`
  Fits the "Search events" placeholder plus icon and clear button with room for a short query.
- `gaps = 12px between groups, 8px inside the control group`
  The tighter inner gap groups the controls visually, and the wider outer gap separates them from the title.

## API

```ts
type CalendarView = "day" | "week" | "month"
function CalendarToolbar(props: { month?: CalendarDate; defaultMonth?: CalendarDate; onMonthChange?: (month: CalendarDate) => void; today?: CalendarDate; onToday?: (today: CalendarDate) => void; view?: CalendarView; defaultView?: CalendarView; onViewChange?: (view: CalendarView) => void; views?: CalendarView[]; searchValue?: string; defaultSearchValue?: string; onSearchChange?: (value: string) => void; showSearch?: boolean; searchPlaceholder?: string; onNewEvent?: () => void; newEventLabel?: string; title?: ReactNode; actions?: ReactNode; locale?: string; className?: string; ref?: Ref<HTMLDivElement> }): JSX.Element
```

- `month / defaultMonth: CalendarDate`
  Shown month, controlled or uncontrolled.
- `onMonthChange: (month: CalendarDate) => void`
  Called with the first day of the month from the stepper or Today.
- `today: CalendarDate` — default `local today`
  Target of the Today button.
- `onToday: (today: CalendarDate) => void`
  Called after Today moved the month.
- `view / defaultView: "day" | "week" | "month"` — default `"month"`
  Selected segment.
- `onViewChange: (view: CalendarView) => void`
  Called when a segment is chosen.
- `views: CalendarView[]` — default `["day", "week", "month"]`
  Segments to show, in order.
- `searchValue / defaultSearchValue / onSearchChange: string / string / (value: string) => void`
  Search text, controlled or uncontrolled.
- `showSearch: boolean` — default `true`
  Render the search field.
- `onNewEvent: () => void`
  Press handler of the primary button.
- `title: ReactNode` — default `formatted month`
  Left heading; `null` hides it.
- `actions: ReactNode`
  Extra controls before New event.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
export function CalendarToolbar({
  month: controlledMonth,
  defaultMonth,
  onMonthChange,
  today,
  onToday,
  view: controlledView,
  defaultView = "month",
  onViewChange,
  views = ["day", "week", "month"],
  searchValue,
  defaultSearchValue = "",
  onSearchChange,
  showSearch = true,
  searchPlaceholder = "Search events",
  onNewEvent,
  newEventLabel = "New event",
  title,
  actions,
  locale = "en-US",
  className,
  ref,
}: CalendarToolbarProps) {
  const [uncontrolledMonth, setUncontrolledMonth] = useState<CalendarDate>(() =>
    startOfMonth(defaultMonth ?? today ?? todayIn(getLocalTimeZone())),
  );
  const month = startOfMonth(controlledMonth ?? uncontrolledMonth);
  const setMonth = (next: CalendarDate) => {
    setUncontrolledMonth(next);
    onMonthChange?.(next);
  };

  const [uncontrolledView, setUncontrolledView] = useState<CalendarView>(defaultView);
  const view = controlledView ?? uncontrolledView;

  const titleFormatter = useMemo(
    () => new DateFormatter(locale, { month: "long", year: "numeric", timeZone: "UTC" }),
    [locale],
  );
  const heading = title === undefined ? titleFormatter.format(month.toDate("UTC")) : title;

  const goToday = () => {
    const target = today ?? todayIn(getLocalTimeZone());
    setMonth(startOfMonth(target));
    onToday?.(target);
  };

  return (
    <div ref={ref} className={cx("flex w-full flex-wrap items-center gap-x-3 gap-y-3", className)}>
      <div className="flex w-full min-w-0 items-center justify-between gap-3 sm:w-auto sm:justify-start">
        {heading !== null ? (
          <h2 aria-live="polite" className="truncate text-title-3-medium text-text-primary">
            {heading}
          </h2>
        ) : null}
        <Button variant="secondary" onClick={goToday}>
          Today
        </Button>
      </div>

      <div className="flex w-full min-w-0 flex-wrap items-center gap-2 sm:w-auto sm:flex-1 sm:justify-end">
        <MonthStepper value={month} onChange={setMonth} locale={locale} className="w-full sm:w-60" />
        <SegmentedControl
          aria-label="Calendar view"
          selectedKeys={[view]}
          onSelectionChange={(keys) => {
            const [next] = [...keys];
            if (typeof next !== "string" || !(next in VIEW_LABELS)) return;
            setUncontrolledView(next as CalendarView);
            onViewChange?.(next as CalendarView);
          }}
        >
          {views.map((v) => (
            <SegmentedControlItem key={v} id={v}>
              {VIEW_LABELS[v]}
            </SegmentedControlItem>
          ))}
        </SegmentedControl>
        {showSearch ? (
          <SearchField
            aria-label={searchPlaceholder}
            placeholder={searchPlaceholder}
            value={searchValue}
            defaultValue={defaultSearchValue}
            onChange={onSearchChange}
            className="w-full min-w-0 sm:w-52"
          />
        ) : null}
        {actions}
        <Button leadingIcon={RiAddLine} onClick={onNewEvent}>
          {newEventLabel}
        </Button>
      </div>
    </div>
  );
}
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** Nothing of its own. The composed kit components clean up their own effects and observers.

**Reduced motion.** The toolbar adds no motion of its own. The month stepper skips its label slide and the segmented control's thumb follows the kit control's own behaviour.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Reading `onSelectionChange` keys as an array. React Aria passes a `Set<Key>`; spread it before destructuring.
- Defaulting `today` with `new Date()` on the server. Pass a fixed `CalendarDate` when the toolbar is server rendered, or the heading and Today target can disagree between server and client around midnight.
- Letting the segmented control allow an empty selection. The kit control sets `disallowEmptySelection`; keep a view selected or the grid under the toolbar has nothing to render.

## Notes

- Use `actions` for the template's notification and inbox icon buttons; they render just before New event.
- The toolbar only reports state. Filtering events by the search text and switching between grid components is the parent's job.

## Definition of done

With month August 2026, the heading reads "August 2026". Pressing the stepper's next chevron changes the heading to "September 2026"; pressing Today returns it to "August 2026". Choosing "Week" in the segmented control marks it selected and reports `"week"`. Typing "sync" in the search reports the text and Escape clears it. New event calls `onNewEvent`. At 360px wide every control remains visible and nothing scrolls sideways.

# Build: Campaigns Table

A bordered card with a result count, a status segmented control and a channel select over the kit Table. Every column sorts through React Aria, and the kit Pagination pages the result.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

A marketing campaigns table with channel icons, delivery status, budget-spent progress bars, CTR and sortable columns.

- Category: display
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: @internationalized/date@^3.12.4, @remixicon/react@^4.9.0, react-aria-components@^1.22.1

## How it works

1. Keep the sort in a React Aria `SortDescriptor` (controlled or local, newest edit first) and hand it to the kit `Table`; every column has `allowsSorting`, so a header click or Enter toggles it and sets `aria-sort`.
2. Derive rows with `sortCampaigns`: filter by status and channel, then compare per column (channel by label, status by rank active, paused, draft, budget by `spent / budget`, dates as ISO strings) times -1 for descending, falling back to the id so ties keep their order.
3. Compute CTR as `clicks / impressions` and return `null` with no impressions; the CTR sort puts null rows last in both directions instead of letting the sign flip them to the top.
4. Draw the budget cell as spend "of" budget, a percent, and the kit `ProgressTrack` at `size="sm"` with the percentage clamped to 100; over budget the fill switches to chart-3 and the percent to the rose status text, so 108% still reads at a glance.
5. Clamp the stored page to the page count and send every sort or filter change back to page 1; dates go through `parseDate(iso).toDate("UTC")` and a UTC formatter so server and client agree.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `pageSize = 6 (demo uses 5)`
  Two-line rows are about 56px; six plus the toolbar and pager keep the card on one dashboard fold.
- `table min width = 860px`
  The budget cell needs about 200px for "$30,884 of $40,000"; below this the kit Table wrapper scrolls instead of squeezing.
- `status rank = active 0, paused 1, draft 2`
  Status sorts by delivery stage, not alphabetically.
- `CTR precision = 2 decimals`
  Ad CTRs mostly sit between 0.5% and 8%, where a whole percent hides real differences.

## API

```ts
type Campaign = { id: string; name: string; channel: "google" | "meta" | "x" | "linkedin" | "email" | "tiktok"; objective: string; status: "active" | "paused" | "draft"; budget: number; spent: number; impressions: number; clicks: number; updated: string }
function CampaignsTable(props: CampaignsTableProps): JSX.Element
function sortCampaigns(rows: Campaign[], sort: SortDescriptor, status?: CampaignStatus | "all", channel?: CampaignChannel | "all"): Campaign[]
```

- `campaigns: Campaign[]`
  All rows; filtering, sorting and paging happen inside.
- `pageSize: number` — default `6`
  Rows per page.
- `sortDescriptor / defaultSortDescriptor / onSortChange: SortDescriptor` — default `{ column: "updated", direction: "descending" }`
  Sort state, controlled or uncontrolled. Columns: name, channel, status, budget, ctr, updated.
- `currency: string` — default `"USD"`
  ISO 4217 code for spend and budget.
- `locale: string` — default `"en-US"`
  Locale for money, percents and dates.
- `label: string` — default `"Campaigns"`
  Accessible name of the card and the table.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the card.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
/** Click-through rate as a fraction, or null before the first impression. */
export function ctrOf(c: Pick<Campaign, "clicks" | "impressions">): number | null {
  return c.impressions > 0 ? c.clicks / c.impressions : null;
}

/** Share of budget spent; a zero budget counts as nothing spent. */
export function spentRatio(c: Pick<Campaign, "spent" | "budget">): number {
  return c.budget > 0 ? c.spent / c.budget : 0;
}

function compare(a: Campaign, b: Campaign, column: Key): number {
  switch (column) {
    case "name":
      return a.name.localeCompare(b.name);
    case "channel":
      return CHANNEL[a.channel].label.localeCompare(CHANNEL[b.channel].label);
    case "status":
      return STATUS[a.status].rank - STATUS[b.status].rank;
    case "budget":
      return spentRatio(a) - spentRatio(b);
    case "updated":
      return a.updated < b.updated ? -1 : a.updated > b.updated ? 1 : 0;
    default:
      return 0;
  }
}

/** Filter by status and channel, then sort. CTR is special-cased so rows
 *  without impressions stay at the bottom in both directions; every other
 *  tie falls back to the id for a stable order across pages. */
export function sortCampaigns(
  rows: Campaign[],
  sort: SortDescriptor,
  status: CampaignStatus | "all" = "all",
  channel: CampaignChannel | "all" = "all",
): Campaign[] {
  const sign = sort.direction === "descending" ? -1 : 1;
  return rows
    .filter((c) => (status === "all" || c.status === status) && (channel === "all" || c.channel === channel))
    .sort((a, b) => {
      if (sort.column === "ctr") {
        const x = ctrOf(a);
        const y = ctrOf(b);
        if (x === null || y === null) return x === y ? a.id.localeCompare(b.id) : x === null ? 1 : -1;
        return sign * (x - y) || a.id.localeCompare(b.id);
      }
      return sign * compare(a, b, sort.column) || a.id.localeCompare(b.id);
    });
}
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** The component adds no timers or listeners. The kit SegmentedControl and Pagination disconnect their ResizeObservers on unmount.

**Reduced motion.** The sort chevron rotates over 150ms and the kit ProgressTrack slides its fill over 500ms; both carry `motion-reduce:transition-none`, so under `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` they change instantly.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Do not multiply null CTRs by the sort sign. Treat "no impressions" as missing and pin it last, or drafts jump to the top of every descending CTR sort.
- Clamp the bar fill to 100% but keep the true percent in the text, otherwise an overspent campaign looks exactly like a fully spent one.
- The progress bar is decorative next to the written figures, so it is `aria-hidden`; giving it a role would make screen readers announce each row twice.

## Notes

- `ctrOf`, `spentRatio` and `sortCampaigns` are exported for server-side sorting with the same rules.
- The status pill is static. Swap it for the kit Select to edit delivery inline.
- Spend and budget take whole currency units; amounts are formatted without decimals.

## Definition of done

The demo card reads "16 campaigns", newest edit first with "Founder story video · US" on top. Sorting CTR descending puts "Brand search · US" (7.50%) first and ascending puts "Creator collab · EU" (0.80%) first, with the three drafts showing "–" at the bottom both ways. "Newsletter promo · EU" shows 108% in rose with a full pink bar. Choosing "Draft" leaves 3 rows; choosing the Meta channel leaves 4 and hides the pager. At 360px the table scrolls inside the card. Light and dark both read correctly.

and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Canvas Handoff Transition

The usual way to put a shader on more than one page is to mount it on each of them, and the price is a new context, a new compile and a new first frame every time the route changes. No easing hides that: a field restarting from t = 0 is visibly a different object. Here one canvas is created imperatively, outside React's ownership, and moved into the destination page with `appendChild` during the layout phase — no paint happens in between, so the context never blinks. What the viewer sees is the surface they were already looking at, travelling from one rectangle to another.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

The live WebGL canvas is handed to the next page and flies to its new slot, instead of being destroyed and rebuilt.

- Category: transition
- Runtime cost: webgl
- Dependencies: three@^0.185.1, gsap@^3.15.0

## How it works

1. Four steps in a fixed order. MEASURE first, inside the click handler, because one `setState` later the outgoing rectangle no longer exists. FLUSH one frame, so the pixels about to travel are current. MOVE in a `useLayoutEffect`, which shares its task with React's DOM mutations and therefore straddles no paint. RESIZE last, on the tween's completion.
2. The move is a plain `target.appendChild(canvas)`. `appendChild` on a node that already has a parent relocates it rather than copying it, and a WebGL context belongs to the canvas element, not to its position in the document — so the context, the compiled program and the drawing buffer all survive being detached and re-attached.
3. The flight is FLIP: `scaleX = first.width / last.width`, `scaleY = first.height / last.height`, and the translation is the difference between the two centre points. Scale, never `width`/`height` — a width tween is 0.72 s of continuous reflow, and writing the canvas's width attribute would reallocate the drawing buffer on every frame of it.
4. The buffer resize is deferred to `onComplete` and the `ResizeObserver` is muted for the duration by a `flying` flag. Assigning `canvas.width` is what reallocates and CLEARS the backing store; do it while the element is mid-flight and the object being animated goes black for a frame. During the flight the old buffer is simply scaled by CSS, which is slightly soft and completely invisible at this duration.
5. Measuring inside the handler also makes interruption correct for free. If a flight is already running, `getBoundingClientRect()` returns the TRANSFORMED rect — where the canvas visually is, mid-air — so a second click continues from that point instead of snapping back to the slot it was heading for.
6. The destination slot has its `overflow` forced to `visible` inline for the length of the flight and restored afterwards. Inline, because the clipping usually comes from a utility class on the consumer's own markup that a rule in our stylesheet would lose to.
7. A `uHandoff` uniform is tweened 0 to 1 and back on the same timeline, shearing the field's sampling coordinate. It disturbs the picture rather than fading it: a fade would hide precisely the frames that prove the surface is the same one.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `HANDOFF_DURATION = 0.72`
  Seconds for the flight. It is long for a page transition, deliberately — the whole point is that you can watch a specific fold of the field travel and see that it never restarts. Under about 0.45 s the eye cannot track it and the effect degrades to a cut; over about 1 s the route change starts to feel withheld.
- `HANDOFF_EASE = 'power3.inOut'`
  Symmetric, because the two rectangles are equally important — the canvas is not leaving somewhere for somewhere, it is the same object being re-placed. An `out` ease would put the acceleration at the origin and imply the old page was the one that mattered.
- `SURGE_EASE = 'sine.inOut'`
  The `uHandoff` shear runs half the flight forward and half back (`yoyo: true, repeat: 1`). Sine, because it is the only common ease with zero slope at both ends, so the disturbance grows out of stillness and returns to it with no visible corner at the turnaround.
- `LEVELS = 6`
  Tones the field is crushed to. Low enough that the quantisation edges are hard and locked to the drawing buffer, which is what makes the mid-flight scaling legible as "these are the pixels that were already there". Above about ten the picture is a smooth gradient again and the proof is lost.
- `CELL = 2`
  Dither cell size in DRAWING-BUFFER pixels, so on a 2x display the pattern is one CSS pixel per cell — fine enough to read as tone, coarse enough to survive the scaling. Measured in buffer pixels rather than CSS pixels on purpose: it is the buffer that stretches during the flight.
- `MAX_DPR = 2`
  Device pixel ratio ceiling. Above 2 the visual gain on a quantised field is nil and the fill-rate cost is quadratic — and this surface is on screen on every page rather than on one hero, so its cost is paid continuously.
- `INK / PAPER = [0.42, 0.65, 1] / [0.035, 0.037, 0.045]`
  The two ends of the quantisation ramp, as raw 0..1 RGB. Passed as `THREE.Vector3` rather than `THREE.Color` because three applies working-colour-space conversion to a Color and none to a Vector3, and a `ShaderMaterial` emits `gl_FragColor` without the output-encoding chunk — Vector3 is the only pairing where the numbers written in the source are the numbers that reach the screen.

## API

```ts
function CanvasHandoffTransition(props: { controller: CanvasHandoff; children: ReactNode; duration?: number; ease?: string; ink?: readonly [number, number, number]; paper?: readonly [number, number, number]; levels?: number; cell?: number; maxDpr?: number; className?: string }): JSX.Element
function CanvasHandoffSlot(props: { controller: CanvasHandoff; id: string; className?: string }): JSX.Element
function useCanvasHandoff(initialId: string): { active: string; fallback: boolean; handoff: (id: string, commit?: () => void) => void }
```

- `controller: CanvasHandoff`
  From `useCanvasHandoff(initialSlotId)`. Shared by the host and every slot.
- `children: ReactNode`
  The pages. Each renders one `CanvasHandoffSlot` for its own landing place.
- `duration: number` — default `0.72`
  Seconds for the flight. `0` moves the canvas instantly with no tween.
- `ease: string` — default `'power3.inOut'`
  Easing for the flight.
- `ink: readonly [number, number, number]` — default `[0.42, 0.65, 1]`
  Bright end of the quantisation ramp, raw 0..1 RGB.
- `paper: readonly [number, number, number]` — default `[0.035, 0.037, 0.045]`
  Dark end of the quantisation ramp, raw 0..1 RGB.
- `levels: number` — default `6`
  How many tones the field is crushed to.
- `cell: number` — default `2`
  Dither cell size in drawing-buffer pixels.
- `maxDpr: number` — default `2`
  Device pixel ratio ceiling.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the host root via `cn`.
- `id: string`
  `CanvasHandoffSlot` only. Stable identity for this landing place, unique within one controller.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
/* ------------------------------------------------------------------------
   BUILD. Depends on the motion preference and the DPR ceiling and nothing
   else — emphatically not on the active slot, or a route change would tear
   down the very context the component exists to preserve.
   ------------------------------------------------------------------------ */
useEffect(() => {
  const rootEl = root.current;
  if (!rootEl) return;

  /* Probed in an effect, never during render: `hasWebGL()` needs `document`,
     and branching the markup on it would be a hydration mismatch rather than
     a graceful degradation. */
  if (!hasWebGL()) {
    setFallback(true);
    return;
  }
  setFallback(false);

  let renderer: THREE.WebGLRenderer;
  try {
    renderer = new THREE.WebGLRenderer({
      antialias: false,
      alpha: false,
      powerPreference: 'low-power',
    });
  } catch {
    // A context can still be refused between the probe and the construction —
    // the tab may have hit the browser's live-context ceiling in between. three
    // throws rather than returning null, and an uncaught throw here takes the
    // page with it.
    setFallback(true);
    return;
  }
  renderer.setPixelRatio(pixelRatio(maxDpr));

  /* three constructs the canvas; React never sees it. This is the whole
     strict-mode story: the second invocation gets a brand new element and a
     brand new context, because the first invocation's cleanup removed and
     released its own. */
  const canvas = renderer.domElement;
  canvas.className = 'kx-handoff-canvas';
  canvas.setAttribute('aria-hidden', 'true');

  const l = look.current;
  const uniforms: HandoffUniforms = {
    uResolution: { value: new THREE.Vector2(1, 1) },
    uTime: { value: 0 },
    uHandoff: { value: 0 },
    uLevels: { value: l.levels },
    uCell: { value: l.cell },
    /* Vector3, not Color: three applies working-colour-space conversion to a
       Color and none to a Vector3, and a `ShaderMaterial` emits `gl_FragColor`
       without the output-encoding chunk. Vector3 is the only pair of ends
       where the numbers written here are the numbers that reach the screen. */
    uInk: { value: new THREE.Vector3(l.ink0, l.ink1, l.ink2) },
    uPaper: { value: new THREE.Vector3(l.paper0, l.paper1, l.paper2) },
  };

  const material = new THREE.ShaderMaterial({
    vertexShader: canvasHandoffVertexShader,
    fragmentShader: canvasHandoffFragmentShader,
    uniforms,
  });
  // A 2x2 plane under an identity ortho camera is a full-screen quad with no
  // projection maths and no camera to keep in sync on resize.
  const geometry = new THREE.PlaneGeometry(2, 2);
  const scene = new THREE.Scene();
  scene.add(new THREE.Mesh(geometry, material));
  const camera = new THREE.OrthographicCamera(-1, 1, 1, -1, 0, 1);

  const render = () => renderer.render(scene, camera);

  const resize = () => {
    const host = canvas.parentElement;
    if (!host) return;
    const w = host.clientWidth;
    const h = host.clientHeight;
    if (w === 0 || h === 0) return;
    // `false` leaves the CSS size alone; the stylesheet's 100%/100% is what
    // keeps the canvas glued to whichever slot currently owns it.
    renderer.setSize(w, h, false);
    uniforms.uResolution.value.set(w, h);
    render();
  };

  // Whatever slot is active right now. `rootEl` is the safety net for a
  // controller whose slots have not registered — the canvas is visible and
  // full-bleed rather than orphaned.
  const home = slots.current.get(activeRef.current) ?? rootEl;
  home.appendChild(canvas);
  resize();

  /* Observed on the CANVAS, not the slot: the observation follows the node
     across the handoff, so one observer covers every slot it will ever live
     in. `setSize(..., false)` never writes the CSS box, so this cannot feed
     back on itself. */
  const observer = new ResizeObserver(() => {
    // The flight deliberately runs at the OLD buffer size, scaled. Honouring
    // the resize here is the black frame the deferral exists to prevent.
    if (engine.current?.flying) return;
    resize();
  });
  observer.observe(canvas);

  if (reduced) {
    // One frame, then nothing. A field that drifts forever is motion, and
    // motion is what was asked not to happen.
    render();
  } else {
    // The timestamp is absolute, so elapsed time survives the handoff with
    // no accumulator to carry across and nothing to reset.
    renderer.setAnimationLoop((time) => {
      uniforms.uTime.value = time / 1000;
      render();
    });
  }

  engine.current = { canvas, uniforms, render, resize, flying: false };

  return () => {
    observer.disconnect();
    gsap.killTweensOf(canvas);
    gsap.killTweensOf(uniforms.uHandoff);
    // Stops the loop before releasing the context; a queued frame rendering
    // into a lost context throws out of the cleanup.
    disposeRenderer(renderer);
    material.dispose();
    geometry.dispose();
    // The effect appended it, the effect removes it. React has no idea this
    // node was ever here and will not try to reconcile it.
    canvas.remove();
    engine.current = null;
  };
}, [reduced, maxDpr, slots, engine, activeRef, setFallback]);

/* ------------------------------------------------------------------------
   HAND OVER. A LAYOUT effect, because React's mutations and its layout
   effects share one task: the canvas leaves the old parent and arrives at
   the new one with no paint in between. The same code in `useEffect` shows a
   frame with a hole where the canvas used to be.
   ------------------------------------------------------------------------ */
useLayoutEffect(() => {
  const e = engine.current;
  const target = slots.current.get(active);
  if (!e || !target) return;

  const from = first.current;
  first.current = null;

  // First run after the build already parked it correctly.
  if (e.canvas.parentElement === target) return;

  // `appendChild` on a node that already has a parent MOVES it. No clone, no
  // re-creation, and the WebGL context rides along untouched.
  target.appendChild(e.canvas);

  /* An interrupted flight leaves an inline transform behind. Clear it before
     measuring or Last is read through the previous flight's scale, and the
     inversion comes out compounded — the canvas leaps somewhere neither slot
     has ever been. `clearProps` rather than a set to identity so the instant
     paths below leave the element genuinely untouched. */
  gsap.killTweensOf(e.canvas);
  gsap.set(e.canvas, { clearProps: 'transform' });

  if (!from || reduced || duration <= 0) {
    e.resize();
    return;
  }

  const to = e.canvas.getBoundingClientRect();
  if (to.width === 0 || to.height === 0) {
    e.resize();
    return;
  }

  // FLIP: invert the measured difference, then animate the inversion away.
  // Scale rather than width/height — width is a layout property and a layout
  // property tweened for 0.7 s is 0.7 s of reflow.
  const scaleX = from.width / to.width;
  const scaleY = from.height / to.height;
  const x = from.left + from.width / 2 - (to.left + to.width / 2);
  const y = from.top + from.height / 2 - (to.top + to.height / 2);

  /* For the length of the flight the canvas is bigger than, and outside, the
     slot it now lives in — so the slot must not clip. Written INLINE and
     restored afterwards, because the thing being overridden is usually a
     utility class on the consumer's own markup, and a rule in our stylesheet
     would lose to it. Skip this and the transition is invisible: the canvas
     is cropped to its destination rectangle from the first frame, which
     looks exactly like no transition at all. */
  const clipped = target.style.overflow;
  target.style.overflow = 'visible';
  const unclip = () => {
    target.style.overflow = clipped;
  };

  e.flying = true;
  const tl = gsap.timeline({
    onComplete: () => {
      e.flying = false;
      unclip();
      gsap.set(e.canvas, { clearProps: 'transform' });
      // The ONE buffer resize, now that nothing is moving.
      e.resize();
    },
  });

  tl.fromTo(
    e.canvas,
    { x, y, scaleX, scaleY, transformOrigin: '50% 50%' },
    { x: 0, y: 0, scaleX: 1, scaleY: 1, duration, ease },
    0,
  ).fromTo(
    e.uniforms.uHandoff,
    { value: 0 },
    { value: 1, duration: duration / 2, ease: SURGE_EASE, yoyo: true, repeat: 1 },
    0,
  );

  return () => {
    tl.kill();
    unclip();
    e.flying = false;
  };
}, [active, duration, ease, reduced, engine, slots, first]);
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** `disposeRenderer` stops the animation loop before releasing the context, so a queued frame cannot render into a lost one and throw out of the cleanup; it then calls `dispose()`, `forceContextLoss()` and zeroes the canvas dimensions to release the backing store immediately. The `ResizeObserver` is disconnected, both the canvas transform tweens and the `uHandoff` tween are killed, the material and geometry are disposed, and the canvas element is removed by the same effect that appended it. The flight effect's own cleanup kills its timeline and restores the destination slot's original `overflow`, so an unmount mid-flight cannot leave a slot permanently unclipped.

**Reduced motion.** No animation loop is started: one frame is drawn when the context is built, and one more after each move and each resize, so the field is a still image rather than a drifting one. The handoff still moves the canvas — that is a DOM relocation, not motion — but the FLIP tween and the `uHandoff` surge are both skipped, and the drawing buffer is resized immediately instead of on a completion that will never fire. `prefers-reduced-motion` is read by the component through `useReducedMotion`, never inferred from the page.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Rendering the canvas from JSX. React unmounts the outgoing page's subtree on a route change, and a `<canvas ref>` inside it is destroyed with it — context, program, buffer and all. That is the exact failure this component exists to avoid, and it cannot be worked around from inside the page: the canvas has to be created by the effect and owned by nobody React can see.
- A React-owned canvas under `reactStrictMode`. The strict-mode remount reuses the SAME element across both effect invocations, so the first cleanup's `forceContextLoss()` hands the second invocation a dead context and the component renders permanently blank — in development only, which is a genuinely expensive way to lose an afternoon. Creating the element inside the effect gives the second run a clean one.
- Doing the move in `useEffect` instead of `useLayoutEffect`. Passive effects run after the browser has painted, so there is one composited frame in which the outgoing page is gone and the canvas has not arrived. It reads as a flash of empty box at exactly the moment the component is supposed to be proving continuity.
- Measuring First inside the layout effect. By then React has already removed the outgoing subtree, so there is nothing left to measure and the FLIP either animates from the wrong rectangle or is skipped. The measurement has to happen in the handler, before `setState`.
- Calling `renderer.setSize()` during the flight. Writing the canvas's width or height reallocates and clears the drawing buffer, so the object mid-animation flashes black for a frame. The `ResizeObserver` fires exactly then, because moving into a differently sized slot changes the border box — which is why it is muted by a `flying` flag rather than trusted.
- A destination slot that clips. `overflow: hidden` on the slot crops the inbound canvas to its final rectangle from the first frame, so the flight is invisible and the result looks identical to no transition. Forcing `overflow: visible` inline for the duration is the only override that reliably beats a utility class.
- Cloning instead of moving. `cloneNode(true)` on a canvas copies the element and NOT its bitmap or its context; `outerHTML` round-trips have the same effect. The clone is blank and the original is gone, so the page shows an empty box with no error anywhere.
- Tweening `width` and `height` instead of `scale`. Besides reflowing on every frame, they are the two properties that reset the drawing buffer, so the animation would clear the surface sixty times a second.
- Mounting the host inside the routed subtree. If the host unmounts on navigation the context goes with it and there is nothing left to hand over — the component silently degrades to the mount-a-new-one behaviour it replaces. It belongs in the layout, above the router outlet.
- Assuming the canvas paints where you expect. It is `position: absolute; z-index: 1` so it can lift over static page content on the way past, which means anything meant to sit ON TOP of the field needs its own stacking context. Text without `relative z-10` disappears under the canvas for the length of the flight.
- Letting the shader carry any state that could reset. Everything visible is a function of the absolute `setAnimationLoop` timestamp, so there is no accumulator to hand over. Drive the field from a per-frame increment instead and it will still restart on the handoff — the exact artefact the component was built to eliminate, hidden one layer deeper.

## Notes

- In Next.js App Router: mount `CanvasHandoffTransition` in `app/layout.tsx`, put a `CanvasHandoffSlot` in each page with an id of its own, and replace `<Link>` with a button calling `handoff(slotId, () => router.push(href))`. The component imports nothing from `next/navigation` — the route change is a callback, so the same host works under React Router or, as in the preview, plain `useState`.
- The slot renders no children while WebGL is live. That is not cosmetic: React only reconciles children it created, so an empty child list is the guarantee that it will never touch the canvas sitting inside. Content that belongs over the field goes in a sibling, not inside the slot.
- One context for the whole site is the real prize. Chromium allows roughly sixteen live WebGL contexts per renderer process and evicts the oldest without warning when you exceed it — a per-page canvas on a site with a persistent background is how an unrelated component three routes away turns black.
- The field is deliberately slow, about eight seconds per visible cycle. Anything faster and the eye cannot hold a specific fold across the transition, which is the only direct evidence the viewer gets that the surface was not rebuilt.
- Under reduced motion there is no animation loop at all — a single frame is drawn on build and again after each move — so the component costs nothing per frame for the people most likely to be on the weakest hardware.

## Definition of done

Watch one bright fold of the field and click a nav item: the same fold is still there when the canvas lands, offset only by the time the flight took. Nothing blanks, blinks, or restarts. The canvas visibly changes proportion in flight — wide banner to tall column — with the dither cells stretching along with it, then snapping to square at the end when the buffer is finally resized. Click twice in quick succession and the second flight starts from wherever the canvas is in the air rather than jumping to the first destination. In React DevTools the canvas element has no owner. Under `reactStrictMode` in development the preview renders on first load, not blank. With reduced motion the field is a still image and the canvas relocates without a flight.

and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Capture-Phase Click Swallow

Throw a drag carousel and let go over a card, and the browser dispatches a `click` on it — `mousedown` and `mouseup` landed in the same subtree, so that is exactly what the spec asks for. The result is that flinging the track navigates somewhere. One listener on the drag surface in the capture phase, which runs before any descendant handler, calls `stopPropagation` and `preventDefault` and the click is gone. The work is in the two edges: it has to swallow exactly one, and it has to let keyboard activation through, because Enter and Space fire a click with no pointer sequence behind it.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

Cancels the single click a finished drag would fire, in the capture phase, without eating the next real click or keyboard activation.

- Category: primitive
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: none beyond React

## How it works

1. The listener is registered with `addEventListener('click', handler, true)` on the drag surface. The third argument is the technique: capture runs root-down, so this handler sees the click before the card's own `onClick` and before a router's link interception. In the bubble phase the navigation has already happened.
2. It calls both `stopPropagation()` and `preventDefault()`. They do different jobs and neither covers the other: propagation stops listeners deeper in the path, while the default action — following an `<a href>`, submitting a form, toggling a `<label>` — is not a listener and is only cancelled by `preventDefault`. A swallow with only `stopPropagation` still navigates.
3. `arm()` is called by the gesture when it ends *having moved*, which `drag-deadzone-capture` reports as `onDragEnd(state, { moved })`. Arming on a stationary press is how the click a user actually meant gets eaten.
4. The arm is consumed inside the handler before the event is cancelled, so exactly one click is swallowed. A flag that stays set is the bug this replaces: the drag is suppressed, and so is the deliberate click that follows it.
5. Two independent stand-downs cover the drag that produces no click at all — one that ends over empty space, or that the browser cancelled. A `pointerdown` on the surface disarms, because a fresh press means the awaited click never came; and a 250 ms timer disarms as a backstop, since the click that follows a `pointerup` is dispatched in the same turn and anything later is not it.
6. `event.detail` is the keyboard test. For a pointer click it is the click count, 1 or more; for Enter, Space, and `element.click()` it is 0. Those return early and pass through untouched, so the widget stays operable from the keyboard.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `TIMEOUT_MS = 250`
  How long an arm survives with no click. The click after a `pointerup` arrives in the same turn, so one frame would do for a mouse; the margin is for the delayed synthetic click some touch browsers still emit. The ceiling is the time a person needs to press and release again — go much past ~400 ms and the arm can outlive its own gesture and reach into the next one, which is exactly the bug the expiry exists to prevent.
- `event.detail threshold = 0`
  Not a tuned number but a specified one: `UIEvent.detail` is the click count for a pointer-driven click and exactly 0 for a keyboard-driven or scripted one. Testing `detail === 0` is the only cross-browser tell available on the click event itself — `pointerId === -1` is only present where `click` is a `PointerEvent`, and the `screenX === 0 && screenY === 0` heuristic misfires on a genuine click in the top-left corner of the screen.

## API

```ts
function useClickSwallow(ref: RefObject<HTMLElement | null>, options?: { timeoutMs?: number; enabled?: boolean; onSwallow?: (event: MouseEvent) => void }): { arm: () => void; disarm: () => void; armed: RefObject<boolean>; swallowed: RefObject<number> }
```

- `timeoutMs: number` — default `250`
  How long an arm survives with no click arriving. Backstop for a drag that ends over nothing clickable.
- `enabled: boolean` — default `true`
  Detach the listeners and stand down when false.
- `onSwallow: (event: MouseEvent) => void`
  The click that was cancelled. Already stopped and prevented by the time this runs.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
/**
 * Milliseconds an arm survives if no click follows. The click that follows a
 * `pointerup` is dispatched in the same turn, so anything over one frame is
 * already generous; the margin is for the delayed click some touch browsers
 * still emit. It has to stay well under the time a person needs to press and
 * release again, or the arm outlives its own gesture.
 */
const TIMEOUT_MS = 250;

/**
 * Suppress the one `click` that a finished drag is about to produce.
 *
 * Pairs with any gesture that reports whether it moved — `drag-deadzone-capture`
 * exposes exactly that as `onDragEnd(state, { moved })`. Arm on `moved`, and
 * only on `moved`: arming after a stationary press is how the click a user
 * meant gets eaten.
 */
export function useClickSwallow(
  ref: RefObject<HTMLElement | null>,
  options: UseClickSwallowOptions = {},
): ClickSwallowHandle {
  const { timeoutMs = TIMEOUT_MS, enabled = true } = options;

  const armed = useRef(false);
  const swallowed = useRef(0);
  const timer = useRef<number | null>(null);

  const config = useRef({ timeoutMs, options });
  config.current = { timeoutMs, options };

  const disarm = useCallback(() => {
    armed.current = false;
    if (timer.current !== null) {
      window.clearTimeout(timer.current);
      timer.current = null;
    }
  }, []);

  const arm = useCallback(() => {
    disarm();
    armed.current = true;
    // An expiry, not a standing flag. A drag that ends over empty space, or
    // one the browser cancelled, produces no click at all — and an arm left
    // standing swallows the user's next real click, whenever that arrives.
    timer.current = window.setTimeout(() => {
      armed.current = false;
      timer.current = null;
    }, config.current.timeoutMs);
  }, [disarm]);

  useEffect(() => {
    const el = ref.current;
    if (!el || !enabled) return;

    const onClickCapture = (e: MouseEvent) => {
      if (!armed.current) return;

      // Enter and Space on a focused link or button dispatch a click with
      // `detail === 0` and no pointer sequence behind it, as does
      // `element.click()`. There is no drag for those to be the tail of, and
      // swallowing them is what makes a drag carousel keyboard-inoperable.
      if (e.detail === 0) return;

      // Consumed here, so exactly one click is swallowed per arm.
      disarm();
      swallowed.current += 1;

      // Both, always. stopPropagation keeps it from the card's own handler and
      // from the router's link interception; preventDefault cancels the
      // default action, which is the part that actually follows an href.
      e.stopPropagation();
      e.preventDefault();

      config.current.options.onSwallow?.(e);
    };

    // A fresh press means the previous gesture is finished and the click it
    // was going to produce never arrived. Second safety net under the timer,
    // and the one that matters — it is deterministic rather than timed.
    const onPointerDown = () => disarm();

    // The third argument is the entire technique. In the bubble phase the
    // card's own handler has already run and the link has already navigated.
    el.addEventListener('click', onClickCapture, true);
    el.addEventListener('pointerdown', onPointerDown);

    return () => {
      el.removeEventListener('click', onClickCapture, true);
      el.removeEventListener('pointerdown', onPointerDown);
      // Without this the timer can fire after unmount and write to a ref that
      // nothing reads, and on a remount the widget starts life armed.
      disarm();
    };
  }, [ref, enabled, disarm]);
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** The effect removes the capture-phase `click` listener with the same capture flag it was added with — passing `true` on the way out is required, since a listener added with capture is a different registration from one added without — removes the `pointerdown` listener, and calls `disarm()`, which clears the pending timeout and resets the flag so a remount does not start armed. No rAF, no pointer capture, nothing else held.

**Reduced motion.** Nothing changes, and the omission is deliberate rather than an oversight: this hook cancels an event, it does not animate anything, and there is no duration, distance, or easing in it to reduce. Behaviour identical under `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`. Note that the keyboard path is unconditional for the same reason it matters here — the pass-through for `detail === 0` is an accessibility guarantee, not a motion setting, and it is not something a preference should be able to switch off.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Registering in the bubble phase. The card's own `onClick` runs first and the link has already navigated by the time the handler sees the event — the listener is correct and completely useless. The third argument to `addEventListener` is the whole fix.
- Calling `stopPropagation()` without `preventDefault()`. Every JavaScript handler is silenced and the `<a href>` still navigates, because following a link is a default action rather than a listener. The failure is confusing precisely because the swallow visibly "works" on buttons and does nothing on links.
- Leaving the flag set after the swallow. It eats the click after the drag as well, so the user drags, then clicks a card deliberately, and nothing happens. Consuming it inside the handler is one line and is the difference between a fix and a new bug.
- Setting the flag with no expiry at all. A drag that ends over empty space never produces a click, so the arm just sits there — and swallows a genuine click a minute later, at which point nobody will connect the two events.
- Swallowing keyboard activation. Enter and Space on a focused card dispatch a click with `detail === 0`, and if the flag happens to be armed the widget silently stops responding to the keyboard. It never shows up in testing because a carousel is tested by dragging it.
- Arming on every gesture instead of only on ones that moved. Without a dead zone upstream reporting `moved`, a two-pixel wobble during a click arms the swallow and the click is cancelled — the exact behaviour that makes drag carousels feel unreliable.
- Assuming the click lands on the element the pointer is over. Click targets the nearest common ancestor of the `mousedown` and `mouseup` targets, and while a pointer is captured the compatibility mouse events are retargeted to the capturing element. Scoping the listener to the drag surface is what makes it see the click at all.
- Reaching for `stopImmediatePropagation()` by default. It also silences capture-phase listeners registered earlier on the same node, which can include analytics or a focus manager that had nothing to do with the drag. Escalate to it only when a library has attached its own capture listener to the same element.
- Leaving the timer running at unmount. It fires against a ref nothing reads, and on remount the widget can start life armed and swallow the first click a user makes.

## Notes

- Designed to pair with `drag-deadzone-capture`: that hook decides whether the gesture moved, this one suppresses the consequence. They are separate because the classification is useful on its own, and because the swallow has edge cases — one click and no more, keyboard passes through — that have nothing to do with dragging.
- A component that activates on `pointerup` rather than on `click` cannot be helped by this; there is no click to cancel. That is a good argument for activating on `click` in a draggable surface, since `click` is also what the keyboard produces.
- `preventDefault` on the click does not undo focus. Focus was moved by `mousedown`, earlier in the sequence, so a swallowed drag can leave the card under the pointer focused. It is invisible in practice because focus from a pointer does not match `:focus-visible`.
- A `dblclick` is dispatched independently of the clicks that preceded it, so a component listening for double-click needs the same treatment applied to `dblclick`.

## Definition of done

Click a card: it opens, and the on-screen counter shows one activation and no swallow. Drag the row and release over a card: the row moves, the card does not open, and the swallow counter goes up by exactly one. Immediately click that same card: it opens — the swallow was consumed by the drag and did not carry over. Drag and release over the gap between cards, then click a card: it opens, because the arm expired instead of waiting for a click that never came. Tab to a card and press Enter, then Space: it opens both times, including immediately after a drag, and the swallow counter does not move. Put a real `<a href>` in the row and drag onto it: the page does not navigate.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Carousel

A horizontally scrolling track with `scroll-snap-type: x mandatory`, not a transformed strip, so touch swipe, trackpad momentum and keyboard scrolling are the browser's own. JavaScript only answers what the DOM will not: which slide is showing and whether either end has been reached. Positions are read from each slide's bounding box rather than computed from a card width, so mixed widths, responsive widths and right-to-left layouts need no extra maths.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

A gallery you slide through on native scroll-snap: swipe, trackpad and arrow keys for free, plus end-aware arrows and a dot indicator.

- Category: display
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: @remixicon/react@^4.9.0

## How it works

1. The track is a flex row with `overflow-x-auto`, `overscroll-x-contain`, `snap-x snap-mandatory` and the scrollbar hidden inline (`[scrollbar-width:none]` plus `[&::-webkit-scrollbar]:hidden`). `gap` is an inline style from the `gap` prop. `tabIndex={0}` makes the track focusable, so once it has focus the arrow keys scroll it natively, and a `focus-visible` ring shows where focus went.
2. Each `CarouselItem` is a `role="group"` with `aria-roledescription="slide"` and `w-full shrink-0 snap-start`, so by default exactly one slide fills the track. The width lives on the item, which lets a consumer pass `w-[85%]` for a peek of the next slide. With `align="center"` the track adds `[&>*]:snap-center` so every slide rests in the middle instead.
3. `Carousel` walks its children with `Children.map` and clones each valid element with `aria-label` set to "`n` of `count`", where `count` is the number of valid elements. Callers never number their own slides. The outer wrapper is a `role="group"` with `aria-roledescription="carousel"` and takes the required `aria-label`.
4. `measure()` reads the track. `inlineScrollOffset(scrollLeft, direction)` turns the physical `scrollLeft` (negative in RTL) into a distance from the inline start. `atStart` is that offset `<= 1` and `atEnd` is `>= scrollWidth - clientWidth - 1`. The active index is pinned to 0 at the start and to the last slide at the end. Between the ends it is the slide whose `scrollOffsetForItem(trackRect, itemRect, 0, direction, align)` is smallest in absolute value, which means the slide closest to its own snap position.
5. One effect attaches a `ResizeObserver` to the track and a passive `scroll` listener, both calling `measure`. The observer fires once on `observe()`, and that call takes the first measurement, so the effect body never calls `setState` synchronously.
6. `scrollToIndex(i)` clamps `i` to the slide range, computes the target `left` with `scrollOffsetForItem(trackRect, targetRect, track.scrollLeft, direction, align)` and calls `track.scrollTo({ left, behavior })`. `behavior` is `"auto"` when `matchMedia("(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)")` matches at click time and `"smooth"` otherwise. The prev and next arrows call it with `active - 1` and `active + 1`, and each dot calls it with its own index.
7. The arrows are two small `IconButton`s ("Previous slide", "Next slide") in a right-aligned row above the track, disabled at the matching end. The dots are real `<button>`s below the track with `aria-current` on the active one. The active dot widens from `w-1.5` to `w-4` and switches to `bg-text-primary`, with `transition-all duration-200 ease-out`.
8. The wrapper sets `dir` from `useDirection()` (React Aria's `useLocale().direction`), so inside an RTL `I18nProvider` the track scrolls from the right and the geometry helpers use the right edges.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `edge slack = 1px`
  `scrollLeft` is fractional on hi-DPI displays, so an exact comparison leaves a fully scrolled track one sub-pixel short of the end and the Next arrow stays enabled. One pixel absorbs the rounding without disabling an arrow while a real slide is still hidden.
- `gap = 16 (px)`
  The default space between slides, applied as an inline `gap`. Snap positions come from each slide's measured box, so changing it never desynchronises the arrows or dots.
- `dot sizes = 6px round, 16px × 6px active, 200ms ease-out`
  The active dot is a short pill rather than a colour swap alone, so the position reads without relying on contrast. 200ms is long enough to see the dot grow and short enough to keep up with a fast swipe across several slides.
- `arrow size = IconButton size="small" (32 × 32)`
  Keeps the control row compact above a card. The arrows sit in their own `justify-end` row so they never overlap slide content or cover a swipe target.

## API

```ts
function Carousel(props: Omit<HTMLAttributes<HTMLDivElement>, "children" | "onScroll"> & { children: ReactNode; "aria-label": string; showArrows?: boolean; showDots?: boolean; align?: "start" | "center"; gap?: number; ref?: Ref<HTMLDivElement> }): JSX.Element
function CarouselItem(props: HTMLAttributes<HTMLDivElement> & { children: ReactNode; ref?: Ref<HTMLDivElement> }): JSX.Element
```

- `aria-label: string`
  Required. Names the carousel group for assistive tech.
- `children: ReactNode`
  `CarouselItem` elements, as direct children. Each one is labelled "n of count" automatically.
- `showArrows: boolean` — default `true`
  Previous and next icon buttons in a right-aligned row above the track. Each disables at its end.
- `showDots: boolean` — default `true`
  Clickable position dots below the track. Only rendered when there are at least two slides.
- `align: "start" | "center"` — default `"start"`
  Where a slide comes to rest when it snaps. Also drives which slide counts as active.
- `gap: number` — default `16`
  Space between slides in px, applied as an inline style.
- `className (CarouselItem): string` — default `"w-full"`
  Override the slide width, such as `w-[85%]` for a peek or `w-[220px]` for fixed cards.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
export function Carousel({
  children,
  showArrows = true,
  showDots = true,
  align = "start",
  gap = 16,
  className,
  ref,
  ...props
}: CarouselProps) {
  const trackRef = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const direction = useDirection();
  const [active, setActive] = useState(0);
  const [atStart, setAtStart] = useState(true);
  const [atEnd, setAtEnd] = useState(false);

  const count = Children.toArray(children).filter(isValidElement).length;

  const items = useCallback(
    () => Array.from(trackRef.current?.children ?? []) as HTMLElement[],
    [],
  );

  const measure = useCallback(() => {
    const track = trackRef.current;
    if (!track) return;

    // 1px of slack: scrollLeft is fractional on hi-DPI displays, so an exact
    // comparison leaves the end arrow enabled on a fully scrolled track.
    const offset = inlineScrollOffset(track.scrollLeft, direction);
    const start = offset <= 1;
    const end = offset >= track.scrollWidth - track.clientWidth - 1;
    setAtStart(start);
    setAtEnd(end);

    const all = items();
    if (all.length === 0) return;

    // At the far end the last cards share the viewport, so the final card can
    // never reach the start edge and "nearest" would settle on the one before
    // it — leaving the last dot permanently unlit and making a click on it
    // look broken. The ends are therefore pinned rather than measured.
    if (end) {
      setActive(all.length - 1);
      return;
    }
    if (start) {
      setActive(0);
      return;
    }

    let nearest = 0;
    let shortest = Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY;
    all.forEach((item, index) => {
      const distance = Math.abs(scrollOffsetForItem(track.getBoundingClientRect(), item.getBoundingClientRect(), 0, direction, align));
      if (distance < shortest) {
        shortest = distance;
        nearest = index;
      }
    });
    setActive(nearest);
  }, [items, direction, align]);

  useEffect(() => {
    const track = trackRef.current;
    if (!track) return;

    // ResizeObserver fires once on observe, which is what takes the first
    // measurement — no synchronous setState in the effect body.
    const observer = new ResizeObserver(measure);
    observer.observe(track);
    track.addEventListener("scroll", measure, { passive: true });
    return () => {
      observer.disconnect();
      track.removeEventListener("scroll", measure);
    };
  }, [measure]);

  const scrollToIndex = (index: number) => {
    const track = trackRef.current;
    const target = items()[Math.max(0, Math.min(index, count - 1))];
    if (!track || !target) return;
    // `matchMedia` rather than a hook: this runs on click, so reading the
    // preference at that moment is both current and cheap.
    const reduce = window.matchMedia("(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)").matches;
    const left = scrollOffsetForItem(track.getBoundingClientRect(), target.getBoundingClientRect(), track.scrollLeft, direction, align);
    track.scrollTo({ left, behavior: reduce ? "auto" : "smooth" });
  };

  return (
    <div
      ref={ref}
      role="group"
      dir={direction}
      aria-roledescription="carousel"
      className={cx("flex w-full flex-col gap-4", className)}
      {...props}
    >
      {showArrows && count > 0 ? (
        <div className="flex items-center justify-end gap-2">
          <IconButton
            icon={RiArrowLeftSLine}
            size="small"
            aria-label="Previous slide"
            disabled={atStart}
            onClick={() => scrollToIndex(active - 1)}
          />
          <IconButton
            icon={RiArrowRightSLine}
            size="small"
            aria-label="Next slide"
            disabled={atEnd}
            onClick={() => scrollToIndex(active + 1)}
          />
        </div>
      ) : null}

      {/* `tabIndex` makes the track focusable so it can be scrolled with the
          arrow keys, which is the browser's own behaviour once it has focus.
          The scrollbar is hidden inline rather than through a global class, so
          the component stays self-contained. */}
      <div
        ref={trackRef}
        tabIndex={0}
        className={cx(
          "relative flex w-full overflow-x-auto overscroll-x-contain outline-none",
          "snap-x snap-mandatory [scrollbar-width:none] [&::-webkit-scrollbar]:hidden",
          "focus-visible:ring-2 focus-visible:ring-border-focus-ring focus-visible:ring-offset-2",
          align === "center" && "[&>*]:snap-center",
        )}
        style={{ gap }}
      >
        {/* The position label is applied here so callers never have to
            hand-number their own slides. */}
        {Children.map(children, (child, index) =>
          isValidElement<CarouselItemProps>(child)
            ? cloneElement(child, { "aria-label": `${index + 1} of ${count}` })
            : child,
        )}
      </div>

      {showDots && count > 1 ? (
        <div className="flex items-center justify-center gap-1.5">
          {Array.from({ length: count }, (_, index) => (
            <button
              key={index}
              type="button"
              aria-label={`Go to slide ${index + 1}`}
              aria-current={index === active}
              onClick={() => scrollToIndex(index)}
              className={cx(
                "h-1.5 cursor-pointer rounded-full transition-all duration-200 ease-out",
                index === active
                  ? "w-4 bg-text-primary"
                  : "w-1.5 bg-background-tertiary-default hover:bg-border-button-active",
              )}
            />
          ))}
        </div>
      ) : null}
    </div>
  );
}
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** The single effect disconnects its `ResizeObserver` and removes the passive `scroll` listener from the track on unmount, or when `direction` or `align` change and `measure` is rebuilt. No timers or animation frames are used.

**Reduced motion.** Arrow and dot clicks jump straight to the target slide (`behavior: "auto"`) instead of smooth-scrolling. The check reads `matchMedia` at click time, so a preference changed mid-session applies immediately. Swipe and trackpad scrolling are the user's own input and stay as they are.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Replacing the scroll track with a `translateX` strip. That throws away native swipe, momentum, trackpad and keyboard scrolling, and then all of them have to be rebuilt by hand. The design depends on the browser doing the scrolling.
- Computing positions as `index * cardWidth`. It breaks for mixed widths, a responsive `w-[85%]` peek, a changed gap and RTL. Always measure bounding rects and go through `scrollOffsetForItem`.
- Choosing the "nearest" slide at the far end. When the last slides share the viewport the final one can never reach the start edge, so the last dot would never light and clicking it would look broken. The ends must stay pinned.
- Wrapping slides in fragments or extra elements. The track reads `children` as DOM slides and the labels come from `Children.map`, so a fragment of three slides counts as one and the labels and dots go out of step. Render `CarouselItem`s as direct children.
- Rendering conditional slides as `{flag && <CarouselItem/>}`. `count` ignores the `false`, but `Children.map` still advances its index for it, so labels read "2 of 2" for the only slide. Filter the array before rendering.
- Hard-coding `behavior: "smooth"`. Under reduced motion the jump must be instant. The component reads the media query at click time, so keep that check when adding new ways to move the track.

## Notes

- There is no controlled index API on purpose. To drive the track yourself, scroll the `.overflow-x-auto` element exactly as `scrollToIndex` does. The arrows and dots pick the change up from the `scroll` event.
- `showArrows={false} showDots={false}` gives a bare swipe-only track, for example a logo strip.

## Definition of done

With four full-width slides, the Previous arrow starts disabled and the first dot is the wide one. Clicking Next smooth-scrolls exactly one slide and the second dot widens. Swiping or trackpad-scrolling snaps to a slide and updates the dots. At the last slide Next disables and the last dot lights, even when slides are narrower than the track. Clicking any dot lands on that slide. With reduced motion the arrows jump instantly. In an RTL locale the track starts at the right edge and Next moves leftward.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Changes Diff Panel

The review side of an agent that edits code: a header with the number of uncommitted changes and their total added and removed lines, then one row per changed file with its path, +/− counts and a New or Deleted tag. Each row opens to an inline unified diff with line numbers and green or red line backgrounds. Accept or reject a file from its row, or every pending file from the header; decided files show an Accepted or Rejected tag with an undo, and the header totals only count what is still pending.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

Uncommitted-changes list with +/− counts, an inline diff per file and accept / reject per file or for all; totals update live.

- Category: display
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: react-aria-components@^1.22.1, @remixicon/react@^4.9.0

## How it works

1. parsePatch reads each file as a unified diff body: an "@@ -a,b +c,d @@" header resets the old and new line counters, "+" lines take the next new number, "-" lines the next old number, context lines advance both, and "\ No newline" markers are skipped. The same pass counts additions and removals, so counts never drift from the diff.
2. Decisions are a map from path to "accepted" or "rejected"; a missing key means pending. They can be controlled (decisions + onDecisionsChange) or left to the panel (defaultDecisions). applyDecision writes one decision, or deletes it for undo, across a list of paths, so a single file and Accept all share one code path.
3. The header derives everything from that map on each render: pending files, their summed +/− lines, and the accepted and rejected counts. When nothing is pending it switches to "All changes reviewed" and the bulk buttons disable.
4. Rows are React Aria Disclosures inside a DisclosureGroup with allowsMultipleExpanded. The trigger button sits inside a heading and the accept / reject buttons are its siblings, so no button is nested in another.
5. Expansion is held by the panel (defaultExpanded seeds it); with collapseOnDecide a decided file folds its diff, so the list shortens as you review.
6. Below 28rem wide the panel hides the folder part of each path and the New / Deleted tag (the file icon still shows the status), so file names stay readable.
7. Rejected files strike through their path and dim their diff instead of hiding it, so the reviewer can still read what was turned down and undo it.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `diff max height = 18rem (max-h-72)`
  Long files scroll inside their own box, so one big diff does not push every other file off the panel.
- `line tones = notification success / error background tokens`
  Soft lime and rose fills that keep code readable in both themes; the +/− signs and counts use the matching foreground tokens.
- `rejected dim = opacity 0.6`
  Clearly secondary while staying legible, unlike hiding the diff, which would make undo a blind action.

## API

```ts
function ChangesDiffPanel(props: { files: { path: string; patch: string; status?: "added" | "modified" | "deleted" }[]; decisions?: Record<string, "accepted" | "rejected">; defaultDecisions?: Record<string, "accepted" | "rejected">; onDecisionsChange?: (next, change: { paths: string[]; decision: "accepted" | "rejected" | null }) => void; defaultExpanded?: string[]; collapseOnDecide?: boolean; title?: string; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `files: { path: string; patch: string; status?: "added" | "modified" | "deleted" }[]`
  Changed files with a unified diff body each.
- `decisions: Record<string, "accepted" | "rejected">`
  Controlled decisions keyed by path; missing means pending.
- `defaultDecisions: Record<string, "accepted" | "rejected">`
  Initial decisions when uncontrolled.
- `onDecisionsChange: (next, change: { paths, decision }) => void`
  Called by every accept, reject and undo, single or bulk.
- `defaultExpanded: string[]` — default `[]`
  Paths whose diff starts open.
- `collapseOnDecide: boolean` — default `true`
  Fold a file once it is accepted or rejected.
- `title: string` — default `"Changes"`
  Accessible name of the panel.
- `className: string`
  Classes for the panel surface (height, width).

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
const HUNK_HEADER = /^@@ -(\d+)(?:,\d+)? \+(\d+)(?:,\d+)? @@/;

/** Turns a unified diff body into rows with old and new line numbers, and counts its additions and removals. */
export function parsePatch(patch: string): ParsedPatch {
  const rows: DiffRow[] = [];
  let oldNo = 1;
  let newNo = 1;
  let added = 0;
  let removed = 0;
  for (const raw of patch.replace(/\n+$/, "").split("\n")) {
    const hunk = HUNK_HEADER.exec(raw);
    if (hunk) {
      oldNo = Math.max(1, Number(hunk[1]));
      newNo = Math.max(1, Number(hunk[2]));
      rows.push({ kind: "hunk", text: raw });
      continue;
    }
    if (raw.startsWith("\\")) continue;
    const sign = raw.charAt(0);
    if (sign === "+") {
      rows.push({ kind: "add", text: raw.slice(1), oldNo: null, newNo: newNo++ });
      added += 1;
    } else if (sign === "-") {
      rows.push({ kind: "del", text: raw.slice(1), oldNo: oldNo++, newNo: null });
      removed += 1;
    } else {
      rows.push({ kind: "ctx", text: sign === " " ? raw.slice(1) : raw, oldNo: oldNo++, newNo: newNo++ });
    }
  }
  return { rows, added, removed };
}

/** Applies one decision (or null to undo) to several paths and returns a new map. */
function applyDecision(prev: ChangeDecisions, paths: string[], decision: ChangeDecision | null): ChangeDecisions {
  const next = { ...prev };
  for (const path of paths) {
    if (decision) next[path] = decision;
    else delete next[path];
  }
  return next;
}
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** No timers, listeners or observers; all state is plain React state.

**Reduced motion.** Only the chevron turn, row hover and the rejected dim fade animate, and all use motion-reduce:transition-none; diffs open and close instantly in every mode.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Paths are the keys for decisions and expansion; two entries with the same path will share one decision.
- In controlled mode, update decisions from onDecisionsChange or the buttons appear dead.
- Pass only the diff body (hunks and lines). File headers such as "diff --git" or "+++ b/file" would be read as added lines.

## Notes

- DiffCounts and parsePatch are exported for summaries elsewhere, for example a commit bar that reads "3 files, +24 −7".
- The status tag is optional: status "added" shows New, "deleted" shows Deleted, anything else shows only the counts.
- Line text is rendered as plain text in a monospace table; plug in your own highlighter if you need colours per token.

## Definition of done

With five pending files the header reads "5 uncommitted changes" with the summed +/− lines; accepting one file drops it from the totals, shows Accepted and folds its diff; Reject all marks every remaining file Rejected and the header reads "All changes reviewed"; undo returns a file to pending and restores the totals; clicking a row toggles its inline diff with old or new line numbers.

and where, so I can check them.
