# Build: Channel Tabs Bar List

A grey card with the kit Tabs on top and an uppercase metric caption on the right. Each tab holds a ranked list where every row sits on a light blue bar sized against the leader, with an optional icon, the label and the row's share of the tab total. Five rows show by default; the last one fades and a chevron button reveals the rest.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

A tabbed card of ranked horizontal bars: switch channels, campaigns or pages and each row shows its share of sessions.

- Category: display
- Runtime cost: css
- Dependencies: @remixicon/react@^4.9.0, react-aria-components@^1.22.1

## How it works

1. Render the kit `Tabs`, `TabList` and one `TabPanel` per tab, selection controlled (`selectedKey`) or uncontrolled (`defaultSelectedKey`, else the first tab); React Aria gives the arrow-key roving focus and `aria-selected`.
2. Rank each tab with `rankBars`: sort by value descending (label as tie-break), take `share = value / total` for the percent label and `width = value / max × 100` for the bar, so the leader always spans the row and the rest read as fractions of it.
3. Draw each row as a `relative isolate` list item with an absolutely positioned bar behind the content (`-z-10`), its width set through a `--bar` custom property and `w-(--bar)`, so the class can also carry `starting:w-0` and the bar grows from zero whenever a panel mounts.
4. Slice to `limit` rows while collapsed, fade the last visible row to 45% and show a small kit `IconButton` with `aria-expanded` and `aria-controls` pointing at the list; expanding rotates its chevron 180° and lists every row.
5. Show the metric caption beside the tabs from `@sm` (24rem), sharing the tab bar's bottom border, and as its own right-aligned line above the list in narrower containers so three tabs still fit at 300px.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `row height = 36px (h-9), 4px gap`
  Matches the 14px body line with room for the bar to read as a block rather than a stripe.
- `limit = 5`
  Five ranked rows cover most of the traffic; the long tail stays one click away.
- `bar grow = 500ms ease-out from 0 via @starting-style`
  Long enough to read the ranking settle when switching tabs, short enough not to delay reading values.
- `teaser opacity = 45%`
  Signals that more rows follow the fifth without hiding its value.

## API

```ts
type BarListItem = { id: string; label: string; value: number; icon?: ComponentType }

function rankBars(items: BarListItem[]): (BarListItem & { share: number; width: number })[]
```

- `tabs: BarListTab[]`
  One tab per grouping, each with its rows in any order.
- `selectedKey / defaultSelectedKey / onSelectionChange: string` — default `first tab id`
  Selected tab, controlled or uncontrolled.
- `metricLabel: string` — default `"Sessions"`
  Caption for the value column and part of each list's accessible name.
- `display: "share" | "value"` — default `"share"`
  Percent of the tab total or the raw number.
- `limit: number` — default `5`
  Rows shown before the expand button.
- `locale: string` — default `"en-US"`
  Locale for numbers and percents.
- `aria-label: string` — default `"Traffic sources"`
  Accessible name of the card and the tab list.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the card.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
/** Sort largest first and size every bar against the leader, so the top row
 *  always spans the track and the rest read as fractions of it. Shares are
 *  of the tab total and drive the percent labels. */
export function rankBars(items: BarListItem[]): RankedRow[] {
  const total = items.reduce((sum, it) => sum + Math.max(0, it.value), 0);
  const max = items.reduce((m, it) => Math.max(m, it.value), 0);
  return [...items]
    .sort((a, b) => b.value - a.value || a.label.localeCompare(b.label))
    .map((it) => ({
      ...it,
      share: total > 0 ? Math.max(0, it.value) / total : 0,
      width: max > 0 ? (Math.max(0, it.value) / max) * 100 : 0,
    }));
}

function BarRows({
  rows,
  limit,
  display,
  label,
  number,
  percent,
}: {
  rows: RankedRow[];
  limit: number;
  display: "share" | "value";
  label: string;
  number: Intl.NumberFormat;
  percent: Intl.NumberFormat;
}) {
  const listId = useId();
  const [expanded, setExpanded] = useState(false);
  const hidden = Math.max(0, rows.length - limit);
  const shown = expanded || hidden === 0 ? rows : rows.slice(0, limit);
  return (
    <div className="flex flex-col gap-2">
      <ol id={listId} aria-label={label} className="flex flex-col gap-1">
        {shown.map((row, i) => {
          const Icon = row.icon;
          // The last collapsed row fades out to say "the list goes on".
          const teaser = !expanded && hidden > 0 && i === shown.length - 1;
          return (
            <li key={row.id} className={cx("relative isolate h-9", teaser && "opacity-45")}>
              <span
                aria-hidden
                className="absolute inset-y-0 start-0 -z-10 w-(--bar) rounded-lg bg-status-blue-background transition-[width] duration-500 ease-out starting:w-0 motion-reduce:transition-none"
                style={{ "--bar": `${row.width.toFixed(2)}%` } as CSSProperties}
              />
              <span className="flex h-full items-center justify-between gap-3 px-2.5">
                <span className="flex min-w-0 items-center gap-2">
                  {Icon ? <Icon className="size-4 shrink-0 text-foreground-icon-secondary" aria-hidden /> : null}
                  <span className="truncate text-body-medium text-text-primary">{row.label}</span>
                </span>
                <span className="shrink-0 text-body-medium text-text-secondary tabular-nums">
                  {display === "share" ? percent.format(row.share) : number.format(row.value)}
                </span>
              </span>
            </li>
          );
        })}
      </ol>
      {hidden > 0 ? (
        <IconButton
          icon={RiArrowDownSLine}
          size="small"
          aria-label={expanded ? "Show fewer" : `Show ${hidden} more`}
          aria-expanded={expanded}
          aria-controls={listId}
          onClick={() => setExpanded((v) => !v)}
          className={cx(
            "self-center [&>svg]:transition-transform [&>svg]:duration-200 [&>svg]:ease-out motion-reduce:[&>svg]:transition-none",
            expanded && "[&>svg]:rotate-180",
          )}
        />
      ) : null}
    </div>
  );
}
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** The component adds no timers or listeners. The kit TabList disconnects its underline ResizeObserver on unmount.

**Reduced motion.** The bars grow over 500ms, the chevron rotates over 200ms and the kit tab underline slides; the bar and chevron carry `motion-reduce:transition-none`, so under `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` they appear at full width and flip instantly.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Size bars against the largest value, not the total. Against the total, a 39% leader fills only 39% of the row and the list looks empty.
- Set the width through a CSS variable and a class. An inline `width` style beats the `starting:w-0` class, so the bars would never animate in.
- The bars are `aria-hidden`; the written percent carries the value, so each row reads once as "Google Ads 39%".

## Notes

- Pass `display="value"` to show raw session counts instead of shares.
- Inactive panels unmount (React Aria default), so the expanded state resets per tab and the bars regrow on every switch.
- `rankBars` is exported for reuse in other ranked lists.

The demo opens on Channels with Google Ads 39%, Meta 25%, X Ads 14%, LinkedIn 8% and a faded Email 7%, each bar sized against Google Ads. Clicking the chevron shows TikTok 4% and Referral 3% and sets aria-expanded. Choosing Campaigns ranks "Free trial push · US" first with five rows and a "Show 1 more" button. At 360px the three tabs fit and the Sessions caption moves above the list. Light and dark both read correctly.

# Build: Char Stagger Then Scale-Up

The headline is on screen from the first frame — small and ghosted, reading as a label. Characters resolve one at a time from left to right, and just before the last one lands the whole word scales to full size with a `back.out` overshoot. It assembles itself, then it asserts itself. Supporting copy fades up a quarter of a second into the scale, so the page is never doing only one thing at a time.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

Characters resolve left to right, then the whole word scales up with an overshoot as the last one lands.

- Category: text
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: gsap@^3.15.0

## How it works

1. The text is split in JSX, not in the DOM: `text.split(" ")` gives word boxes, `Array.from(word)` gives one `inline-block` span per character. React owns every node, so no library mutates the tree and no `revert()` is needed to restore it.
2. The idle state — `opacity: dimOpacity` per character and `transform: scale(scaleFrom)` on the word — is written as inline JSX styles, not by GSAP. That makes the server-rendered markup and the no-JS render identical to the pre-animation frame, and it means a parent re-render cannot wipe out what GSAP wrote, because React only ever diffs props against props.
3. A `gsap.timeline` first tweens `[data-char]` to `opacity: 1` with `stagger: 0.07` and `duration: 0.28` on `power1.out`.
4. The word scale is appended at position `">-0.05"` — 50 ms *before* the character stagger ends. The overlap is what fuses two phases into one gesture; at `">"` they read as two separate animations queued back to back.
5. Supporting copy (`[data-fade]`) is appended at `"<0.25"` — 250 ms after the *scale started*, not after it finished. Relative-to-previous-start positioning is what keeps the choreography overlapping rather than sequential.
6. `transformOrigin: "50% 50%"` is set explicitly on the scale tween even though it is the default: a heading inside a flex column can inherit an origin from an earlier transform on an ancestor, and the word then grows out of one corner.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `SCALE_FROM = 0.42`
  Starting scale of the word. Around 0.4 the text reads as a caption; past ~0.65 the growth is not large enough to register as a change of role, and below ~0.3 the characters are illegible while they stagger, so the first half of the animation is wasted.
- `DIM_OPACITY = 0.24`
  Resting strength of an unresolved character, as opacity on `currentColor`. Zero would make the reveal a pop-in and lose the ghosted-label reading; above ~0.4 there is not enough contrast between resolved and unresolved for the sweep to be visible.
- `CHAR_STAGGER = 0.07`
  Seconds between adjacent characters. A ten-character word takes 0.7s to sweep. Below ~0.04 the characters resolve as a block; above ~0.12 a long headline outlasts the reader's patience.
- `CHAR_DURATION = 0.28`
  Seconds for one character. Deliberately four times the stagger, so several characters are always mid-resolve — that overlap is what makes it a sweep rather than a sequence of individual pops.
- `SCALE_DURATION = 0.9`
  Seconds for the scale-up. `back.out` spends most of its curve on the settle, so a shorter duration compresses the overshoot into something that reads as a bounce artefact.
- `OVERSHOOT = 1.3`
  The `back.out(n)` parameter. Around 1.3 the word passes a few percent beyond full size and returns. At 1.7 (GSAP's default) the overshoot on large type is tens of pixels and reads as a wobble.
- `FADE_STAGGER / FADE_DURATION / FADE_Y = 0.12 / 0.7 / 18`
  Supporting copy rises 18px over 0.7s, 0.12s apart. The travel is small on purpose — body copy that moves as far as the headline competes with it.
- `VIEW_THRESHOLD = 0.35`
  Fraction visible before the timeline runs. A headline is tall; requiring more than about a third means it has to be nearly centred before anything happens, and requiring less starts it while it is still a sliver at the bottom edge.

## API

```ts
function CharStaggerScaleUp(props: { text: string; children?: ReactNode; scaleFrom?: number; dimOpacity?: number; charStagger?: number; charDuration?: number; scaleDuration?: number; overshoot?: number; delay?: number; startOnView?: boolean; className?: string; textClassName?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `text: string`
  The headline. Split per word and per character in JSX.
- `children: ReactNode`
  Supporting copy. Fades up after the scale has begun.
- `scaleFrom: number` — default `0.42`
  Starting scale of the whole word.
- `dimOpacity: number` — default `0.24`
  Starting opacity of each character.
- `charStagger: number` — default `0.07`
  Seconds between character reveals.
- `charDuration: number` — default `0.28`
  Seconds for one character to resolve.
- `scaleDuration: number` — default `0.9`
  Seconds for the scale-up.
- `overshoot: number` — default `1.3`
  The `back.out(n)` parameter — how far past 100% the word travels.
- `delay: number` — default `0`
  Seconds before the timeline starts.
- `startOnView: boolean` — default `true`
  Run when scrolled into view rather than on mount.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the wrapper via `cn`.
- `textClassName: string`
  Merged onto the headline span — this is where type size and tracking go.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
const SCALE_FROM = 0.42;
const DIM_OPACITY = 0.24;
const CHAR_STAGGER = 0.07;
const CHAR_DURATION = 0.28;
const SCALE_DURATION = 0.9;
const OVERSHOOT = 1.3;
const FADE_DURATION = 0.7;
const FADE_STAGGER = 0.12;
const FADE_Y = 18;
const VIEW_THRESHOLD = 0.35;

export function CharStaggerScaleUp({
  text,
  children,
  scaleFrom = SCALE_FROM,
  dimOpacity = DIM_OPACITY,
  charStagger = CHAR_STAGGER,
  charDuration = CHAR_DURATION,
  scaleDuration = SCALE_DURATION,
  overshoot = OVERSHOOT,
  delay = 0,
  startOnView = true,
  className,
  textClassName,
}: CharStaggerScaleUpProps) {
  const root = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const word = useRef<HTMLSpanElement>(null);
  const reduced = useReducedMotion();
  const { inView } = useInView(root, { threshold: VIEW_THRESHOLD, once: true });

  useEffect(() => {
    const el = root.current;
    const wordEl = word.current;
    // Reduced motion needs no branch here: the idle state written into the
    // JSX below is already the finished state, so doing nothing is correct.
    if (!el || !wordEl || reduced) return;
    if (startOnView && !inView) return;

    const chars = Array.from(el.querySelectorAll<HTMLElement>('[data-char]'));
    const fades = Array.from(el.querySelectorAll<HTMLElement>('[data-fade]'));

    const ctx = gsap.context(() => {
      const tl = gsap.timeline({ delay });

      tl.to(chars, {
        opacity: 1,
        duration: charDuration,
        ease: 'power1.out',
        stagger: charStagger,
      }).to(
        wordEl,
        {
          scale: 1,
          duration: scaleDuration,
          ease: `back.out(${overshoot})`,
          // Set explicitly even though it is the default: a block-level
          // heading inside a flex column can inherit an origin from an
          // earlier transform, and the word then grows out of one corner.
          transformOrigin: '50% 50%',
        },
        '>-0.05',
      );

      if (fades.length > 0) {
        tl.to(
          fades,
          {
            opacity: 1,
            y: 0,
            duration: FADE_DURATION,
            ease: 'power3.out',
            stagger: FADE_STAGGER,
          },
          '<0.25',
        );
      }
    }, el);

    // revert(), not kill(): it also strips the inline transform and opacity
    // GSAP wrote, handing the nodes back in exactly the state React rendered.
    return () => ctx.revert();
  }, [
    text,
    reduced,
    inView,
    startOnView,
    delay,
    charDuration,
    charStagger,
    scaleDuration,
    overshoot,
  ]);
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** The timeline is built inside a `gsap.context` scoped to the root, and teardown calls `ctx.revert()`. That kills the tweens and strips the inline `transform` and `opacity` GSAP wrote, handing the nodes back in exactly the state React rendered — which matters under React 19 StrictMode, where the effect runs twice on mount.

**Reduced motion.** The idle inline styles collapse to the finished state (`scale(1)`, `opacity: 1`, no translate) and the effect returns before building a timeline. The headline and its supporting copy are fully rendered at full size on first paint — nothing is hidden and nothing waits for a trigger.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Splitting text before the webfont has loaded. Character and word boxes are measured against the fallback face, so widths and line breaks are wrong and never re-flow once the real font arrives — see `font-safe-text-split` for the gating and re-split lifecycle this class of component needs.
- Letting a splitting library mutate the DOM under React. React has no record of the injected spans, so the next parent render replaces the whole subtree and the animation targets nodes that are no longer in the document. Splitting in JSX avoids the problem entirely.
- Writing the idle state with `gsap.set` in the effect. The first paint then shows the finished headline at full size before the effect runs, and it visibly snaps down before animating up.
- Splitting straight to characters without word boxes. A line break can then land between two letters of the same word.
- Hardcoding the dim colour as a hex value. `#3d3d3d` is invisible on a light background; opacity on `currentColor` composites correctly against any theme.
- Queuing the scale at `">"` instead of `">-0.05"`. The two phases stop overlapping and the headline reads as "characters appear… then a separate thing happens".
- Cleaning up with `kill()` rather than `revert()`. `kill()` stops the tweens but leaves GSAP's inline `transform` and `opacity` on the nodes, so a remount starts from the finished state.

## Notes

- No text-splitting dependency: the split is declarative JSX. GSAP `SplitText` is reserved for the two components whose subject *is* SplitText (`nested-splittext-restore`, `font-safe-text-split`); everything else here splits in React so consumers are not forced to adopt a DOM-mutating splitter for a per-character stagger.
- Each word is one `inline-block whitespace-nowrap` box with a real text node for the space between words, so lines still wrap normally between words.

## Definition of done

On entering the viewport the characters brighten one at a time from left to right, and the word begins growing before the last character has finished. The word overshoots full size once and settles. Supporting copy starts rising while the word is still growing, not after. Unmount mid-animation and the nodes carry no inline `transform` or `opacity`. With reduced motion enabled the finished headline is present on first paint.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Chat Message Bubble

One row of an AI chat transcript. User messages sit on the right in a filled bubble with an initials avatar, and assistant messages sit on the left in an outlined bubble with a sparkle avatar. Each row shows its time and an action row that appears on hover or focus. Copy writes to the real clipboard; assistant rows also get regenerate and a like/dislike pair. Single-backtick spans render as inline code.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

User and assistant chat rows with avatar, bubble, time and inline code. Hovering shows copy, regenerate and like/dislike actions.

- Category: display
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: @remixicon/react@^4.9.0, react-aria-components@^1.22.1

## How it works

1. The row is an `<article>` with the avatar and a bubble column. `from="user"` adds `flex-row-reverse` and `items-end`, so the same markup mirrors to the right. The bubble column is capped at `min(85%, 36rem)`, and the corner nearest the avatar is cut to `rounded-*-md` so the bubble points at its sender.
2. `renderMessageText` splits the text on blank lines into `<p>` elements, then splits each paragraph with the capturing regex ``/(`[^`\n]+`)/``. Because the group is captured, every code span lands at an odd index and becomes a `<code>` in mono at 0.875em on the opposite surface colour. Anything else, including a lone backtick, stays plain text.
3. The action row starts at `opacity-0` and is revealed by `group-hover/message`, `group-focus-within/message` and `data-[pinned]`, which is set while the copy result is showing. On `@media (hover: none)` it is always visible. It uses opacity rather than `hidden`, so the buttons stay in the tab order and tabbing onto one reveals the row.
4. Copy calls `navigator.clipboard.writeText`. If that rejects (an insecure origin or a refused permission), it copies from a hidden, selected `<textarea>` with `document.execCommand("copy")`, removes it and puts focus back. A success swaps the icon to a check in lime and the label to "Copied", and a failure shows a rose warning and "Copy failed". A visually hidden `role="status"` announces the result, and a 1600ms timer resets it.
5. Like and dislike are React Aria `ToggleButton`s that both read one `rating` value, so pressing one clears the other and pressing it again clears the rating. They work controlled (`feedback`) or uncontrolled (`defaultFeedback`), and the selected one swaps to the filled thumb icon. Regenerate is a plain React Aria `Button` that only renders on assistant rows when `onRegenerate` is passed.
6. Every action is wrapped in the kit `TooltipTrigger` with a 300ms delay, and its tooltip text matches its `aria-label`.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `COPY_RESET_MS = 1600ms`
  Long enough to read "Copied" after moving the pointer away, short enough that a second copy a moment later starts from the normal icon.
- `tooltip delay = 300ms`
  Four small icon buttons sit side by side. Without a delay, moving the pointer along the row flashes a tooltip for each one.
- `bubble max width = min(85%, 36rem)`
  About 70 characters per line on a wide screen. On a phone, 85% leaves room for the avatar and keeps user and assistant sides apart.
- `action button = 28px, 16px icon`
  Fits under the bubble next to the time without making the row taller than the caption needs.

## API

```ts
function ChatMessageBubble(props: { from: "user" | "assistant"; text: string; time?: string; dateTime?: string; name?: string; avatar?: ReactNode; feedback?: "like" | "dislike" | null; defaultFeedback?: "like" | "dislike" | null; onFeedbackChange?: (value: "like" | "dislike" | null) => void; onRegenerate?: () => void; onCopy?: (text: string) => void; className?: string }): JSX.Element
function renderMessageText(text: string, codeClassName?: string): ReactNode
```

- `from: "user" | "assistant"`
  Which side the row sits on, which bubble style it uses and which actions it gets.
- `text: string`
  Message text. Single backticks make inline code; a blank line starts a paragraph. This is also what Copy writes.
- `time: string`
  Time shown under the bubble, already formatted.
- `dateTime: string`
  Machine-readable value for the `<time>` element.
- `name: string` — default `"You" / "Assistant"`
  Sender name for the initials avatar and the row's accessible label.
- `avatar: ReactNode`
  Replaces the default avatar.
- `feedback: "like" | "dislike" | null`
  Controlled rating for an assistant row.
- `defaultFeedback: "like" | "dislike" | null` — default `null`
  Starting rating when uncontrolled.
- `onFeedbackChange: (value: "like" | "dislike" | null) => void`
  Called with the new rating, or null when it is cleared.
- `onRegenerate: () => void`
  Shows the regenerate button on an assistant row.
- `onCopy: (text: string) => void`
  Called after the text reaches the clipboard.
- `className: string`
  Classes for the row.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
async function writeClipboard(text: string): Promise<boolean> {
  try {
    await navigator.clipboard.writeText(text);
    return true;
  } catch {
    // No Clipboard API (insecure origin) or permission refused: copy from a
    // hidden, selected textarea instead, then hand focus back.
    const previous = document.activeElement instanceof HTMLElement ? document.activeElement : null;
    const area = document.createElement("textarea");
    area.value = text;
    area.setAttribute("readonly", "");
    area.style.position = "fixed";
    area.style.opacity = "0";
    document.body.appendChild(area);
    area.select();
    let ok = false;
    try {
      ok = document.execCommand("copy");
    } catch {
      ok = false;
    }
    area.remove();
    previous?.focus({ preventScroll: true });
    return ok;
  }
}

function useCopy(text: string, onCopy?: (text: string) => void) {
  const [state, setState] = useState<CopyState>("idle");
  const timer = useRef<ReturnType<typeof setTimeout> | null>(null);
  const alive = useRef(true);

  useEffect(() => {
    alive.current = true;
    return () => {
      alive.current = false;
      if (timer.current !== null) clearTimeout(timer.current);
    };
  }, []);

  const copy = async () => {
    const ok = await writeClipboard(text);
    // The promise can settle after the message unmounts.
    if (!alive.current) return;
    if (ok) onCopy?.(text);
    setState(ok ? "copied" : "failed");
    if (timer.current !== null) clearTimeout(timer.current);
    timer.current = setTimeout(() => setState("idle"), COPY_RESET_MS);
  };

  return [state, copy] as const;
}
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** The copy reset timer is cleared when copy runs again and on unmount. A mounted ref stops a late clipboard promise from setting state, and the fallback textarea is removed straight after copying.

**Reduced motion.** The action row fade and the button colour and press-scale transitions use `motion-reduce:transition-none`, and the press scale is held at 100%. The row still appears on hover and focus, just without fading. Tooltips follow the kit's own reduced-motion rule.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Hiding the actions with `hidden` or `display: none` until hover. That removes them from the tab order, so keyboard users can never reach them. Opacity plus `group-focus-within` keeps them focusable.
- Giving like and dislike their own `isSelected` state. Both can end up pressed. Derive both from one value.
- Splitting on backticks with a non-capturing regex. The code spans are dropped from the result. With a capturing group they come back at odd indices.
- Setting state when the clipboard promise settles after the row has unmounted. The hook checks a mounted ref first and clears its timer on unmount.

## Notes

- `text` is a plain string, not Markdown. Only blank-line paragraphs and single-backtick code are handled; fenced blocks, links and lists are not.
- In the dark theme the primary and tertiary backgrounds are the same grey, so the user bubble, the code chips in assistant bubbles and the user avatar step up to the quaternary background with `dark:`.
- A user avatar uses the kit `Avatar` with initials from `name` ("Ada Park" becomes AP). Pass `avatar` to replace either avatar.
- The demo is a four-message thread. Regenerate cycles each reply through canned alternatives and clears its rating, both replies use controlled `feedback`, and a status line at the bottom reports each copy, rating and regenerate.

## Definition of done

Hover or Tab onto a message and its actions fade in under the bubble. Copy puts the exact text on the clipboard and shows a check and "Copied" for about 1.6s. Like and dislike are exclusive and pressing one again clears it. Regenerate appears only on assistant rows. Backtick spans show as inline code.

and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Chat Starter

A full chat page: the kit dashboard sidebar on the left and a rounded chat card holding the first screen of a conversation. With no messages the card centres a greeting, a pill composer and a row of suggestion chips; a chip fills the composer instead of sending, so the visitor can edit first. Set `apiKeyMissing` and the card shows a setup checklist for adding a provider key, with a button that skips straight to the demo. Sending posts the message and answers with a scripted reply after a short thinking state, so the screen works with no backend.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

Empty AI chat screen with a greeting, suggestion chips that fill the pill composer, and an "Add an API key to start" setup card.

- Category: block
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: @remixicon/react@^4.9.0

## How it works

1. State is local: `draft` (the composer text), `messages` (an array of `{ id, role, text }` with ids from a counter ref, never `Math.random`), `thinking`, the chosen `model`, and `skipped`. The setup card renders while `apiKeyMissing && !skipped`; "Skip, show me the demo" sets `skipped` and calls `onSkip`.
2. The composer zone is one element in both layouts. With no messages it gets `my-auto` inside a flex column, which centres the greeting, composer and chips vertically. Once a message exists, a scrolling list is inserted before it as a sibling, so the composer drops to the bottom without remounting and keeps focus.
3. A suggestion chip calls `setDraft(prompt ?? label)`, focuses the textarea and raises a `caretToEnd` ref. The layout effect that sizes the field runs after the new value is in the DOM, so it is the place that parks the caret at the end and clears the flag.
4. The textarea auto-grows: the layout effect sets `height: auto`, reads `scrollHeight` and writes it back capped at 6 lines × 20px + 16px of vertical padding. Past the cap the field scrolls.
5. Enter sends and Shift+Enter inserts a newline. The keydown handler skips Enter while `nativeEvent.isComposing` is true, so confirming an IME candidate never sends a half-typed message. The send button is a real `type="submit"` in a `<form>`, disabled while the trimmed draft is empty or a reply is pending.
6. Send appends the user message, clears the draft and starts one timeout (`replyDelay`, 900ms). When it fires it appends the reply of the suggestion whose prompt matches the sent text exactly, else `fallbackReply`. The timer id lives in a ref and is cleared on reset, before a new send, and on unmount.
7. The model chip is the kit `Dropdown`, controlled through `isOpen` so picking a row can close it. The selected row shows a check. The header "Start a new chat" button clears messages, draft and any pending reply.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `composer radius = 26px`
  Half of the 52px single-line height (36px controls + 8px padding top and bottom), so a one-line composer is a true pill. When the field grows to several lines the same radius reads as a soft card instead of a stretched capsule.
- `MAX_LINES = 6`
  Enough to see a pasted paragraph without the composer covering the conversation on an 800px-tall screen. Past six lines the field scrolls inside itself.
- `replyDelay = 900ms`
  Long enough for the thinking indicator to register as a state, not a flicker. Much longer and the scripted demo feels broken.
- `content column = max-w-[720px]`
  Keeps line length near 90 characters at 14px, which stays readable on a wide screen while the card itself stretches.

## API

```ts
function ChatStarter(props: { apiKeyMissing?: boolean; onSkip?: () => void; greeting?: string; subtitle?: string; suggestions?: ChatStarterSuggestion[]; placeholder?: string; models?: string[]; onSubmit?: (text: string) => void; fallbackReply?: string; replyDelay?: number; navItems?: DashboardNavItem[] | null; className?: string }): JSX.Element
interface ChatStarterSuggestion { label: string; prompt?: string; icon?: RemixiconComponentType; reply?: string }
```

- `apiKeyMissing: boolean` — default `false`
  Show the "Add an API key to start" setup card instead of the greeting and composer, until the visitor skips it.
- `onSkip: () => void`
  Called when "Skip, show me the demo" is pressed. The card hides either way.
- `greeting: string` — default `"What can I help with?"`
  Heading of the empty state.
- `subtitle: string` — default `"Ask anything, or start from one of these."`
  Line under the greeting. Pass an empty string to hide it.
- `suggestions: ChatStarterSuggestion[]` — default `[]`
  Chips under the composer. A click fills the composer with `prompt ?? label`; `reply` is the scripted answer for that exact prompt.
- `placeholder: string` — default `"Ask me anything"`
  Composer placeholder.
- `models: string[]` — default `["Swift 2", "Swift 2 Mini", "Deep 1"]`
  Names listed in the model chip. The first is selected.
- `onSubmit: (text: string) => void`
  Called with the trimmed text on every send.
- `fallbackReply: string`
  Scripted answer for prompts that match no suggestion.
- `replyDelay: number` — default `900`
  Milliseconds of thinking state before the scripted answer lands.
- `navItems: DashboardNavItem[] | null` — default `CHAT_STARTER_NAV`
  Sidebar rows (Chat, Dashboard, Components and Blocks, Sign in, Sign up). `null` hides the sidebar.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the root.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
const fillFromSuggestion = (s: ChatStarterSuggestion) => {
  const text = s.prompt ?? s.label;
  setDraft(text);
  // Focus now; the layout effect parks the caret at the end once the value lands.
  caretToEnd.current = true;
  inputRef.current?.focus();
};

const send = () => {
  const text = draft.trim();
  if (!text || thinking) return;
  onSubmit?.(text);
  const match = suggestions.find((s) => (s.prompt ?? s.label) === text);
  setMessages((m) => [...m, { id: nextId.current++, role: "user", text }]);
  setDraft("");
  setThinking(true);
  if (timerRef.current) clearTimeout(timerRef.current);
  timerRef.current = setTimeout(() => {
    timerRef.current = null;
    setThinking(false);
    setMessages((m) => [
      ...m,
      { id: nextId.current++, role: "assistant", text: match?.reply ?? fallbackReply },
    ]);
  }, replyDelay);
};

const onKeyDown = (e: KeyboardEvent<HTMLTextAreaElement>) => {
  // Enter sends, Shift+Enter breaks the line; never send mid IME composition.
  if (e.key === "Enter" && !e.shiftKey && !e.nativeEvent.isComposing) {
    e.preventDefault();
    send();
  }
};
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** One `setTimeout` for the scripted reply, held in a ref and cleared on unmount, on "Start a new chat" and before every new send. The model dropdown and the sidebar clean up after themselves.

**Reduced motion.** Composer, chip and button transitions carry `motion-reduce:transition-none`, the send button no longer scales on press, and new replies appear without the fade-in because that animation is behind `motion-safe:`. The kit thinking indicator falls back to its static frame. The scripted delay stays, since it is a state, not motion.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Sending on a suggestion click. The chip only fills the composer. Prompts usually need a word changed, and sending on click also makes it impossible to read the chips before committing.
- Moving the caret with `setSelectionRange` straight after `setDraft`. The DOM still holds the old value at that point, so the caret lands at the old length. Do it in the layout effect after the value commits.
- Sending on Enter during IME composition. Japanese, Chinese and Korean input confirm candidates with Enter, so check `nativeEvent.isComposing` first.
- Rendering the composer twice, once centred and once docked. The swap remounts the textarea and drops focus and the caret on the first send. Keep one element and change the layout around it.
- Leaving the reply timeout running on unmount or reset. A late `setMessages` writes an answer into a fresh chat.

## Notes

- The setup copy names Vercel and `AI_API_KEY` because that is the deploy path of the starter. Change the card copy to match your own host and variable name.
- Pass `navItems={null}` to drop the sidebar and use the chat card alone inside another layout. The sidebar is also hidden below the `lg` breakpoint.

## Definition of done

With `apiKeyMissing` the setup card shows; "Skip, show me the demo" reveals the greeting, composer and chips. Clicking a chip fills the composer with its prompt without sending. Enter sends, Shift+Enter adds a line, and the send button is disabled while the field is empty. A sent message appears on the right, "Thinking" shows, then a reply appears on the left.

# Build: Checkbox

React Aria's `Checkbox` wrapped around a shared `CheckboxGlyph`: a 16px (or 14px) box with a 4px radius that fills with the accent gradient when checked, while a white tick draws itself on over 200ms. The indeterminate state swaps the tick for a flat dash, which is what a "select all" parent shows when only some of its children are on. The glyph lives in its own file so Checkbox Card renders the identical box.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

React Aria checkbox in two sizes: a gradient box whose white tick draws itself on, plus an indeterminate dash for partial selections.

- Category: form
- Runtime cost: css
- Dependencies: react-aria-components@^1.22.1

## How it works

1. `Checkbox` spreads every React Aria prop onto `AriaCheckbox`, which renders a `<label>` around the native input (hence `ref?: Ref<HTMLLabelElement>`). Its children are a render function: the state object (`isSelected`, `isIndeterminate`, `isHovered`, `isFocusVisible`, `isDisabled`) goes straight into `<CheckboxGlyph state={state} size={size} />`, and `children`, when not null, becomes a label span in the size's type style.
2. The glyph derives `isMarked = isSelected || isIndeterminate`. Marked boxes paint `bg-linear-to-b from-accent-500 to-accent-600` plus `shadow-checkbox-selected` (the inner highlight), lightening to `from-accent-400 to-accent-500` on hover. Unmarked boxes are a 1px `border-border-checkbox-default` on `bg-background-primary-default` with `shadow-xs`, and the border darkens to `border-border-checkbox-hover` on hover. Hover only counts when the box is not disabled.
3. The box transitions `background-color`, `border-color` and `box-shadow` over 150ms. The gradient itself is a `background-image`, which does not interpolate, so the fill switches at once and the tick carries the motion.
4. Inside a 16×16 `viewBox`, indeterminate wins over selected: it renders the dash `M4.5 8H8H11.5`. A selected box renders the tick path with `pathLength={1}` and `animate-check-draw`. The theme gives that class `stroke-dasharray: 1; stroke-dashoffset: 1` and animates the offset to 0 over 200ms `cubic-bezier(0.65, 0, 0.35, 1)` with `forwards`. Because `pathLength` is 1, the same numbers mean "the whole stroke" at either size.
5. An unchecked box renders no path at all. So every check mounts a fresh path and replays the draw, and unchecking removes the tick immediately with no reverse animation.
6. Sizes come from `checkboxSizes`: md is a `size-4` box, `text-body-medium` label and `gap-2`; sm is a `size-3.5` box, `text-body-2-medium` label and `gap-1.5`. Focus draws `ring-2 ring-border-focus-ring ring-offset-2` only while `isFocusVisible` is true, so it shows for keyboard focus and not for a mouse click. Disabled dims the glyph to `opacity-50` and sets `cursor-not-allowed` on the label. `className` accepts a string or React Aria's state function and is merged last through `cx`.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `box size = md 16px (size-4), sm 14px (size-3.5), radius 4px (rounded-sm)`
  Figma's two sizes. Each is paired with its own label style (14px Body 1 for md, 13px Body 2 for sm), so box and text centre on one line.
- `tick draw = 200ms cubic-bezier(0.65, 0, 0.35, 1), forwards`
  A symmetric ease-in-out, so the stroke starts and lands softly like a pen mark. It is short enough to finish before the pointer has moved on. `forwards` holds the final frame, otherwise the tick would vanish when the animation ends.
- `pathLength = 1`
  Normalises the dash arithmetic. A dasharray and offset of 1 mean "the whole path" whatever the rendered size, so one keyframe serves both sizes.
- `stroke = 2px white, round caps and joins`
  The Figma glyph. Round caps keep a 2px stroke from looking clipped inside a 14px box.
- `colour transition = 150ms ease on background-color, border-color, box-shadow`
  The hover border change and the focus ring arrive quickly without looking abrupt.

## API

```ts
function Checkbox(props: Omit<AriaCheckboxProps, "children"> & { children?: ReactNode; size?: "sm" | "md"; ref?: Ref<HTMLLabelElement> }): JSX.Element
function CheckboxGlyph(props: { state: CheckboxGlyphState; size?: CheckboxSize }): JSX.Element
```

- `size: "sm" | "md"` — default `"md"`
  16px box with a 14px label, or 14px box with a 13px label.
- `children: ReactNode`
  The label. Omit it for a bare box, and pass `aria-label` instead.
- `isSelected / defaultSelected: boolean`
  Controlled or uncontrolled checked state (React Aria).
- `onChange: (isSelected: boolean) => void`
  Called with the new checked state.
- `isIndeterminate: boolean`
  Shows the dash instead of the tick. Presentational; the parent clears it.
- `isDisabled: boolean`
  Dims the glyph to 50% and blocks interaction.
- `className: string | ((state) => string)`
  Merged onto the label element after the defaults.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
export function Checkbox({ className, children, size = "md", ref, ...props }: CheckboxProps) {
  const s = checkboxSizes[size];

  return (
    <AriaCheckbox
      ref={ref}
      {...props}
      className={(state) =>
        cx(
          "group inline-flex items-center select-none",
          s.gap,
          state.isDisabled ? "cursor-not-allowed" : "cursor-pointer",
          typeof className === "function" ? className(state) : className,
        )
      }
    >
      {(state) => (
        <>
          <CheckboxGlyph state={state} size={size} />
          {children !== undefined && children !== null && (
            <span className={cx(s.label, "text-text-primary")}>{children}</span>
          )}
        </>
      )}
    </AriaCheckbox>
  );
}
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** Nothing to release. There are no effects, listeners or timers, and the tick animation belongs to the SVG path, which unmounts with the component.

**Reduced motion.** The theme's `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` rule sets `animation: none` and `stroke-dashoffset: 0` on `.animate-check-draw`, so the tick appears whole at once. The 150ms colour and border transition still runs. It changes colour only, nothing moves.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Rendering the tick path all the time and toggling its opacity. The draw is a CSS animation that runs when the path mounts, so it would play once on page load and never again. The glyph returns `null` for an unchecked box for this reason.
- Expecting `isIndeterminate` to clear itself. It is presentational: React Aria keeps showing the dash until the parent stops passing it. A "select all" parent has to compute it from its children on every render (some but not all selected).
- Wrapping `Checkbox` in another `<label>`, or putting a link or button in `children`. `AriaCheckbox` already renders the label, so a nested interactive element toggles the box as well as doing its own job.
- Rendering a bare box (no `children`) without `aria-label`. The box then has no accessible name, and a screen reader announces only "checkbox".

## Notes

- `CheckboxGlyph` takes a plain state object (five booleans), so any component that can supply them can draw the same box. Checkbox Card is the in-kit example.
- Disabled dims only the glyph. The label text keeps full colour, as the Figma states do; pass a `className` if a form needs the whole row dimmed.

## Definition of done

Clicking the label or pressing Space toggles the box. When it is checked, the white tick draws on from left to right over about 200ms on a blue gradient, and an indeterminate box shows a flat white dash instead. With reduced motion the tick appears at once. Tab focus shows a 2px ring offset from the box, and a mouse click does not.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Checkbox Card

A larger hit target for an on/off choice: a 10px-radius bordered card with a medium-weight title and an optional secondary description, and the same checkbox glyph the plain Checkbox uses, pinned to the trailing edge. The card is the React Aria `Checkbox` label, so clicking the text, the padding or the box all toggle it, and the tick draws itself on exactly as it does in the small control.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

Bordered option card with title and description on the left and the kit checkbox on the right; a click anywhere on it toggles.

- Category: form
- Runtime cost: css
- Dependencies: react-aria-components@^1.22.1

## How it works

1. `CheckboxCard` renders `AriaCheckbox` directly. React Aria makes that a `<label>` wrapping a visually hidden native `<input type="checkbox">`, so the whole card is the click target, Space toggles it when focused, and it takes part in forms and `CheckboxGroup`s like any checkbox. Every Aria prop (`isSelected`, `defaultSelected`, `onChange`, `isDisabled`, `isIndeterminate`, `name`, `value`) passes through.
2. The card class comes from the render-state function: `flex w-full items-center justify-between gap-3 rounded-2lg border border-border-button-default py-3 pe-5 ps-4 select-none`, with `transition-colors duration-150`. When hovered and not disabled the background is `bg-background-primary-hover`, otherwise `bg-background-primary-default`. Disabled adds `cursor-not-allowed opacity-50`.
3. The children render function receives the same state object and lays out a text column (`flex min-w-0 flex-col gap-0.5`) with the title in `text-body-medium text-text-primary` and, when `description` is not null or undefined, a second line in `text-body-regular text-text-secondary`. Both lines `truncate`, so long copy never pushes the box off the card.
4. On the trailing side, `<CheckboxGlyph state={state} />` (wrapped in `shrink-0 py-1`) draws the 16px box: accent gradient and a white tick that draws on over 200ms when selected, a dash when indeterminate, and a focus ring only while `isFocusVisible`. Sharing the glyph is what keeps the card and the plain Checkbox identical.
5. Physical padding is logical (`ps-4 pe-5`), so in RTL the box moves to the left edge and the extra 4px of padding stays on the box side.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `padding = ps-4 pe-5 py-3 (16 / 20 / 12px)`
  Taken from the Figma checkbox item (node 3793:2966). The trailing side is 4px wider so the 16px box sits optically centred in its corner rather than tight against the border.
- `radius = rounded-2lg (10px)`
  The kit's card-level control radius, the same as the gray pill tab and other selectable surfaces, so a stack of option cards matches the inputs around it.
- `hover transition = 150ms transition-colors`
  Only the background changes on hover. 150ms is the kit-wide timing for surface colour changes.

## API

```ts
function CheckboxCard(props: Omit<AriaCheckboxProps, "children"> & { title: ReactNode; description?: ReactNode; ref?: Ref<HTMLLabelElement> }): JSX.Element
```

- `title: ReactNode`
  Main label in body medium. Also the accessible name of the checkbox.
- `description: ReactNode`
  Optional secondary line in body regular, truncated to one line.
- `isSelected / defaultSelected: boolean`
  Controlled or uncontrolled checked state, from React Aria.
- `onChange: (isSelected: boolean) => void`
  Called when the card is toggled.
- `isIndeterminate: boolean`
  Shows the dash instead of the tick.
- `isDisabled: boolean`
  Dims the card to 50%, sets a not-allowed cursor and ignores input.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
export function CheckboxCard({
  className,
  title,
  description,
  ref,
  ...props
}: CheckboxCardProps) {
  return (
    <AriaCheckbox
      ref={ref}
      {...props}
      className={(state) =>
        cx(
          "group flex w-full items-center justify-between gap-3 rounded-2lg border border-border-button-default py-3 pe-5 ps-4 select-none",
          "transition-colors duration-150 ease",
          state.isHovered && !state.isDisabled
            ? "bg-background-primary-hover"
            : "bg-background-primary-default",
          state.isDisabled ? "cursor-not-allowed opacity-50" : "cursor-pointer",
          typeof className === "function" ? className(state) : className,
        )
      }
    >
      {(state) => (
        <>
          <span className="flex min-w-0 flex-col gap-0.5">
            <span className="truncate text-body-medium text-text-primary">{title}</span>
            {description !== undefined && description !== null && (
              <span className="truncate text-body-regular text-text-secondary">{description}</span>
            )}
          </span>
          <span className="flex shrink-0 items-center py-1">
            <CheckboxGlyph state={state} />
          </span>
        </>
      )}
    </AriaCheckbox>
  );
}
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** Nothing to clean up. The card holds no state, listeners or timers of its own; React Aria owns the checkbox state.

**Reduced motion.** The card itself only fades its background over 150ms. The tick draw animation comes from the shared checkbox glyph, which plays the theme's `animate-check-draw`. The component does not check `prefers-reduced-motion` itself, so remove that animation globally if the tick should appear instantly.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Do not put a link or a button inside `title` or `description`. The card is a `<label>`, so any click inside it toggles the checkbox, and an interactive child would both fire and toggle.
- Do not wrap the card in your own `<label>` or attach an extra `onClick`. React Aria already makes the whole card the label of the hidden input.
- Do not remove `truncate` from the text spans. Without it a long description wraps unpredictably and pushes the checkbox glyph down off the centre line.
- Do not signal selection with the card border. In this kit the card keeps its neutral border and only the checkbox shows the state.

## Notes

- Put several cards in a React Aria `CheckboxGroup` with `value` props to get a multi-select option list with one shared value array.

## Definition of done

Three stacked cards show a title, a description and a box on the right. Clicking anywhere on a card, including its text, checks it and the white tick draws on. Clicking again clears it. Hovering a card tints its background. Tab focuses each card in turn with a focus ring on the box, and Space toggles it. A disabled card is at half opacity and ignores clicks.

and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Chip

A single `<span>` label with a tinted background and a matching text colour, used for statuses ("Completed", "Waiting"), percentage deltas, prices and role tags. Three variants change only the vertical padding and type style, and ten colours map to semantic background/text pairs, so a chip follows light and dark mode without any `dark:` classes. The colour map is exported as `CHIP_COLORS` and reused by Tag Group.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

Coloured status, delta and role chips in three emphasis levels and ten theme-aware colour pairs on a 6px radius.

- Category: display
- Runtime cost: css
- Dependencies: none beyond React

## How it works

1. Export `CHIP_COLORS`, a `Record<ChipColor, string>` of background + text pairs. The seven hues use `bg-status-<hue>-background text-status-<hue>-text`. `neutral`, `gray` and `soft` reuse surface tokens (`bg-background-tertiary-default` / `bg-background-secondary-default` with `text-text-secondary` or `text-text-primary`).
2. Build the style map with `sortCx`: `base` is `inline-flex items-center justify-center rounded-md px-1.5 whitespace-nowrap`, and `variant` sets `py-0.5 text-body-medium` (bold), `py-1 text-body-medium` (subtle) or `py-1 text-caption-1-medium` (caption).
3. Define the status tokens per theme. Light pairs the 200 step background with 800 text (purple: 100 with 600). Dark mixes the 950 step at 60% with `transparent` behind 500/400/300 text (purple: 900 at 50% behind 300), so chips glow softly on dark cards instead of sitting as bright blocks.
4. Render one `<span>` whose classes are `cx(base, variant, color, className)`. `cx` is the kit's `tailwind-merge`, so a caller `px-2` or `rounded-full` replaces the default instead of fighting it.
5. Add `transition-[padding,font-size] duration-200` to the base, so a chip that changes variant in place (for example when a table switches density) eases its size instead of jumping.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `horizontal padding / radius = px-1.5 (6px), rounded-md (6px)`
  Shared by every variant so chips of different emphasis line up on their left edges in a column and keep the same corner.
- `variant padding = bold py-0.5 (2px), subtle py-1 (4px), caption py-1 (4px)`
  Bold is the dense status chip that fits a 32px table row (20px line + 4px). Subtle is the roomier price chip. Caption pairs 4px padding with the 12px type style for role tags.
- `type = text-body-medium (14/20, 500) or text-caption-1-medium (12/16, 500)`
  Medium weight keeps the coloured text readable on a tinted fill; the caption tier exists for secondary tags that must not compete with the row's main label.
- `dark status fill = color-mix(in srgb, <hue>-950 60%, transparent)`
  A translucent fill takes on the colour of whatever card it sits on, so the same chip works on primary and secondary dark surfaces.

## API

```ts
type ChipColor = "orange" | "lime" | "rose" | "yellow" | "cyan" | "blue" | "purple" | "neutral" | "gray" | "soft"
const CHIP_COLORS: Record<ChipColor, string>
interface ChipProps extends HTMLAttributes<HTMLSpanElement> { variant?: "bold" | "subtle" | "caption"; color?: ChipColor; ref?: Ref<HTMLSpanElement> }
function Chip(props: ChipProps): JSX.Element
```

- `variant: "bold" | "subtle" | "caption"` — default `"bold"`
  Vertical padding and type style: 2px + 14px, 4px + 14px, or 4px + 12px.
- `color: ChipColor` — default `"neutral"`
  One of ten background/text pairs from `CHIP_COLORS`.
- `className: string`
  Merged last through `tailwind-merge`.
- `ref: Ref<HTMLSpanElement>`
  Forwarded to the span (React 19 ref-as-prop).

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
/** Background and text pair per colour, shared with Tag Group's tags. */
export const CHIP_COLORS: Record<ChipColor, string> = {
  orange: "bg-status-orange-background text-status-orange-text",
  lime: "bg-status-lime-background text-status-lime-text",
  rose: "bg-status-rose-background text-status-rose-text",
  yellow: "bg-status-yellow-background text-status-yellow-text",
  cyan: "bg-status-cyan-background text-status-cyan-text",
  blue: "bg-status-blue-background text-status-blue-text",
  purple: "bg-status-purple-background text-status-purple-text",
  neutral: "bg-background-tertiary-default text-text-secondary",
  gray: "bg-background-secondary-default text-text-primary",
  soft: "bg-background-secondary-default text-text-secondary",
};

export interface ChipProps extends HTMLAttributes<HTMLSpanElement> {
  variant?: ChipVariant;
  color?: ChipColor;
  ref?: Ref<HTMLSpanElement>;
}

const styles = sortCx({
  base: "inline-flex items-center justify-center rounded-md px-1.5 whitespace-nowrap transition-[padding,font-size] duration-200 ease",
  variant: {
    bold: "py-0.5 text-body-medium",
    subtle: "py-1 text-body-medium",
    caption: "py-1 text-caption-1-medium",
  },
  color: CHIP_COLORS,
});

export function Chip({
  variant = "bold",
  color = "neutral",
  className,
  ref,
  ...props
}: ChipProps) {
  return (
    <span
      ref={ref}
      className={cx(styles.base, styles.variant[variant], styles.color[color], className)}
      {...props}
    />
  );
}
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** Nothing to clean up. The component is stateless markup with no listeners, timers or effects.

**Reduced motion.** The only motion is a 200ms padding/font-size transition when a chip changes variant in place. It is not disabled under `prefers-reduced-motion`, since it is a size change, not movement across the screen.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Do not hard-code palette classes such as `bg-lime-200 text-lime-800` on a chip. The semantic `status-*` tokens are what switch to the translucent dark-mode pair.
- Do not remove `whitespace-nowrap`. A two-word status such as "In review" wraps inside a narrow table cell and doubles the row height.
- Do not encode meaning in colour alone. A rose chip still needs its "Failed" or "-3.2%" text.
- Do not add a new colour only to `ChipColor`. It has to exist in `CHIP_COLORS` and as a token in both themes, or the chip renders with no fill.

## Notes

- `CHIP_COLORS` is imported by `tag-group`, so its tags share the exact chip palette.
- The default is `variant="bold"` and `color="neutral"`.

## Definition of done

Twelve chips across all three variants and the ten colours wrap into a ragged cloud. Bold chips are 24px tall, subtle 28px and caption 24px, all with 6px side padding and 6px corners. In light mode the hue chips show a pale fill with dark text; in dark mode the same chips show a translucent dark fill with lighter text. Text never wraps inside a chip.

# Build: CSS Variable Clip-Path Tween

A panel reveal that tweens a CSS custom property instead of a CSS property. The stage clips itself with `inset(var(--kx-clip))`, and because custom properties inherit, any descendant carrying `.kx-clip-follow` clips with the same value in its own box — one tween, several clip boxes, no possible drift. The media pushes from 1.4 to 1 over half again the clip duration and the lines slide up on a stagger; the exit is the same timeline reversed, which turns the positive stagger into a last-line-first peel and the scale-down back into a push.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

One tweened custom property drives every clip-path on the panel, and reversing the timeline is the exit.

- Category: transition
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: gsap@^3.15.0

## How it works

1. GSAP's CSSPlugin special-cases any property whose name starts with `--`: it reads the start value with `getComputedStyle(target).getPropertyValue(prop)` and writes with `style.setProperty(prop, value)`. Because neither end is a plain number, the tween routes through the complex-string interpolator, which walks both strings and interpolates every number it finds pairwise — `100% 0% 0% 0%` to `0% 0% 0% 0%` is four independent number tweens in one string.
2. The tweened value feeds `clip-path: inset(var(--kx-clip))` on the stage. `inset()` takes `top right bottom left`, so a top inset of 100% collapses the box to nothing and 0% leaves it whole: the reveal is the top edge travelling down.
3. The reason to tween a variable rather than `clipPath` itself is inheritance. `.kx-clip-follow` on any descendant re-uses the same inherited value against its own border box, so a caption reveals in proportion with the panel without a second tween. Tweening `clipPath` on each element instead means N tweens that agree only until someone edits one.
4. The initial `--kx-clip` is declared in the injected stylesheet, not in React's inline style. GSAP writes the tweened value inline, and a React re-render owning that same inline property would reset it mid-tween. It also has to be declared somewhere: an undeclared custom property computes to the empty string, and a tween with no readable start value snaps to its end.
5. One paused timeline is built and then `play()`ed or `reverse()`d. Reversing is not a shortcut — it is the exit the source had: a reversed positive stagger runs last-element-first, and a reversed `scale: 1.4 -> 1` runs `1 -> 1.4`, so the panel leaves with its lines peeling off in reverse while the media is still pushing in.
6. The timeline is built inside `gsap.context()` with `open` deliberately absent from its dependencies. Rebuilding per state change would call `context.revert()`, which strips the inline value GSAP wrote — the closing tween would then read the stylesheet default, fully shut, as its start and animate from nowhere to nowhere.
7. Media and line timings are ratios of the clip duration (1.5x, 0.6x, offset 0.35x) rather than independent numbers, so retuning the reveal cannot desynchronise the three groups.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `duration = 1.2`
  Seconds for the clip. The source ran 2 s, but that timeline was scrubbed against scroll where duration is only a proportion of the scroll range. Played back at real time, 2 s is a panel you wait for; below ~0.8 s the `power3.inOut` has no room for its slow start and the edge appears to jump.
- `mediaScale = 1.4`
  Start scale of the media. Big enough that the settle is legible for the full duration, small enough that a 1x asset is not visibly softened. Also the reason the media needs an `overflow: hidden` wrapper: at 1.4 it is 40% wider than its box.
- `lineStagger = 0.125`
  Seconds between lines. Exactly the source value. At 0 the block arrives as one slab; past ~0.2 s the last line is still climbing after the clip has finished and the reveal appears to have two endings.
- `MEDIA_DURATION_RATIO = 1.5`
  The push outlives the clip by half again. The clip is the event; the scale still resolving after it is what stops the panel feeling like it stopped dead on arrival.
- `LINE_OFFSET_RATIO = 0.35`
  Fraction of the clip before the lines start. Any earlier and they climb inside a box that is still mostly clipped, so the first thing the eye catches is text being cut in half.
- `CLIP_SHUT = '100% 0% 0% 0%'`
  Four percentages, matching the four in `CLIP_OPEN`. The complex-string interpolator pairs numbers positionally, so `inset(100%)` against `inset(0% 0% 0% 0%)` would interpolate one number and leave the other three as literal text.

## API

```ts
function ClipPathVariableTween(props: { open: boolean; children: ReactNode; duration?: number; mediaScale?: number; lineStagger?: number; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `open: boolean`
  `true` plays the reveal, `false` reverses it. Every change re-drives the same timeline.
- `children: ReactNode`
  Content. `[data-clip-media]` is pushed from `mediaScale` to 1; `[data-clip-line]` slides up from 120%.
- `duration: number` — default `1.2`
  Seconds for the clip. Media and line timings are ratios of it.
- `mediaScale: number` — default `1.4`
  Scale the media starts at. 1 disables the push.
- `lineStagger: number` — default `0.125`
  Seconds between lines. Reversed on exit, so the last line leaves first.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the stage, which is the element that carries the clip.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
/** `inset(top right bottom left)`. Top at 100% collapses the box entirely. */
const CLIP_SHUT = '100% 0% 0% 0%';
const CLIP_OPEN = '0% 0% 0% 0%';

/**
 * Media scale outlives the clip by half again. The clip is the event; the push
 * continuing past it is what stops the panel feeling like it stopped dead.
 */
const MEDIA_DURATION_RATIO = 1.5;
const LINE_DURATION_RATIO = 0.6;
/** Lines start when the clip is a third open — before that they are hidden. */
const LINE_OFFSET_RATIO = 0.35;

const CLIP_CSS = `
.kx-clip-stage {
  /* Declared in CSS, never in React's inline style: GSAP writes the tweened
     value to the inline style, and a React re-render would reset it mid-tween.
     It also has to be declared SOMEWHERE — an undeclared custom property
     computes to the empty string, and a tween with no start value snaps. */
  --kx-clip: ${CLIP_SHUT};
  clip-path: inset(var(--kx-clip));
}
/* Any descendant clipped by the same inherited variable. */
.kx-clip-follow {
  clip-path: inset(var(--kx-clip));
}
`;

export interface ClipPathVariableTweenProps {
  /** `true` reveals, `false` clips away. Every change plays or reverses. */
  open: boolean;
  /**
   * Content. Two opt-in hooks:
   * `[data-clip-media]` is pushed from `mediaScale` to 1, and
   * `[data-clip-line]` slides up from 120% with a stagger.
   */
  children: ReactNode;
  /** Seconds for the clip itself. Media and lines are derived ratios of it. */
  duration?: number;
  /** Scale the media starts at. 1 disables the push. */
  mediaScale?: number;
  /** Seconds between lines. Reversed on exit, so the last line leaves first. */
  lineStagger?: number;
  className?: string;
}

export function ClipPathVariableTween({
  open,
  children,
  duration = 1.2,
  mediaScale = 1.4,
  lineStagger = 0.125,
  className,
}: ClipPathVariableTweenProps) {
  const root = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const timeline = useRef<ReturnType<typeof gsap.timeline> | null>(null);
  const reduced = useReducedMotion();

  // Built once and held paused. Rebuilding it per `open` change would be
  // wrong twice over: `gsap.context().revert()` strips the inline value GSAP
  // wrote, so a closing tween would read the CSS default — fully shut — as its
  // start and animate from nowhere to nowhere.
  useGsap(
    gsap,
    () => {
      const el = root.current;
      if (!el) return;

      const media = el.querySelectorAll<HTMLElement>('[data-clip-media]');
      const lines = el.querySelectorAll<HTMLElement>('[data-clip-line]');

      const tl = gsap.timeline({ paused: true });

      tl.fromTo(
        el,
        { '--kx-clip': CLIP_SHUT },
        { '--kx-clip': CLIP_OPEN, duration, ease: 'power3.inOut' },
        0,
      );

      if (media.length > 0) {
        tl.fromTo(
          media,
          { scale: mediaScale },
          {
            scale: 1,
            duration: duration * MEDIA_DURATION_RATIO,
            ease: 'power2.out',
          },
          0,
        );
      }

      if (lines.length > 0) {
        tl.fromTo(
          lines,
          { yPercent: 120 },
          {
            yPercent: 0,
            duration: duration * LINE_DURATION_RATIO,
            ease: 'power3.out',
            stagger: lineStagger,
          },
          duration * LINE_OFFSET_RATIO,
        );
      }

      timeline.current = tl;
      return () => {
        timeline.current = null;
      };
    },
    root,
    [duration, mediaScale, lineStagger],
  );

  // Same dependency list plus `open`, so this always runs after the effect
  // above has rebuilt the timeline rather than driving a stale one.
  useEffect(() => {
    const tl = timeline.current;
    if (!tl) return;

    if (reduced) {
      // A jump, not a zero-duration tween: the timeline is seeked to the
      // correct end state and stays paused there. Clip, scale and line offsets
      // all land correctly because they are all on this one timeline.
      tl.progress(open ? 1 : 0).pause();
      return;
    }

    if (open) tl.play();
    else tl.reverse();
  }, [open, reduced, duration, mediaScale, lineStagger]);

  return (
    <div ref={root} className={cn('kx-clip-stage', className)}>
      <style href="kinetic-clip-path-variable-tween" precedence="medium">
        {CLIP_CSS}
      </style>
      {children}
    </div>
  );
}
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** `useGsap` runs everything inside `gsap.context()` and calls `revert()` on unmount, which kills the timeline and removes the inline `--kx-clip`, `transform` and `scale` GSAP wrote so React never inherits a stray style. The context callback also nulls the timeline ref, so the effect that plays it cannot touch a reverted timeline.

**Reduced motion.** The timeline is seeked with `tl.progress(open ? 1 : 0).pause()` — a jump to the correct end state, not a zero-duration tween. Because the clip, the media scale and every line offset all live on that one timeline, one seek lands all of them correctly, which is the practical argument for putting them there in the first place.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Writing the custom property through React's inline `style` as well. React owns that attribute and GSAP writes to it; the first re-render during a tween resets the value and the clip snaps back.
- Never declaring the custom property. An undeclared custom property computes to the empty string, so GSAP has nothing to parse as a start value and the tween jumps straight to its end on the first frame.
- Mismatching the number count between the two clip strings. The interpolator pairs numbers positionally, so `inset(100%)` to `inset(0% 0% 0% 0%)` animates the first number and carries the rest through as text.
- Rebuilding the timeline whenever the open state changes. `gsap.context().revert()` removes the inline value GSAP wrote, so the reverse tween reads the stylesheet default as its start and animates from the closed state to the closed state — the exit silently does nothing.
- Tweening `clipPath` on each element instead of one shared variable. It works on the day you write it and drifts the first time one of the durations is tuned, because nothing structural keeps them equal.
- Forgetting `overflow: hidden` on the media wrapper and on each line. A 1.4x scale overflows its box by 40%, and a line entering from `yPercent: 120` is visible below its own box the entire way up.
- Assuming a clipped-away panel is inert. `clip-path` does clip hit-testing, but anything positioned outside the clip region — a fixed-position child, a focusable control — can still be reached by the keyboard, so the panel also needs its interactive state driven from the same flag.
- Tweening `--kx-clip` with a scrubbed ScrollTrigger and expecting sub-pixel smoothness. Custom property writes invalidate style for the whole inheritance subtree, so a stage with hundreds of descendants pays for it on every frame. The technique earns its keep with a handful of followers, not hundreds.

## Notes

- The `open` flag is the API surface, so a faked route change, a real router, an `IntersectionObserver` or a click all drive it identically. Nothing here imports a router.
- Registering the property with `@property { syntax: "<percentage>+" }` is not needed: GSAP interpolates the string itself and never asks the browser to. Register it only if you also want CSS transitions or keyframes to animate the same variable.
- `inset()` is the only basic shape whose numbers interpolate this cleanly. `polygon()` works the same way as long as both sides have the same vertex count, which is the same constraint stated differently.
- For a full-page version, put the stage on the layout wrapper and the follower class on the header rule and the footer — one tween, three clip boxes, and the whole chrome resolves together.

## Definition of done

Click an index row: the panel's top edge travels down over 1.2 s, the media resolves from a 1.4x push, the three lines climb into place 0.125 s apart, and the meta rule at the bottom clips itself in step without a tween of its own. Click Close: the panel clips back up, the last line leaves first, and the media pushes in again — the index underneath is revealed, not covered by a second animation. With reduced motion the panel is simply present or absent with the media at 1x and the lines in place.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.
