# Build: Copy Page Button

The "Copy Page" control that sits beside a docs page title. One bordered 36px shell is split by a 1px rule into a copy button and a chevron trigger. The copy half writes the page Markdown to the clipboard and swaps its icon and label to a lime check and "Copied" for a moment. The chevron opens the kit Dropdown with "Copy as Markdown", "View as Markdown" and any extra actions you pass.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

Docs split button: the main half copies the page as Markdown and flips to Copied, the chevron opens Copy and View as Markdown.

- Category: action
- Runtime cost: css
- Dependencies: @remixicon/react@^4.9.0

## How it works

1. `markdown` is a string or a function, sync or async, resolved at click time by `resolveMarkdown`. A page can then build or fetch its Markdown only when someone asks for it. A `busy` ref drops repeat clicks while an async source is still pending.
2. The resolved text goes through `useCopyToClipboard` from `code-block-copy`. It tries the async Clipboard API, falls back to a hidden textarea with `execCommand("copy")`, and sets `copied` for `resetMs` (1600ms). The copy icon scales to 50% and fades out while the check scales in, and the label switches to `copiedLabel`.
3. The chevron half is a `DropdownTrigger` inside a `Dropdown` whose open state is held here, controlled or uncontrolled. The chevron can then rotate 180 degrees while the menu is open. The `DropdownPopover` opens at `bottom end` with a 6px offset and 288px width, so its right edge lines up with the button.
4. Each menu row closes the menu first and then runs its action. "Copy as Markdown" uses the same `copyPage` path, so the main half shows the copied state even though the click happened in the menu. "View as Markdown" becomes a real `<a target="_blank">` when `markdownHref` is set. Otherwise it calls `onViewMarkdown(text)`, or, as the fallback, opens a `text/plain` Blob URL in a new tab and revokes it after 60s.
5. A visually hidden `role="status"` span announces "Page copied as Markdown" while `copied` is true, because the visible label change alone is not read out.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `shell = h-9, rounded-2lg (10px), 1px border-button-default, shadow-xs`
  This matches the kit secondary Button at medium size, so the split button lines up with other toolbar buttons.
- `chevron half = w-9 (36px square)`
  It gives the trigger a square hit area the same height as the shell, like an icon-only medium button.
- `resetMs = 1600`
  Long enough to read "Copied", short enough that a second copy still gives fresh feedback.
- `menu = placement bottom end, offset 6, w-[288px]`
  The button sits at the right of the title row, so the panel aligns to its end edge and stays inside the content column.
- `blob revoke = 60_000 ms`
  The new tab needs the object URL alive while it loads. Revoking at once would show a blank tab in some browsers.

## API

```ts
function CopyPageButton(props: { markdown: string | (() => string | Promise<string>); markdownHref?: string; onViewMarkdown?: (markdown: string) => void; actions?: readonly { id: string; label: string; description?: string; icon?: ComponentType; onAction: () => void }[]; label?: string; copiedLabel?: string; resetMs?: number; onCopied?: (markdown: string) => void; isMenuOpen?: boolean; onMenuOpenChange?: (isOpen: boolean) => void; className?: string; ref?: Ref<HTMLDivElement> }): JSX.Element
```

- `markdown: string | (() => string | Promise<string>)`
  The page as Markdown, or a function resolved at click time.
- `markdownHref: string`
  URL of the raw Markdown. "View as Markdown" becomes a new-tab link.
- `onViewMarkdown: (markdown: string) => void`
  Custom "View as Markdown" handler, used when no `markdownHref` is set.
- `actions: readonly CopyPageAction[]` — default `[]`
  Extra menu rows under the built-in two.
- `label: string` — default `"Copy Page"`
  Main button label.
- `copiedLabel: string` — default `"Copied"`
  Label while the copied state lasts.
- `resetMs: number` — default `1600`
  Duration of the copied state in ms.
- `onCopied: (markdown: string) => void`
  Called after a successful copy.
- `isMenuOpen / onMenuOpenChange: boolean / (isOpen: boolean) => void` — default `uncontrolled`
  Controlled menu state.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
const copyPage = async () => {
  // Ignore double clicks while an async source is still resolving.
  if (busy.current) return;
  busy.current = true;
  try {
    const text = await resolveMarkdown(markdown);
    if (await copy(text)) onCopied?.(text);
  } finally {
    busy.current = false;
  }
};

const viewMarkdown = async () => {
  setOpen(false);
  if (markdownHref) return; // the anchor navigates on its own
  const text = await resolveMarkdown(markdown);
  if (onViewMarkdown) onViewMarkdown(text);
  else openMarkdownBlob(text);
};

const runFromMenu = (action: () => void | Promise<void>) => () => {
  setOpen(false);
  void action();
};
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** The copied-state timeout belongs to `useCopyToClipboard` and is cleared on unmount and before each new copy. The Blob URL fallback revokes its object URL after 60 seconds. Outside-press listeners belong to the kit Dropdown and go away when it closes.

**Reduced motion.** The icon cross-fade, the chevron rotation and the hover colours all carry `motion-reduce:transition-none`. The kit Dropdown panel skips its fade, scale and blur. Under reduced motion the state still changes, only without animation.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Awaiting a slow network fetch before `clipboard.writeText`. Safari drops the user activation after a long await and rejects the write. Keep async sources fast, or pass a string.
- Leaving the menu open after "Copy as Markdown". The copied feedback is on the main button, so the menu has to close first or the reader never sees it.
- Rendering "View as Markdown" as a button that calls `window.open` with a server URL. A plain anchor keeps middle-click and "open in new tab" working, which is why `markdownHref` renders an `<a>`.

## Notes

- `actions` appends rows such as "Open in ChatGPT" or "Copy page link". Each row closes the menu before its `onAction` runs.
- The copy logic is shared with the Code Block copy button through `useCopyToClipboard` in `code-block-copy.tsx`.

## Definition of done

Clicking "Copy Page" puts the exact Markdown on the clipboard, and the button reads "Copied" with a lime check for about 1.6s before going back. Clicking the chevron opens a menu below the button, aligned to its right edge, with "Copy as Markdown" and "View as Markdown", and the chevron points up. Choosing "Copy as Markdown" closes the menu and shows the same copied state. Choosing "View as Markdown" closes the menu and calls `onViewMarkdown` with the text, or opens `markdownHref` in a new tab. Escape closes the menu.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Raycaster-Free Hover Picking

A ring of plates spins entirely on the compositor, so the main thread has no idea where anything is. Instead of measuring the DOM, the component recomputes the same transform in JavaScript — rotate, tilt, perspective divide — and hit-tests the resulting screen points against the pointer. A crosshair marks the computed position so you can see the mirror agreeing with the pixels.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

Run the GPU's transform again on the CPU and hit-test the result. No raycaster, no rect reads.

- Category: primitive
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: none beyond React

## How it works

1. The spin is one `Element.animate` keyframe pair with `iterations: Infinity`. It runs off the main thread, which means it keeps time even while JS is busy, and means the main thread must reconstruct the angle rather than remember it: `animation.currentTime` divided by the period gives the exact phase the compositor is drawing.
2. The mirror is four lines that shadow the CSS one for one. Two nested `rotateY` (ring spin, plate angle) collapse into a single angle sum, so a plate centre sits at `(r·sin a, 0, r·cos a)`. The stage `rotateX` turns that depth into vertical offset. The perspective divide `d / (d − z)` reproduces what the browser does with the `perspective` property.
3. Picking runs once per frame, not per `pointermove`. The geometry moves under a stationary cursor, so the correct answer changes on frames where no input arrived at all. An event-driven hit test would leave the hover state stuck on whatever plate happened to be there when the pointer last moved.
4. Plates with `z <= 0` are rejected before the distance compare. They are on the far side of the ring, drawn behind the near plates, and picking them would let a click pass through the front of the object.
5. The winner is the nearest projected point within a squared pick radius. Squared, because a comparison against `r²` gives the same ordering as a comparison against `r` without the square root.
6. This is the only correct approach when a vertex shader, a CSS transform, or GPU skinning moves the geometry after it leaves JavaScript. The CPU-side geometry never changed, so `Raycaster` intersects the undeformed mesh and reports hits on a shape that is not on screen. Mirroring the vertex transform on the CPU is the fix — the same maths, applied to one point instead of every vertex.
7. Everything inside the perspective root is `pointer-events: none`. There is nothing for the browser to hit-test; the container takes the pointer and the mirror decides what was under it.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `PERSPECTIVE = 900`
  Shared by the CSS `perspective` property and the JS divide. If the two ever disagree the crosshair drifts away from the plate it is meant to mark — which makes this the single most important value to keep in one place.
- `TILT = 16`
  Degrees of stage lean. Enough that the ring reads as a ring rather than a row; past ~30° the far plates hide behind the near ones and picking gets ambiguous even with the depth rejection.
- `PICK_RADIUS = 44`
  The pointer must land within 44 px of a projected centre. Matches the 44 px minimum touch target, and is wide enough to forgive the plate scaling down as it recedes.
- `PICK_RADIUS_SQ = PICK_RADIUS * PICK_RADIUS`
  Compared against squared distance so the loop never calls `Math.sqrt`. Fourteen square roots a frame is not a real cost, but the squared compare is free and is the habit worth having in a loop that might hold a thousand points.
- `RADIUS_RATIO = 0.36`
  Ring radius as a fraction of container width. Keeps the ring inside the box at its widest and leaves room for the pick-radius halo at the edges.
- `SPIN_PERIOD = 26`
  Seconds per revolution. Slow enough that a plate stays under the cursor long enough to click, fast enough that the per-frame re-pick is visibly necessary.

## API

```ts
function CpuMirrorPicking(props: { count?: number; period?: number; showMirror?: boolean; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `count: number` — default `14`
  Plates around the ring.
- `period: number` — default `26`
  Seconds per revolution. The mirror divides the animation clock by this.
- `showMirror: boolean` — default `true`
  Draw the computed crosshair and the pick-radius halo.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the perspective root via `cn`.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
/** Must match the CSS `perspective` exactly — the mirror divides by this. */
const PERSPECTIVE = 900;
/** Stage lean, degrees. Matches the CSS `rotateX`. */
const TILT = 16;
const SIN_TILT = Math.sin((TILT * Math.PI) / 180);
const COS_TILT = Math.cos((TILT * Math.PI) / 180);
/** Pointer-to-plate distance that counts as a hit, in CSS pixels. */
const PICK_RADIUS = 44;
const PICK_RADIUS_SQ = PICK_RADIUS * PICK_RADIUS;
const RADIUS_RATIO = 0.36;
const MIN_RADIUS = 64;
const MAX_RADIUS = 190;
const SPIN_PERIOD = 26;

interface Projected {
  x: number;
  y: number;
  z: number;
  scale: number;
}

/**
 * The mirror. Every line here has a counterpart in the element's CSS:
 *
 *   ul   transform: rotateY(spin)              <- from the running animation
 *   li   transform: rotateY(theta) translateZ(radius)
 *   root perspective: PERSPECTIVE
 *   stage transform: rotateX(TILT)
 *
 * A plate's centre starts at the ring origin, so `rotateY(a) translateZ(r)`
 * puts it at (r·sin a, 0, r·cos a) with a = theta + spin. Composing the two
 * rotateY into one addition is the whole trick — the rest is the standard
 * perspective divide.
 */
function project(theta: number, spin: number, radius: number, cx: number, cy: number, out: Projected): void {
  const a = theta + spin;
  const x = Math.sin(a) * radius;
  const depth = Math.cos(a) * radius;
  // rotateX(t): y' = y·cos t − z·sin t, z' = y·sin t + z·cos t. y is 0 here,
  // so the tilt turns depth into vertical offset and shortens the ring.
  const y = -depth * SIN_TILT;
  const z = depth * COS_TILT;
  // CSS perspective: everything at depth z scales by d / (d − z).
  const scale = PERSPECTIVE / (PERSPECTIVE - z);
  out.x = cx + x * scale;
  out.y = cy + y * scale;
  out.z = z;
  out.scale = scale;
}

/**
 * `Animation.currentTime` is typed `CSSNumberish | null`: a plain number in
 * every shipping engine, but the spec permits a CSSNumericValue. Narrow it
 * rather than cast, and treat a null clock (animation not yet started) as 0.
 */
function readMs(anim: Animation | null): number {
  if (!anim) return 0;
  const t = anim.currentTime;
  if (t === null) return 0;
  return typeof t === 'number' ? t : t.to('ms').value;
}

export function CpuMirrorPicking({
  count = 14,
  period = SPIN_PERIOD,
  showMirror = true,
  className,
}: CpuMirrorPickingProps) {
  const root = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const ring = useRef<HTMLUListElement>(null);
  const plates = useRef<(HTMLLIElement | null)[]>([]);
  const probe = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const halo = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);

  const anim = useRef<Animation | null>(null);
  /** Pointer in the root's own coordinate space. Null when it has left. */
  const pointer = useRef<{ x: number; y: number } | null>(null);
  const hovered = useRef(-1);
  const scratch = useRef<Projected>({ x: 0, y: 0, z: 0, scale: 1 });

  const [hover, setHover] = useState(-1);
  const [picked, setPicked] = useState(-1);

  const reduced = useReducedMotion();
  const size = useResizeObserver(root);
  const radius = clamp(size.width * RADIUS_RATIO, MIN_RADIUS, MAX_RADIUS);

  // The compositor owns the spin. One keyframe pair, then the main thread is
  // out of the loop entirely — which is exactly why it has to reconstruct the
  // angle instead of remembering it.
  useEffect(() => {
    const el = ring.current;
    if (!el || reduced) return;
    const a = el.animate(
      [{ transform: 'rotateY(0deg)' }, { transform: 'rotateY(360deg)' }],
      { duration: period * 1000, iterations: Infinity, easing: 'linear' },
    );
    anim.current = a;
    return () => {
      a.cancel();
      anim.current = null;
    };
  }, [period, reduced]);

  const readPointer = useCallback((e: ReactPointerEvent<HTMLDivElement>) => {
    const el = root.current;
    if (!el) return;
    // One rect read per pointer event, for the container only. Reading a rect
    // per plate per event is the version that costs fourteen forced layouts.
    const rect = el.getBoundingClientRect();
    pointer.current = { x: e.clientX - rect.left, y: e.clientY - rect.top };
  }, []);

  const clearPointer = useCallback(() => {
    pointer.current = null;
  }, []);

  useRaf((_dt) => {
    if (size.width === 0) return;

    // Picking runs per frame, not per pointermove. The ring moves under a
    // stationary cursor, so the hit answer changes when nothing was pointed.
    const spin = reduced ? 0 : (readMs(anim.current) / (period * 1000)) * TAU;
    const cx = size.width / 2;
    const cy = size.height / 2;
    const p = pointer.current;
    const out = scratch.current;

    let best = -1;
    let bestDist = PICK_RADIUS_SQ;
    let bestX = 0;
    let bestY = 0;

    for (let i = 0; i < count; i += 1) {
      project((i / count) * TAU, spin, radius, cx, cy, out);

      // The projection pass already knows the depth, so the fade rides along
      // rather than needing a second traversal.
      const el = plates.current[i];
      if (el) {
        const depth = out.z / (radius * COS_TILT);
        el.style.opacity = (0.18 + 0.82 * (depth * 0.5 + 0.5)).toFixed(3);
      }

      // z <= 0 is the far half of the ring: drawn, but behind the near plates
      // and never the intended target of a click.
      if (!p || out.z <= 0) continue;
      const dx = p.x - out.x;
      const dy = p.y - out.y;
      const dist = dx * dx + dy * dy;
      if (dist < bestDist) {
        bestDist = dist;
        best = i;
        bestX = out.x;
        bestY = out.y;
      }
    }

    const marker = probe.current;
    if (marker) {
      marker.style.opacity = best >= 0 ? '1' : '0';
      if (best >= 0) {
        marker.style.transform = `translate3d(${bestX.toFixed(1)}px, ${bestY.toFixed(1)}px, 0) translate(-50%, -50%)`;
      }
    }
    const cursor = halo.current;
    if (cursor) {
      cursor.style.opacity = p ? '1' : '0';
      if (p) {
        cursor.style.transform = `translate3d(${p.x.toFixed(1)}px, ${p.y.toFixed(1)}px, 0) translate(-50%, -50%)`;
      }
    }

    if (best !== hovered.current) {
      hovered.current = best;
      setHover(best);
    }
  });
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** The animation is cancelled on unmount or period change, which releases the compositor animation and nulls the ref. The frame loop unsubscribes with the hook; the shared RAF parks itself once no subscriber is left. No listeners are attached outside React.

**Reduced motion.** The spin animation is never created, so the ring holds still at phase zero. Picking is unaffected — the mirror simply reads a spin of 0 — which is the point: the technique is about where things are, not about them moving.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- `getBoundingClientRect()` per plate per pointermove. That is N forced layouts per event, and the rects are wrong anyway: a compositor-driven transform does not update layout boxes, so every rect reports the plate's unanimated position.
- Hit-testing only on `pointermove`. The ring rotates under a still cursor, so hover has to be re-evaluated every frame or it freezes on a stale plate.
- Letting the CSS and the mirror drift apart. A tweak to `perspective`, the tilt, or the transform order in one place and not the other produces a crosshair that is subtly, maddeningly offset. Keep both reading the same constants.
- Putting `overflow: hidden` on a `transform-style: preserve-3d` element. Overflow is a grouping property: it silently forces the subtree back to flat and the ring collapses into a line.
- Trusting `Raycaster` against a shader-deformed mesh. The vertex shader runs on the GPU; the `BufferGeometry` in memory is the rest pose. The ray intersects the rest pose and hits nothing you can see.
- Reading `animation.currentTime` as a number without narrowing. It is typed `CSSNumberish | null` — null before the animation starts, and permitted by spec to be a `CSSNumericValue`.
- Forgetting the far-half rejection. Without it the ring picks through itself, and a click near the centre selects a plate on the back.

## Notes

- The depth fade rides along on the projection pass that was going to run anyway — one extra style write per plate, no second traversal and no extra maths.
- The same mirror generalises: for a three.js scene, project the object's world position with `vector.project(camera)` and compare in NDC; for a shader-deformed mesh, re-run the deformation for that one vertex on the CPU. The principle is identical — hit-test the transform, not the source geometry.

## Definition of done

Hold the pointer still over a plate: the crosshair tracks the plate as it rotates away and hover releases at the pick radius, with no pointer events involved. Move to the middle of the ring and nothing on the far side lights up. Click and the plate under the crosshair — not the one under a stale rect — is the one that selects. With reduced motion the ring is static and picking still works.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: CSS Variable Stagger Reveal

A reveal system where JavaScript writes one number per element and then gets out of the way. The stagger delay is `calc(var(--kx-reveal-index) * var(--kx-reveal-step))`, so duration, travel, easing and the delay ramp all live in CSS where they can be retuned — or overridden from an unrelated stylesheet — without touching the component. The observer measures against the nearest scrollable ancestor, so the same component works inside a card, a modal, or the document.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

Groups reveal as they enter their scroll container; the stagger delay is a CSS calc over an index the JS writes once.

- Category: scroll
- Runtime cost: css
- Dependencies: none beyond React

## How it works

1. On mount the component collects `[data-reveal-group]` descendants, falling back to itself as a single group, and writes `--kx-reveal-index` as an inline custom property on each `[data-reveal]` inside each group. Index restarts at zero per group, so a second group does not inherit a delay whose beginning the reader never saw.
2. One shipped rule computes the per-element delay: `--kx-reveal-delay: calc(var(--kx-reveal-index, 0) * var(--kx-reveal-step, 90ms))`, and both the opacity and transform transitions use it as their `transition-delay`. This is the entire stagger — there is no timeline object and no rAF loop anywhere in the component.
3. The start state (`opacity: 0`, `translate3d(0, var(--kx-reveal-distance), 0)`) is a CSS rule rather than an inline style, so it is already in effect before hydration and there is no frame of un-hidden content.
4. An IntersectionObserver with `threshold: 0.15` and `rootMargin: "0px 0px -8% 0px"` sets `data-kx-revealed` on the group. The negative bottom margin shrinks the observation box up from the bottom edge, so an element must be genuinely inside the container rather than merely touching its edge — without it, a reveal fires while the element is still one pixel of its own height into view.
5. The observer `root` is resolved in three steps: an explicit `scroller` ref if given, otherwise a walk up the ancestor chain for the first element whose computed `overflow-x` or `overflow-y` is `auto`, `scroll` or `overlay`, otherwise `null`, which is the value that means the viewport. Nothing in the component references `window`, so it behaves identically in a 320 px preview card and on a full page.
6. Revealed groups are unobserved immediately unless `repeat` is set, so a long page is not still servicing a hundred settled groups. `repeat` instead deletes the attribute on exit, and CSS runs the same transition backwards.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `stepMs = 90`
  Delay per index. Below ~50 ms the elements read as arriving together and the stagger is wasted; above ~140 ms a group of six takes over three quarters of a second to finish and the last line is still moving after the eye has reached it.
- `durationMs = 700`
  Per-element transition duration, roughly 8x the step. Keeping duration well above step is what makes the group overlap into one motion rather than resolve as six separate events.
- `distance = 28px`
  Travel. Small enough that the text never leaves its own line box — a reveal that starts 100 px down reads as an element flying in from elsewhere, which fights the impression that the content was always there.
- `ease = cubic-bezier(0.22, 1, 0.36, 1)`
  An ease-out-quint. Nearly all of the travel happens in the first third, so the element appears to arrive and settle rather than to decelerate the whole way. A symmetric ease-in-out on a reveal always reads as slow.
- `threshold = 0.15`
  Fraction of the group that must be visible. At 0 the reveal fires on a single pixel of intersection, which for a tall group means the stagger completes before the content is on screen. Past ~0.4 a group taller than the container can never satisfy it and never reveals at all.
- `rootMargin = 0px 0px -8% 0px`
  Shrinks the observation box 8% up from the bottom, so the element is genuinely inside the container before it fires. Positive values here are the usual mistake: they fire the reveal below the fold and the user scrolls onto content that has already finished animating.

## API

```ts
function CssVarStaggerReveal(props: { children: ReactNode; scroller?: RefObject<HTMLElement | null>; stepMs?: number; durationMs?: number; distance?: string; ease?: string; threshold?: number; rootMargin?: string; repeat?: boolean; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `children: ReactNode`
  Mark groups with `data-reveal-group` and targets with `data-reveal`. A scope with no groups is treated as one group.
- `scroller: RefObject<HTMLElement | null>`
  Scroll container for the observer. Omit and the nearest scrollable ancestor is found by walking computed overflow.
- `stepMs: number` — default `90`
  Milliseconds of delay per index step. Written as `--kx-reveal-step`.
- `durationMs: number` — default `700`
  Transition duration. Written as `--kx-reveal-duration`.
- `distance: string` — default `'28px'`
  Starting vertical offset, any CSS length. Written as `--kx-reveal-distance`.
- `ease: string` — default `'cubic-bezier(0.22, 1, 0.36, 1)'`
  Timing function. Written as `--kx-reveal-ease`.
- `threshold: number` — default `0.15`
  Fraction of a group that must be visible before it reveals.
- `rootMargin: string` — default `'0px 0px -8% 0px'`
  Observation box inset. The negative bottom means "genuinely in view".
- `repeat: boolean` — default `false`
  Re-hide groups that leave the container. Off by default, which also lets settled groups be unobserved.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the scope element.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
/**
 * Nearest ancestor that actually scrolls. `overflow: auto` on an element that
 * has not overflowed yet still counts — it is the container the reveal will
 * live inside once content arrives, and testing `scrollHeight > clientHeight`
 * on mount would pick the document instead and fire everything at once.
 *
 * Returns `null` for "the viewport", which is the IntersectionObserver
 * `root` value that means the document.
 */
function nearestScrollParent(node: Element | null): Element | null {
  let el = node?.parentElement ?? null;
  while (el) {
    const { overflowY, overflowX } = getComputedStyle(el);
    const scrollable = /(auto|scroll|overlay)/.test(overflowY + overflowX);
    if (scrollable) return el;
    el = el.parentElement;
  }
  return null;
}

export function CssVarStaggerReveal({
  children,
  scroller,
  stepMs = 90,
  durationMs = 700,
  distance = '28px',
  ease = 'cubic-bezier(0.22, 1, 0.36, 1)',
  threshold = 0.15,
  rootMargin = '0px 0px -8% 0px',
  repeat = false,
  className,
}: CssVarStaggerRevealProps) {
  const root = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    const rootEl = root.current;
    if (!rootEl) return;

    const groups = Array.from(rootEl.querySelectorAll<HTMLElement>(GROUP_SELECTOR));
    // A subtree with no declared groups is one group: the scope itself.
    const scopes: HTMLElement[] = groups.length > 0 ? groups : [rootEl];

    // Index is per group, not per document. Two sibling groups both start
    // their stagger at zero, so the second one does not inherit a delay the
    // reader never sees the beginning of.
    for (const group of scopes) {
      const targets = group.querySelectorAll<HTMLElement>(REVEAL_SELECTOR);
      targets.forEach((target, i) => {
        target.style.setProperty('--kx-reveal-index', String(i));
      });
    }

    const reveal = (group: HTMLElement) => {
      group.dataset.kxRevealed = 'true';
    };

    // No observer available: reveal rather than leave the content at
    // opacity 0 forever. A missing API must degrade to visible content.
    if (typeof IntersectionObserver === 'undefined') {
      for (const group of scopes) reveal(group);
      return;
    }

    // `undefined` from the prop means "find it"; `null` from the walk means
    // "the document", which is what IntersectionObserver's root expects.
    const container = scroller ? scroller.current : nearestScrollParent(rootEl);

    const observer = new IntersectionObserver(
      (entries) => {
        for (const entry of entries) {
          const target = entry.target;
          if (!(target instanceof HTMLElement)) continue;
          if (entry.isIntersecting) {
            reveal(target);
            // One-shot is the default: stop watching immediately so a long
            // page is not still servicing a hundred settled groups.
            if (!repeat) observer.unobserve(target);
          } else if (repeat) {
            delete target.dataset.kxRevealed;
          }
        }
      },
      { root: container ?? null, rootMargin, threshold },
    );

    for (const group of scopes) observer.observe(group);
    return () => observer.disconnect();
  }, [scroller, threshold, rootMargin, repeat]);
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** `observer.disconnect()` in the effect teardown, which releases the observer's references to every group. The inline `--kx-reveal-index` properties and the `data-kx-revealed` attributes live on nodes React owns and are discarded with them. There is no rAF, no listener and no timer to cancel — the hoisted `<style>` is reference-counted and removed by React when the last instance unmounts.

**Reduced motion.** A `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` block in the shipped rule set resolves every target to its END state — `opacity: 1`, `transform: none`, `transition: none` — so the content is simply present, with no travel and no delay ramp to sit through. The observer still runs and still sets `data-kx-revealed`, so anything else keyed off that attribute keeps working; it just has nothing to transition.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Writing the delay as an inline `transition-delay` per element. It works, and it moves the choreography into JavaScript where a designer cannot reach it and a stylesheet cannot override it. The point of the index-as-custom-property indirection is that JS contributes a number and CSS owns every unit.
- Numbering targets across the whole scope instead of per group. The second group starts at index 6 and sits at a 540 ms delay, so the reader watches nothing happen for half a second after it enters view.
- Assuming the scroll container is the window. Inside any `overflow-y: auto` panel, an observer with `root: null` compares against the viewport: everything in the panel is "in view" from the start, so the entire page reveals at once on mount and never staggers again.
- Testing `scrollHeight > clientHeight` when hunting for the scroll parent. A panel that has not overflowed yet is still the container the reveal will live inside once content arrives; rejecting it picks the document and fires everything at once.
- Putting the hidden start state in an inline style set from an effect. The server-rendered markup then paints visible, hides on hydration, and animates — a flash of correct content followed by a reveal, which is worse than no reveal.
- Shipping a hidden-by-default rule with no escape hatch for a document that never runs scripts. `@media (scripting: none)` restores opacity and transform; without it the page is simply blank for anyone who has JS off.
- Leaving the observer connected. It keeps a strong reference to every observed group, so an unmounted section is still measured on every scroll of the container that outlived it.
- Adding only `[data-kx-revealed] [data-reveal]` as the revealed selector. When the scope declares no groups, the marker lands on the scope element itself, which is not a descendant of itself — so the reveal silently never applies.

## Notes

- Every knob is a custom property, which means a consumer can retune the whole system from any ancestor: `--kx-reveal-step`, `--kx-reveal-duration`, `--kx-reveal-distance`, `--kx-reveal-ease`. The props are conveniences that write those same properties onto the scope element.
- This is the CSS-owned sibling of the GSAP reveal systems in the registry. Choose this one when the choreography is a fade-and-rise and the value is that a designer can retune it; choose a GSAP builder when the reveal needs scrubbing, a per-element timeline, or to be measured against a horizontal container animation.
- The observer watches groups, not individual elements. A group that is taller than its container reveals when 15% of it is visible — if a section is very tall, wrap the parts you want revealed separately in their own `data-reveal-group`.

## Definition of done

Scroll the container: each group's children rise and fade in one after another, about 90 ms apart, and the group does not start until it is genuinely inside the box rather than touching its bottom edge. Inspect a revealed child and its computed `transition-delay` equals index x 90 ms. Set `--kx-reveal-step: 200ms` on any ancestor in dev tools and the stagger widens immediately with no re-render. With reduced motion on, everything is already visible and in place. Unmount the scroller and no observer callbacks fire.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: CTA Section

The last section of a landing page. A fanned stack of product cards (the Stacked Card Fan, with its lower edge masked into the page and a "See all" pill) sits above a large two-line headline, a short paragraph and a row of actions, all centred on a full-width surface. The first time a quarter of the section scrolls into view, the visual, headline, copy and actions rise, unblur and fade in one after another. The cards stay live: hovering spreads them, clicking cycles them and the pill lays them all out.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

Closing call-to-action: a faded stack of product cards, a large headline, copy and buttons that rise in one after another on scroll.

- Category: block
- Runtime cost: css
- Dependencies: none beyond React

## How it works

1. Reveal flag: the kit `useInView` hook (shared IntersectionObserver, `once`, threshold 0.25) sets `data-shown` on the section. Each part carries the same transition class and is hidden by `group-data-[shown=false]/cta:` variants (16px lower, `opacity-0`, `blur-sm`). Flipping the one flag starts every transition.
2. Stagger: parts are numbered in render order, skipping any that are not passed, and each gets an inline `transition-delay` of `order × 90ms`. A text-only CTA therefore starts with the headline and has no gap where the visual would be.
3. Visual: `cards` are passed to `StackedCardFan` with `fade` (a `mask-b-from-55%` gradient mask) at 320×280px inside a 680px column. `fanProps` overrides any of its props, such as the pill label or the controlled front card.
4. Fit: the section is a size container (`@container/cta`). Below `@2xl` the headline steps down from display-2 to display-4 and the copy from 16px to 14px, so it reads the same in a narrow preview as on a phone. `text-balance` keeps the headline lines even and `max-w-[18ch]` breaks it in two.
5. Semantics: a `section` labelled by its `h2` through `useId`, so it appears as a named region; the action row takes any buttons or links.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `stagger = 90ms per part`
  Close enough that the four parts read as one movement, far enough apart that the order shows.
- `entrance = 700ms, 16px rise, blur-sm, cubic-bezier(0.22, 1, 0.36, 1)`
  A soft settle, matching the card fan transition, without a bounce on a closing section.
- `trigger = 25% visible, once`
  Starts when the section is clearly arriving, and does not replay when it is scrolled past again.
- `visual = 320 × 280px cards in a 680px column`
  Large enough that the front card reads, narrow enough that the fan stays above the headline width.

## API

```ts
function CtaSection(props: { title: ReactNode; description?: ReactNode; actions?: ReactNode; cards?: StackedCardFanItem[]; fanProps?: Omit<StackedCardFanProps, "items">; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `title: ReactNode`
  Headline; rendered as the `h2` that labels the section.
- `description: ReactNode`
  Supporting copy under the headline.
- `actions: ReactNode`
  Buttons or links, in a centred wrapping row.
- `cards: StackedCardFanItem[]`
  Cards for the faded stack above the headline; omit for text only.
- `fanProps: Omit<StackedCardFanProps, "items">`
  Overrides for the card stack (pill label, size, controlled state).
- `className: string`
  Classes for the section.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
/**
 * Entrance: the visual, headline, copy and actions rise 16px, unblur and fade
 * in one after another the first time a quarter of the section is on screen.
 * Each part waits `order * STAGGER_MS` before starting, so one shared flag on
 * the root (`data-shown`) drives the whole sequence with CSS transitions only.
 * Hidden styles are keyed to `data-shown="false"`, so a reduced-motion visitor,
 * for whom the flag starts true, never sees a hidden frame.
 */
const STAGGER_MS = 90;

const REVEAL =
  "transition-[opacity,translate,filter] duration-700 ease-[cubic-bezier(0.22,1,0.36,1)] motion-reduce:transition-none " +
  "group-data-[shown=false]/cta:translate-y-4 group-data-[shown=false]/cta:opacity-0 group-data-[shown=false]/cta:blur-sm";

function revealDelay(order: number): CSSProperties {
  return { transitionDelay: `${order * STAGGER_MS}ms` };
}
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** The shared IntersectionObserver stops watching the section after the first reveal (`once`) and on unmount. The entrance is CSS transitions with nothing to cancel.

**Reduced motion.** The reveal flag starts true and the transitions are off (`motion-reduce:transition-none`), so everything is visible at once. The card fan changes state instantly under the same preference.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Hiding parts with an `opacity-0` class that a reveal removes: reduced-motion visitors and anything rendered before the observer fires get a blank section. Key the hidden state to the flag being false and start it true under reduced motion.
- Animating `transform` while the cards inside also animate theirs: the entrance uses the standalone `translate` property and filter, so it composes with the fan transforms without overriding them.
- Using `md:` breakpoints for the headline size: in a scaled preview or a narrow column they follow the window. Use container queries on the section.

## Notes

- Imports Stacked Card Fan and is shown with its `AGENT_DASHBOARD_CARDS` faces; any `StackedCardFanItem[]` works.
- Omit `cards` for a text-only CTA; the stagger starts at the headline.
- The demo actions are kit `ButtonLink`s with hash links.

## Definition of done

Scrolling the section in shows the card stack, then the headline, copy and two buttons rising and unblurring in that order. The stack fades into the page at the bottom with the See all five pill over the fade; hovering spreads it and the pill lays the cards out. At 360px the headline is smaller and wraps, the buttons wrap onto two lines and nothing overflows. Light and dark both read.

# Build: Cursor Clip-Path Mask

An upper layer is clipped to a circle that trails the pointer, so a disc of alternate content moves across a base layer. GSAP never tweens `clip-path`; it tweens a plain `{ x, y, r }` object and one `onUpdate` writes both the clip string and the ring outline from the same numbers on the same frame.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

A disc of a second layer follows the pointer; hovering the trigger grows it until it covers the panel.

- Category: cursor
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: gsap@^3.15.0

## How it works

1. The animated value is a proxy object, not a DOM property. `gsap.to(proxy, { x, y, onUpdate: write })` gives normal tween semantics — easing, overwrite, duration — over three plain numbers, and `write()` turns them into a `clip-path` string plus a transform for the ring.
2. That indirection is the whole point. Tweening `clipPath` directly means GSAP parses and re-serialises a string each frame, and the ring outline drawn on top must be animated by a second, independent tween. Two interpolations of the same idea drift under fast movement, and a visible sliver of base layer appears between the ring and the edge of the disc.
3. It also lets position and radius be separate tweens with different durations and eases — 0.4s linear for the follow, 0.55s `power3.inOut` for the expansion — while still producing one coherent write. That is not expressible as a single `clipPath` tween.
4. The radius is written in px, not `%`. A percentage radius in `circle()` resolves against `sqrt(w^2 + h^2) / sqrt(2)`, not against the width, so the same percentage is a different physical size at every aspect ratio and the px-sized ring stops matching the disc it is supposed to outline.
5. Expansion targets `Math.hypot(clientWidth, clientHeight)` — one full diagonal, which is enough to cover the panel from any point inside it, including a corner.
6. The ring is a fixed-diameter element scaled by `r / radius` rather than an element whose width and height are rewritten, so each frame is a composited transform instead of a layout pass.
7. Hover detection uses `pointerover`/`pointerout` on the container, which bubble, so one listener pair covers every trigger in the subtree regardless of how React re-renders it. `pointerenter` does not bubble and would need a listener per trigger plus subscription bookkeeping.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `radius = 130`
  Resting disc radius in px. Small enough that the base layer still dominates and the disc reads as an instrument, large enough to show a readable fragment of the layer underneath. Below ~60 you are looking through a keyhole and cannot tell what the reveal layer is.
- `FOLLOW_DURATION = 0.4`
  Seconds of catch-up on position. Long enough that the disc reads as being dragged rather than teleported, short enough that it is still under the pointer when you stop to read what is inside it.
- `ease: 'none' on the follow = linear`
  Deliberately linear, unlike most cursor follows. The end value is remutated on every pointer event, so an eased tween re-eases from a fresh start each time and the disc reads as surging and stalling. Linear catch-up gives one steady drag speed no matter how the pointer moves.
- `EXPAND_DURATION = 0.55`
  Seconds for the disc to grow to a full diagonal and back. The distance travelled is large, so a follow-length 0.4s makes it feel like a cut; past ~0.8s the reveal has not finished before an impatient pointer has left the trigger.
- `expand ease 'power3.inOut' = power3.inOut`
  In-out for the expansion because it is a discrete state change with a beginning and an end, unlike the follow. The slow start keeps the growth from looking explosive; the slow finish stops the edge whipping off-panel.
- `ring opacity ramp = clamp(0, 1, 2 - scale)`
  The ring is scaled, so its 1px border thickens with it. Fading it out by the time the disc has doubled hides that artefact before it becomes visible, and it also gets the outline out of the way of a full-panel reveal.
- `off-panel park = -radius * 3`
  Where the disc sits before the first move and after leaving. Three radii guarantees no part of it clips back into view at any aspect ratio, and the reveal layer is invisible until the pointer earns it.

## API

```ts
function CursorClipPathMask(props: { base: ReactNode; reveal: ReactNode; radius?: number; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `base: ReactNode`
  Always-visible bottom layer, and the layer that keeps all pointer events. Put `[data-mask-trigger]` elements here.
- `reveal: ReactNode`
  Top layer, visible only inside the disc. Clipped, `aria-hidden` and non-interactive.
- `radius: number` — default `130`
  Resting disc radius in CSS px.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the root container via `cn`.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
const FOLLOW_DURATION = 0.4;
const EXPAND_DURATION = 0.55;

export function CursorClipPathMask({
  base,
  reveal,
  radius = 130,
  className,
}: CursorClipPathMaskProps) {
  const root = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const overlay = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const ring = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    const el = root.current;
    const layer = overlay.current;
    const outline = ring.current;
    if (!el || !layer || !outline) return;

    const fine = window.matchMedia('(pointer: fine)').matches;
    const reduced = window.matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)').matches;

    /* One object, three numbers, tweened by GSAP like any DOM property. The
       clip string is derived from it — never tweened itself. */
    const proxy = { x: 0, y: 0, r: radius };

    const write = () => {
      /* Radius in px, not `%`. A percentage radius in `circle()` resolves
         against sqrt(w^2 + h^2) / sqrt(2), NOT against the width — so a
         percentage hole is a different physical size on every panel aspect
         ratio, and the px-sized ring drawn on top of it stops matching. */
      layer.style.clipPath = `circle(${proxy.r}px at ${proxy.x}px ${proxy.y}px)`;

      /* Same frame, same numbers. The ring is a fixed-diameter element scaled
         to the current radius, so this is one composited transform rather than
         a width/height write that would relayout every frame. */
      const scale = proxy.r / radius;
      outline.style.transform = `translate3d(${proxy.x - radius}px, ${proxy.y - radius}px, 0) scale(${scale})`;
      // The border thickens with the scale, so the ring is faded out well
      // before the expansion makes that obvious.
      outline.style.opacity = String(gsap.utils.clamp(0, 1, 2 - scale));
    };

    if (!fine || reduced) {
      /* No pointer to follow, or motion the user declined. Park a static hole
         left-of-centre so both layers are legible at once and the component
         reads as a composed still rather than a blank panel. */
      const rect = el.getBoundingClientRect();
      proxy.x = rect.width * 0.34;
      proxy.y = rect.height * 0.5;
      write();
      return () => {
        layer.style.clipPath = '';
        outline.style.transform = '';
        outline.style.opacity = '';
      };
    }

    // Start off-panel so nothing is revealed before the first move.
    proxy.x = -radius * 3;
    proxy.y = -radius * 3;
    write();

    let entered = false;

    const onMove = (e: PointerEvent) => {
      const rect = el.getBoundingClientRect();
      const x = e.clientX - rect.left;
      const y = e.clientY - rect.top;

      if (!entered) {
        entered = true;
        // Teleport on entry, otherwise the hole slides in from the corner
        // over 400ms and reveals a diagonal streak of the layer beneath.
        gsap.set(proxy, { x, y });
        write();
        return;
      }

      /* `ease: 'none'` is deliberate. An eased follow re-eases from a new
         start value on every event, which under continuous movement reads as
         the hole surging and stalling. Linear catch-up at 0.4s gives a steady
         drag. `overwrite: 'auto'` claims x and y and leaves the radius tween
         from the trigger running underneath. */
      gsap.to(proxy, {
        x,
        y,
        duration: FOLLOW_DURATION,
        ease: 'none',
        overwrite: 'auto',
        onUpdate: write,
      });
    };

    const onLeave = () => {
      entered = false;
      gsap.to(proxy, {
        x: -radius * 3,
        y: -radius * 3,
        duration: 0.35,
        ease: 'power2.in',
        overwrite: 'auto',
        onUpdate: write,
      });
    };

    /* Enough radius to cover the panel from any point inside it: the far
       corner is at most one diagonal away. */
    const full = () => Math.hypot(el.clientWidth, el.clientHeight);

    const onEnterTrigger = (e: Event) => {
      const target = e.target;
      if (!(target instanceof Element) || !target.closest('[data-mask-trigger]')) return;
      gsap.to(proxy, {
        r: full(),
        duration: EXPAND_DURATION,
        ease: 'power3.inOut',
        overwrite: 'auto',
        onUpdate: write,
      });
    };

    const onLeaveTrigger = (e: Event) => {
      const target = e.target;
      if (!(target instanceof Element) || !target.closest('[data-mask-trigger]')) return;
      gsap.to(proxy, {
        r: radius,
        duration: EXPAND_DURATION,
        ease: 'power3.inOut',
        overwrite: 'auto',
        onUpdate: write,
      });
    };

    el.addEventListener('pointermove', onMove, { passive: true });
    el.addEventListener('pointerleave', onLeave);
    /* `pointerover`/`pointerout` bubble, so one pair of listeners covers every
       trigger in the subtree no matter how React re-renders it. `pointerenter`
       does not bubble and would need a listener per trigger. */
    el.addEventListener('pointerover', onEnterTrigger);
    el.addEventListener('pointerout', onLeaveTrigger);

    return () => {
      el.removeEventListener('pointermove', onMove);
      el.removeEventListener('pointerleave', onLeave);
      el.removeEventListener('pointerover', onEnterTrigger);
      el.removeEventListener('pointerout', onLeaveTrigger);
      gsap.killTweensOf(proxy);
      layer.style.clipPath = '';
      outline.style.transform = '';
      outline.style.opacity = '';
    };
  }, [radius]);
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** Removes all four container listeners, calls `gsap.killTweensOf(proxy)` so no tween can write to a detached node after React releases it, then clears the inline `clipPath`, `transform` and `opacity` that `write()` set. The proxy is a local object and is garbage-collected with the closure.

**Reduced motion.** No listeners attach. The disc is written once, parked at 34% across and vertically centred, and never moves. Both layers stay readable and the composition still communicates what the component does; it simply does not animate.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Tweening `clipPath` as a string. GSAP re-parses it each frame and the ring must then be animated separately; the two interpolations diverge under fast movement and a crescent of the base layer shows between the outline and the disc edge.
- A percentage radius. `circle(20% at ...)` resolves against `sqrt(w^2 + h^2) / sqrt(2)`, so the disc is a different size on a wide panel than a tall one and no px-based outline can be made to match it.
- Forgetting `pointer-events: none` on the clipped layer. `clip-path` clips hit testing, not just paint, so the overlay becomes a region that swallows events inside the disc and passes them through everywhere else — hover targets then work or do not work depending on where the disc happens to be.
- Putting the trigger inside the reveal layer. It is clipped away, so it is only hoverable when it is already inside the disc, which is exactly when you no longer need to hover it. Triggers belong in the base layer.
- Easing the position follow. Because the tween restarts from a new end value on every event, an ease-out curve reads as the disc lunging and hesitating rather than being dragged.
- Animating the ring by writing `width` and `height`. That is a layout invalidation on every frame of the expansion, and it shows as jank on the exact interaction that is meant to feel expensive.
- Not teleporting on entry. Without the `gsap.set` on the first move, the disc eases in from its parked corner over 0.4s and drags a diagonal streak of the reveal layer across the panel every time the pointer enters.
- `overwrite: true` on either tween. It kills the other one, so the disc either freezes mid-expansion or stops following. `overwrite: "auto"` claims only the properties that tween actually animates, which is why position and radius can coexist on one proxy.

## Notes

- Gated on `(pointer: fine)`. On touch there is no pointer to follow: `pointermove` only fires mid-drag, so the disc would sit under the finger hiding it, and it would be stranded wherever the finger lifted. The touch path parks a static disc at 34% across and vertically centred, so both layers are legible at once and the panel reads as a composed still rather than blank.
- Reduced motion takes the same static path — the entire effect is continuous movement, so there is nothing to slow down honestly.
- The reveal layer is `aria-hidden`: it is a second rendering of content the base layer already presents, and exposing both would double every heading to a screen reader.
- Scoped to its own container rather than the viewport. Position is measured against the container rect, so the component composes anywhere and does not assume it owns the page.

## Definition of done

Move across the panel and a disc of the second layer drags along behind the pointer at a steady speed, with a thin ring exactly on its edge — no gap, no crescent of the base layer showing between them, even when you flick the pointer. Hover the trigger and the disc grows smoothly past the corners until the reveal layer fills the panel, with the ring fading out as it goes; leave and it shrinks back to the pointer. Resize the panel to a very wide or very tall aspect ratio and the disc stays circular and stays the same physical size. On touch the disc is parked left-of-centre and static.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.
