# Build: Important Alerts Card

The alerts card from BoardUI's medical profile dashboard. A header shows "Important alerts" with a large weekly count (12 this week) and a static week pill ("29 Jun - 5 Jul"). Below it, a fixed-height feed lists the six most recent alerts: a coloured circle with a white Remix icon, a title, a description and a date tag pinned to the row's top-right corner. The feed runs flush to the card's bottom edge and clips there, so the third row is cut off as in the Figma frame, and a card-coloured gradient fades in over the top of the feed once it has been scrolled.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

A health dashboard card: weekly alert count, a week pill, and a scrolling feed of tinted-icon alerts that fades under its header.

- Category: display
- Runtime cost: css
- Dependencies: @remixicon/react@^4.9.0

## How it works

1. The `section` is a fixed `h-[330px]` flex column with `overflow-hidden rounded-[20px]` and 10px padding on the top and sides only, so the feed meets the bottom edge. Its 1px border is the same colour as its background: invisible, but content clips inside it so rows stop 1px short of the rounded corner.
2. The header is a flex row: label in `text-body-medium text-text-secondary`, the count `12` in `text-title-1-medium tabular-nums` with "this week" baseline-aligned beside it, and `WeekRangePill` on the end.
3. The feed is `flex-1 min-h-0 overflow-y-auto overscroll-contain` with `gap-2.5` and `pb-2.5`, so it scrolls inside the card without chaining to the page and the last row has room at the bottom.
4. Each alert row is `rounded-2lg bg-background-inner-default p-2.5`: a `size-8` circle in the alert's colour with an 18px white icon, the title (`text-body-medium`, no wrap) and description (`text-body-2-regular`), plus an absolutely positioned date tag at `top-2.5 end-2.5`.
5. An `onScroll` handler sets `scrolled` to `scrollTop > 0`. An `aria-hidden` 40px `bg-linear-to-b from-background-secondary-default to-transparent` overlay at the top of the feed transitions to `opacity-100` while scrolled, so rows dissolve under the header instead of being cut by it.
6. `WeekRangePill` renders a 32px tall, min-151px pill with a 1px button border and `shadow-xs`. Without `onPrev`/`onNext` both chevrons are `aria-hidden` spans and the label is plain text.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `card height = 330px, rounded-[20px], px-2.5 pt-2.5 (no bottom padding)`
  Matches the Figma frame, where the feed is deliberately cut by the card's bottom edge to show it scrolls.
- `ALERTS_THIS_WEEK_COUNT = 12`
  The week's total, higher than the six rows in the feed, which only lists the most recent alerts.
- `top fade = h-10 (40px) gradient, opacity 200ms ease-out`
  Shown only once `scrollTop > 0`, so the first row is never dimmed at rest.
- `icon tints = rose-600, amber-400, emerald-500, blue-400, purple-400, teal-400`
  One hue per alert type (heart rate, Medical ID, lab results, medication, sleep, blood oxygen) so a row can be recognised at a glance.
- `week pill = h-8, min-w-[151px], rounded-2lg, border-border-button-default, shadow-xs`
  The same 151×32 chrome as the dashboard's other range pills; min-width rather than width so a longer label grows the pill.

## API

```ts
function ImportantAlertsCard(props?: { className?: string }): JSX.Element
function WeekRangePill(props: { label: string; onPrev?: () => void; onNext?: () => void; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `className: string`
  ImportantAlertsCard: merged onto the card section, e.g. to set its width.
- `label: string`
  WeekRangePill: the range text, e.g. "29 Jun - 5 Jul".
- `onPrev / onNext: () => void`
  WeekRangePill: makes the chevrons buttons and turns on the rolling label.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
export function ImportantAlertsCard({ className }: { className?: string } = {}) {
  const localize = useTemplateCopy();
  const [scrolled, setScrolled] = useState(false);

  return localize((
    <section
      className={cx(
        // The 1px border matches the card's own bg — invisible as a line,
        // but content clips at the padding box (inside the border), so the
        // white alert rows stop 1px shy of the rounded edge instead of
        // touching it when scrolled to the bottom.
        "flex h-[330px] w-full min-w-0 flex-col gap-4 overflow-hidden rounded-[20px] border border-background-secondary-default bg-background-secondary-default px-2.5 pt-2.5",
        className,
      )}
    >
      <div className="flex w-full items-start justify-between gap-2 px-1.5 pt-1.5">
        <div className="flex min-w-0 flex-1 flex-col gap-0.5">
          <p className="text-body-medium text-text-secondary">Important alerts</p>
          <div className="flex items-baseline gap-1">
            <p className="text-title-1-medium whitespace-nowrap text-text-primary tabular-nums">
              {ALERTS_THIS_WEEK_COUNT}
            </p>
            <span className="text-caption-1-medium whitespace-nowrap text-text-secondary">this week</span>
          </div>
        </div>
        <WeekRangePill label="29 Jun - 5 Jul" />
      </div>

      <div className="relative min-h-0 w-full flex-1">
        <div
          className="flex h-full w-full flex-col gap-2.5 overflow-y-auto overscroll-contain pb-2.5"
          onScroll={(e) => setScrolled(e.currentTarget.scrollTop > 0)}
        >
          {ALERTS.map((alert, index) => (
            <div
              key={`${alert.title}-${index}`}
              className="relative flex w-full shrink-0 flex-col gap-2 rounded-2lg bg-background-inner-default p-2.5"
            >
              <span className={cx("flex size-8 shrink-0 items-center justify-center rounded-full", alert.iconBg)}>
                <alert.icon className="size-[18px] text-white" aria-hidden />
              </span>
              <div className="flex flex-col gap-0.5">
                <p className="text-body-medium whitespace-nowrap text-text-primary">{alert.title}</p>
                <p className="text-body-2-regular text-text-secondary">{alert.description}</p>
              </div>
              <span className="absolute top-2.5 end-2.5 rounded-md bg-background-secondary-default px-1.5 py-px text-body-medium whitespace-nowrap text-text-secondary">
                {alert.date}
              </span>
            </div>
          ))}
        </div>
        {/* Top fade — card-colored gradient that eases in once the feed is
            scrolled, so rows dissolve under the header instead of cutting. */}
        <div
          aria-hidden
          className={cx(
            "pointer-events-none absolute inset-x-0 top-0 h-10 bg-linear-to-b from-background-secondary-default to-transparent",
            "transition-opacity duration-200 ease-out",
            scrolled ? "opacity-100" : "opacity-0",
          )}
        />
      </div>
    </section>
  ));
}
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** Nothing to clean up. The scroll handler is a React prop and the only state is a boolean.

**Reduced motion.** The only motion in the card is the 200ms opacity fade of the top gradient while scrolling. It does not move anything, so there is no reduced-motion branch; scrolling itself is native.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- The alerts, the count and the week label are constants inside the file. To use real data, lift `ALERTS` and the count into props; the component takes only `className` today.
- Do not give the card a fixed height and remove `min-h-0` from the feed wrapper. Without it the flex child grows to its content and the feed stops scrolling.
- Do not add bottom padding to the card. The flush bottom edge is what tells people the feed scrolls.
- If you change the card background, change the fade's `from-` colour and the border colour with it, or the fade shows as a band and the border as a line.

## Notes

- The date tag is absolutely positioned, so a very long title can run under it; titles are kept short and `whitespace-nowrap`.
- `WeekRangePill` also has an interactive mode: pass `onPrev`/`onNext` and the chevrons become real buttons and the label rolls like a counter (220ms `label-out` / `label-in` keyframes). This card uses the static mode.
- All copy passes through `useTemplateCopy`, which translates display strings when a `TemplateCopyProvider` is present and is a no-op otherwise.

## Definition of done

The card renders 330px tall with "Important alerts", a large 12 and "this week", and a "29 Jun - 5 Jul" pill with chevrons on the right. The feed starts with High Heart rate and is cut off mid-row by the card's bottom edge. Scrolling the feed fades a gradient in under the header within 200ms and fades it out again when scrolled back to the top; the page does not scroll when the feed reaches its end. Each row has a coloured circle with a white icon and a date tag in its top-right corner.

# Build: Input

The kit's text field in three layers: `TextField` (React Aria field plus a size context), `InputBase` (the filled shell with icons or addons around the `<input>`) and `Input`, which composes a label, the shell and a hint or error line. The shell has no border; hover and focus draw a 2px inset ring and an invalid field tints red, all over 150ms. React Aria wires the label, description and error message to the input.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

React Aria text field on a filled shell with an inset ring for hover and focus, label with required mark, hint or error line, and icons.

- Category: form
- Runtime cost: css
- Dependencies: @remixicon/react@^4.9.0, react-aria-components@^1.22.1

## How it works

1. `TextField` renders `AriaTextField` as `group flex h-max w-full flex-col items-start gap-1` with `data-input-size`, and provides `TextFieldContext` with `size`, `fieldClassName` and `inputClassName`, so an `InputBase` (or the kit Textarea) further down picks them up without prop drilling. Children may be a render function that receives `isRequired`, `isInvalid`, `isDisabled` and `isReadOnly`.
2. `InputBase` renders `AriaGroup`, whose className function calls `inputFieldClassName(state, size, hasAddon)`. The base shell is `rounded-2lg bg-background-tertiary-default` with `ring-2 ring-inset ring-transparent` and a `transition-[background-color,box-shadow,color]` over `var(--input-transition-ms)` (150ms in the theme). Hover, when not focused, disabled or invalid, sets `ring-border-button-hover`; focus within sets `ring-border-button-active`; disabled sets `bg-input-disabled-background`; invalid sets `bg-background-tertiary-error text-foreground-icon-error`.
3. Inside the shell, a leading `leadingAddon` (if given) or `leadingIcon` (a component rendered at `size-5`, `aria-hidden`) sits before `AriaInput`, then `trailingAddon` or `trailingIcon`. Icons have no colour of their own, so they inherit the shell's text colour and turn red with it when invalid.
4. The `<input>` is transparent and borderless in `text-body-regular text-text-primary`. Its placeholder is `text-text-tertiary`, darkens to `text-text-primary` on focus and turns `text-text-error-placeholder` when `aria-invalid`. `useLocale` decides `pl-1 text-left` or, in RTL, `pr-1 text-right`.
5. `Input` composes the three: it renders `Label` (when `label` is given) with the field's `isRequired`, then `InputBase`, then React Aria's `FieldError` styled by `hintTextClassName(true)` when the field is invalid and `errorMessage` is set, otherwise `HintText` with `hint`. With no `label` and no `aria-label`, a string `placeholder` becomes the `aria-label`. For `type` email, url or tel it sets `dir="ltr"` on the input unless `inputDir` says otherwise.
6. `Label` wraps React Aria `Label` in `text-body-medium text-text-primary` with a 2px gap, adds an `aria-hidden` red `*` when `isRequired`, and a 16px `RiInformationFill` when `tooltip` is set. `HintText` wraps React Aria `Text` with `slot="description"` (or `slot="errorMessage"` when `isInvalid`) in `pt-px text-caption-1-medium`, `text-text-secondary` or `text-text-error-primary`.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `--input-transition-ms = 150ms`
  One theme variable for every field shell (Input, Textarea and others read it), so ring and fill changes run at the same speed across a form.
- `ring = ring-2 ring-inset, transparent at rest`
  An inset box shadow instead of a border, so the hover and focus outlines appear without the field growing or the text shifting by a pixel.
- `sizes = medium p-2 (36px with a 20px line) · small h-8 px-1.5 py-2 (32px)`
  Figma node 3665:1849. With a `leadingAddon` the start padding drops to 4px so an addon such as a country picker sits close to the edge.
- `icon = size-5 (20px)`
  The same height as the 20px body line, so icons and text centre on one axis inside the 36px shell.

## API

```ts
function Input(props: Omit<TextFieldProps, "children"> & { label?: ReactNode; hint?: ReactNode; errorMessage?: FieldErrorProps["children"]; tooltip?: boolean | string; placeholder?: string; inputDir?: "ltr" | "rtl" | "auto"; leadingIcon?: IconComponent; trailingIcon?: IconComponent; leadingAddon?: ReactNode; fieldClassName?: string; ref?: Ref<HTMLInputElement>; groupRef?: Ref<HTMLDivElement> }): JSX.Element
function TextField(props: AriaTextFieldProps & { size?: "medium" | "small"; fieldClassName?: string; inputClassName?: string }): JSX.Element
function InputBase(props: Omit<AriaInputProps, "size" | "className"> & { size?: "medium" | "small"; className?: string; leadingIcon?: IconComponent; trailingIcon?: IconComponent; leadingAddon?: ReactNode; trailingAddon?: ReactNode; fieldClassName?: string; ref?: Ref<HTMLInputElement>; groupRef?: Ref<HTMLDivElement> }): JSX.Element
```

- `label: ReactNode`
  Visible label above the field, wired to the input by React Aria.
- `hint: ReactNode`
  Caption below the field, wired as the description.
- `errorMessage: ReactNode | (validation) => ReactNode`
  Replaces the hint while the field is invalid.
- `value / defaultValue / onChange: string / (value: string) => void`
  Controlled or uncontrolled value, from React Aria.
- `isRequired: boolean`
  Adds the red asterisk to the label and `aria-required`.
- `isInvalid: boolean`
  Red-tinted shell, red placeholder and the error line.
- `isDisabled: boolean`
  Grey shell and text, not-allowed cursor.
- `size: "medium" | "small"` — default `"medium"`
  36px or 32px shell.
- `leadingIcon / trailingIcon: ComponentType`
  20px icon components on either side of the text.
- `tooltip: boolean | string`
  Shows an info glyph after the label.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
/**
 * The field shell's classes for a state. InputBase uses it, and so do fields
 * whose editable part isn't an <input> (Time Field's segments).
 */
export function inputFieldClassName(
  { isFocusWithin, isHovered, isDisabled, isInvalid }: InputFieldState,
  size: InputSize = "medium",
  hasAddon = false,
) {
  return cx(
    inputStyles.field,
    hasAddon ? inputStyles.fieldWithAddonSize[size] : inputStyles.fieldSize[size],
    // Hover: idle, no focus, no disabled, no invalid
    isHovered && !isFocusWithin && !isDisabled && !isInvalid && "ring-border-button-hover",
    // Focus wins over hover
    isFocusWithin && !isDisabled && !isInvalid && "ring-border-button-active",
    // Disabled
    isDisabled && "bg-input-disabled-background text-input-disabled-foreground",
    // Invalid
    isInvalid && "bg-background-tertiary-error text-foreground-icon-error",
  );
}

export function InputBase({
  size: sizeProp,
  leadingIcon: Leading,
  trailingIcon: Trailing,
  leadingAddon,
  trailingAddon,
  fieldClassName,
  className,
  ref,
  groupRef,
  ...inputProps
}: InputBaseProps) {
  const { direction } = useLocale();
  const ctx = useContext(TextFieldContext);
  const size: InputSize = sizeProp ?? ctx.size ?? "medium";
  const hasAddon = leadingAddon !== undefined && leadingAddon !== null;

  return (
    <AriaGroup
      ref={groupRef}
      className={(state) => cx(inputFieldClassName(state, size, hasAddon), ctx.fieldClassName, fieldClassName)}
    >
      <div className={inputStyles.content}>
        <div className={inputStyles.leftSection}>
          {hasAddon ? (
            leadingAddon
          ) : Leading ? (
            <Leading className={inputStyles.icon} aria-hidden />
          ) : null}
          <AriaInput
            ref={ref}
            {...inputProps}
            // Align to the field's start even when email/URL values use LTR.
            className={cx(inputStyles.input, direction === "rtl" ? "pr-1 text-right" : "pl-1 text-left", ctx.inputClassName, className)}
          />
        </div>
        {trailingAddon ?? (Trailing ? (
          <Trailing className={inputStyles.icon} aria-hidden />
        ) : null)}
      </div>
    </AriaGroup>
  );
}
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** Nothing to clean up. The components hold no state, listeners or timers of their own; React Aria owns the field state.

**Reduced motion.** The component does not check `prefers-reduced-motion`. The only motion is the 150ms colour and ring transition on the shell, which a global rule that removes transitions turns into an instant change.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Do not add a `border` to show focus. The shell uses an inset ring that takes no layout space; a border would shift the content by a pixel on focus.
- Do not pass an element to `leadingIcon` (`<RiMailLine />`). It expects the component (`RiMailLine`) and renders it with the shell's classes.
- Do not set `isInvalid` without an `errorMessage` or `hint` if users need to know why. Only the shell tints red; the error text comes from those props.
- Do not leave a field with no `label`, no `aria-label` and no string `placeholder`. Then nothing names it and React Aria warns.

## Notes

- `inputFieldClassName` is exported for fields whose editable part is not an `<input>` (date and time segments), so they share the exact shell states.
- `Label`'s `isInvalid` prop is accepted but unused; it is reserved for invalid styling later.

## Definition of done

A labelled field shows a grey filled shell with no visible border. Hovering draws a light inset ring; clicking in darkens the ring and the placeholder, with no shift in layout. A required field shows a red asterisk after its label. Typing an invalid email in a field marked invalid tints the shell and its icon red and swaps the hint for the error message. A disabled field is lighter and ignores input. Screen readers announce the label, the hint and, when invalid, the error.

# Build: Input OTP

A verification-code field that looks like six boxes but holds one digit string. Every box is a real `<input>` with `autoComplete="one-time-code"`, and all edits go through one `writeFrom` function, so typing, pasting and OS autofill all write digits from the current box onward and move focus to the next empty one. It has no dependency beyond React and works controlled or uncontrolled.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

One-time-code field: a monospace box per digit that advances on type, steps back on Backspace, spreads a paste and accepts OS autofill.

- Category: form
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: none beyond React

## How it works

1. The value is a single string of digits. `code` is the controlled `value` (or internal state seeded from `defaultValue`) with every non-digit removed (`/\D/g`) and cut to `length`. Box `i` shows `code[i]`, or an empty string.
2. `writeFrom(index, digits)` strips non-digits, pads `code` to `length` with spaces, overwrites positions from `index` onward, and passes the result to `commit`, then calls `focusBox(index + digits.length)`. `focusBox` clamps the index to the last box, focuses it and selects its content, so the next keystroke replaces rather than appends.
3. `commit` strips non-digits again, sets internal state when uncontrolled, calls `onChange`, and calls `onComplete` whenever the result has `length` digits. Each box's `onChange` calls `writeFrom(index, event.target.value)`. `maxLength` is `length`, not 1, so when iOS or Chrome autofill drops the whole code into one box, all of it is distributed instead of five digits being lost.
4. `onKeyDown` handles Backspace itself (`preventDefault`): on a filled box it clears that position and keeps focus; on an empty box it clears the previous position and moves focus back. ArrowLeft and ArrowRight move focus without editing. `onPaste` prevents the default and sends the clipboard text to `writeFrom` from the box with the caret. `onFocus` selects the box content.
5. The wrapper is `role="group"` with the `aria-label` (default "One-time code") and `dir="ltr"`, so digits run left to right even in an RTL page. Each input has `aria-label="Digit i of n"`, `type="text"` with `inputMode="numeric"`, and `aria-invalid` when `isInvalid`. `groupEvery` adds `ms-3` before every nth box to split the code, for example into 3 + 3.
6. Each box is `size-12 rounded-2lg` with `font-mono text-title-3-medium tabular-nums`, a 1px `border-border-button-default` and `shadow-xs`. Hover darkens the border; `focus-visible` draws the focus border and a 2px ring; `isInvalid` sets a red border and tint; `isDisabled` greys it out. These changes transition over 150ms.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `length = 6 (default)`
  The common length for email and SMS codes, and the default the `aria-label`s count against ("Digit 1 of 6").
- `maxLength = length (not 1)`
  OS autofill writes the whole code into the focused box. With `maxLength={1}` the browser would keep only the first digit.
- `box = size-12 (48px), rounded-2lg, font-mono text-title-3-medium tabular-nums`
  Monospace digits keep a row of fixed boxes optically even; in a proportional face a 1 is visibly narrower than an 8.
- `group gap = gap-2 between boxes, extra ms-3 at each groupEvery boundary`
  An 8px gap keeps the boxes separate; the extra 12px reads as a break, so 000 000 is easier to copy from a phone.

## API

```ts
function InputOtp(props: { length?: number; value?: string; defaultValue?: string; onChange?: (value: string) => void; onComplete?: (value: string) => void; isDisabled?: boolean; isInvalid?: boolean; groupEvery?: number; "aria-label"?: string; className?: string; ref?: Ref<HTMLDivElement> }): JSX.Element
```

- `length: number` — default `6`
  Number of digit boxes.
- `value / defaultValue: string`
  Controlled or uncontrolled digits. Non-digits are dropped and the string is cut to `length`.
- `onChange: (value: string) => void`
  Called with the new digit string on every edit.
- `onComplete: (value: string) => void`
  Called after any edit that leaves every box filled, so editing a digit of a full code calls it again.
- `groupEvery: number`
  Adds a wider gap before every nth box, for example 3.
- `isInvalid: boolean` — default `false`
  Red border and tint, `aria-invalid` on every box.
- `isDisabled: boolean` — default `false`
  Disables every box.
- `aria-label: string` — default `"One-time code"`
  Name of the group.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
const commit = (next: string) => {
  const clean = next.replace(DIGITS_ONLY, "").slice(0, length);
  if (!controlled) setInternal(clean);
  onChange?.(clean);
  if (clean.length === length) onComplete?.(clean);
};

const focusBox = (index: number) => {
  const target = inputsRef.current[Math.max(0, Math.min(index, length - 1))];
  target?.focus();
  target?.select();
};

/** Writes `digits` starting at `index`, which covers typing and autofill. */
const writeFrom = (index: number, digits: string) => {
  const clean = digits.replace(DIGITS_ONLY, "");
  if (clean === "") return;

  const chars = code.padEnd(length, " ").split("");
  for (let offset = 0; offset < clean.length && index + offset < length; offset += 1) {
    chars[index + offset] = clean.charAt(offset);
  }
  commit(chars.join("").trimEnd());
  focusBox(index + clean.length);
};

const onKeyDown = (event: KeyboardEvent<HTMLInputElement>, index: number) => {
  if (event.key === "Backspace") {
    event.preventDefault();
    if (code[index]) {
      // Clear in place; the caret only steps back on an already-empty box,
      // which is what makes holding Backspace feel right.
      const chars = code.padEnd(length, " ").split("");
      chars[index] = " ";
      commit(chars.join("").trimEnd());
      return;
    }
    const chars = code.padEnd(length, " ").split("");
    chars[Math.max(0, index - 1)] = " ";
    commit(chars.join("").trimEnd());
    focusBox(index - 1);
    return;
  }

  if (event.key === "ArrowLeft") {
    event.preventDefault();
    focusBox(index - 1);
  } else if (event.key === "ArrowRight") {
    event.preventDefault();
    focusBox(index + 1);
  }
};

const onPaste = (event: ClipboardEvent<HTMLInputElement>, index: number) => {
  event.preventDefault();
  writeFrom(index, event.clipboardData.getData("text"));
};
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** Nothing to clean up. The component keeps a ref array of inputs and at most one piece of state; it sets no timers or listeners outside React's own handlers.

**Reduced motion.** The component does not check `prefers-reduced-motion`. Its only motion is the 150ms border, background and shadow transition on each box, which a global rule that removes transitions makes instant.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Do not use `type="number"` for the boxes. It adds spinners, accepts `e` and `-`, and reports an empty value for input it considers malformed. Use `type="text"` with `inputMode="numeric"`.
- Do not set `maxLength={1}`. Autofill hands the full code to one box and the browser would drop the rest.
- Do not put `aria-invalid` on the `role="group"` wrapper. The group role does not support it; each input carries its own.
- Do not remove `dir="ltr"` from the wrapper. In an RTL page the code would otherwise read right to left.

## Notes

- The value is stored as a compact digit string, so clearing a box in the middle of a full code shifts the digits after it one place left.
- Arrow keys are not mirrored; the wrapper is always left to right.

## Definition of done

Six empty boxes sit in a row. Typing 7 fills the first box and moves focus to the second. Pasting "731428" into the first box fills all six and calls `onComplete`. Backspace on a filled box clears it and keeps focus; Backspace on an empty box clears the previous one and moves back. Arrow keys move between boxes without changing anything. Letters are ignored. With `groupEvery={3}` a wider gap separates 3 + 3. `isInvalid` turns every box red.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Install Command Tabs

The install box from a docs page. A grey shell holds a row of package-manager tabs and a copy button above a white command line. The runner (`npx`, `pnpm dlx`, `bun add` and so on) is set in the stronger purple and the arguments in the lighter command accent. Commands are derived from one description (a binary to run, or packages to add), so the four spellings never drift apart. A controlled `value` keeps every block on the page on the manager the reader picked. `InstallSteps` and `InstallStep` lay blocks out as numbered steps joined by the `docs-install-rail` line.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

pnpm, npm, yarn and bun tabs that spell the same install or run command four ways, with copy and numbered docs steps on a rail.

- Category: display
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: react-aria-components@^1.22.1

## How it works

1. `getInstallCommand(manager, source)` builds each spelling. An explicit `commands[manager]` wins. Otherwise `run` is prefixed with the manager's runner (`npx`, `pnpm dlx`, `yarn dlx`, `bunx --bun`), or `install` packages follow its add verb (`npm install`, `pnpm add`, `yarn add`, `bun add`), with `-D` or `--dev` when `dev` is set.
2. React Aria `Tabs` provide one `Tab` and one `TabPanel` per manager, with roving focus, arrow keys and `aria-controls`. Selection is controlled through `value` and `onValueChange` or uncontrolled through `defaultValue`. A `value` that is not in `managers` falls back to the first one rather than leaving nothing selected.
3. Each panel splits its command with `splitRunner`, which matches the longest known runner first so that `pnpm dlx` beats `pnpm`. The runner renders in `status-purple-text` and the rest in `docs-command-accent`, inside a horizontally scrollable `whitespace-pre` line.
4. The header `CopyButton` takes a function value, so it copies the command of the tab selected at click time, and its accessible name follows the tab ("Copy yarn command"). It shows the shared copy-to-check feedback from `code-block-copy`.
5. `InstallStep` is an `<li>` with a 28px zero-padded number badge and a 1px `bg-docs-install-rail` line that fills the remaining height down to the next badge. The `group-last/step:hidden` modifier removes the rail on the last step without a prop.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `tab pill = h-7, px-2.5, rounded-lg, white + shadow-2xs when selected`
  The selected pill sits 6px inside the rounded-2xl shell, like the file chip in the code block, so the two docs pieces line up.
- `runner order = longest runner first`
  `pnpm dlx` and `pnpm add` both start with `pnpm`, so matching the shortest first would colour only `pnpm`.
- `step badge = size-7, rounded-full, mono caption-1, zero-padded`
  Two-digit labels (`01`, `02`) keep the badge text the same width from step 1 to step 12.
- `rail = w-px, docs-install-rail, mt-2 below the badge`
  The token is the button border in light mode and a 60% neutral-800 in dark mode, so the rail stays visible without competing with the code panels.

## API

```ts
type PackageManager = "pnpm" | "npm" | "yarn" | "bun";
function InstallCommandTabs(props: { run?: string; install?: string | readonly string[]; dev?: boolean; commands?: Partial<Record<PackageManager, string>>; managers?: readonly PackageManager[]; value?: PackageManager; defaultValue?: PackageManager; onValueChange?: (manager: PackageManager) => void; "aria-label"?: string; onCopied?: (command: string) => void; className?: string; ref?: Ref<HTMLDivElement> }): JSX.Element
function getInstallCommand(manager: PackageManager, source: { run?: string; install?: string | readonly string[]; dev?: boolean; commands?: Partial<Record<PackageManager, string>> }): string
function InstallSteps(props: { children: ReactNode; className?: string }): JSX.Element
function InstallStep(props: { step: number; title: ReactNode; description?: ReactNode; children?: ReactNode }): JSX.Element
```

- `run: string`
  Arguments for a one-off binary run, e.g. `boardui@latest add line-chart-card`.
- `install: string | readonly string[]`
  Packages to add to the project.
- `dev: boolean` — default `false`
  With `install`, add as dev dependencies.
- `commands: Partial<Record<PackageManager, string>>`
  Exact command per manager. Overrides `run` and `install`.
- `managers: readonly PackageManager[]` — default `["pnpm", "npm", "yarn", "bun"]`
  Tabs to show, in order.
- `value / defaultValue / onValueChange: PackageManager` — default `uncontrolled, first manager`
  Selected manager. Share it to sync blocks.
- `aria-label: string` — default `"Package manager"`
  Accessible name of the tab list.
- `onCopied: (command: string) => void`
  Called with the copied command.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
// Every command is derived, never stored: changing `run` or `install`
// updates all four spellings at once, and the copy button reads the one
// that matches the selected tab at click time.
const source: InstallCommandSource = { run, install, dev, commands };
const lines = managers.map((manager) => {
  const command = getInstallCommand(manager, source);
  const [runner, rest] = splitRunner(command);
  return { manager, command, runner, rest };
});
const current = lines.find((line) => line.manager === active)?.command ?? "";

const select = (key: PackageManager) => {
  setUncontrolled(key);
  onValueChange?.(key);
};
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** There are no effects, timers or listeners in this file. The copy reset timeout lives in `useCopyToClipboard` and is cleared on unmount.

**Reduced motion.** Nothing travels. The tab pill fades its colour and shadow over 150ms, and the copy glyph cross-fades over 200ms. Both have `motion-reduce:transition-none`, so they switch at once.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Storing the copied text in state when the tab changes. A stale closure would copy the npm command after the reader switched to bun. The copy button reads the selected command at click time.
- Assuming every runner is one word. `pnpm dlx`, `yarn dlx` and `bunx --bun` are two tokens, and colouring by first word would split them wrongly.
- Giving each block its own state on a multi-step page. The reader would have to pick their manager once per block. Lift the value and pass `value` and `onValueChange` to every block.

## Notes

- `getInstallCommand` and `PACKAGE_MANAGERS` are exported for building other docs pieces, such as an llms.txt entry or a shell snippet.
- Use `commands` for anything the builder does not cover, such as `npm create` or a global install.

## Definition of done

With `run="boardui@latest add line-chart-card"`, the pnpm tab shows `pnpm dlx boardui@latest add line-chart-card`, npm shows `npx …`, yarn `yarn dlx …` and bun `bunx --bun …`, with the runner in a darker purple than the arguments. Clicking yarn, or arrowing to it, switches the command and renames the copy button to "Copy yarn command", which copies exactly the visible text. When two blocks share `value`, choosing bun in one switches the other. Step badges read 01 and 02, and a rail joins them but not past the last step.

and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Instanced Quad Particles

Four vertices and six indices are shared by every particle; three instanced attributes carry position, size, spin, alpha, tint and shape. One `drawElementsInstanced` puts the whole field on screen. Quads instead of `gl_PointSize` because point sprites are capped at 255px on many drivers, cannot be rotated, and are culled whole the instant their centre leaves the viewport — a large sprite disappears while half of it is still visible.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

Up to 1800 drifting particles in one draw call — quads rather than point sprites, so each one has its own size, spin and shape.

- Category: webgl
- Runtime cost: webgl
- Dependencies: ogl@^1.0.11

## How it works

1. The geometry is one unit quad in `position` (-0.5..0.5) plus an index buffer, and three attributes marked `instanced: 1`: `aOrigin` (field-space rest position), `aParams` (size in CSS px, signed spin rate, base alpha, tint mix) and `aSeed` (two flow phases, spin phase, shape mix). Ten floats per particle, 72 KB at the 1800 ceiling.
2. Buffers are allocated once at `maxCount` and never reallocated. The visible population comes from `geometry.setInstancedCount(count)` where `count` is derived from container area — `clamp(round(megapixels * density), 250, maxCount)` — so the same density reads correctly in a 320px card and a 2000px hero. Because the scatter is random, any prefix of the buffer is still a spatially even field.
3. The vertex shader rotates the quad corner in PIXEL space and only then divides by the drawing-buffer resolution to reach clip space. Rotating in clip space would shear the quad by the container aspect ratio, and a square particle would become a lozenge that changes shape as it spins.
4. Drift is a pure function of `elapsed` and the per-particle seed: the field marches upward with `fract(y + t * RISE)`, then two out-of-phase sinusoids sampled at the particle's own position add wander. No per-particle state is stored, so a resize, a tab switch or a reduced-motion still can all be drawn from one number.
5. `fract` teleports a particle from the top edge to the bottom, which is a visible pop. `uFadeBand` smoothsteps alpha to zero within 12% of each end, so the population always arrives and leaves at zero opacity.
6. One rounded-box SDF in the fragment shader covers both shapes. At `shape` 0 the half-extents and the corner radius are both 0.5, which reduces exactly to `length(uv) - 0.5` — a true circle. At 1 it is a narrow shard, and the shard is the only reason per-particle rotation is visible at all.
7. Blending is additive (`ONE, ONE`) onto an opaque clear colour, which is order independent — a thousand overlapping instances need no depth sort, which is what makes one draw call possible. The canvas is opaque rather than transparent because additive blending onto transparency would have to brighten the page background, and the GPU cannot see it.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `density = 900`
  Particles per megapixel. Tuned so a typical card holds 250-400 and a full-width hero approaches the ceiling. Doubling it does not double the perceived density — it doubles the fill rate and flattens the depth cue that comes from having gaps.
- `maxCount = 1800`
  Ceiling and allocation size. Not a performance limit on the vertex side — 1800 quads is 7200 vertices, nothing — but the fill cost of 1800 soft additive quads averaging 12px is roughly one full screen of blended pixels per frame.
- `MAX_DPR = 1.5`
  Additive fill is the entire cost of this component and it scales with the square of the pixel ratio. Dust has no fine detail that a third sample per axis resolves, so 3x phones render at 1.5x and the frame budget drops by a factor of four against an uncapped ratio.
- `SIZE_BIAS = 2.2`
  Exponent on the uniform random used for size. At 1 a quarter of the population lands in the largest quarter of the range, and a hundred 28px blobs is fog rather than dust. At 2.2 the large sizes are rare enough to read as individuals.
- `RISE = 0.045`
  Field heights per second at `speed` 1 — about 22 seconds to cross. Slow enough that the eye reads drift rather than travel; above ~0.15 the field looks like falling snow played in reverse.
- `FADE_BAND = 0.12`
  Fraction of the field height the wrap fade occupies at each end. Below ~0.06 the pop at the seam becomes visible for the largest particles, whose radius alone is a couple of percent of the height. Above 0.2 a quarter of the field is permanently dim.
- `FLOW_SCALE = 1.4`
  Cycles of wander across the field. Under 1 the whole population slides sideways as a sheet; well above 2 adjacent particles move in opposite directions and the motion reads as noise rather than air.
- `X_MIN / X_MAX = -0.08 / 1.08`
  Field-space x range. Seeding wider than the container means horizontal wander can never bare a strip at the left or right edge. The off-screen quads are clipped by the rasteriser and cost nothing — which is exactly what a point sprite could not do.
- `alpha per particle = 1 - 0.78 * sizeT`
  Large particles are dimmed so total emitted light is roughly independent of size. Without it the few big instances dominate every additive overlap and the field looks like it has hot spots.

## API

```ts
function InstancedQuadParticles(props: { density?: number; maxCount?: number; sizeRange?: readonly [number, number]; softness?: number; spin?: number; speed?: number; wander?: number; opacity?: number; colorA?: string; colorB?: string; background?: string; seed?: number | string; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `density: number` — default `900`
  Particles per megapixel of container area. The count is derived from this, not fixed.
- `maxCount: number` — default `1800`
  Population ceiling, and the size the buffers are allocated at.
- `sizeRange: readonly [number, number]` — default `[5, 28]`
  Particle size in CSS pixels. The distribution is biased toward the small end.
- `softness: number` — default `0.62`
  Edge width, 0..1. 0 is a hard silhouette, 1 is a pure gradient. Floored at one device pixel.
- `spin: number` — default `0.5`
  Peak spin in radians per second; each particle takes a signed fraction of it.
- `speed: number` — default `1`
  Multiplier on the whole drift, including the upward march.
- `wander: number` — default `0.06`
  Sinusoidal wander amplitude in field units, where 1 is the container.
- `opacity: number` — default `0.55`
  Overall alpha multiplier applied in the fragment shader.
- `colorA: string` — default `'#9fb4cc'`
  First tint. Any value ogl's `Color` accepts.
- `colorB: string` — default `'#e8ddc9'`
  Second tint; each particle mixes between the two by a seeded amount.
- `background: string` — default `'#07090d'`
  Opaque clear colour the additive field is composited onto.
- `seed: number | string` — default `'instanced-quad-particles'`
  Seeds the scatter. Same seed, same field on every reload and on the server.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the host element via `cn`.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
export function InstancedQuadParticles({
  density = 900,
  maxCount = 1800,
  sizeRange = [5, 28],
  softness = 0.62,
  spin = 0.5,
  speed = 1,
  wander = 0.06,
  opacity = 0.55,
  colorA = '#9fb4cc',
  colorB = '#e8ddc9',
  background = '#07090d',
  seed = 'instanced-quad-particles',
  className,
}: InstancedQuadParticlesProps) {
  const host = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const stage = useRef<Stage | null>(null);
  const [unsupported, setUnsupported] = useState(false);

  const { width, height } = useResizeObserver(host);
  const size = useRef({ width, height });
  size.current = { width, height };

  const reduced = useReducedMotion();
  const visible = useVisibility();
  const { inView } = useInView(host, { rootMargin: '10%' });
  const ready = width > 1 && height > 1;

  const [minSize = 5, maxSize = 28] = sizeRange;

  useEffect(() => {
    const el = host.current;
    if (!el || !ready) return;

    if (!hasWebGL()) {
      setUnsupported(true);
      return;
    }

    // ogl creates its own canvas, and it is appended and removed per effect
    // run. Reusing one React-owned canvas would break under StrictMode: the
    // cleanup force-loses the context, and `getContext` on that same element
    // afterwards hands back the dead one rather than a fresh context.
    const renderer = new Renderer({
      dpr: pixelRatio(MAX_DPR),
      // Opaque, so the field owns every pixel and reads the same on a light or
      // a dark page. Additive blending onto a transparent canvas would have to
      // brighten whatever is behind it, which is the page background, which
      // the GPU cannot see.
      alpha: false,
      // Nothing is sorted and nothing occludes anything, so a depth buffer is
      // memory and a clear per frame for no result.
      depth: false,
      antialias: false,
      // The field is fill-bound, not shader-bound. Asking for the discrete GPU
      // on a laptop costs battery and buys nothing.
      powerPreference: 'low-power',
    });

    const gl = renderer.gl;
    const canvas = gl.canvas;

    const bg = new Color(background);
    gl.clearColor(bg.r, bg.g, bg.b, 1);

    // Four vertices, six indices, shared by every instance.
    const quad = new Float32Array([-0.5, -0.5, 0.5, -0.5, 0.5, 0.5, -0.5, 0.5]);
    const index = new Uint16Array([0, 1, 2, 0, 2, 3]);

    const total = Math.max(MIN_COUNT, Math.round(maxCount));
    const origins = new Float32Array(total * 2);
    const params = new Float32Array(total * 4);
    const seeds = new Float32Array(total * 4);

    const rng = createRng(seed);
    const lo = Math.max(1, Math.min(minSize, maxSize));
    const hi = Math.max(lo + 0.5, Math.max(minSize, maxSize));

    for (let i = 0; i < total; i += 1) {
      origins[i * 2] = randRange(rng, X_MIN, X_MAX);
      origins[i * 2 + 1] = rng();

      // Biased toward small: a linear distribution puts a quarter of the
      // population in the largest quarter of the size range, and a hundred
      // 28px blobs is fog rather than dust.
      const sizeT = Math.pow(rng(), SIZE_BIAS);
      params[i * 4] = lo + (hi - lo) * sizeT;
      params[i * 4 + 1] = randRange(rng, -1, 1) * spin;
      // Big particles are dimmer. Alpha per particle rather than per pixel
      // keeps the total light roughly constant as the size scales.
      params[i * 4 + 2] = 1 - 0.78 * sizeT;
      params[i * 4 + 3] = rng();

      seeds[i * 4] = rng() * Math.PI * 2;
      seeds[i * 4 + 1] = rng() * Math.PI * 2;
      seeds[i * 4 + 2] = rng();
      // A third are discs. The rest are shards, and the shards are the only
      // reason per-particle rotation is visible at all.
      seeds[i * 4 + 3] = rng() < 0.34 ? 0 : randRange(rng, 0.55, 1);
    }

    const geometry = new Geometry(gl, {
      index: { data: index },
      position: { size: 2, data: quad },
      aOrigin: { size: 2, data: origins, instanced: 1 },
      aParams: { size: 4, data: params, instanced: 1 },
      aSeed: { size: 4, data: seeds, instanced: 1 },
    });

    const uniforms: Uniforms = {
      uResolution: { value: [1, 1] },
      uPixelRatio: { value: renderer.dpr },
      uElapsed: { value: 0 },
      uDrift: { value: speed },
      uRise: { value: RISE },
      uFlowScale: { value: FLOW_SCALE },
      uWander: { value: wander },
      uFadeBand: { value: FADE_BAND },
      uColorA: { value: new Color(colorA) },
      uColorB: { value: new Color(colorB) },
      uSoftness: { value: clamp(softness, 0, 1) },
      uOpacity: { value: opacity },
    };

    const program = new Program(gl, {
      vertex: INSTANCED_QUAD_PARTICLES_VERT,
      fragment: INSTANCED_QUAD_PARTICLES_FRAG,
      uniforms,
      transparent: true,
      depthTest: false,
      depthWrite: false,
      // ogl defaults `cullFace` to BACK. The quad's index winding is not
      // guaranteed to face the way the driver expects once it is rotated in
      // the vertex shader, and a culled particle is simply absent.
      cullFace: false,
    });
    // Additive, overriding the source-over that `transparent: true` selected.
    // Order independent, so a thousand overlapping instances need no sort —
    // which is what makes one draw call possible in the first place.
    program.setBlendFunc(gl.ONE, gl.ONE);

    const mesh = new Mesh(gl, { geometry, program });

    el.appendChild(canvas);
    canvas.style.display = 'block';

    const resize = (w: number, h: number) => {
      renderer.setSize(w, h);
      // `setSize` writes literal px into the canvas's inline style, which wins
      // over any class. Re-asserting percentages keeps the element fluid
      // between resize notifications.
      canvas.style.width = '100%';
      canvas.style.height = '100%';

      uniforms.uResolution.value = [gl.drawingBufferWidth, gl.drawingBufferHeight];
      uniforms.uPixelRatio.value = renderer.dpr;

      // Population from area, not from a fixed number: the same density looks
      // right in a 320px card and in a 2000px hero. The buffers already hold
      // `total` particles in scattered order, so a prefix of them is still a
      // spatially even field — no rebuild, no reallocation.
      const megapixels = (w * h) / 1_000_000;
      const count = clamp(Math.round(megapixels * density), MIN_COUNT, total);
      geometry.setInstancedCount(count);
    };

    const draw = (elapsed: number) => {
      uniforms.uElapsed.value = elapsed;
      renderer.render({ scene: mesh });
    };

    resize(size.current.width, size.current.height);
    stage.current = { renderer, geometry, program, mesh, uniforms, resize, draw };
    draw(STATIC_ELAPSED);

    // An unheard context loss is a field that goes blank and never returns —
    // no error, no fallback — so it is routed into the same no-WebGL path. The
    // `preventDefault` is mandatory: without it a restore can never be offered.
    const onLost = (event: Event): void => {
      event.preventDefault();
      setUnsupported(true);
    };
    canvas.addEventListener('webglcontextlost', onLost);

    return () => {
      stage.current = null;
      canvas.removeEventListener('webglcontextlost', onLost);
      // ogl has no `dispose()`: `remove()` on the geometry deletes its VAOs and
      // every buffer, `remove()` on the program deletes the shaders and the
      // program, and only then is the context worth handing back.
      geometry.remove();
      program.remove();
      loseContext(gl);
      canvas.width = 0;
      canvas.height = 0;
      canvas.remove();
    };
  }, [
    ready,
    density,
    maxCount,
    minSize,
    maxSize,
    softness,
    spin,
    speed,
    wander,
    opacity,
    colorA,
    colorB,
    background,
    seed,
  ]);

  // Resize is its own effect: a reflow costs a `setSize` and an instanced-count
  // change, never a buffer rebuild.
  useEffect(() => {
    stage.current?.resize(width, height);
    if (reduced) stage.current?.draw(STATIC_ELAPSED);
  }, [width, height, reduced]);

  useRaf(
    (_dt, elapsed) => stage.current?.draw(elapsed),
    ready && inView && visible && !reduced && !unsupported,
  );
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** `geometry.remove()` deletes every VAO and every buffer, `program.remove()` deletes the shaders and the program, then `loseContext(gl)` hands the context back through `WEBGL_lose_context` — ogl has no `dispose()` and nothing else releases a context. The canvas backing store is zeroed and the node removed, so the drawing buffer goes with it rather than waiting for GC.

**Reduced motion.** The rAF subscription is never made and the field is drawn once at `elapsed` 0. That is a complete, correct frame rather than a collapsed one: the scatter, sizes, tints, shapes and spin phases are all per-particle seeds that already vary at t=0, and the wrap fade applies exactly as it does in motion. Resizing redraws the same still.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Reaching for `gl_PointSize`. It is capped — 255px on a great many drivers, and the cap is silent — it cannot be rotated, and the sprite is culled by its centre point, so anything large blinks out while half of it is still on screen.
- Leaving ogl's `cullFace` at its default. `Program` defaults it to `gl.BACK`; once the quad corners are rotated in the vertex shader the winding the driver sees is not the winding you authored, and culled particles are simply absent with no error anywhere.
- Rotating the corner offset after converting to clip space. The container aspect ratio shears it, so a particle is square only when the container is, and it visibly changes shape through a spin.
- Rebuilding the buffers on resize to change the particle count. `setInstancedCount` selects a prefix of what is already uploaded; reallocating 72 KB of GPU memory on every ResizeObserver notification is a stall for no visual difference.
- Wrapping with `fract` and no fade. The seam is a hard teleport, and at 1800 particles something is crossing it constantly, so the field flickers along one edge.
- Compositing an additive field onto a transparent canvas. Additive needs to know what it is adding to; with `alpha: true` the destination is zero, the result is the particle colour flat, and the field looks pasted on rather than glowing.
- Reusing one React-owned canvas across effect runs. Cleanup force-loses the context, and `getContext` on that same element afterwards returns the dead one — under StrictMode's mount / unmount / mount that means every instance is permanently black. ogl creates its own canvas, which is appended and removed per run.
- Assuming `renderer.setSize` leaves the CSS alone. ogl writes literal px into the canvas's inline `style`, which beats any class; the percentages have to be re-asserted after every call or the element stops being fluid.

## Notes

- ogl rather than three: the whole component is one instanced mesh with no lights, no camera and no scene graph, and ogl's `Geometry` exposes instanced attributes directly with `instanced: 1` instead of through an `InstancedBufferGeometry` wrapper.
- No camera is passed to `renderer.render`, which is deliberate. Without one ogl skips frustum culling and the matrix uniforms entirely — the shader writes clip space itself, so a projection matrix would be an identity multiply per vertex.
- `depth: false` on the context. Nothing occludes anything under additive blending, so a depth buffer would be memory plus a clear per frame for no result.
- Sizes are authored in CSS pixels and multiplied by the pixel ratio in the shader, so the field looks identical across a dpr change and nothing needs rebuilding when one happens.
- GLSL ES 1.00 with no derivative functions: the edge anti-aliasing floor is `1.0 / sizePx`, which is exact for a quad of that pixel size, so the same source compiles under a WebGL1 fallback context where `fwidth` needs an extension.

## Definition of done

The field drifts upward and sideways with no visible seam at the top or bottom edge, and no particle ever appears or vanishes abruptly. Individual particles spin, and the shards are visibly rotating rather than shimmering. Resize the container narrow and wide: particles stay square at every aspect ratio, and the population changes without a stutter. One draw call per frame in a frame capture, whatever the count. Mount and unmount a dozen instances and none of the earlier ones go black.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Inverse Scroll Scale

The inverse of the usual scroll-scale. Instead of growing as it rises, the media starts oversized and resolves down to exactly 1.0 over the first 60% of the scroller, so it settles into its frame rather than bursting out of it — and it is at rest for the whole time it is the thing you are actually looking at. No animation library: one rAF callback, gated by an IntersectionObserver.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

Media enters oversized at 1.25x and settles to exactly 1.0 as it rises through the first 60% of the scroller.

- Category: scroll
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: none beyond React

## How it works

1. Each frame the component reads the frame element's `getBoundingClientRect().top`, converts it to a position inside the scroller by subtracting the scroller's own rect top, and computes `t = clamp((height - top) / (span * height), 0, 1)`.
2. `t` is 0 while the frame's top edge sits on the bottom of the scroller and reaches 1 once it has climbed `span` of the scroller's height — 60% by default, so it is finished long before the element is centred.
3. Scale is a straight linear ramp: `from - (from - 1) * t`. It ends on exactly 1.0 by construction, which matters because a scale below 1 on an element sized to its frame would let the frame show through at the edges.
4. Optional smoothing runs the result through `damp(current, wanted, smoothing, dt)`, which raises the retention factor to the power of elapsed time and so converges at the same rate on 60Hz and 120Hz displays. The naive `x += (target - x) * 0.1` would run twice as fast on the faster display.
5. The frame is rounded to four decimals and compared against what was last written; on the many frames where nothing changed the style write is skipped entirely, so an idle instance costs one rect read.
6. An IntersectionObserver with a 20% rootMargin flips an `active` ref, and the rAF callback returns immediately when it is false. The observer is hand-rolled rather than pooled because it needs the demo's scroller as its `root`.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `from = 1.25`
  Starting scale. Must be at least 1 — anything less shows the frame through the edges of the media, because the media is sized to exactly fill the frame. Past ~1.4 the visible crop at the start is severe enough that the composition changes rather than just the size.
- `span = 0.6`
  Fraction of scroller height over which the scale resolves, measured up from the bottom edge. The whole argument for the effect: at 1.0 the media is still moving while it is centred and being read, which is exactly when it should be still. At 0.6 it lands well before that.
- `smoothing = 0`
  Off by default. The mapping from scroll position to scale is already continuous, so smoothing adds lag with nothing to hide. It exists for the case where the scroll source is itself steppy (a trackpad-free mouse wheel, or a snapped container).
- `rootMargin = '20% 0px 20% 0px'`
  Starts the rAF work a fifth of a scroller height before the frame is visible, so the first painted frame is already at the correct scale. Without the margin the element pops from its authored scale to its computed one on the frame it enters.
- `toFixed precision = 4`
  Below one device pixel of difference on a 4000px-wide element, so the rounding is invisible; its purpose is to make the "unchanged" comparison actually hit, which it never would on raw floats.

## API

```ts
function InverseScrollScale(props: { children: ReactNode; from?: number; span?: number; smoothing?: number; scrollerRef?: RefObject<HTMLElement | null>; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `children: ReactNode`
  The media. Sized to fill the frame; this is what gets scaled.
- `from: number` — default `1.25`
  Starting scale. Must be >= 1.
- `span: number` — default `0.6`
  Fraction of scroller height over which the scale resolves.
- `smoothing: number` — default `0`
  Fraction of the remaining gap left after one second. 0 disables smoothing.
- `scrollerRef: RefObject<HTMLElement | null>`
  The scroll container that owns the scroll position. Omit for the document.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the frame via `cn`. Set the frame size here.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
export function InverseScrollScale({
  children,
  from = 1.25,
  span = 0.6,
  smoothing = 0,
  scrollerRef,
  className,
}: InverseScrollScaleProps) {
  const frame = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const media = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const active = useRef(false);
  const scale = useRef(from);
  const written = useRef(-1);
  const reduced = useReducedMotion();

  // Gate the rAF work on visibility. Hand-rolled rather than `useInView`
  // because the observer needs a custom `root` — the demo's own scroller —
  // and a pooled observer keyed only by threshold would hand back one rooted
  // at the document.
  useEffect(() => {
    const el = frame.current;
    if (!el || reduced) return;

    const observer = new IntersectionObserver(
      (entries) => {
        for (const entry of entries) active.current = entry.isIntersecting;
      },
      { root: scrollerRef?.current ?? null, rootMargin: '20% 0px 20% 0px' },
    );
    observer.observe(el);
    return () => observer.disconnect();
  }, [reduced, scrollerRef]);

  useRaf(
    (dt) => {
      const el = frame.current;
      const target = media.current;
      if (!el || !target || !active.current) return;

      // One read pass, then one write pass. Reading the rect after writing a
      // transform in the same frame forces a synchronous layout.
      const scroller = scrollerRef?.current ?? null;
      const rect = el.getBoundingClientRect();
      const height = scroller ? scroller.clientHeight : window.innerHeight;
      const top = scroller ? rect.top - scroller.getBoundingClientRect().top : rect.top;

      // t is 0 while the frame's top edge is at the bottom of the scroller and
      // reaches 1 once it has risen `span` of the scroller's height.
      const t = clamp((height - top) / (span * height), 0, 1);
      const wanted = from - (from - 1) * t;

      scale.current =
        smoothing > 0 ? damp(scale.current, wanted, smoothing, dt) : wanted;

      // Four decimals is below one device pixel on a 4000px element, and the
      // equality check skips the style write on the many frames where nothing
      // changed — an idle instance then costs a rect read and nothing else.
      const next = Number(scale.current.toFixed(4));
      if (next === written.current) return;
      written.current = next;
      target.style.transform = `scale(${next})`;
    },
    !reduced,
  );
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** `useRaf` unsubscribes on unmount and drops the shared loop entirely when it was the last subscriber; the IntersectionObserver is disconnected in its own effect cleanup. Without the disconnect the observer holds a reference to a removed element and keeps firing on every scroll of a container the component no longer participates in.

**Reduced motion.** The media renders at scale 1 — its resolved state, filling the frame — and neither the IntersectionObserver nor the rAF subscription is created, so there is no per-frame work at all.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Using `window.innerHeight` when the element scrolls inside a container. Inside a 300px-tall panel on a 1000px-tall window, `t` never exceeds about 0.3, so the media stays visibly oversized for the whole scroll and never resolves.
- Scaling from below 1 up to 1 instead. The media is sized to its frame, so any scale under 1 leaves a gap at the edges and the background shows through as a hairline border that grows and shrinks.
- Reading `getBoundingClientRect()` after writing the transform in the same callback. That is a forced synchronous layout every frame, and it appears in a profile as a long purple bar attached to the rAF, not as anything obviously related to this component.
- Running the rAF callback for every instance on the page. Ten of these in a long article means ten rect reads per frame for elements that are nowhere near the viewport; the IntersectionObserver gate is what keeps the cost proportional to what is on screen.
- A per-frame lerp constant instead of `damp` when smoothing is enabled. On a 120Hz display the media reaches its target in half the scroll distance, so the effect is materially different on a MacBook Pro than on an external 60Hz monitor.
- Omitting `overflow: hidden` on the frame. At 1.25 the media is 25% larger than its box and overlaps whatever is next to it, which is most visible as text from the following section being covered as you scroll.

## Notes

- No animation library. The whole component is one rAF subscription and one IntersectionObserver.
- The transform is written imperatively rather than through React state, so no scroll frame causes a render.

## Definition of done

Scroll the frame up from the bottom of the scroller: the media is visibly cropped and oversized as it appears, and reaches its natural size a little past halfway up — after which it does not move at all while you read it. Scroll back down and it re-expands. No hairline of background is ever visible inside the frame. With reduced motion on, the media is at natural size at all scroll positions.

and where, so I can check them.
