# Build: Nav Dot Wave

One keyframe block and N elements. Each nav item writes its own index into an inline `--i`, and the stylesheet turns that index into an animation delay, so a crest travels along the row. Adding a nav item requires no change to the CSS and no JavaScript at all.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

Nav dots that lift in sequence. The index is an inline custom property; CSS derives the delay.

- Category: primitive
- Runtime cost: css
- Dependencies: none beyond React

## How it works

1. Every list item carries `style={{ "--i": i }}`. The dot's rule reads `animation-delay: calc(var(--i, 0) * var(--kx-dot-stagger, 60ms))`, so the phase offset of each dot is derived from its position rather than authored per item. The index is data; the timing is a function of it.
2. The keyframe is deliberately mostly flat: `0%, 60%, 100%` is the resting pose and only `30%` lifts. The dot therefore rests for 40% of every 1400 ms cycle. That long rest is what makes a staggered set read as a single crest travelling along the row instead of a row of dots vibrating in place.
3. 0% is the resting pose, not the lifted one, and that ordering is load-bearing. A positive `animation-delay` holds an element at its 0% pose until the delay expires, so if 0% were the lift, every dot would sit visibly raised for its share of the stagger on first paint and the row would *settle* into place rather than start from it.
4. The active item swaps to a second keyframe (`kx-dotwave-active`) with identical geometry but a constant `opacity: 1`. It participates in the wave so the row stays coherent, but it never dims, because a location marker that fades to 45% twice a second is a marker you cannot trust.
5. The lift is written with the `translate` property, not `transform`, so the active state's `scale: 1.6` composes independently and can carry its own spring transition without either value clobbering the other.
6. `reverse` negates the stagger to `-60ms`. Negative delays start an animation already partway through its cycle, so the phase gradient inverts and the crest runs right-to-left with no second keyframe.
7. The CSS ships in a `<style href="kinetic-nav-dot-wave" precedence="medium">` element. React 19 deduplicates and hoists it to the head by `href`, so the rules exist exactly once no matter how many navs are mounted, and nothing has to be added to a global stylesheet.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `durationMs = 1400`
  One dot's full cycle. Below ~900 ms the lift reads as a nervous twitch; above ~2000 ms the crest is so slow that a user glancing at the nav sees a static row and the effect is paid for but not perceived.
- `staggerMs = 60`
  Phase gap between neighbours. The crest travels at one item per 60 ms. Under ~30 ms the dots look simultaneous; over ~120 ms the wave breaks into visibly separate blips because the leading dot has finished its lift before the next begins.
- `keyframe rest span = 0%, 60%, 100%`
  The dot is flat for 40% of the cycle. Shrink the rest and adjacent dots overlap enough that the whole row appears raised at once, which is a vibration, not a wave.
- `peak position = 30%`
  The lift peaks in the first third and eases back over the next third. Symmetric timing (peak at 50%) makes each dot look like it is hovering rather than being flicked, and the crest loses its direction.
- `lift = 3`
  Pixels. A nav dot is 5px; 3px is a lift of over half its diameter, which is legible at a glance. Past ~6px the dots start colliding with the label baseline and the row looks broken rather than animated.
- `resting opacity = 0.45`
  Low enough that the peak at 1.0 registers as a change, high enough that an inactive nav item is still readable. Below ~0.3 the dots vanish against a dark surface and the row appears to lose items.
- `active scale = 1.6`
  The current-page dot has to win against five siblings that are all moving. Under ~1.3 it is lost in the wave; over ~2 it stops reading as the same kind of object as its neighbours.

## API

```ts
function NavDotWave(props: { items: readonly { label: string; href?: string }[]; activeIndex?: number; staggerMs?: number; durationMs?: number; lift?: number; size?: number; reverse?: boolean; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `items: readonly NavDotWaveItem[]`
  Nav entries. Each is `{ label, href? }`; the label is also the React key.
- `activeIndex: number` — default `0`
  Index of the current page. Its dot grows, takes the accent colour and stops dimming.
- `staggerMs: number` — default `60`
  Milliseconds between one dot's phase and the next.
- `durationMs: number` — default `1400`
  Full cycle of a single dot, in milliseconds.
- `lift: number` — default `3`
  Peak lift in pixels.
- `size: number` — default `5`
  Dot diameter in pixels.
- `reverse: boolean` — default `false`
  Negates the stagger so the crest runs right-to-left.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the `nav` element.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
const DOT_WAVE_CSS = `
/* 0% is the RESTING pose, not the lifted one. That matters: a positive
   animation-delay holds the element at its 0% pose until the delay expires,
   so if 0% were the lift, every dot would sit visibly raised for its share of
   the stagger on first paint and the row would settle rather than start. */
@keyframes kx-dotwave {
  0%, 60%, 100% { opacity: 0.45; translate: 0 0; }
  30%           { opacity: 1;    translate: 0 var(--kx-dot-lift, -3px); }
}

/* The current item never dims — it is a location marker, and a marker that
   fades to 45% twice a second is a marker you cannot trust. */
@keyframes kx-dotwave-active {
  0%, 60%, 100% { opacity: 1; translate: 0 0; }
  30%           { opacity: 1; translate: 0 var(--kx-dot-lift, -3px); }
}

.kx-dotwave-list {
  display: flex;
  align-items: center;
  gap: var(--kx-dot-gap, 1.5rem);
  list-style: none;
  margin: 0;
  padding: 0;
}

.kx-dotwave-link {
  display: inline-flex;
  align-items: center;
  gap: 0.5rem;
  color: var(--color-muted, currentColor);
  transition: color 200ms linear;
}

.kx-dotwave-link:hover,
.kx-dotwave-item[data-active="true"] .kx-dotwave-link {
  color: var(--color-fg, currentColor);
}

.kx-dotwave-dot {
  width: var(--kx-dot-size, 5px);
  height: var(--kx-dot-size, 5px);
  border-radius: 9999px;
  background-color: currentColor;
  flex: none;
  scale: 1;

  animation: kx-dotwave var(--kx-dot-duration, 1400ms) ease-in-out infinite;
  animation-delay: calc(var(--i, 0) * var(--kx-dot-stagger, 60ms));

  /* 'translate' and 'opacity', not 'transform' — the scale below belongs to
     the active state and has to survive independently of the wave. */
  will-change: translate, opacity;
  transition: scale 260ms cubic-bezier(0.34, 1.56, 0.64, 1);
}

.kx-dotwave-item[data-active="true"] .kx-dotwave-dot {
  animation-name: kx-dotwave-active;
  background-color: var(--color-accent, currentColor);
  scale: 1.6;
}

/* No motion: the crest is decoration, so it goes. Everything that carries
   information stays — the current item keeps its accent colour and its larger
   dot, the rest keep their dimmed one. */
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  .kx-dotwave-dot {
    animation: none;
    opacity: 0.45;
    will-change: auto;
  }
  .kx-dotwave-item[data-active="true"] .kx-dotwave-dot {
    opacity: 1;
  }
}
`;

export function NavDotWave({
  items,
  activeIndex = 0,
  staggerMs = 60,
  durationMs = 1400,
  lift = 3,
  size = 5,
  reverse = false,
  className,
}: NavDotWaveProps) {
  const rootStyle: StyleWithVars = {
    '--kx-dot-stagger': `${reverse ? -staggerMs : staggerMs}ms`,
    '--kx-dot-duration': `${durationMs}ms`,
    '--kx-dot-lift': `${-lift}px`,
    '--kx-dot-size': `${size}px`,
  };

  return (
    <>
      <style href="kinetic-nav-dot-wave" precedence="medium">
        {DOT_WAVE_CSS}
      </style>
      <nav className={cn('kx-dotwave', className)} style={rootStyle}>
        <ul className="kx-dotwave-list">
          {items.map((item, i) => {
            // The index is the only per-item data the stylesheet needs. Every
            // timing decision is derived from it in CSS.
            const itemStyle: StyleWithVars = { '--i': i };
            const active = i === activeIndex;
            return (
              <li
                key={item.label}
                className="kx-dotwave-item"
                data-active={active ? 'true' : 'false'}
                style={itemStyle}
              >
                <a
                  href={item.href ?? '#'}
                  className="kx-dotwave-link text-xs tracking-tight"
                  aria-current={active ? 'page' : undefined}
                >
                  <span className="kx-dotwave-dot" aria-hidden="true" />
                  {item.label}
                </a>
              </li>
            );
          })}
        </ul>
      </nav>
    </>
  );
}
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** Nothing imperative to tear down. The stylesheet is a React-managed `<style>` with an `href` key, so React owns its lifetime and deduplicates it across instances; unmounting the nav removes the elements and the animations with them.

**Reduced motion.** A `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` block in the component's own stylesheet sets `animation: none` and `will-change: auto` on the dots, drops them to the resting opacity, and holds the active dot at full opacity. The accent colour and the 1.6x active scale stay, so the nav still shows where you are — only the travelling crest is removed.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Putting the lift at 0% of the keyframe. `animation-delay` freezes the element at its 0% pose, so on first paint the whole row sits raised and drops in sequence — the animation appears to run once backwards before starting.
- Animating `transform` for both the lift and the active scale. The last-declared transform wins, so the active dot either loses its lift or snaps back to scale 1 every cycle. Separate `translate` and `scale` properties compose instead.
- Driving the stagger from JavaScript with a timer or a per-item inline delay string. It costs a re-render per item, drifts out of phase with the CSS clock, and stops working the moment items are added dynamically.
- Letting the active dot dim with the rest. It is the only element on the page telling the user where they are; a marker at 45% opacity for most of every cycle is worse than no marker.
- Leaving `will-change: translate, opacity` on under reduced motion. The animation is gone but the compositor layer is not, so a nav that no longer moves still holds GPU memory on every dot.
- Removing the animation under reduced motion and removing the active state with it. The accent colour and the larger dot carry information, not decoration — only the crest should go.
- Keying the list by index while items reorder. The `--i` and the label desynchronise for one frame and a dot appears to jump across the row.

## Notes

- Nothing here is JavaScript-driven: no rAF, no observers, no state. The component's entire runtime cost is one style element and one inline custom property per item, which is why it is safe in a header that mounts on every route.
- The `--i` pattern generalises. Any staggered CSS animation — list entrances, grid reveals, letter-by-letter text — can take its delay from an index custom property instead of from generated per-item rules or a JavaScript timeline.
- Set `activeIndex` from your router. `aria-current="page"` is applied to the matching link, so the state is announced as well as drawn.

## Definition of done

A crest travels left-to-right along the dots once every 1.4 s and each dot is flat for most of that time. On first paint no dot is raised. The current item's dot is accent-coloured, 1.6x larger, and never dims while its neighbours do. Set `reverse` and the crest runs the other way. With reduced motion nothing moves, but the active dot is still larger and still accented.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: In-Shader Mouse Bulge

The pointer is a screen-space quantity and the mesh is a world-space one, so something has to convert between them. Instead of unprojecting the pointer on the CPU with a raycaster, every vertex projects ITSELF once, compares its own normalised device position against the pointer, and displaces by the result. Each vertex gets an exact distance, the cost is one extra matrix multiply per vertex, and nothing about it depends on the CPU knowing the mesh's real shape.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

A soft lens that follows the cursor, measured by projecting every vertex to screen space instead of raycasting.

- Category: webgl
- Runtime cost: webgl
- Dependencies: three@^0.185.1

## How it works

1. The vertex shader runs `projectionMatrix * modelViewMatrix * vec4(pos, 1.0)` twice. The first is a probe: dividing its xy by w gives this vertex's own NDC position, which is the only common space the pointer and the geometry both live in.
2. NDC spans -1..1 on both axes whatever the viewport is, so a raw distance is stretched by the aspect ratio. The x component of the delta is multiplied by `uAspect` before the length is taken, which is what keeps the lens circular on a 16:9 canvas instead of an ellipse 1.78 times too wide.
3. The weight is `exp(-dot(delta, delta) * falloff)`. A Gaussian never actually reaches zero, so there is no radius at which the deformation visibly stops, and its derivative is continuous, so the sheen has no hard edge either — a smoothstep would give both a visible boundary ring.
4. The vertex is lifted by `bulge * uLift` and the weight is passed to the fragment shader, which pushes the centred UV outward by `centered * vBulge * uMagnify`. Lift alone is a bump; lift plus UV magnification is a lens, and that is the difference between a dent in the surface and glass sitting on top of it.
5. The second projection is the one that ships the vertex, evaluated after the displacement the first one made possible. The extra matrix multiply per vertex is the entire cost of the technique.
6. The strength uniform is damped toward the pointer's active state rather than switched, so the lens fades in on enter and out on leave instead of appearing at, and vanishing from, the last known position.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `falloff = 5`
  Tightness of the Gaussian in aspect-corrected NDC units, where the full viewport is 2 wide. At 5 the lens is roughly a third of the height across. Below ~2 it swells to cover the whole plane and reads as a global warp; above ~15 it collapses to a pinpoint that the vertex grid cannot resolve smoothly.
- `lift = 0.5`
  World units the crown rises, against a plane about 2.5 units tall at a camera distance of 3. Above ~1.2 the crown passes the camera's near plane and the lens punches a hole through itself when the cursor is centred.
- `magnify = 0.12`
  UV displacement at the crown. This is what makes it a lens rather than a bump. Above ~0.3 the magnification outruns the geometry, the texture visibly slides across the surface, and the illusion of glass breaks into a smear.
- `sheen = 0.18`
  Extra brightness at the crown. Small on purpose: the eye reads a slight highlight as curvature, and anything past ~0.4 reads as a blown-out light source instead.
- `segments = 128`
  The bulge is per-vertex, so the mesh density is the resolution of the lens. At 16 the Gaussian resolves into a faceted pyramid chasing the cursor; past ~192 the extra vertices land inside a single pixel of the highlight.
- `STRENGTH_SMOOTHING = 0.0008`
  Fraction of the gap left after one second, so the lens fades in over roughly a fifth of a second. Instant switching leaves the lens visible at the last known position for one frame after the cursor leaves, which flickers.
- `pointer smoothing = 0.0008`
  Matches the strength smoothing so the lens grows and moves at the same rate. A pointer smoothed much harder than the strength arrives late and the lens appears to be dragged; much softer and it inherits every jitter in the raw pointer stream.
- `CAMERA_FOV / CAMERA_Z = 45 / 3`
  Sets how much perspective the lift reads against. At a narrow FOV the raised crown barely changes size and the bulge looks flat; at a wide one the plane's own edges keystone enough to compete with the effect.

## API

```ts
function NdcMouseBulge(props: { strength?: number; falloff?: number; lift?: number; magnify?: number; sheen?: number; segments?: number; paint?: (ctx: CanvasRenderingContext2D, size: { width: number; height: number }) => void; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `strength: number` — default `1`
  Peak displacement weight. 0 disables the effect.
- `falloff: number` — default `5`
  Gaussian tightness. Higher is a smaller, sharper lens.
- `lift: number` — default `0.5`
  World units the crown of the bulge rises toward the camera.
- `magnify: number` — default `0.12`
  How far the lens magnifies at the crown, in UV units.
- `sheen: number` — default `0.18`
  Extra brightness at the crown.
- `segments: number` — default `128`
  Plane subdivisions per axis. The resolution of the lens.
- `paint: (ctx, size) => void`
  Override the surface. Receives a 2D context for a 1024x1024 canvas.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the wrapper via `cn`.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
export function NdcMouseBulge({
  strength = 1,
  falloff = 5,
  lift = 0.5,
  magnify = 0.12,
  sheen = 0.18,
  segments = 128,
  paint,
  className,
}: NdcMouseBulgeProps) {
  const host = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const stage = useRef<Stage | null>(null);

  const { width, height } = useResizeObserver(host);
  const { inView } = useInView(host, { threshold: 0 });
  const visible = useVisibility();
  const reduced = useReducedMotion();
  // Already in NDC, which is exactly the space the shader compares in — no
  // conversion, no cached bounding rect to go stale on scroll.
  const pointer = useSmoothPointer({ target: host, smoothing: 0.0008 });

  const [supported, setSupported] = useState(true);
  useEffect(() => setSupported(hasWebGL()), []);

  const engaged = useRef(0);

  const live = useRef({ strength, falloff, lift, magnify, sheen });
  live.current = { strength, falloff, lift, magnify, sheen };

  const ready = width > 1 && height > 1 && supported;

  useEffect(() => {
    const el = host.current;
    if (!el || !ready) return;

    let renderer: THREE.WebGLRenderer;
    try {
      renderer = new THREE.WebGLRenderer({ antialias: true, alpha: true });
    } catch {
      // A context can still be refused between the probe and the construction —
      // the tab may have hit the browser's live-context ceiling in between. three
      // throws rather than returning null, and an uncaught throw here takes the
      // page with it.
      setSupported(false);
      return;
    }
    renderer.setPixelRatio(pixelRatio());
    renderer.setSize(el.clientWidth, el.clientHeight, false);
    renderer.setClearColor(0x000000, 0);
    renderer.domElement.style.display = 'block';
    renderer.domElement.style.width = '100%';
    renderer.domElement.style.height = '100%';
    el.appendChild(renderer.domElement);

    const scene = new THREE.Scene();
    const camera = new THREE.PerspectiveCamera(CAMERA_FOV, 1, 0.1, 100);
    camera.position.z = CAMERA_Z;

    const canvas = document.createElement('canvas');
    canvas.width = TEXTURE_SIZE;
    canvas.height = TEXTURE_SIZE;
    const ctx = canvas.getContext('2d');
    if (ctx) (paint ?? paintSurface)(ctx, { width: TEXTURE_SIZE, height: TEXTURE_SIZE });

    const texture = new THREE.CanvasTexture(canvas);
    texture.colorSpace = THREE.SRGBColorSpace;
    texture.wrapS = THREE.ClampToEdgeWrapping;
    texture.wrapT = THREE.ClampToEdgeWrapping;
    texture.anisotropy = Math.min(4, renderer.capabilities.getMaxAnisotropy());

    const uniforms: BulgeUniforms = {
      uTexture: { value: texture },
      uMouseNdc: { value: new THREE.Vector2(0, 0) },
      uAspect: { value: 1 },
      uStrength: { value: 0 },
      uFalloff: { value: falloff },
      uLift: { value: lift },
      uMagnify: { value: magnify },
      uSheen: { value: sheen },
    };

    // Dense. The bulge is evaluated per vertex, so the lens can only be as
    // round as the mesh is fine: at 16 segments the Gaussian resolves into a
    // faceted pyramid that follows the cursor.
    const geometry = new THREE.PlaneGeometry(1, 1, segments, segments);
    const material = new THREE.ShaderMaterial({
      vertexShader: ndcMouseBulgeVertexShader,
      fragmentShader: ndcMouseBulgeFragmentShader,
      uniforms,
    });
    const mesh = new THREE.Mesh(geometry, material);
    // The lift happens after the bounding sphere was computed; leaving culling
    // on lets three blank a plane that is filling the viewport.
    mesh.frustumCulled = false;
    scene.add(mesh);

    stage.current = { renderer, scene, camera, mesh, geometry, material, texture, uniforms };

    return () => {
      stage.current = null;
      scene.remove(mesh);
      // Inside `uniforms`, where `disposeObject` cannot see it.
      texture.dispose();
      disposeObject(scene);
      geometry.dispose();
      material.dispose();
      disposeRenderer(renderer);
      renderer.domElement.remove();
    };
    // eslint-disable-next-line react-hooks/exhaustive-deps
  }, [ready, segments, paint]);

  useEffect(() => {
    const current = stage.current;
    if (!current || width < 1 || height < 1) return;
    const aspect = width / height;
    current.renderer.setPixelRatio(pixelRatio());
    current.renderer.setSize(width, height, false);
    current.camera.aspect = aspect;
    current.camera.updateProjectionMatrix();

    // Cover the frustum exactly at z = 0. Derived from the camera, because the
    // visible extent at this distance has no fixed relationship to the pixel
    // width of the container.
    const visibleHeight = 2 * Math.tan((CAMERA_FOV * Math.PI) / 360) * CAMERA_Z;
    current.mesh.scale.set(visibleHeight * aspect, visibleHeight, 1);
    // The shader corrects its screen-space distance with this, so a stale
    // value turns the lens into an ellipse the moment the container reshapes.
    current.uniforms.uAspect.value = aspect;
  }, [width, height]);

  useRaf(
    (dt) => {
      const current = stage.current;
      if (!current) return;
      const { strength: peak, falloff: tightness, lift: rise, magnify: zoom, sheen: light } =
        live.current;

      // Fade the whole effect in and out with the pointer rather than snapping
      // it. Snapping leaves a lens sitting at the last known position for one
      // frame after the cursor leaves, which flickers.
      const wanted = pointer.current.active && !reduced ? peak : 0;
      engaged.current = damp(engaged.current, wanted, STRENGTH_SMOOTHING, dt);

      current.uniforms.uMouseNdc.value.set(pointer.current.ndcX, pointer.current.ndcY);
      current.uniforms.uStrength.value = engaged.current;
      current.uniforms.uFalloff.value = tightness;
      current.uniforms.uLift.value = rise;
      current.uniforms.uMagnify.value = zoom;
      current.uniforms.uSheen.value = light;

      current.renderer.render(current.scene, current.camera);
    },
    ready && inView && visible,
  );
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** Removes the mesh from the scene, disposes the `CanvasTexture` explicitly because it sits inside `material.uniforms` beyond `disposeObject`'s reach, runs `disposeObject` over the scene, disposes the geometry and material, then `disposeRenderer` — `setAnimationLoop(null)`, `dispose()`, `forceContextLoss()` — and removes the canvas from the DOM. The stage ref is nulled first so a frame already queued on the shared RAF loop exits before touching anything. `useSmoothPointer` removes its own listeners on unmount.

**Reduced motion.** The strength target is held at 0, so no vertex is ever displaced, the UV is never magnified and no sheen appears — the surface is a completely static image that ignores the pointer. The value is still damped to zero rather than assigned, so a lens that is on screen when the preference changes retracts smoothly instead of popping flat.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Comparing raw NDC distances. NDC is -1..1 on both axes regardless of the viewport, so on a 16:9 canvas the falloff is 1.78 times wider than it is tall and the lens is a visible ellipse. The x component of the delta is weighted by the aspect before the length is taken.
- Raycasting the pointer against the plane instead. It costs a matrix inversion per frame, returns exactly one hit point, and — decisively — it intersects the CPU-side geometry, which this shader has already moved. Once anything displaces vertices, the raycast answers a question about a surface that is not on screen.
- Projecting once and reusing `gl_Position`. The probe has to happen before the displacement and the final projection has to happen after it, so the two cannot be shared. Displacing after computing `gl_Position` simply has no effect at all.
- Using a linear or smoothstep falloff. Both reach exactly zero at a finite radius, which draws a visible ring on the surface where the deformation stops. The Gaussian is asymptotic and leaves no boundary.
- Lifting the vertex without magnifying the UV. The result is a bump, not a lens — the surface moves but the image printed on it does not, so it reads as a dent in a rigid sheet rather than glass laid over it.
- Leaving `frustumCulled` on. The lift happens after the bounding sphere was computed, so three can decide a plane that is filling the viewport is off screen and blank it.
- Sizing the plane from the container's pixel dimensions. The plane has to cover the frustum at z = 0, which is `2 * tan(fov/2) * distance` tall; a pixel width has no fixed relationship to that and the plane ends up short of the edges or overscaled.
- Forgetting to update `uAspect` on resize. The lens silently turns elliptical the moment the container reshapes, and because it still follows the cursor correctly the bug looks like a design decision.
- Calling `renderer.dispose()` alone on unmount. GPU objects are freed but the WebGL context survives, and Chromium drops the oldest once a renderer process holds about 16. `disposeRenderer` calls `forceContextLoss`.

## Notes

- `useSmoothPointer` already exposes `ndcX` / `ndcY`, so the pointer reaches the uniform without a single conversion and without a cached bounding rect that could go stale on scroll.
- This is the same two-projections-per-vertex trick `cylinder-gallery` uses; there it has to be in-shader, because the CPU geometry is a flat plane and the visible drum exists only on the GPU.

## Definition of done

Move the cursor over the surface and a round highlight follows it, swelling the lattice cells underneath rather than merely brightening them. The highlight is circular at any container aspect — resize from square to wide and it stays round. It has no visible outer edge or ring where the effect stops. Leave the surface and the lens retracts over about a fifth of a second rather than vanishing. Nothing changes when the cursor moves outside the component. With `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` the surface is completely inert and the cursor has no effect at all.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Nested Split With True Restore

Splitting text destroys the markup inside it: a paragraph containing an `<em>` and an `<a>` goes into SplitText as semantic HTML and comes out as a flat pile of divs. This component splits into masked lines that rise into view, preserves each child element's own tag through the split, and on teardown restores the container's `innerHTML` byte-identically to what it was before anything touched it.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

Splits rich markup into masked lines and restores the original innerHTML byte-for-byte on teardown.

- Category: text
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: gsap@^3.15.0

## How it works

1. `const originalHTML = el.innerHTML` is captured **before** any pre-processing. This string is the contract — everything else is arranged so it can be reapplied exactly.
2. The nested pre-pass walks the container's element children. Each child is split to lines on its own with a throwaway `new SplitText(child, { type: "lines" })`; the line markup is read while that split is live, the split is reverted, and each line is re-emitted inside a **shallow clone** of the child (`child.cloneNode(false)`) before the child is removed. A shallow clone carries the tag and every attribute and none of the content — `cloneNode(true)` would duplicate the child's entire text into every line.
3. The container is then split for real with `new SplitText(el, { type, mask: "lines", linesClass, aria: "auto" })`, and `gsap.from(split.lines, { yPercent: 110, duration: 0.9, stagger: 0.08, ease: "power3.out" })` runs inside a `gsap.context` scoped to the element.
4. The build is deferred behind `document.fonts.ready`, because line boxes measured against the fallback face break in the wrong places and never re-flow when the real font arrives. A `cancelled` flag closes the async gap so a build cannot start after unmount.
5. Teardown runs in a fixed order: `ctx.revert()` first, so the tween's inline styles are removed while the split nodes still exist; then `split.revert()`; then `if (el.innerHTML !== originalHTML) el.innerHTML = originalHTML`.
6. That last line is the whole point. GSAP's `revert()` restores the string SplitText itself captured at construction time — which, after a nested pre-pass, is the *intermediate* markup, not the original. The explicit restore is what makes the guarantee real.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `Y = 110`
  Percent of a line's own height it starts below the mask. Past 100 rather than at it, because `mask: "lines"` clips to the line box and descenders on the first frame otherwise peek below the mask edge on tall faces.
- `DURATION = 0.9`
  Seconds per line. Long enough that `power3.out` has room for its deceleration; below ~0.5s the ease flattens and the lines read as snapping into place.
- `STAGGER = 0.08`
  Seconds between lines. About a tenth of the duration, so five or six lines are always in motion together and the block reads as one rising mass rather than as a queue.
- `VIEW_THRESHOLD = 0.25`
  Fraction of the block visible before splitting and revealing. A paragraph is tall, so requiring more than about a quarter means it must be nearly centred before anything happens.
- `cloneNode(false) = false`
  Shallow, always. `true` copies the child's descendants, so every line of a five-line paragraph contains the whole paragraph and the block renders five times its own height.

## API

```ts
function NestedSplitRestore(props: { children: ReactNode; type?: string; mask?: boolean; nested?: boolean; y?: number; duration?: number; stagger?: number; delay?: number; startOnView?: boolean; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `children: ReactNode`
  Markup to split. Element children keep their own tags and attributes through the pre-pass.
- `type: string` — default `'lines'`
  SplitText `type`. Lines are what the mask and the reveal use.
- `mask: boolean` — default `true`
  Wrap each line in an overflow-hidden box so it rises out of nothing.
- `nested: boolean` — default `true`
  Run the per-child pre-pass. Turn off for a single flat paragraph.
- `y: number` — default `110`
  Percent of a line's height it starts below the mask.
- `duration: number` — default `0.9`
  Seconds per line.
- `stagger: number` — default `0.08`
  Seconds between lines.
- `delay: number` — default `0`
  Seconds before the first line moves.
- `startOnView: boolean` — default `true`
  Split and reveal when scrolled into view rather than on mount.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the container via `cn`.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
const Y = 110;
const DURATION = 0.9;
const STAGGER = 0.08;
const VIEW_THRESHOLD = 0.25;

/**
 * Replace each element child of `host` with one shallow clone per visual line.
 * Text nodes sitting directly under `host` are left alone — they have no tag
 * to preserve, so the outer split handles them correctly already.
 */
function flattenChildrenToLines(host: HTMLElement): void {
  for (const child of Array.from(host.children)) {
    if (!(child instanceof HTMLElement)) continue;

    const inner = new SplitText(child, { type: 'lines' });
    // Read the line markup while the split is live, then put the child back
    // exactly as it was. Reading after revert would read the un-split child.
    const lines = inner.lines.map((line) => line.innerHTML);
    inner.revert();

    for (const markup of lines) {
      // cloneNode(false) — the tag and every attribute, none of the content.
      // cloneNode(true) would duplicate the child's entire text into each line.
      const clone = child.cloneNode(false);
      if (!(clone instanceof HTMLElement)) continue;
      clone.innerHTML = markup;
      host.insertBefore(clone, child);
    }
    host.removeChild(child);
  }
}

/**
 * A stable string identity for `children`: the text that will be split, plus
 * the element tags the pre-pass above re-emits around every line.
 *
 * React builds a fresh node object on every parent render for anything that is
 * not a bare string, so naming `children` in a dependency array actually says
 * "re-run whenever the parent renders, for any reason at all". Here that is
 * destructive rather than merely wasteful. The cleanup reverts the split and
 * writes `originalHTML` back; the next run re-splits and calls `gsap.from`
 * again; and because `useInView` is `once: true` the gate is still open, so it
 * happens immediately. A reader half way down the paragraph watches it drop
 * back below the mask and rise a second time, and whatever tween was in flight
 * is thrown away with the context that owned it. A sibling toggling a menu is
 * enough to trigger it.
 *
 * Dropping the dependency outright is not the fix either — the split would
 * then describe a paragraph that is no longer on screen. So the node is
 * flattened to the only things the split actually depends on, and that string
 * is the dependency. Same content, same string, no re-run.
 */
function childrenSignature(node: ReactNode): string {
  if (node === null || node === undefined || typeof node === 'boolean') return '';
  if (typeof node === 'string' || typeof node === 'number' || typeof node === 'bigint') {
    return String(node);
  }
  if (Array.isArray(node)) {
    // A separator that cannot occur in text, so ['ab', 'c'] and ['a', 'bc'] do
    // not collapse onto the same key.
    return (node as ReactNode[]).map(childrenSignature).join('\u0001');
  }
  if (isValidElement<{ children?: ReactNode }>(node)) {
    // The tag belongs in the signature: `flattenChildrenToLines` clones it
    // around each line, so <h2>Same words</h2> and <p>Same words</p> are two
    // different splits of identical text.
    const { type } = node;
    const tag =
      typeof type === 'string'
        ? type
        : (type as { displayName?: string; name?: string }).displayName ||
          (type as { name?: string }).name ||
          'component';
    return `<${tag}>${childrenSignature(node.props.children)}`;
  }
  // Iterables, portals and promises have no cheap textual identity. A constant
  // under-reports a change, which is the safe direction: the alternative is a
  // fresh value every render, i.e. exactly the bug this function exists to
  // remove.
  return '';
}

export function NestedSplitRestore({
  children,
  type = 'lines',
  mask = true,
  nested = true,
  y = Y,
  duration = DURATION,
  stagger = STAGGER,
  delay = 0,
  startOnView = true,
  className,
}: NestedSplitRestoreProps) {
  const root = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const reduced = useReducedMotion();
  const { inView } = useInView(root, { threshold: VIEW_THRESHOLD, once: true });
  // Compared by value, not by identity. The node itself still goes into the
  // tree below — only the effect's notion of "the content changed" is derived
  // from this string. See `childrenSignature` for what listing `children` here
  // costs.
  const contentKey = childrenSignature(children);

  useEffect(() => {
    const el = root.current;
    // Reduced motion never splits at all. The markup React rendered is the
    // finished state, and leaving it untouched is both the accessible answer
    // and the fast one.
    if (!el || reduced) return;
    if (startOnView && !inView) return;

    gsap.registerPlugin(SplitText);

    // Captured before the pre-pass, not after. This string is the contract.
    const originalHTML = el.innerHTML;

    let cancelled = false;
    let split: SplitText | null = null;
    let ctx: gsap.Context | null = null;

    const build = () => {
      if (cancelled) return;

      if (nested) flattenChildrenToLines(el);

      const s = new SplitText(el, {
        type,
        mask: mask ? 'lines' : undefined,
        linesClass: 'kinetic-split-line',
        // SplitText restores the original text to the accessibility tree
        // itself; without this the reveal is read out one line per node.
        aria: 'auto',
      });
      split = s;

      ctx = gsap.context(() => {
        gsap.from(s.lines, {
          yPercent: y,
          duration,
          stagger,
          delay,
          ease: 'power3.out',
        });
      }, el);
    };

    // Measuring line boxes before the webfont arrives measures the fallback,
    // so the lines break in the wrong places and never re-flow. See
    // `font-safe-text-split` for the full resize and late-font lifecycle.
    void document.fonts.ready.then(build);

    return () => {
      cancelled = true;
      // Order matters. The context reverts the tween's inline styles while the
      // split nodes still exist; reverting the split first would leave those
      // styles orphaned on nodes GSAP can no longer find.
      ctx?.revert();
      split?.revert();
      // The true restore. Only writes when something actually differs, so the
      // no-pre-pass case hands React back the very nodes it created.
      if (el.innerHTML !== originalHTML) el.innerHTML = originalHTML;
    };
  }, [
    contentKey,
    type,
    mask,
    nested,
    y,
    duration,
    stagger,
    delay,
    startOnView,
    inView,
    reduced,
  ]);
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** A `cancelled` flag guards the async `document.fonts.ready` boundary. Teardown then runs `ctx.revert()` (kills the tweens and strips their inline styles while the split nodes still exist), `split.revert()`, and finally an explicit `el.innerHTML = originalHTML` when the two differ — the true restore.

**Reduced motion.** No split happens at all — the effect returns before touching the DOM. The markup React rendered is the finished state, so the text is fully visible and fully semantic on first paint, with every `<em>` and `<a>` intact. This is both the accessible answer and the fast one.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Trusting `revert()` to restore the original markup after a nested pre-pass. SplitText snapshots `innerHTML` at construction, which by then is your intermediate line markup — `revert()` faithfully restores the wrong thing, and the `<em>` and `<a>` are gone for good.
- Splitting before the webfont loads. Lines are measured against the fallback face, so they break in the wrong places and never re-flow; the mask then clips text that has moved outside its line box. See `font-safe-text-split`.
- Using `cloneNode(true)` in the pre-pass. Each line inherits the child's full contents and the block explodes to several times its height.
- Reading the line markup after reverting the inner split. Revert restores the child to its unsplit state, so you read the whole child back and produce one "line" containing everything.
- Reverting the split before the context. GSAP's inline styles are then orphaned on nodes the context can no longer find, so a remount starts from a half-animated state.
- Letting SplitText's line divs into the accessibility tree. Without `aria: "auto"` a screen reader announces one fragment per line, mid-sentence; with it SplitText restores the original text for assistive technology.
- Splitting at all under reduced motion. There is nothing to gain and a whole DOM tree to rebuild — the markup React rendered is already the finished state.

## Notes

- This is one of the two components that deliberately use GSAP `SplitText`, because the technique *is* SplitText: nested splitting and the shortcomings of its `revert()`. `SplitText` ships inside the main `gsap` package and is free to use; it is imported from `gsap/SplitText` rather than vendored, so this is a use grant and no redistribution is involved. The other text components here split declaratively in JSX so consumers are not forced into GSAP for effects that do not need it.
- The acceptance criterion is exact and testable: after teardown, `element.innerHTML` is byte-identical to what it was before the split — tags, attributes and whitespace included, not merely visually equivalent.
- The `nested` prop can be turned off for a single flat paragraph, in which case the pre-pass is skipped and the restore write never fires because the strings already match.

## Definition of done

Record `element.innerHTML` before mounting, unmount, and compare: the two strings are byte-identical, including the `<em>` and `<a>` tags and their attributes. Visually, lines rise from behind their own mask edge, staggered, with no character visible below the mask on the first frame. A screen reader reads the paragraph as continuous prose rather than as one fragment per line. With reduced motion enabled the paragraph is fully rendered on first paint and the DOM is never modified.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Newsletter Card

A centred sign-up card: a title, a line of copy and the kit `Input` with a mail icon beside a Subscribe button, under soft coloured streaks. Submitting validates the address inline. A valid address enters a submitting state that lasts at least `submitDelay` ms. The card then shows a success panel with the address and a "Use a different address" reset, or puts the failure message on the field. With no `onSubscribe` the delay alone simulates the request.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

Email sign-up card with inline validation, a submitting state on a cleaned-up timer, success with reset, and an error path.

- Category: form
- Runtime cost: css
- Dependencies: @remixicon/react@^4.9.0

## How it works

1. Four states (`idle`, `submitting`, `success`, `error`) plus an `error` string drive the render. The form has `noValidate` and the field `validationBehavior="aria"`, so the browser never shows its own bubble. `validate(email)` returns a message or null, and the message goes into the kit Input as `isInvalid` plus `errorMessage`, rendered through React Aria's FieldError. Editing the field clears the message and leaves the error state.
2. On a valid submit the card bumps a run counter and enters `submitting`. It wraps `onSubscribe(email)` so a return, a rejection and a synchronous throw all become a settled value, and starts a `window.setTimeout(submitDelay)` stored in a ref. It waits on `Promise.all` of the two, so a fast response still shows the spinner for the full delay and a slow one holds it longer.
3. When both settle, the result applies only if the run counter still matches. A reset or unmount bumps the counter and clears the timer, so a late result from an abandoned submission cannot overwrite the current state. Failures go through `messageOf` (Error message, then string, then a fallback) and land on the field.
4. Focus follows the state. A `focusRef` names the target ("input" or "success"), and an effect keyed on `[status, error]` focuses it after the new state has rendered: the field after an invalid submit, an error or a reset, and the `tabIndex=-1` success panel after success. While submitting, the field is `isReadOnly` and the button `aria-disabled` rather than disabled, because disabling the focused element would drop focus to `<body>`.
5. A visually hidden `role="status"` paragraph announces "Subscribing…" and "Subscribed as …". The success panel enters with a 320ms fade and 6px rise from a hoisted `@keyframes`, applied only under `motion-safe`. The streaks are six blurred rounded bars in accent and chart tones, faded out downward by `mask-b-from-10% mask-b-to-100%`.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `submitDelay = 1200ms`
  The minimum time in the submitting state. Long enough to read the spinner as "working" rather than a flicker, and short enough not to feel slow. It is also the full simulated request when there is no `onSubscribe`.
- `email pattern = /^[^\s@]+@[^\s@.]+(\.[^\s@.]+)+$/`
  Catches the typos people actually make (no @, no dot in the domain, stray spaces, `name@.com`) without rejecting valid but unusual addresses. The server stays the real authority.
- `success entrance = 320ms cubic-bezier(0.2, 0.8, 0.2, 1), opacity 0 → 1, translateY 6px → 0`
  A short ease-out rise reads as the form turning into the confirmation, rather than the content being swapped.
- `form width = max-w-[380px], row from @md (28rem)`
  Fits the 380px input-and-button row of the landing card. Below 28rem of container width the button moves under the field at full width.

## API

```ts
function NewsletterCard(props: { title?: ReactNode; description?: ReactNode; placeholder?: string; submitLabel?: ReactNode; onSubscribe?: (email: string) => void | Promise<void>; submitDelay?: number; validate?: (email: string) => string | null; successTitle?: ReactNode; successMessage?: (email: string) => ReactNode; resetLabel?: ReactNode; onStatusChange?: (status: "idle" | "submitting" | "success" | "error") => void; decoration?: boolean; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `title: ReactNode` — default `"Get new components in your inbox"`
  Card heading (an h3 that labels the section).
- `description: ReactNode`
  Copy under the title.
- `placeholder: string` — default `"you@company.com"`
  Field placeholder.
- `submitLabel: ReactNode` — default `"Subscribe"`
  Button text when idle. It reads "Subscribing" while submitting.
- `onSubscribe: (email: string) => void | Promise<void>`
  Called with the trimmed, validated address. A throw or rejection shows the error state with its message.
- `submitDelay: number` — default `1200`
  Minimum time in the submitting state, in ms.
- `validate: (email: string) => string | null` — default `validateEmail`
  Returns a message to block submission.
- `successTitle: ReactNode` — default `"You're on the list"`
  Heading of the success panel.
- `successMessage: (email: string) => ReactNode`
  Body of the success panel, given the subscribed address.
- `resetLabel: ReactNode` — default `"Use a different address"`
  Reset button text.
- `onStatusChange: (status: NewsletterStatus) => void`
  Fired on every state change.
- `decoration: boolean` — default `true`
  Show the coloured streaks along the top edge.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
export function NewsletterCard({
  title = "Get new components in your inbox",
  description = "One short email when a component, block or template ships. No digests, no drip sequences, and you can leave any time.",
  placeholder = "you@company.com",
  submitLabel = "Subscribe",
  onSubscribe,
  submitDelay = 1200,
  validate = validateEmail,
  successTitle = "You're on the list",
  successMessage = (email) => (
    <>
      We'll write to <span className="font-medium text-text-primary">{email}</span> when something new ships.
    </>
  ),
  resetLabel = "Use a different address",
  onStatusChange,
  decoration = true,
  className,
}: NewsletterCardProps) {
  const [value, setValue] = useState("");
  const [status, setStatus] = useState<NewsletterStatus>("idle");
  const [error, setError] = useState<string | null>(null);
  const [subscribed, setSubscribed] = useState("");

  const inputRef = useRef<HTMLInputElement>(null);
  const successRef = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const timerRef = useRef<number | undefined>(undefined);
  const runRef = useRef(0);
  const focusRef = useRef<"input" | "success" | null>(null);
  const statusChangeRef = useRef(onStatusChange);
  const titleId = useId();

  useEffect(() => {
    statusChangeRef.current = onStatusChange;
  });

  // Unmount: stop the timer and orphan any pending result.
  useEffect(
    () => () => {
      window.clearTimeout(timerRef.current);
      runRef.current += 1;
    },
    [],
  );

  // Move focus once the next state has rendered, so keyboard users are never left on a removed node.
  useEffect(() => {
    const target = focusRef.current;
    focusRef.current = null;
    if (target === "input") inputRef.current?.focus();
    if (target === "success") successRef.current?.focus();
  }, [status, error]);

  const go = (next: NewsletterStatus) => {
    setStatus(next);
    statusChangeRef.current?.(next);
  };

  const submit = (event: FormEvent<HTMLFormElement>) => {
    event.preventDefault();
    if (status === "submitting") return;
    const email = value.trim();
    const invalid = validate(email);
    if (invalid) {
      setError(invalid);
      if (status !== "idle") go("idle");
      focusRef.current = "input";
      return;
    }

    const run = ++runRef.current;
    setError(null);
    go("submitting");

    let outcome: Promise<unknown>;
    try {
      outcome = Promise.resolve(onSubscribe?.(email)).then(
        () => null,
        (reason: unknown) => ({ reason }),
      );
    } catch (reason) {
      outcome = Promise.resolve({ reason });
    }
    const delay = new Promise<void>((resolve) => {
      timerRef.current = window.setTimeout(resolve, Math.max(0, submitDelay));
    });

    void Promise.all([outcome, delay]).then(([failure]) => {
      if (runRef.current !== run) return;
      timerRef.current = undefined;
      if (failure) {
        setError(messageOf((failure as { reason: unknown }).reason));
        focusRef.current = "input";
        go("error");
      } else {
        setSubscribed(email);
        focusRef.current = "success";
        go("success");
      }
    });
  };

  const reset = () => {
    window.clearTimeout(timerRef.current);
    runRef.current += 1;
    setValue("");
    setError(null);
    setSubscribed("");
    focusRef.current = "input";
    go("idle");
  };

  const submitting = status === "submitting";
  const announcement =
    status === "submitting" ? "Subscribing…" : status === "success" ? `Subscribed as ${subscribed}.` : "";
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** An unmount effect clears the submit timer and bumps the run counter, so a promise still in flight resolves into nothing. A reset does the same. There are no listeners or observers.

**Reduced motion.** The success entrance is behind `motion-safe:`, so with reduced motion the panel simply appears. The streaks never move, and the opacity change on success transitions only under `motion-safe`. The spinner still turns, because it is the status indicator and not decoration.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Disabling the field or button while submitting. If either has focus, the browser moves focus to `<body>` and a keyboard user has to tab back in from the top of the page. Read-only and `aria-disabled` keep focus where it was, and the submit handler ignores repeats.
- Letting a stale request finish. If someone resets, or the card unmounts mid-request, the old promise still resolves. Without the run-counter check it would flip a fresh form to success or call setState after unmount.
- Using `Promise.all([onSubscribe(), delay])` directly. A rejection short-circuits `all`, the error appears before the minimum delay, and a synchronous throw escapes the handler entirely. Settle the call into a value first.
- Leaving native validation on. `type="email"` with `required` shows the browser bubble on submit, which ignores the theme and does not reach the FieldError slot.

## Notes

- Pass your own `validate` to add rules such as blocking disposable domains. It receives the trimmed address.
- The exported `validateEmail` is the default validator, so a custom one can call it and add rules on top.

## Definition of done

Submitting an empty field shows "Enter your email address." under it, keeps focus there and makes no request. Submitting "abc" shows the format message, and typing clears it. A valid address disables repeat submits, shows "Subscribing" with a spinner for about 1.2s, then shows the success panel naming the address. "Use a different address" returns to an empty, focused field. An address that `onSubscribe` rejects shows its message on the field after the delay. Unmounting mid-submit leaves no timer running.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Not Found Page

The page a site shows when a link leads nowhere. A large gradient error code sits over a small "Error 404 · /the/path" line, so the visitor sees what they asked for. Below them come the title, a plain explanation and two ways out: Back home and Browse components. A grid of suggested destination cards follows, and an optional footnote, here machine-readable entry points for agents. Every link reports through `onNavigate`, so a client router can take over.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

A 404 block: big error code, the missing path, home and browse actions, suggested page cards and an agent footnote, staggered in.

- Category: block
- Runtime cost: css
- Dependencies: @remixicon/react@^4.9.0

## How it works

1. The root is an `@container` `<section>` with a centred `max-w-[672px]` column, so the block sizes by its own width, not the viewport. The destination grid goes from one column to two at `@xl`. The code grows from Display 2 to the 4rem Large Title, and the title from Display 4 to Display 3, at the same breakpoint.
2. The code is decorative (`aria-hidden`) and painted with `bg-linear-to-b from-text-primary to-text-tertiary bg-clip-text text-transparent`. Both stops are theme tokens, so the fade flips with dark mode. The readable "Error 404" and the path in `<code>` sit on the caption line under it.
3. The entry is pure CSS. Each band gets `transition-[opacity,translate] duration-500 ease-out` with `starting:opacity-0 starting:translate-y-2`, so the browser animates from the `@starting-style` values on first render. A step index picks a static `delay-*` class (0 to 500ms): the code, then the caption and title, the description, the actions, the card rows and the footnote.
4. Destination cards are `<a>` elements in a `<ul>` inside `<nav aria-label="Suggested pages">`. The whole card is the link target, hover lifts the surface to `background-secondary-hover`, and the arrow after the title nudges 2px (mirrored under RTL with `directionalIconClass`).
5. The actions are kit `ButtonLink`s: primary with a leading back arrow (which flips in RTL) and secondary with a grid icon. The footnote styles any `<code>` and `<a>` in its body through arbitrary child variants, and renders its links as mono underlined entries followed by "— description".

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `column = max-w-[672px], py-12 → py-20 at @3xl`
  At this width the description stays under about 75 characters a line at the 20px size, and two cards sit side by side at about 320px each.
- `entry = 500ms ease-out, 8px rise, delays 0, 75, 150, 200, 300, 400, 500ms`
  Short enough that the page is settled before the visitor has read the title, and the stagger reads top to bottom without feeling like a sequence to wait for.
- `code size = Display 2 (3rem) → Large Title (4rem) at @xl`
  The code is the first thing the eye lands on, but it stays smaller than a hero headline, so the title and the ways out keep the weight.

## API

```ts
function NotFoundPage(props: { code?: string; path?: string; title?: ReactNode; description?: ReactNode; homeAction?: { label: string; href: string } | false; browseAction?: { label: string; href: string } | false; destinations?: { title: string; description: string; href: string; icon?: ComponentType }[]; footnote?: { title: string; body?: ReactNode; links?: { label: string; href: string; description?: string }[] }; onNavigate?: (href: string, event: MouseEvent<HTMLAnchorElement>) => void; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `code: string` — default `"404"`
  The big error code, also shown as "Error {code}" in the caption.
- `path: string`
  The requested path, shown in mono after the code.
- `title: ReactNode` — default `"Page not found"`
  The h1.
- `description: ReactNode`
  The explanation under the title.
- `homeAction: { label, href } | false` — default `{ label: "Back home", href: "/" }`
  Primary button with a back arrow.
- `browseAction: { label, href } | false` — default `{ label: "Browse components", href: "/components" }`
  Secondary button with a grid icon.
- `destinations: NotFoundDestination[]` — default `[]`
  `{ title, description, href, icon? }` cards in a two-column grid.
- `footnote: NotFoundFootnote`
  `{ title, body?, links?: { label, href, description? }[] }`, shown under a divider.
- `onNavigate: (href, event) => void`
  Called for every link the block renders. `preventDefault()` there to route client-side.
- `className: string`
  Classes for the root section.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
/** Entry stagger: each band starts 8px low and transparent, then settles. Static strings so Tailwind sees them. */
const STEP_DELAYS = ["delay-0", "delay-75", "delay-150", "delay-200", "delay-300", "delay-[400ms]", "delay-500"] as const;

function rise(step: number) {
  return cx(
    "transition-[opacity,translate] duration-500 ease-out starting:translate-y-2 starting:opacity-0 motion-reduce:transition-none",
    STEP_DELAYS[Math.min(step, STEP_DELAYS.length - 1)],
  );
}

function DestinationCard({
  item,
  step,
  onNavigate,
}: {
  item: NotFoundDestination;
  step: number;
  onNavigate?: NotFoundPageProps["onNavigate"];
}) {
  const Icon = item.icon;
  return (
    <li className={rise(step)}>
      <a
        href={item.href}
        data-destination=""
        onClick={(event) => onNavigate?.(item.href, event)}
        className="group flex h-full items-start gap-3 rounded-xl border border-border-component-detail-container bg-background-secondary-default p-4 outline-none transition-colors duration-150 ease-out hover:bg-background-secondary-hover focus-visible:ring-2 focus-visible:ring-border-focus-ring motion-reduce:transition-none"
      >
        {Icon ? (
          <span className="flex size-9 shrink-0 items-center justify-center rounded-lg border border-border-button-default bg-background-primary-default shadow-xs">
            <Icon aria-hidden className="size-[18px] text-foreground-icon-secondary" />
          </span>
        ) : null}
        <span className="min-w-0 flex-1">
          <span className="flex items-center gap-1 text-headline-semibold text-text-primary">
            {item.title}
            <RiArrowRightLine
              aria-hidden
              className={cx(
                "size-4 text-foreground-icon-tertiary transition-[translate,color] duration-150 ease-out group-hover:translate-x-0.5 group-hover:text-foreground-icon-secondary motion-reduce:transition-none motion-reduce:group-hover:translate-x-0 rtl:group-hover:-translate-x-0.5",
                directionalIconClass(RiArrowRightLine),
              )}
            />
          </span>
          <span className="mt-1 block text-body-regular text-text-secondary">{item.description}</span>
        </span>
      </a>
    </li>
  );
}
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** There are no effects, timers or listeners. The entry is CSS `@starting-style` transitions, and the only handlers are React `onClick` props on the links.

**Reduced motion.** Every band has `motion-reduce:transition-none`, so under prefers-reduced-motion the `@starting-style` values never animate and the page renders settled. The card arrow nudge is removed (`motion-reduce:group-hover:translate-x-0`) and hover colours change instantly.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Building the stagger delay with string interpolation (`delay-${n}`). Tailwind only generates classes it can see, so the delays silently vanish. The delays live in a static array.
- Making the big code the only place the error appears. It is decorative and `aria-hidden`, so screen readers would never hear "404". The caption line carries it as text.
- Returning a 404 page with a 200 status. The block is visual only. In Next.js render it from `not-found.tsx` (or call `notFound()`), so the response status is 404 and crawlers drop the URL.
- Running the entry with JavaScript on mount. A hydration-timed fade flashes the content in and out on slow devices. `@starting-style` runs on first style resolution, with no effect and no state.

## Notes

- Pass `onNavigate={(href, e) => { e.preventDefault(); router.push(href) }}` for client routing. It covers the actions, the cards and the footnote links. Links inside a custom `footnote.body` are yours to wire.
- Pass the requested pathname as `path` (for example from `usePathname()`), so visitors can spot a typo.
- Set `homeAction={false}` or `browseAction={false}` to drop a button, and leave `destinations` empty to hide the grid.

## Definition of done

At 1280px a gradient "404" sits over "Error 404 · /charts/bubble-chart", then "Page not found", the explanation, and Back home and Browse components buttons. Four cards follow in two columns (Components, Documentation, Installation, MCP server), then the "Reading this site as an agent" footnote with four mono links. On load the bands rise in top to bottom. Clicking any link calls `onNavigate` with its href (the demo status reads "Would open /components"). Under reduced motion nothing moves. At 360px the cards stack in one column.
