# Build: Orders Chart Card

A 344px dashboard card that charts twelve months of orders as grouped Recharts bars, last year in neutral grey beside this year in indigo. The header shows the year total with a delta chip and the year-earlier figure. Hovering a month swaps all three for that month, and the number counts to its new value. It shares its frame and header with the revenue chart card and the stat cards, so it drops into the same dashboard row.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

A dashboard card of monthly orders as paired bars, this year beside last, whose count-up headline follows the hovered month.

- Category: display
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: recharts@^3.10.1

## How it works

1. One piece of state, `activeIndex`, drives the header. `BarChart`'s `onMouseMove` reads `state.activeTooltipIndex`, and when `isTooltipActive` is true and the index is finite it stores it. `onMouseLeave` resets it to `null`. A `<Tooltip content={() => null}>` keeps Recharts tracking the hovered category and drawing its cursor band (`fill: var(--color-chart-track)`, opacity 0.5) without rendering a tooltip box.
2. With no month hovered the headline is the sum of `current` over `data` and the comparison is the sum of `previous`. With a month hovered they are that point's two values, and the label becomes the full month name looked up from the short `label` through `MONTHS` and `MONTHS_FULL` (it falls back to the raw label).
3. `describeDelta` turns the pair into a chip. A zero `previous` gives "New" in neutral. Otherwise the percentage change is rounded to one decimal: 0 gives "0%" in neutral, a rise gives "+x%" in lime and a fall "-x%" in rose.
4. The figure is passed through `useCountUp(headlineValue)`, which eases from the shown value to the new one over 320ms with an ease-out cubic on `requestAnimationFrame`. The `<p>` holding it is keyed by `activeIndex ?? "total"`, so each change remounts it and replays `.animate-number-fade` (220ms, opacity 0.35 to 1). The digits are `tabular-nums` and formatted with `toLocaleString("en-US")`.
5. The chart fills the rest of the card through `ResponsiveContainer` at 100% by 100% inside a `min-h-0 flex-1` box. `barCategoryGap="28%"` and `barGap={3}` keep each month's pair together. The Y axis is fixed at 40px wide with `domain={[0, yMax * 1.1]}`, four ticks and `formatK` labels ("2.5k"). The X axis uses `interval="preserveStartEnd"`, so narrow cards drop middle months but keep January and December.
6. Both bars use `radius={[4, 4, 0, 0]}` and grow in over 450ms on mount. Colours are CSS variables (`--color-chart-neutral`, `--color-chart-9-active`) passed to Recharts as `fill`, so the chart follows the light and dark theme without re-rendering.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `card height = h-[344px], gap-6, px-4 pt-4 pb-3`
  Matches the revenue chart card and the stat-card rows, so chart cards placed side by side line up. The chart takes whatever height the header leaves.
- `y domain = [0, yMax * 1.1]`
  The 10% headroom keeps the tallest bar off the top edge. The axis starts at 0 because a bar's length is the value, and a cut axis would exaggerate the gap between years.
- `bar spacing = barCategoryGap 28%, barGap 3`
  A 3px gap reads the two bars as one pair, and the 28% gap between months separates pairs clearly, so twelve pairs still fit at about 560px.
- `count-up and fade = useCountUp 320ms ease-out cubic, number-fade 220ms`
  Fast enough to keep up with a pointer sweeping across months. The fade restarts on every change and covers the first frames of the count, so the swap never looks like a jump.
- `bar entrance = animationDuration 450`
  Long enough to show the bars growing on first paint, short enough to finish before a user reaches for the chart.

## API

```ts
function OrdersChartCard(props?: { data?: OrdersPoint[]; title?: string; className?: string }): JSX.Element
type OrdersPoint = { label: string; current: number; previous: number }
const ORDERS_DATA: OrdersPoint[]
```

- `data: OrdersPoint[]` — default `ORDERS_DATA`
  Twelve points, one per month, each with this year's and last year's orders.
- `title: string` — default `"Orders"`
  Header label shown while no month is hovered.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the card section, for example to set a width.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
export function OrdersChartCard({
  data = ORDERS_DATA,
  title = "Orders",
  className,
}: {
  /** Twelve points, one per month; defaults to the demo year. */
  data?: OrdersPoint[];
  /** Headline label when no month is hovered. */
  title?: string;
  className?: string;
} = {}) {
  const [activeIndex, setActiveIndex] = useState<number | null>(null);

  const totalCurrent = data.reduce((sum, point) => sum + point.current, 0);
  const totalPrevious = data.reduce((sum, point) => sum + point.previous, 0);
  const hovering = activeIndex !== null && activeIndex < data.length;
  const point = hovering ? data[activeIndex] : null;

  const headlineValue = point ? point.current : totalCurrent;
  const comparison = point ? point.previous : totalPrevious;
  const delta = describeDelta(headlineValue, comparison);
  const monthIndex = point ? MONTHS.indexOf(point.label) : -1;
  const label = point ? (monthIndex >= 0 ? MONTHS_FULL[monthIndex] : point.label) : title;
  const display = useCountUp(headlineValue);

  const yMax = Math.max(...data.map((d) => Math.max(d.current, d.previous)));

  return (
    <section
      className={cx(
        "flex h-[344px] min-w-0 flex-1 flex-col gap-6 rounded-2xl bg-background-secondary-default px-4 pt-4 pb-3",
        className,
      )}
    >
      {/* Header: label over the count-up figure and its delta; legend on the right */}
      <div className="flex w-full flex-col gap-3 sm:flex-row sm:items-start sm:justify-between">
        <div className="flex min-w-0 flex-col gap-0.5">
          <p className="w-full text-body-medium text-text-secondary">{label}</p>
          <div className="flex w-full items-center gap-2">
            <p
              key={activeIndex ?? "total"}
              className="animate-number-fade text-title-1-medium whitespace-nowrap text-text-primary tabular-nums"
            >
              {display.toLocaleString("en-US")}
            </p>
            <Chip variant="bold" color={delta.color}>
              {delta.label}
            </Chip>
          </div>
          <p className="text-body-2-medium text-text-tertiary tabular-nums">
            {comparison.toLocaleString("en-US")} {point ? "a year earlier" : "last year"}
          </p>
        </div>
        <dl className="flex shrink-0 items-center gap-4 text-body-2-medium text-text-secondary">
          <div className="flex items-center gap-1.5">
            <span className="size-2 rounded-full bg-chart-9-active" aria-hidden />
            <dt>This year</dt>
          </div>
          <div className="flex items-center gap-1.5">
            <span className="size-2 rounded-full bg-chart-neutral" aria-hidden />
            <dt>Last year</dt>
          </div>
        </dl>
      </div>

      {/* Chart */}
      <div className="min-h-0 w-full flex-1">
        <ResponsiveContainer width="100%" height="100%">
          <BarChart
            data={data}
            margin={{ top: 4, right: 6, bottom: 0, left: 0 }}
            barCategoryGap="28%"
            barGap={3}
            onMouseMove={(state) => {
              const index = Number(state?.activeTooltipIndex);
              if (state?.isTooltipActive && Number.isFinite(index)) setActiveIndex(index);
            }}
            onMouseLeave={() => setActiveIndex(null)}
          >
            <YAxis
              width={40}
              domain={[0, yMax * 1.1]}
              tickCount={4}
              tickFormatter={formatK}
              tickLine={false}
              axisLine={false}
              tick={{ fontSize: 12, fill: "var(--color-text-tertiary)" }}
            />
            <XAxis
              dataKey="label"
              tickLine={false}
              axisLine={false}
              tickMargin={12}
              interval="preserveStartEnd"
              tick={{ fontSize: 13, fill: "var(--color-text-tertiary)" }}
            />
            <Tooltip content={() => null} cursor={{ fill: "var(--color-chart-track)", opacity: 0.5 }} />
            <Bar
              dataKey="previous"
              fill="var(--color-chart-neutral)"
              radius={[4, 4, 0, 0]}
              isAnimationActive
              animationDuration={450}
            />
            <Bar
              dataKey="current"
              fill="var(--color-chart-9-active)"
              radius={[4, 4, 0, 0]}
              isAnimationActive
              animationDuration={450}
            />
          </BarChart>
        </ResponsiveContainer>
      </div>
    </section>
  );
}
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** `useCountUp` cancels its pending animation frame when the value changes and on unmount. `ResponsiveContainer` disconnects its resize observer when the card unmounts. The card adds no listeners of its own.

**Reduced motion.** There is no reduced-motion branch. The bars grow in over 450ms on mount, the headline counts over 320ms through `useCountUp` and the number fades in over 220ms on each hover change. All three are short and none moves the layout, but they play regardless of the user's setting.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Dropping the `<Tooltip>`. Without it Recharts does not track the active category, `activeTooltipIndex` never arrives in `onMouseMove`, and the headline never follows the pointer. It renders `content={() => null}` on purpose.
- Putting the card in a parent with no height. The chart is `ResponsiveContainer height="100%"` inside a flex child, and the card sets `h-[344px]` itself. Overriding that with `h-auto` collapses the chart to zero height.
- Passing more or fewer than twelve points without matching labels. The month names come from looking up `label` in `MONTHS`; a label like "Q1" still works but shows as "Q1" in the header.
- Hard-coding hex colours into the `Bar` fills. They are theme variables, so the chart follows the theme with no re-render.

## Notes

- `ORDERS_DATA` and `OrdersPoint` are exported. The default data adds up to 25,162 orders against 20,968 the year before, which the chip shows as "+20%".
- Recharts is forced to `direction: ltr` and its focus outlines are hidden by the theme stylesheet, so the chart reads left to right in an RTL page while the header mirrors.

## Definition of done

The card is 344px tall with "Orders", "25,162" (shown at once, with no count on mount), a lime "+20%" chip and "20,968 last year" in the header, and "This year" and "Last year" legend dots at the end. Twelve pairs of rounded bars grow in. Hovering a month bands it, the label becomes the full month name, and the number counts to that month's orders with its own delta. Leaving the chart returns to the total.

and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Key-Replayed Page Reveal

Two opaque layers and one CSS keyframe do the whole job of a route transition. The inbound layer carries `key={revealKey}`, so a route change unmounts it and mounts a new one — and a freshly mounted element runs its animation from frame zero, which replays the fade with no state, no library and nothing to reset. The outbound layer fades up to opaque and the navigation commits at 80% of that, while the screen is already covered, so the two halves hand off invisibly without ever referring to each other.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

An opaque overlay that fades away on every route change, replayed by nothing more than a changed React key.

- Category: transition
- Runtime cost: css
- Dependencies: none beyond React

## How it works

1. The inbound layer is `<div key={revealKey} className="kinetic-reveal-in" />`. Its animation runs `from { opacity: 1 }` to `to { opacity: 0; visibility: hidden }` over 0.55 s on `cubic-bezier(0.4, 0, 0.2, 1)` with `forwards`. Changing `revealKey` is the entire replay mechanism: React sees a different key, discards the node, mounts a new one, and the new node starts its animation at frame zero.
2. `visibility: hidden` in the `to` frame, held by `forwards`, is what retires the layer. At `opacity: 0` alone a full-viewport opaque surface stays composited for the rest of the page's life; `visibility` removes it from the compositor without unmounting anything.
3. `usePageCover(coverDuration)` returns `{ covering, cover }`. `cover(commit)` sets `covering` true — which flips `data-covering` on the outbound layer and runs `opacity: 0 -> 1` over `coverDuration` on `cubic-bezier(0.4, 0, 1, 1)` — then, after `coverDuration * 0.8` seconds, calls `setCovering(false)` and `commit()` in the same tick.
4. Both calls in one tick matters: React batches them into a single commit, so the cover drops to transparent on the exact frame the re-keyed inbound layer mounts at opacity 1. Split them across two ticks and there is one frame of bare destination content visible between the two halves.
5. The transition property is declared on the `[data-covering="true"]` rule only, never on the base rule, so release is a hard cut rather than a fade. The inbound layer is opaque and stacked above the cover at that instant, so the cut is invisible — and a symmetric fade there would compound two opacities and hold the screen dark past the end of the reveal.
6. The stylesheet is emitted through React 19's `<style href precedence>` hoisting, which dedupes by `href`. Per-instance values — durations, colour, z-index — ride in CSS custom properties set on the root, because there is only ever one copy of the rule block.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `revealDuration = 0.55`
  Seconds for the inbound fade. Under ~0.35 s the reveal reads as a flicker of the wrong colour rather than a curtain lifting; over ~0.8 s the destination is legible through a haze for long enough that people start clicking through it.
- `PAGE_COVER_DURATION = 0.32`
  Seconds for the outbound cover. Deliberately about half the reveal: leaving should feel decisive and arriving should feel gradual. Exported as a constant so the hook that times the commit and the layer that runs the transition cannot be handed two different numbers.
- `COMMIT_FRACTION = 0.8`
  Fraction of the cover the commit waits for. On `cubic-bezier(0.4, 0, 1, 1)` the layer is roughly 96% opaque at 80% of the way through, so the step to fully covered is imperceptible while a fifth of the perceived navigation latency disappears. At 1.0 every click pays a full 0.32 s of dead time; below ~0.6 the destination is visibly swapped behind a translucent sheet.
- `cover ease = cubic-bezier(0.4, 0, 1, 1)`
  Ease-in, no ease-out. The cover must be at its steepest as it approaches opaque, which is what makes 80% look like 100%. An ease-out cover crawls through its last 20% and the early commit becomes visible.
- `zIndex = 195`
  Above a custom cursor (150) and a scroll progress bar (120) — both of which must be hidden during a transition — and below a preloader (200), which must be able to sit over a reveal on first load.

## API

```ts
function PageRevealOverlay(props: { revealKey: string; revealDuration?: number; coverDuration?: number; covering?: boolean; color?: string; zIndex?: number; position?: "fixed" | "absolute"; className?: string }): JSX.Element
function usePageCover(coverDuration?: number): { covering: boolean; cover: (commit: () => void) => void }
```

- `revealKey: string`
  Identity of the current page. A change replays the reveal. `usePathname()` in Next.js.
- `revealDuration: number` — default `0.55`
  Seconds the inbound cover takes to fade away.
- `coverDuration: number` — default `0.32`
  Seconds the outbound cover takes to reach opaque. Pass the same value to `usePageCover`.
- `covering: boolean` — default `false`
  Drive from `usePageCover().covering`.
- `color: string` — default `'#000'`
  Any CSS colour. Must be opaque, or the page shows through the handoff.
- `zIndex: number` — default `195`
  Above the site and any custom cursor, below a preloader.
- `position: "fixed" | "absolute"` — default `"fixed"`
  `absolute` inside a bounded container; `fixed` for a real page transition.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the root via `cn`.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
/**
 * Seconds the outbound cover takes to reach opaque. Shared default so the hook
 * that times the commit and the layer that runs the transition cannot be given
 * two different numbers.
 */
export const PAGE_COVER_DURATION = 0.32;

/**
 * Fraction of the cover the commit waits for. On the `cubic-bezier(0.4, 0, 1,
 * 1)` cover, 80% of the way through the screen is about 96% opaque, so the
 * step to fully covered is imperceptible — and a fifth of the perceived
 * navigation latency is gone. Waiting for 100% is a fifth of a second of dead
 * time on every single click.
 */
const COMMIT_FRACTION = 0.8;

const REVEAL_CSS = `
@keyframes kinetic-page-reveal {
  from { opacity: 1; }
  to   { opacity: 0; visibility: hidden; }
}
.kinetic-reveal-root {
  /* Never eats a click, not even mid-fade. The layer is opaque and covers the
     whole viewport; one swallowed click on a nav item is a dead site. */
  pointer-events: none;
  z-index: var(--kx-reveal-z, 195);
}
.kinetic-reveal-layer {
  position: absolute;
  inset: 0;
  background: var(--kx-reveal-color, #000);
}
/* Inbound. Starts opaque because it is mounted at the moment the destination
   is mounted, and holds the end frame with 'forwards' so 'visibility: hidden'
   retires the layer from compositing instead of leaving an invisible
   full-screen surface alive for the rest of the page's life. */
.kinetic-reveal-in {
  opacity: 1;
  animation: var(--kx-reveal-duration, 0.55s) cubic-bezier(0.4, 0, 0.2, 1)
    forwards kinetic-page-reveal;
}
/* Outbound. Idle is hidden as well as transparent, for the same reason. */
.kinetic-reveal-cover {
  opacity: 0;
  visibility: hidden;
}
/* The transition is declared on the covering state ONLY, so release is a cut.
   That is deliberate: at release the re-keyed inbound layer is already sitting
   at opacity 1 directly above this one, so a second fade here would compound
   two opacities and hold the screen dark past the end of the reveal. */
.kinetic-reveal-cover[data-covering='true'] {
  opacity: 1;
  visibility: visible;
  transition: opacity var(--kx-cover-duration, 0.32s)
    cubic-bezier(0.4, 0, 1, 1);
}
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  /* Not 'animation: none' — that would leave the inbound layer parked at its
     opaque from-frame, permanently covering the site. The layers are removed
     entirely, and 'usePageCover' commits synchronously, so navigation is a
     hard cut to the destination with no flash of overlay in either direction. */
  .kinetic-reveal-layer { display: none; }
}
`;

export interface PageRevealOverlayProps {
  /**
   * Identity of the current page. A change replays the reveal. In Next.js App
   * Router this is `usePathname()`; in the demo it is a local state value.
   */
  revealKey: string;
  /** Seconds the inbound cover takes to fade away. */
  revealDuration?: number;
  /** Seconds the outbound cover takes to reach opaque. */
  coverDuration?: number;
  /** Drive from `usePageCover().covering`. */
  covering?: boolean;
  /** Any CSS colour. Must be opaque, or the page shows through the handoff. */
  color?: string;
  /** Above the site, below a preloader. */
  zIndex?: number;
  /** `absolute` to demo inside a bounded box; `fixed` for a real page. */
  position?: 'fixed' | 'absolute';
  className?: string;
}

export function PageRevealOverlay({
  revealKey,
  revealDuration = 0.55,
  coverDuration = PAGE_COVER_DURATION,
  covering = false,
  color = '#000',
  zIndex = 195,
  position = 'fixed',
  className,
}: PageRevealOverlayProps) {
  return (
    <>
      {/* React 19 hoists and dedupes by `href`, so a hundred navigations and
          any number of instances still emit exactly one rule block. Per
          instance values ride in custom properties for that reason. */}
      <style href="kinetic-page-reveal-overlay" precedence="medium">
        {REVEAL_CSS}
      </style>

      <div
        aria-hidden
        className={cn(
          'kinetic-reveal-root',
          position === 'fixed' ? 'fixed inset-0' : 'absolute inset-0',
          className,
        )}
        style={
          {
            '--kx-reveal-duration': `${revealDuration}s`,
            '--kx-cover-duration': `${coverDuration}s`,
            '--kx-reveal-color': color,
            '--kx-reveal-z': zIndex,
          } as CSSProperties
        }
      >
        {/* Cover first, reveal second: later in the DOM paints on top, and the
            inbound layer's opaque first frame is what hides the cover's cut. */}
        <div
          className="kinetic-reveal-layer kinetic-reveal-cover"
          data-covering={covering ? 'true' : 'false'}
        />
        <div key={revealKey} className="kinetic-reveal-layer kinetic-reveal-in" />
      </div>
    </>
  );
}

export interface PageCover {
  /** Feed to `PageRevealOverlay`. */
  covering: boolean;
  /** Raise the cover, then run `commit` — your navigation — under it. */
  cover: (commit: () => void) => void;
}

/**
 * The outbound half. `commit` is a callback rather than a router call so
 * nothing here depends on a routing library.
 */
export function usePageCover(coverDuration = PAGE_COVER_DURATION): PageCover {
  const [covering, setCovering] = useState(false);
  const timer = useRef<ReturnType<typeof setTimeout> | null>(null);
  const reduced = useReducedMotion();

  useEffect(
    () => () => {
      if (timer.current !== null) clearTimeout(timer.current);
      timer.current = null;
    },
    [],
  );

  const cover = useCallback(
    (commit: () => void) => {
      // Reduced motion: no cover at all, and the commit is synchronous. A
      // zero-duration cover would still be one frame of opaque colour, which
      // is a flash — the single most unpleasant thing to show someone who has
      // asked for less motion.
      if (reduced) {
        commit();
        return;
      }
      // A second click while a cover is already up would schedule a second
      // commit and navigate twice. The live timer is the lock.
      if (timer.current !== null) return;

      setCovering(true);
      timer.current = setTimeout(
        () => {
          timer.current = null;
          // Both in one tick, so React batches them into a single commit: the
          // cover drops to transparent on the exact frame the re-keyed reveal
          // layer mounts at opacity 1. Split across two ticks and there is one
          // frame of bare destination content between them.
          setCovering(false);
          commit();
        },
        coverDuration * COMMIT_FRACTION * 1000,
      );
    },
    [coverDuration, reduced],
  );

  return { covering, cover };
}
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** The only resource is the commit timer, cleared in an unmount effect and nulled so the lock cannot survive a remount. There are no listeners, no rAF and no tweens; the animations are CSS and die with the nodes React removes.

**Reduced motion.** Both layers get `display: none`, and `usePageCover` calls the commit synchronously rather than starting a timer. Navigation is a hard cut straight to the destination — no cover, no reveal, and crucially not a zero-duration overlay, which would still be one frame of opaque colour.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Animating the overlay with a tween and a timeline. There is nothing to tween: the whole reason this is bulletproof is that a remount restarts a CSS animation, so there is no in-flight animation to kill, no state to reset, and a double navigation cannot leave the overlay half-faded.
- Using `animation: none` for reduced motion. That leaves the inbound layer parked on its opaque `from` frame, permanently covering the site — the failure looks like a blank page. The layers get `display: none` and `usePageCover` commits synchronously instead.
- Committing the navigation after the cover finishes. A fifth of a second of nothing happening after a click is exactly where a visitor decides the link is broken and clicks again.
- Omitting `pointer-events: none`. A full-viewport opaque div swallows the click on whatever the visitor aims at next, and mid-transition that is usually another nav item.
- Letting `cover()` run while a cover is already up. Without the live-timer lock a fast double click schedules two commits and navigates twice, so the visitor lands one page past where they aimed.
- Leaving the finished inbound layer at `opacity: 0` without `visibility: hidden`. It is still a composited full-viewport surface, and on a page that also runs a WebGL hero it costs a measurable slice of fill rate for the rest of the session.
- Fading the cover back out symmetrically. Two opaque layers both mid-fade multiply, not add: the screen stays darker for longer and the reveal appears to stall before it starts.

## Notes

- In Next.js App Router: mount once in `app/layout.tsx` with `revealKey={usePathname()}` and `position="fixed"`, then replace nav `<Link>` elements with buttons calling `cover(() => router.push(href))`. Nothing in this file imports `next/navigation` — the commit is a callback so the same component works under React Router or a plain state switch.
- The overlay colour must be opaque. A translucent colour makes both halves show the wrong page through the handoff, which is the one artefact this technique exists to prevent.
- The root carries `aria-hidden`: it is a purely decorative surface, and a screen reader announcing it on every navigation would be worse than no transition at all.
- Browser back and forward change the key without going through `cover()`, so they get the reveal but not the cover. That is correct — a history navigation has already happened by the time your code hears about it, so there is nothing left to cover.

## Definition of done

Click a nav item: the panel fades to the overlay colour, the destination content swaps while it is covered, and the overlay fades away over roughly half a second. The heading is never visible in an intermediate state, and there is no frame where old and new content are both on screen. Click two nav items in quick succession and you land on the second one, not past it. With reduced motion the content swaps instantly with no coloured frame in either direction.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Pagination

A controlled page navigator: secondary small `Button`s for Previous and Next at either end, and a row of 32px page cells between them that collapses long ranges to first, last, a window around the current page, and "…" placeholders. The active page borrows the raised secondary-button surface; the rest are ghost cells. A `ResizeObserver` on the nav switches it to an icon-only, zero-sibling layout when its own container is narrow, so it never clips.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

Controlled pager with Previous/Next buttons, 32px page cells and ellipsis collapsing that turns compact below a 420px container.

- Category: navigation
- Runtime cost: css
- Dependencies: @remixicon/react@^4.9.0

## How it works

1. `paginationRange(current, total, sibling)` builds the item list. If `sibling * 2 + 5` (first, last, current, the siblings on both sides and two dots) is at least `total`, every page is shown. Otherwise it computes `leftSibling = max(current - sibling, 1)` and `rightSibling = min(current + sibling, total)`, and shows left dots only when `leftSibling > 2` and right dots only when `rightSibling < total - 2`.
2. The three collapsed shapes keep the row a constant length: near the start it is `1…(3 + 2·sibling), …, total`; near the end `1, …, (total − 2 − 2·sibling)…total`; in the middle `1, …, leftSibling…rightSibling, …, total`. With the default `siblingCount` of 1 this is always 7 items, so the Next button does not jump sideways as you page.
3. `useIsCompact` returns a callback ref for the `<nav>`. When the nav mounts it measures `offsetWidth` at once (during commit, so the first paint already has the right layout), then observes the border box with a `ResizeObserver`; `isCompact` is `width < 420`, and a width of 0 (hidden, not laid out) is ignored so the last layout stays. The ref's cleanup disconnects the observer when the nav unmounts. In compact mode both arrow buttons become `iconOnly` with the label moved to `aria-label`, and `paginationRange` is called with sibling 0, which trims the row to 5 items.
4. The nav is `flex w-full items-center justify-between gap-2`, so Previous sits flush left, Next flush right and the `<ul>` of cells (`gap-0.5`) floats between them. Previous is disabled on page 1 and Next on the last page, and each calls `onChange(page ∓ 1)`.
5. Each page is a `<button type="button" aria-label="Go to page N">` in a shared `cell` class: `size-8 rounded-lg text-body-medium`, centred. The current page gets `aria-current="page"` and the secondary-button surface (`border border-border-button-default bg-background-primary-default text-text-primary shadow-xs`). Others are `text-text-secondary` with `hover:bg-background-secondary-hover hover:text-text-primary`. Dots are `aria-hidden` `<li>`s in `text-text-tertiary`.
6. The cells deliberately have no transition. Animating background, shadow and colour makes the previously active number visibly fade out on every page change, which reads as a flicker.
7. With `totalPages <= 1` the component returns `null` after its hooks have run. The whole tree passes through `useTemplateCopy()`, which is the identity unless a `TemplateCopyProvider` supplies a translator for the labels.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `COMPACT_WIDTH = 420px`
  The full-label, one-sibling layout starts clipping somewhere between 380 and 420px depending on how many digits `totalPages` has. Switching at the upper end of that range means it never clips.
- `cell = size-8 (32×32), rounded-lg, gap-0.5`
  32px matches the small secondary `Button` height on either side, so the whole row shares one baseline and one height. The 2px gap keeps hover backgrounds from touching.
- `item count = siblingCount × 2 + 5 (7 at the default of 1)`
  First, last, current, the siblings and two dot slots. Keeping the count constant across the three collapsed shapes is what stops the row from changing width while paging.
- `siblingCount default = 1`
  One neighbour each side is enough to step through pages by clicking without overfilling a card footer. Compact mode forces 0.

## API

```ts
function Pagination(props: { page: number; totalPages: number; onChange: (page: number) => void; siblingCount?: number; className?: string; previousLabel?: string; nextLabel?: string; "aria-label"?: string }): JSX.Element | null
```

- `page: number`
  Current page, 1-based. Controlled.
- `totalPages: number`
  Number of pages. At 1 or fewer the component renders nothing.
- `onChange: (page: number) => void`
  Called with the target page from a cell, Previous or Next.
- `siblingCount: number` — default `1`
  Pages shown on each side of the current one. Forced to 0 below a 420px container.
- `previousLabel / nextLabel: string` — default `"Previous" / "Next"`
  Button labels, used as `aria-label` in compact mode.
- `aria-label: string` — default `"Pagination"`
  Accessible name of the `<nav>` landmark.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
const DOTS = "dots";

function range(start: number, end: number): number[] {
  return Array.from({ length: end - start + 1 }, (_, i) => start + i);
}

function paginationRange(
  current: number,
  total: number,
  sibling: number,
): (number | typeof DOTS)[] {
  // first + last + current + 2*sibling + 2 dots
  const totalPageNumbers = sibling * 2 + 5;
  if (totalPageNumbers >= total) return range(1, total);

  const leftSibling = Math.max(current - sibling, 1);
  const rightSibling = Math.min(current + sibling, total);
  const showLeftDots = leftSibling > 2;
  const showRightDots = rightSibling < total - 2;

  if (!showLeftDots && showRightDots) {
    return [...range(1, 3 + 2 * sibling), DOTS, total];
  }
  if (showLeftDots && !showRightDots) {
    return [1, DOTS, ...range(total - (2 + 2 * sibling), total)];
  }
  return [1, DOTS, ...range(leftSibling, rightSibling), DOTS, total];
}

// No transition on the cells: animating background/shadow/color makes the
// previously-active number visibly fade out ("flicker") on every page change.
const cell = "flex size-8 shrink-0 items-center justify-center rounded-lg text-body-medium";

/** Below this nav width, Previous/Next drop their labels and siblingCount
 *  clamps to 0 — the full-label, full-sibling layout starts clipping
 *  somewhere around 380–420px depending on totalPages' digit count. */
const COMPACT_WIDTH = 420;

function useIsCompact() {
  const [isCompact, setIsCompact] = useState(false);

  // A callback ref, so the observer follows the nav itself: it attaches when
  // the nav mounts (also when `totalPages` grows past 1 after a `null` render)
  // and disconnects when the nav unmounts. A mount-only effect would have run
  // once while the nav was absent and never observed it.
  const ref = useCallback((el: HTMLElement | null) => {
    if (!el) return;
    const measure = (width: number) => {
      // 0 means hidden or not laid out (display: none, a closed tab or panel).
      // Keep the last layout instead of flipping to compact, which would then
      // paint for a frame when the nav is shown again.
      if (width > 0) setIsCompact(width < COMPACT_WIDTH);
    };
    // Measure now, during commit, so the first paint already has the right
    // layout. The observer's first callback lands after that paint, so on a
    // narrow container the full labels would flash before switching.
    measure(el.offsetWidth);
    // Border box, like offsetWidth, and unaffected by a scaled ancestor.
    const observer = new ResizeObserver(([entry]) => {
      if (entry) measure(entry.borderBoxSize?.[0]?.inlineSize ?? entry.contentRect.width);
    });
    observer.observe(el, { box: "border-box" });
    return () => observer.disconnect();
  }, []);

  return [ref, isCompact] as const;
}
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** The `ResizeObserver` on the nav is disconnected by the callback ref's cleanup whenever the nav unmounts (component unmount, or `totalPages` dropping to 1). There are no timers or animation frames.

**Reduced motion.** Nothing animates. The page cells have no transitions by design, and the arrow buttons only have the shared button press, which `Button` already removes under `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Do not add `transition-colors` to the page cells. The old active cell then fades out while the new one fades in, which looks like a flicker on every click.
- Do not decide compact mode only in the `ResizeObserver` callback, and do not let a 0 width count. The first callback lands after the first paint, so a narrow pager flashes its full labels, and a hidden pager (0 wide) would flip to compact and flash that when shown again.
- Do not switch to compact mode on a viewport media query. The pager lives in cards and table footers, so it observes its own nav width with a `ResizeObserver`.
- Do not drop the `aria-label` on the icon-only arrows. In compact mode the visible label is gone and the button would otherwise be announced as just "button".
- Do not use the array index as the key for page cells. They are keyed by page number so a cell keeps its identity, and focus, when the window shifts. Only the dots use an index key.
- Do not treat it as uncontrolled. It renders whatever `page` it is given and only reports clicks through `onChange`, so the parent must store the page.

## Notes

- The observer follows the nav, not the component: if `totalPages` starts at 1 (the pager renders `null`) and grows later, the nav attaches and is measured then; dropping back to 1 disconnects it.
- The arrow icons come through `Button`, which mirrors directional glyphs in RTL, so Previous and Next point the reading direction automatically.

## Definition of done

With page 3 of 10 the row reads Previous, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, …, 10, Next, with 3 raised and bordered. Clicking 4 moves the raised cell instantly with no fade and the row becomes 1, …, 3, 4, 5, …, 10, still seven items. Previous is disabled on page 1 and Next on page 10. Narrowing the container below 420px turns both arrows into icon-only buttons and the row becomes 1, …, 3, …, 10 without clipping. Each page cell announces "Go to page N" and the current one has `aria-current="page"`.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Staggered Panel Wipe

The counter, the word list and the exit wipe are three parts of a single `gsap.timeline`, not three independent animations racing each other. The number is tweened on a plain object with `power2.inOut`, so it accelerates and settles instead of ticking linearly — the difference between a loading count and a progress bar wearing a costume.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

An eased 0-100 counter, a word list and a five-column wipe, all on one timeline so they cannot drift.

- Category: transition
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: gsap@^3.15.0

## How it works

1. A plain object `{ v: 0 }` is tweened to 100 over `countDuration` seconds. `onUpdate` writes `String(Math.round(count.v)).padStart(3, "0")` into a ref'd span. Tweening the object rather than the DOM keeps the eased value in one place and means the number is interpolated by the same engine, on the same clock, as everything else on the timeline.
2. The words are placed with `tl.set(wordEl, { textContent: w }, i * step)` where `step = countDuration / words.length` — for five words over 1.6 s that is one word every 320 ms. Because they are positioned on the timeline rather than scheduled with `setTimeout`, they stay locked to the counter if the timeline is retimed, paused, or seeked.
3. When the count lands, the content block leaves on `yPercent: -120, opacity: 0` over 0.5 s with `power3.inOut`. -120 rather than -100 clears the block past its own height plus a margin, so a descender never lingers at the top edge.
4. The five columns then retract with `scaleY: 0` and `transformOrigin: "top"`, 0.9 s of `power4.inOut`, staggered 0.08 s apart, inserted at `-=0.2` so the wipe begins while the content is still leaving. `scaleY` is a compositor-friendly transform; animating `height` here would relayout five elements every frame.
5. The whole build runs inside `useGsap`, which wraps it in a `gsap.context` scoped to the root and calls `ctx.revert()` on unmount, so a preloader torn down mid-count leaves no inline transforms behind.
6. Only after the timeline's `onComplete` fires does React set `gone` and return `null`. Unmounting on a timer instead would pull the nodes out from under running tweens.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `countDuration = 1.6`
  Seconds for 0 to 100. Under ~1.2 s the digits change too fast to read as a count and the word list flickers; over ~2.5 s people have already decided the site is slow.
- `CONTENT_DURATION = 0.5`
  Content exit. Long enough to read as a departure rather than a cut, short enough that it is finished before the panels have opened far enough to reveal what is behind it.
- `PANEL_DURATION = 0.9`
  Per-column retract. `power4.inOut` spends most of its time near the ends, so a shorter duration collapses the slow start and the whole wipe reads as a single instant cut.
- `PANEL_STAGGER = 0.08`
  Gap between columns. At 0 the five columns are one panel; past ~0.15 the last column is still standing after the first has finished, which reads as a stuck element rather than a sequence.
- `PANEL_OVERLAP = 0.2`
  Seconds the wipe is pulled back into the content exit. Without the overlap there is a dead beat between the number disappearing and the panels moving, and that pause is where the eye decides something has hung.
- `padStart(3, "0") = 3`
  Fixed three-digit width. Without it the counter changes character count at 10 and 100 and the number visibly jumps sideways twice mid-tween.

## API

```ts
function PanelWipePreloader(props: { words?: string[]; panels?: number; countDuration?: number; onDone?: () => void; position?: "fixed" | "absolute"; className?: string }): JSX.Element | null
```

- `words: string[]` — default `['Assets', 'Type', 'Shaders', 'Layout', 'Ready']`
  Words shown under the counter, spread evenly across the count.
- `panels: number` — default `5`
  Number of collapsing columns.
- `countDuration: number` — default `1.6`
  Seconds the counter takes to reach 100.
- `onDone: () => void`
  Fires from the timeline's `onComplete`, after the last column has collapsed.
- `position: "fixed" | "absolute"` — default `"fixed"`
  Use `absolute` inside a bounded container; `fixed` for a real full-page preloader.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the root via `cn`.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
export function PanelWipePreloader({
  words = ['Assets', 'Type', 'Shaders', 'Layout', 'Ready'],
  panels = 5,
  countDuration = 1.6,
  onDone,
  position = 'fixed',
  className,
}: PanelWipePreloaderProps) {
  const root = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const content = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const counter = useRef<HTMLSpanElement>(null);
  const word = useRef<HTMLSpanElement>(null);
  const reduced = useReducedMotion();
  const [gone, setGone] = useState(false);

  const done = useRef(onDone);
  done.current = onDone;

  useGsap(
    gsap,
    () => {
      const el = root.current;
      const contentEl = content.current;
      const counterEl = counter.current;
      const wordEl = word.current;
      if (!el || !contentEl || !counterEl || !wordEl) return;

      const columns = Array.from(el.querySelectorAll<HTMLElement>('[data-wipe-panel]'));

      if (reduced) {
        counterEl.textContent = '100';
        wordEl.textContent = words[words.length - 1] ?? '';
        setGone(true);
        done.current?.();
        return;
      }

      const count = { v: 0 };
      const tl = gsap.timeline({
        onComplete: () => {
          setGone(true);
          done.current?.();
        },
      });

      tl.to(count, {
        v: 100,
        duration: countDuration,
        ease: 'power2.inOut',
        onUpdate: () => {
          counterEl.textContent = String(Math.round(count.v)).padStart(3, '0');
        },
      });

      // Positioned on the SAME timeline as the counter, at computed times, so
      // the words stay locked to the number no matter how the timeline is
      // retimed, paused or seeked.
      const step = countDuration / Math.max(words.length, 1);
      words.forEach((w, i) => {
        tl.set(wordEl, { textContent: w }, i * step);
      });

      tl.to(contentEl, {
        yPercent: -120,
        opacity: 0,
        duration: CONTENT_DURATION,
        ease: 'power3.inOut',
      });

      if (columns.length > 0) {
        // transformOrigin top + scaleY 0 retracts each column upward like a
        // blind. The -0.2 overlap fuses the wipe with the tail of the content
        // exit so the two read as one gesture.
        tl.to(
          columns,
          {
            scaleY: 0,
            transformOrigin: 'top',
            duration: PANEL_DURATION,
            ease: 'power4.inOut',
            stagger: PANEL_STAGGER,
          },
          `-=${PANEL_OVERLAP}`,
        );
      }
    },
    root,
    [reduced],
  );
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** `useGsap` runs the whole build inside a `gsap.context` scoped to the root and calls `ctx.revert()` on unmount, which kills the counter tween, the positioned `set` calls and the panel stagger, and restores every property they touched — including the span's original `textContent`.

**Reduced motion.** No timeline is built at all. The counter is written straight to 100, the last word is set, the component unmounts itself and `onDone` fires on the same tick — so a reduced-motion visitor sees the real page immediately rather than a silent panel that still has to be waited out.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Driving the counter with `setInterval` and the panels with GSAP. Two clocks, and on a loaded main thread the number finishes after the wipe has already covered it.
- Tweening a linear counter. It is the ease that sells the count — `power2.inOut` slows near 100, which is the shape of real work finishing.
- Animating panel `height` instead of `scaleY`. Five elements relayouting every frame on a page that is simultaneously mounting its real content is the one place the jank is guaranteed to be visible.
- Unmounting the preloader on a `setTimeout` sized to match the timeline. The two drift under load; unmount from `onComplete` instead.
- Leaving the preloader in the tree with `opacity: 0`. It still swallows every click on the page underneath. This returns `null`.
- Forgetting `transformOrigin: "top"`. The default centre origin makes the columns shrink to a band in the middle of the screen instead of retracting like a blind.

## Notes

- In a Next.js App Router project this mounts once in `app/layout.tsx`, above `{children}`, and calls `onDone` to flip a context flag the hero listens to. It is deliberately not keyed to the pathname — a preloader that replays on every navigation is a bug, not a feature.
- If the real site has an actual load signal (fonts ready, hero image decoded), gate `onDone` on both the timeline and that promise. See `safe-preloader` for the ceiling-and-floor version of that problem.
- The counter is decorative. The root carries `aria-hidden`, so a screen reader is never read a number climbing to 100.

## Definition of done

The number counts 000 to 100 with a visible ease, never changing width. Five words swap under it at even intervals and the last word lands as the number does. The content lifts away and five columns retract upward in sequence, the wipe starting before the content has finished leaving. `onDone` fires once, after the last column. With reduced motion the preloader is gone on the first frame. Unmount mid-count and no transforms or altered text remain.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Patients Table

A patient list for a clinic dashboard. A toolbar shows the result count (and how many rows are picked) next to status and condition filters and a rounded search field; the table lists each patient with a selection checkbox, initials avatar, name and age, an inline admission select, a coloured status pill, condition chips, the next appointment with the last visit under it, and three row actions. Selection, sorting and paging run on React Aria's own Table state, with selection kept across pages and filters.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

A clinic patient list: initials, age, admission select, status pill, conditions, next and last visit, row selection, sort, filter, pages.

- Category: display
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: @internationalized/date@^3.12.4, @remixicon/react@^4.9.0, react-aria-components@^1.22.1

## How it works

1. Rows are filtered in a `useMemo` by status, condition and a case-insensitive name search, then copied and sorted when the React Aria `sortDescriptor` names a sortable column: `name` uses `localeCompare`, `nextAppointment` compares ISO strings, and a missing date always sorts last.
2. The sorted rows are sliced into pages of `pageSize` (default 6). The page index is clamped to the page count so a filter that shrinks the list never leaves an empty page, and every filter, search keystroke and sort change resets to page 1. The kit `Pagination` footer appears only when there is more than one page.
3. The table uses React Aria `selectionMode="multiple"`: a `Checkbox slot="selection"` in the Patient column header is the select-all-on-this-page box (React Aria makes it indeterminate for a partial page) and one in each Patient cell selects the row. Clicking anywhere else on a row also toggles it.
4. Selection is one `Set` of patient ids (controlled via `selectedKeys` or uncontrolled via `defaultSelectedKeys`). React Aria only receives the ids on the visible page; its `onSelectionChange` result, `"all"` meaning every id on the page, replaces that page's ids in the full set, so picks on other pages and on filtered-out rows survive.
5. Inline controls are React Aria buttons (the admission `Select` trigger, the chart and edit buttons, the more-menu `DropdownTrigger`), whose presses stop at the button and never toggle the row. Admission changes live in a per-id state map and call `onAdmissionChange`; row actions call `onAction(action, patient)`.
6. Dates are ISO strings parsed with `parseDate` and printed with an `@internationalized/date` `DateFormatter` (`month: "short", day: "2-digit", year: "numeric"`, UTC), so server and client render the same "Oct 03, 2026".

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `pageSize = 6`
  Default rows per page; the demo uses 5 so the card fits a dashboard panel.
- `table min width = 1060px`
  Six columns keep their widths; narrower viewports scroll the table inside its own overflow-x-auto wrapper.
- `search width = 153px`
  Matches the kit data table search pill; it grows to fill the row on mobile.

## API

```ts
export function PatientsTable({ patients, pageSize = 6, selectedKeys, defaultSelectedKeys, onSelectionChange, onAdmissionChange, onAction, conditionOptions, locale = "en-US", className, "aria-label": ariaLabel = "Patients" }: PatientsTableProps): JSX.Element
```

- `patients: Patient[]`
  Rows: id, name, optional initials/avatarColor/age, admission, status, conditions, optional lastVisit and nextAppointment ISO dates.
- `pageSize: number` — default `6`
  Rows per page.
- `selectedKeys: Iterable<Key>`
  Controlled selected patient ids, kept across pages and filters.
- `defaultSelectedKeys: Iterable<Key>`
  Initial selection when uncontrolled.
- `onSelectionChange: (keys: Set<Key>) => void`
  Called with the full selection after any checkbox or row press.
- `onAdmissionChange: (id: string, admission: Admission) => void`
  Called when a row's admission select changes.
- `onAction: (action: PatientAction, patient: Patient) => void`
  Chart, edit, book, message or archive from the row actions.
- `conditionOptions: string[]`
  Condition filter options; defaults to every condition in the data.
- `locale: string` — default `"en-US"`
  Locale for the date columns and the result count.
- `className: string`
  Classes on the outer section.
- `aria-label: string` — default `"Patients"`
  Accessible name of the table.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
// Filter → sort → page. Selection is kept as one Set of ids across every
// page; React Aria only ever sees the ids that are on the visible page, and
// its answers are merged back so off-page picks are never lost.
const selected = useMemo(
  () => (selectedKeys !== undefined ? new Set(selectedKeys) : ownSelection),
  [selectedKeys, ownSelection],
);

const rows = useMemo(() => {
  const q = query.trim().toLowerCase();
  const filtered = patients.filter(
    (p) =>
      (statusFilter === "all" || p.status === statusFilter) &&
      (conditionFilter === "all" || p.conditions.includes(conditionFilter)) &&
      (q === "" || p.name.toLowerCase().includes(q)),
  );
  if (!sort || !SORTABLE.has(sort.column)) return filtered;
  const dir = sort.direction === "ascending" ? 1 : -1;
  return [...filtered].sort((a, b) =>
    sort.column === "name"
      ? a.name.localeCompare(b.name, locale) * dir
      : compareOptional(a.nextAppointment, b.nextAppointment, dir),
  );
}, [patients, query, statusFilter, conditionFilter, sort, locale]);

const totalPages = Math.max(1, Math.ceil(rows.length / pageSize));
const currentPage = Math.min(page, totalPages);
const pageRows = rows.slice((currentPage - 1) * pageSize, currentPage * pageSize);
const pageSelection = new Set<Key>(pageRows.filter((p) => selected.has(p.id)).map((p) => p.id));

const commitSelection = (next: Set<Key>) => {
  if (selectedKeys === undefined) setOwnSelection(next);
  onSelectionChange?.(next);
};

const handleSelectionChange = (keys: Selection) => {
  const pageIds = pageRows.map((p) => p.id);
  const next = new Set(selected);
  for (const id of pageIds) next.delete(id);
  for (const id of keys === "all" ? pageIds : keys) next.add(id);
  commitSelection(next);
};

const resetPage = () => setPage(1);
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** No timers, listeners or observers of its own; the Select, Dropdown and Tooltip release their popovers when unmounted.

**Reduced motion.** Nothing moves except colour transitions; the sort chevron flip and the row button colour fades are dropped with motion-reduce:transition-none.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Do not hand React Aria the full selection set: it only knows the rendered page, so `"all"` would be read as every patient. Merge its answer back into the page's ids only.
- Do not use the kit IconButton (a plain <button>) for row actions inside a selectable row; a React Aria Button keeps the press from toggling selection.
- Do not format dates with `toLocaleDateString` on a `Date` built in local time; parse ISO strings with `parseDate` and format in UTC so SSR and hydration agree.

## Notes

- The condition filter lists every condition found in `patients` unless `conditionOptions` is passed.
- Age and last visit are optional per patient and are simply omitted when missing; a missing next appointment shows an em dash.

## Definition of done

Ticking a row checkbox adds it to "N selected", the header box selects the whole page, sorting Patient orders names A to Z, the status filter narrows the rows, and choosing a new admission does not change selection.

and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Pause, Don't Unmount

A rotating stack of slabs mounted twice over: once behind `<Activity mode="hidden">` and once behind a plain conditional, switchable live. Hiding tears the Effects down either way — the WebGL context is released, which is what you want, since contexts are a scarce per-process resource. What Activity keeps is everything React owns: the fiber, the DOM, and every `useState` and `useRef` value inside. So the stack resumes at the angle it left, and the build counter on its fiber survives to be incremented again. Requires React 19.2 or newer.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

React 19's Activity hides a WebGL scene without losing its state. Effects still tear down, so the GL context is genuinely released.

- Category: primitive
- Runtime cost: webgl
- Dependencies: three@^0.185.1

## How it works

1. `<Activity mode="hidden">` does three separable things, and conflating them is where the misuse starts: it sets `display: none` on the host children, it destroys the Effects inside — cleanup functions run, in order, exactly as on unmount — and it keeps the fiber alive, so state, refs and DOM nodes are all still there when `mode` goes back to `visible`. Children continue to re-render, at a priority below anything visible.
2. Because Effects are destroyed, the scene's cleanup runs on every hide: materials and geometry are disposed and `disposeRenderer` calls `renderer.forceContextLoss()`. That is the correct behaviour rather than a shortfall — Chromium hands out roughly sixteen WebGL contexts per renderer process and evicts the oldest past that, so a context parked behind `display: none` is the thing that blanks an unrelated canvas three sections down the page.
3. The rotation phase lives in a `useRef` inside the hidden subtree, and the build Effect seeds the slab rotations from it BEFORE the first draw. On re-show the scene is correct on frame one; there is no snap from zero up to the resumed angle. Under the `unmount` arm the same ref is a fresh zero because the fiber it lived on was collected.
4. The build counter is the proof, and it needs both halves to move: it increments inside the Effect, so it only rises if the Effect really re-ran, and it survives between runs only if the fiber was preserved. Under `activity` it climbs 1, 2, 3; under `unmount` it is pinned, because each show starts a new fiber whose counter is new too.
5. Build cost is measured with `performance.now()` from the top of the Effect to the end of the first completed `render`, so it covers context acquisition, program linking and the initial upload — the work Activity does not save. On a desktop GPU it lands in the tens of milliseconds; the point of the readout is that the number is not zero.
6. The size hook re-seeds synchronously from `getBoundingClientRect` on every Effect run, and its state is preserved across the hide as well, so the re-shown scene already knows its dimensions and skips the zero-sized first render that a fresh mount has to pass through. That one saved render round-trip is a second, quieter thing the preserved fiber buys.
7. The renderer creates its own canvas inside the Effect and it is removed in cleanup. A React-rendered `<canvas ref>` cannot work here: with `forceContextLoss()` in cleanup, StrictMode's double-invoke hands the second run a permanently dead element, and Activity turns that from a once-per-mount hazard into a once-per-toggle one.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `GAP = 0.2`
  Vertical spacing between slabs in world units, at a slab height of 1.15. Tight enough that the group reads as one stack rather than seven separate cards, wide enough that the back-to-front transparent sort has visible separation to work with.
- `TWIST = 0.24`
  Radians of rotation between neighbouring slabs — about 14 degrees, so seven slabs fan through 84 degrees, just under a quarter turn. Past a full turn the stack becomes rotationally ambiguous and "it resumed where it left" stops being checkable by eye.
- `count / period = 7 / 24`
  Seven slabs at 24 seconds a revolution: 15 degrees per second. Slow enough that a hide and a show a second apart leaves a gap the eye can measure against the readout, which is the entire experiment.
- `CAM_Y / CAM_Z = 2.05 / 4.4`
  A camera lean of about 25 degrees above the stack. Flatter and the slabs collapse into a single silhouette; steeper and it reads as a plan view where the vertical stacking disappears.
- `opacity ramp = 0.34 to 0.80`
  Bottom slab to top. The ramp is what makes the stack legible through itself; a constant alpha turns seven slabs into one muddy plane.

## API

```ts
function PauseDontUnmount(props: { strategy?: 'activity' | 'unmount'; count?: number; period?: number; color?: string; accent?: string; seed?: number | string; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `strategy: 'activity' | 'unmount'` — default `'activity'`
  Which arm the switch starts on.
- `count: number` — default `7`
  Slabs in the stack.
- `period: number` — default `24`
  Seconds for one full rotation.
- `color: string` — default `'#5f6873'`
  Colour of the bottom slab.
- `accent: string` — default `'#e8e4dc'`
  Colour of the top slab. The stack lerps between the two.
- `seed: number | string` — default `'pause-dont-unmount'`
  Seeds the per-slab size jitter.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the host element via `cn`.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
useEffect(() => {
  const el = host.current;
  if (!el || !ready) return;

  if (!hasWebGL()) {
    setUnsupported(true);
    return;
  }

  // Timed from here to the first completed draw: allocating the context,
  // linking the programs and uploading the geometry are what re-showing
  // actually costs, and the number is the honest counterweight to "Activity
  // makes hiding free".
  const t0 = performance.now();

  // The renderer makes its own canvas inside the effect. Two reasons, and
  // both bite here: StrictMode double-invokes this effect, so a React-owned
  // `<canvas ref>` would be handed back after `forceContextLoss()` killed
  // it; and Activity destroys and re-runs this effect on every show, which
  // is the same hazard once per toggle instead of once per mount.
  let renderer: THREE.WebGLRenderer;
  try {
    renderer = new THREE.WebGLRenderer({ antialias: true, alpha: true });
  } catch {
    // A context can still be refused between the probe and the construction —
    // the tab may have hit the browser's live-context ceiling in between. three
    // throws rather than returning null, and an uncaught throw here takes the
    // page with it.
    setUnsupported(true);
    return;
  }
  renderer.setPixelRatio(pixelRatio());
  renderer.setClearAlpha(0);

  const scene = new THREE.Scene();
  const camera = new THREE.PerspectiveCamera(FOV, 1, 0.1, 100);
  camera.position.set(0, CAM_Y, CAM_Z);
  camera.lookAt(0, 0, 0);

  const geometry = new THREE.PlaneGeometry(SLAB_W, SLAB_H);
  const rng = createRng(seed);
  const base = new THREE.Color(color);
  const tint = new THREE.Color(accent);

  const slabs: Slab[] = [];
  const span = Math.max(count - 1, 1);

  for (let i = 0; i < count; i += 1) {
    const t = i / span;
    const material = new THREE.MeshBasicMaterial({
      color: base.clone().lerp(tint, t),
      transparent: true,
      opacity: 0.34 + 0.46 * t,
      side: THREE.DoubleSide,
      // The slabs are flat and stacked along Y with nothing between them, so
      // the transparent pass sorted back to front is already correct. Writing
      // depth would let the upper slabs clip the lower ones they overhang.
      depthWrite: false,
    });
    const mesh = new THREE.Mesh(geometry, material);
    const k = 0.66 + rng() * 0.46;
    mesh.scale.set(k, k, 1);
    mesh.position.y = (i - span / 2) * GAP;
    scene.add(mesh);
    slabs.push({ mesh, material });
  }

  el.appendChild(renderer.domElement);
  renderer.domElement.style.display = 'block';
  renderer.domElement.style.width = '100%';
  renderer.domElement.style.height = '100%';

  const resize = (w: number, h: number) => {
    renderer.setSize(w, h, false);
    camera.aspect = w / Math.max(h, 1);
    camera.updateProjectionMatrix();
    dirty.current = true;
  };
  resize(size.current.width, size.current.height);

  // Seed the scene from the PRESERVED phase before the first draw. Under
  // Activity this is wherever the stack was when it went away; under a
  // conditional the ref is new and this reads zero. Doing it before the
  // timed draw also means the resumed frame is correct on frame one, with
  // no snap from zero to the real angle.
  for (let i = 0; i < slabs.length; i += 1) {
    const slab = slabs[i];
    if (slab) slab.mesh.rotation.set(-Math.PI / 2, 0, phase.current + i * TWIST);
  }
  renderer.render(scene, camera);

  builds.current += 1;
  buildMs.current = performance.now() - t0;

  stage.current = { renderer, scene, camera, slabs, geometry, resize };
  report(true);

  return () => {
    stage.current = null;
    for (const slab of slabs) {
      scene.remove(slab.mesh);
      slab.material.dispose();
    }
    geometry.dispose();
    // Not optional. `dispose()` alone leaves the context alive and counting
    // against the per-process budget; only `forceContextLoss()`, which
    // `disposeRenderer` calls, actually gives it back. Every hide runs this.
    disposeRenderer(renderer);
    renderer.domElement.remove();
  };
}, [ready, count, color, accent, seed, report]);
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** The Effect removes each slab and disposes its material, disposes the one shared geometry, calls `disposeRenderer` — which stops the loop, disposes the renderer and calls `forceContextLoss()` — and removes the canvas it appended. This runs on unmount, on a StrictMode double-invoke, and on every Activity hide, so it is exercised constantly rather than once. `useRaf` unsubscribes and the shared loop parks when its last subscriber leaves; the `ResizeObserver` unobserves with its hook. A separate Effect reports the scene as gone on teardown so the readout does not freeze on a stale row.

**Reduced motion.** The stack holds still — the phase is integrated from delta time, so freezing it is a matter of adding nothing — and with nothing marking the frame dirty the renderer draws once per build and then idles. The demonstration survives the loss of motion because it was never really about the motion: the build counter still climbs under `activity` and stays pinned under `unmount`, and the rebuild cost in milliseconds is still charged on every show. Only the resumed rotation angle stops being informative, since both arms sit at zero degrees.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Expecting Activity to keep the WebGL context alive. It does not, by design — Effects are destroyed on hide, so your cleanup runs and the context is released. If you had assumed otherwise and skipped disposal, you leak instead; if you assumed re-showing is free, the rebuild millisecond readout says otherwise.
- Lifting the state you wanted preserved above the boundary. Anything outside the `<Activity>` was never at risk, and anything the parent owns is not evidence of anything. The value has to live on a fiber inside the boundary or the comparison proves nothing.
- Changing the element at the boundary position instead of changing `mode`. Swapping `<Activity>{scene}</Activity>` for `{scene}` reconciles as a different type at that slot, so React unmounts the subtree and every preserved value goes with it. Keep the boundary mounted and toggle `mode`.
- Treating hidden as unrendered. Children keep re-rendering, only at a lower priority, so a parent state update still walks the hidden subtree. Anything expensive in render — not in an Effect — is still paid for while hidden.
- Assuming a ref into hidden DOM behaves the same as a ref into visible DOM. The DOM nodes themselves survive, but ref attachment is part of the layout-effect phase that the offscreen path tears down and replays, and this component does not depend on the answer either way. Do the work in an Effect, which is re-run on show, rather than caching a node in a closure that outlives the hide.
- Handing three's renderer a React-rendered `<canvas ref>`. Cleanup calls `forceContextLoss()`, and the next Effect run — from StrictMode or from a re-show — is given the same dead element. Let the renderer build its own canvas in the Effect and remove it in cleanup.
- Reading the build counter in development and taking the absolute number literally. StrictMode double-invokes Effects on mount, so the first build reads 2, not 1. The claim to check is the shape: climbing under `activity`, pinned under `unmount`.

## Notes

- `Activity` is exported from `react` from 19.2 (verified against 19.2.8: `exports.Activity = REACT_ACTIVITY_TYPE`, typed as `ExoticComponent<ActivityProps>` with `mode?: "hidden" | "visible"`). On anything older the import is undefined at runtime, not a build error, which fails as a blank subtree.
- The strongest real use is not a canvas at all — it is a tab, a route the user is likely to come back to, or a filter panel: scroll offsets, uncontrolled input values and list virtualisation windows are all preserved for free, and none of them cost a GPU context to rebuild.
- Pre-rendering the other direction, `mode="hidden"` on a subtree that has never been visible, mounts it at low priority without running Effects. Useful for warming a route, useless for warming a renderer, for the same reason as above.

## Definition of done

On `activity`: press hide, wait, press show. The stack picks up at the angle the readout froze at, `builds` has gone up by one, and the rebuild cost is a real number of milliseconds. On `unmount`: the same sequence returns the stack to zero degrees and `builds` never moves. Hide on either arm and the canvas is gone from the DOM inspector under `unmount` but present with `display: none` under `activity`. Neither arm accumulates WebGL contexts — toggle twenty times and the other previews on the page stay drawn.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.
