# Build: Sidebar

A floating `<aside>` with an account switcher at the top, Quick Search, the primary nav and, at the bottom, Support, Settings and a team card. One button folds it from 260px to a 60px rail. The panel width animates, and every label, badge and shortcut hint blurs and narrows away while the icons stay where they were. The account and team cards open React Aria popovers beside the rail, and Settings opens the kit's `SettingsModal`.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

A floating dashboard sidebar that folds from 260px to a 60px icon rail, with ⌘L nav search, team and account menus and a settings entry.

- Category: block
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: @remixicon/react@^4.9.0, react-aria-components@^1.22.1

## How it works

1. Collapsing animates two things on the same 300ms ease-in-out clock. The aside's `width` goes from 260px to 60px, and each text slot is wrapped in `Collapsible`, which moves `max-width` from full to 0, `opacity` from 1 to 0 and `filter` from blur(0) to blur(3px). The icons are never re-centred, so they stay pinned to the left edge while the panel closes over them.
2. Each row is an `<a>` with `aria-label`, `aria-current` on the selected row and a `title` tooltip only while collapsed. The selected row is filled with a top-to-bottom accent gradient and `shadow-nav-selected`, and its badge switches to the primary colour. Rows passed through `items` are filtered against the search query by a separate `NavRows` component, so the closures over the query and `collapsed` stay out of the sidebar body.
3. Quick Search has three ways in: the button, ⌘L or Ctrl+L, and expanding the rail first if it is collapsed. All of them set `searchActive`. The field replaces the button with a 2px inset ring and its input is focused one animation frame later, once it exists. A document `click` listener closes the search when a click lands outside the field. Escape clears it and puts focus back on the trigger on the next frame. Support and Settings are filtered too, and "No results" appears only when nothing in either list matches.
4. The scroller is wider than the rail by 16px (`-m-2 p-2 w-[calc(100%+16px)]`). A vertical `overflow-y: auto` box also clips horizontally, so without that extra room the selected row's ring, the focus rings and the account trigger's 6px hover pill would be cut off at the rail edge. The negative margin gives the space back, so nothing moves.
5. The account and team cards are React Aria `DialogTrigger` + `Popover` pairs, 265px wide and offset 8px. The account menu opens to the right and aligned to the top of its trigger, and the team menu to the right and aligned to the bottom. In RTL they open to the left, and below 640px they drop under the trigger. Both animate 150ms ease-out from `data-[entering]` / `data-[exiting]` states at opacity 0, scale 0.95 and blur 2px. React Aria handles focus containment, Escape and outside-click dismissal.
6. Expanding the rail sets `suppressHover` on the account trigger. Its hover pill is drawn by a `::before` with `-inset-x-1.5 -inset-y-[5px]`. Without the flag, the newly expanded trigger would slide under a pointer that has not moved and light its pill. The flag is cleared on the trigger's next `pointerleave`.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `rail widths = 260px expanded, 60px collapsed (px 11, py 12)`
  The collapsed width is 1px border + 11px padding on each side, which leaves exactly 36px, the width of a `w-9` icon row. So icons sit centred in the rail without being moved, and the selected fill fits the column with no clipping.
- `collapse timing = 300ms ease-in-out, label blur 3px`
  Width, label fade and icon flip share one duration, so the panel edge and the disappearing text arrive together. A 3px blur is enough to soften the text as it is squeezed, so it never reads as being cut off.
- `popover motion = 150ms ease-out, scale 0.95, blur 2px, offset 8px`
  Menus are opened often and should feel instant, so they run at half the rail's duration. A 0.95 scale from the corner nearest the trigger (`origin-top-left` / `origin-bottom-left`) makes the panel read as coming out of the card.
- `search shortcut = ⌘L / Ctrl+L on window`
  Matches the Kbd hint on the button. The handler calls `preventDefault`, so while the sidebar is mounted the shortcut opens the nav search instead of focusing the browser's address bar.
- `mobile breakpoint = (max-width: 639px)`
  Below Tailwind's `sm`, the sidebar can span the whole viewport, and a 265px popover placed to its right would render off-screen. Both menus switch to `bottom start` under that query.

## API

```ts
interface DashboardNavItem { key: string; label: string; icon: IconComponent; href?: string; badge?: string | number }
const DASHBOARD_NAV: DashboardNavItem[]
function DashboardSidebar(props?: { mobile?: boolean; onClose?: () => void; fluid?: boolean; showThemeToggle?: boolean; selected?: DashboardNavKey; items?: DashboardNavItem[]; flat?: boolean; className?: string }): JSX.Element
function DashboardTeamMenu(props: { collapsed?: boolean; className?: string; showThemeToggle?: boolean }): JSX.Element
function DashboardUserMenu(props: { collapsed?: boolean; suppressHover?: boolean; onHoverSuppressionEnd?: () => void; avatarClassName?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `selected: string` — default `"home"`
  Key of the row drawn in the filled accent state.
- `items: DashboardNavItem[]` — default `DASHBOARD_NAV`
  Primary navigation rows: key, label, icon component, optional href and badge.
- `showThemeToggle: boolean` — default `true`
  Shows the light/dark segmented control above the footer. It toggles the document theme, so hide it when the sidebar is used as artwork.
- `fluid: boolean` — default `false`
  Expanded width fills the container below `lg` instead of a fixed 260px. The collapsed rail stays 60px.
- `mobile: boolean` — default `false`
  Drawer mode: always expanded, with a close button in place of the collapse toggle.
- `onClose: () => void`
  Called by the mobile close button.
- `flat: boolean` — default `false`
  Removes the border, radius and shadow and paints the full background.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the aside.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
/**
 * Collapsible text/badge slot: blurs + fades + shrinks away when the rail
 * closes, and blurs back in on expand. The icons/rows themselves stay pinned in
 * place — only these label/badge slots animate — so nothing jumps to center.
 */
function Collapsible({ collapsed, children, className }: { collapsed: boolean; children: ReactNode; className?: string }) {
  const localize = useTemplateCopy();
  return localize((
    <span
      className={cx(
        "flex min-w-0 items-center overflow-hidden transition-[max-width,opacity,filter] duration-300 ease-in-out",
        // Expanded, the cap is the row itself: a fixed cap (it was 160px)
        // clipped any label wider than it, "Components and Blocks" included.
        collapsed ? "max-w-0 opacity-0 blur-[3px]" : "max-w-full opacity-100 blur-none",
        className,
      )}
    >
      {children}
    </span>
  ));
}

function NavItem({
  icon: Icon,
  label,
  badge,
  isSelected = false,
  collapsed = false,
  href = "#",
  onClick,
}: {
  icon: IconComponent;
  label: string;
  badge?: ReactNode;
  isSelected?: boolean;
  collapsed?: boolean;
  href?: string;
  /** Action rows (e.g. Settings → modal) intercept the navigation. */
  onClick?: () => void;
}) {
  const localize = useTemplateCopy();
  return localize((
    <a
      href={href}
      onClick={
        onClick
          ? (event) => {
              event.preventDefault();
              onClick();
            }
          : undefined
      }
      aria-current={isSelected ? "page" : undefined}
      aria-label={label}
      title={collapsed ? label : undefined}
      className={cx(
        "flex items-center justify-between overflow-hidden rounded-2lg p-2",
        "transition-[width,background-color] duration-300 ease-in-out",
        collapsed ? "w-9" : "w-full",
        isSelected
          ? "bg-linear-to-b from-accent-500 to-accent-600 shadow-nav-selected"
          : "hover:bg-background-secondary-hover",
      )}
    >
      <span className="flex min-w-0 items-center gap-2">
        <Icon
          className={cx("size-5 shrink-0", isSelected ? "text-white" : "text-foreground-icon-secondary")}
          aria-hidden
        />
        <Collapsible collapsed={collapsed}>
          <span
            className={cx(
              "text-body-medium whitespace-nowrap",
              isSelected ? "text-white" : "text-text-secondary",
            )}
          >
            {label}
          </span>
        </Collapsible>
      </span>
      {badge && <Collapsible collapsed={collapsed}>{badge}</Collapsible>}
    </a>
  ));
}
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** Every listener is scoped to an effect: the window `keydown` for ⌘L (always), the document `click` for outside-click (only while search is active) and the rAF that focuses the search input (cancelled if search closes first). Each is removed on unmount or when its condition ends. The account menu removes its `matchMedia` change listener, and the team menu reads the same query through `useSyncExternalStore`, which unsubscribes itself. React Aria tears down the popovers' focus scope and dismiss handlers when they close.

**Reduced motion.** Not handled. The rail width, label blur, search field and popover transitions run at full duration under `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`, and none of the three files uses `motion-reduce:` variants. The motion is short (150 to 300ms) and never loops, but to honour the setting add `motion-reduce:transition-none` to the aside, `Collapsible` and the two popovers. The theme toggle, when shown, already skips its view-transition reveal under reduced motion.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Clipping the nav scroller to the rail's own box. `overflow-y: auto` forces `overflow-x` to clip too, and the selected ring, the focus rings and the account trigger's hover pill all extend past the rows. Keep the padded, negatively-margined scroller.
- Centring icons when the rail collapses (`justify-center` on the rows). The icons then jump sideways while the width animates. Only the label slots should change. The 60px rail is sized so the left-aligned icons already end up centred.
- Animating labels with `width` or `display`. `display: none` cannot transition, and a fixed `max-width` cap (an earlier version used 160px) truncates long labels such as "AI Image Generation". The slot animates `max-width` between `full` and 0.
- Rendering two sidebars on one page. Each registers its own window ⌘L listener, so a single shortcut opens search in both.
- Rendering the sidebar inside a parent without a height. The aside is `h-full` and its nav scrolls inside it, so a parent with no height gives the nav nothing to scroll in and the footer is pushed below the fold.

## Notes

- `items` replaces the primary rows (the default is `DASHBOARD_NAV`), and `selected` takes any row `key`. Rows without an `href` fall back to `#`, so a host app that routes client-side should pass real paths.
- `flat` drops the floating panel treatment for a sidebar revealed beneath mobile content. `mobile` swaps the collapse button for a close button, and with `flat` it turns search into an expanding pill next to the account trigger.
- Settings is an action row. Its click handler calls `preventDefault` and opens `SettingsModal`, so the settings dialog comes with the sidebar as a registry dependency.

## Definition of done

The sidebar fills the page height beside the content, with Home selected and its 152 badge. Clicking the fold icon narrows the panel to a 60px rail as labels, badges and the ⌘L hint blur away, and the icons do not move sideways. Clicking it again restores everything. Pressing ⌘L or Ctrl+L, or clicking Quick Search, opens a ringed search field (expanding the rail if needed). Typing filters the rows, "zzz" shows "No results", and Escape or a click outside closes it. Clicking the Jordan Lee trigger opens an account list to the right that blurs and scales in, and clicking the Acme team card opens the team menu to the right, aligned with the card's bottom edge. Escape closes either. Settings opens the settings dialog, which is closed until then.

and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Site Footer

The footer that closes a marketing site. The brand mark and tagline sit on the left, with social buttons and one call to action on the right. Up to six link columns follow, each with an optional "View all (N) →" link. The bottom bar holds the Language Select, the kit theme toggle, a centre slot (the demo uses the accent swatches companion) and the copyright and legal links. Every link reports through `onLinkClick`, so a client router can take over.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

Marketing footer: logo, tagline and socials, six link columns with View all counts, then a language, theme, swatch and legal bar.

- Category: block
- Runtime cost: css
- Dependencies: @remixicon/react@^4.9.0

## How it works

1. The root is an `@container` `<footer>` with a top border. Inside, a `max-w-[1152px]` column has three bands: the brand row, a `<nav aria-label="Footer">` grid, and the bottom bar. Layout follows the footer's own width, not the viewport: the brand row splits left and right from `@3xl`, and the grid goes from 2 columns to 3 at `@xl` and 6 at `@5xl`.
2. Socials branch on `count`. Without one, a social renders the kit `IconLinkButton` (36px square) named by `label`. With one, it renders a secondary `ButtonLink` with the icon and the count as visible text, named "GitHub stars, 2.4k". All socials open in a new tab with `rel="noopener noreferrer"`.
3. Each column is an uppercase caption `h2` over a `ul` of links. A `badge` renders a status-blue pill after the label. `viewAll` adds a medium-weight link with a tertiary "(N)" and an arrow that nudges 2px on hover and flips under RTL.
4. The bottom bar is a one-column grid that becomes `grid-cols-[1fr_auto_1fr]` from `@3xl`. That keeps the centre slot centred whatever the widths of the language and theme controls on the left and the legal text on the right. `language` takes `LanguageSelect` props (or `false`) and `themeToggle` renders the kit `ThemeToggle` as a small segmented control.
5. `AccentSwatches` (companion) is a `role="radiogroup"` of `role="radio"` buttons with a roving tab stop. Only the checked dot has `tabIndex=0`. Arrow keys (mirrored under RTL), Home and End move focus and select. Each dot is SVG artwork: a linear gradient through its stops, a white radial highlight at (35%, 30%) and a 12% black hairline.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `content width = max-w-[1152px], px-0 from a 1200px container`
  This matches the landing page grid, so the footer columns line up with the sections above. Below 1200px, 16 or 24px gutters return.
- `grid breakpoints = 2 cols, @xl (36rem) 3 cols, @5xl (64rem) 6 cols`
  Six columns of about 170px need 64rem before "Marketing Dashboard" fits on one line. Three columns keep two rows readable on tablets.
- `link rhythm = gap-3 between Body 1 links, mt-4 under the heading`
  A roughly 33px row pitch makes a 9-link column about 300px tall, so all six columns end on the same baseline band.
- `swatch = 24px dot, gap-1.5, ring-2 + ring-offset-1 when checked, hover scale 1.1 over 150ms`
  The ring offset leaves a gap in the bar colour between the dot and the ring, so the checked state reads on every hue, including the pale spectrum dot.

## API

```ts
function SiteFooter(props: { logo?: ReactNode; brandLabel?: string; brandHref?: string; tagline?: ReactNode; socials?: FooterSocial[]; cta?: ReactNode; columns: FooterColumn[]; language?: false | LanguageSelectProps; themeToggle?: boolean; bottomCenter?: ReactNode; copyright?: ReactNode; legal?: FooterLink[]; onLinkClick?: (href: string, event: MouseEvent<HTMLAnchorElement>) => void; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `columns: FooterColumn[]`
  `{ title, links: { label, href, badge?, external? }[], viewAll?: { href, count?, label? } }` per column.
- `logo: ReactNode`
  Brand mark, wrapped in a link to `brandHref`.
- `brandLabel: string` — default `"Home"`
  Accessible name of the logo link.
- `brandHref: string` — default `"/"`
  Logo link target.
- `tagline: ReactNode`
  Paragraph under the logo, at most 430px wide.
- `socials: FooterSocial[]` — default `[]`
  `{ label, href, icon, count? }`. With `count` it renders a labelled button, otherwise an icon button.
- `cta: ReactNode`
  Action after the socials, e.g. a "Get Pro" `ButtonLink`.
- `language: false | LanguageSelectProps` — default `{}`
  Props for the bottom-bar Language Select, or false to hide it.
- `themeToggle: boolean` — default `true`
  Show the kit segmented ThemeToggle.
- `bottomCenter: ReactNode`
  Centre slot of the bottom bar, e.g. `<AccentSwatches />`.
- `copyright: ReactNode`
  Leading text of the legal line.
- `legal: FooterLink[]` — default `[]`
  Links after the copyright, separated by middle dots.
- `onLinkClick: (href, event) => void`
  Called for every footer link. `preventDefault()` there to route client-side.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
export function SiteFooter({
  logo,
  brandLabel = "Home",
  brandHref = "/",
  tagline,
  socials = [],
  cta,
  columns,
  language = {},
  themeToggle = true,
  bottomCenter,
  copyright,
  legal = [],
  onLinkClick,
  className,
}: SiteFooterProps) {
  const click = (href: string) => (event: MouseEvent<HTMLAnchorElement>) => onLinkClick?.(href, event);

  return (
    <footer className={cx(styles.root, className)}>
      <div className={styles.inner}>
        <div className={styles.top}>
          <div className="min-w-0">
            {logo ? (
              <a
                href={brandHref}
                aria-label={brandLabel}
                onClick={click(brandHref)}
                className={cx(styles.link, "inline-flex")}
              >
                {logo}
              </a>
            ) : null}
            {tagline ? <p className={styles.tagline}>{tagline}</p> : null}
          </div>

          {socials.length > 0 || cta ? (
            <div className={styles.actions}>
              {socials.map((social) =>
                social.count !== undefined ? (
                  <ButtonLink
                    key={social.label}
                    href={social.href}
                    variant="secondary"
                    leadingIcon={social.icon}
                    aria-label={countLabel(social)}
                    onClick={click(social.href)}
                    {...externalProps(true)}
                  >
                    {social.count}
                  </ButtonLink>
                ) : (
                  <IconLinkButton
                    key={social.label}
                    href={social.href}
                    icon={social.icon}
                    aria-label={social.label}
                    onClick={click(social.href)}
                    {...externalProps(true)}
                  />
                ),
              )}
              {cta}
            </div>
          ) : null}
        </div>

        <nav aria-label="Footer" className={styles.grid}>
          {columns.map((column) => (
            <div key={column.title} className="min-w-0">
              <h2 className={styles.heading}>{column.title}</h2>
              <ul className={styles.list}>
                {column.links.map((link) => (
                  <li key={link.href}>
                    <a
                      href={link.href}
                      onClick={click(link.href)}
                      className={styles.link}
                      {...externalProps(link.external)}
                    >
                      {link.label}
                      {link.badge ? <span className={styles.badge}>{link.badge}</span> : null}
                    </a>
                  </li>
                ))}
                {column.viewAll ? (
                  <li>
                    <a
                      href={column.viewAll.href}
                      onClick={click(column.viewAll.href)}
                      className={cx(styles.link, styles.viewAll)}
                    >
                      {column.viewAll.label ?? "View all"}
                      {column.viewAll.count !== undefined ? (
                        <span className="text-body-regular text-text-tertiary">({column.viewAll.count})</span>
                      ) : null}
                      <RiArrowRightLine
                        aria-hidden
                        className="size-4 transition-transform duration-150 ease-out group-hover/view:translate-x-0.5 motion-reduce:transition-none motion-reduce:group-hover/view:translate-x-0 rtl:-scale-x-100"
                      />
                    </a>
                  </li>
                ) : null}
              </ul>
            </div>
          ))}
        </nav>

        <div className={styles.bottom}>
          <div className={styles.bottomStart}>
            {language !== false ? <LanguageSelect {...language} /> : null}
            {themeToggle ? <ThemeToggle appearance="segmented" size="small" /> : null}
          </div>
          <div className={styles.bottomCenter}>{bottomCenter}</div>
          {copyright || legal.length > 0 ? (
            <p className={styles.legal}>
              {copyright ? <span>{copyright}</span> : null}
              {legal.map((link, i) => (
                <span key={link.href} className="inline-flex items-center gap-2">
                  {copyright || i > 0 ? <span aria-hidden>·</span> : null}
                  <a
                    href={link.href}
                    onClick={click(link.href)}
                    className={styles.legalLink}
                    {...externalProps(link.external)}
                  >
                    {link.label}
                  </a>
                </span>
              ))}
            </p>
          ) : null}
        </div>
      </div>
    </footer>
  );
}
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** There are no effects, timers or listeners. The swatch keyboard handler is a React prop on the radio group. The Language Select and ThemeToggle own and clean up their own listeners.

**Reduced motion.** All motion is hover feedback: link colour fades, the View all arrow nudge and the swatch scale. They are CSS transitions with `motion-reduce:` variants that remove the transition and the transform. The theme toggle keeps the kit behaviour.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Using viewport breakpoints. A footer placed in a narrower shell, such as a docs layout with a sidebar, would still get six columns and overflow. Container queries size it by its own width.
- Repeating the same SVG gradient `id` in two marks or swatches. Browsers resolve `url(#id)` to the first match, so a later swatch can paint with another's gradient. Ids come from `useId()`.
- Giving every swatch `tabIndex=0`. Tab would then stop seven times in the bottom bar. A radio group has one tab stop and uses the arrow keys inside.

## Notes

- Pass `onLinkClick={(href, e) => { e.preventDefault(); router.push(href) }}` for client-side routing. External links (`external: true`) can be skipped in that handler.
- The theme toggle is the kit `ThemeToggle`. It writes the document theme and persists it, so set `themeToggle={false}` when the host page already has one.

## Definition of done

At 1280px the footer shows the logo and tagline on the left and X, Discord, a "2.4k" GitHub button and Get Pro on the right. Six columns follow, Components and Charts ending in "View all (96) →" and "View all (18) →", and Affiliate carries an "Earn 40%" pill. The bottom bar reads, left to right: the English select and the sun/moon toggle, seven centred colour dots, then "© 2026 Tessera Labs · Privacy · Terms · License". Clicking a link calls `onLinkClick` with its href. Tabbing reaches the swatches once, and ArrowRight checks the next dot. At 360px the columns become two and the bottom bar stacks.

and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Site Header

The landing page's top bar: a brand lockup, a row of nav links where any link with `items` becomes a menu button, and an action cluster of search pill, social icons, GitHub star count, a free slot and the kit ThemeToggle. It responds to its own width through a container query, so the same header collapses to a menu button that opens the kit Drawer whenever its container is under 896px, whatever the window size.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

Marketing header with a menu link, a ⌘K search pill, a GitHub star pill and the theme toggle, folding into a drawer in narrow containers.

- Category: block
- Runtime cost: css
- Dependencies: @remixicon/react@^4.9.0

## How it works

1. The `<header>` is an `@container/site-header`. Every responsive switch is a container variant (`@4xl/site-header:` = 56rem = 896px): the desktop `<nav>`, the socials/GitHub/actions/theme cluster and the full search pill appear at that width, and the menu IconButton hides at it. Media queries are never used, so a header placed in a narrow column or a scaled preview still picks the right layout.
2. Links with an `items` array render through `NavMenu`, which wraps the kit `Dropdown`. Open state lives in the header (`openMenu` holds the label of the one open menu), so opening a second menu closes the first. The trigger is a React Aria button (Enter, Space and Escape for free); its chevron rotates 180deg on open; the panel holds plain `<a>` rows, so destinations keep native link behaviour, and picking a row calls `onNavigate` then closes the panel.
3. Current page: `isCurrentLink` marks a link current when its `href`, or any row of its menu, equals `currentHref`. Current anchors get `aria-current="page"`, which the shared link class styles as primary text, and current menu rows take the dropdown hover fill.
4. The search trigger is a `<button>` that calls `onSearch`. The shortcut chip is display only (it sets `aria-keyshortcuts="Meta+K"` for the default label); the key binding belongs to whatever the search opens, e.g. the kit CommandPalette, whose `shortcut="k"` already toggles it. Below 896px the pill shrinks to a 40px icon button.
5. The narrow layout puts the same data in a `DrawerTrigger` + `Drawer placement="end" size="sm"`: plain links become full-width menu rows, each menu becomes a labelled group of its rows, and the GitHub pill, actions and a ThemeToggle sit under a divider. Every row calls `close()` from the Drawer render prop after `onNavigate`, so navigating dismisses the sheet.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `bar height = h-[72px]`
  Matches the reference: a 40px control row (search pill, GitHub pill, theme toggle) with 16px of air above and below.
- `collapse width = @4xl (896px container)`
  Below it the four links plus a 220px search pill, two socials, the GitHub pill, Get Pro and the toggle no longer fit on one line at 1280px max width.
- `search pill = w-[220px] h-10 rounded-full`
  Wide enough for "Quick Search" plus the ⌘K chip without truncation; 40px matches the toggle and GitHub pill so the cluster shares one baseline.
- `menu panel = w-[320px]`
  Room for a 32px icon tile plus a one-line description; the default 266px menu width wraps the descriptions.

## API


- `links: SiteHeaderLink[]` — default `[]`
  `{ label, href?, items? }`. A link with `items` (`{ label, href, description?, icon? }`) becomes a menu button.
- `currentHref: string`
  Marks the matching link or menu row with `aria-current="page"`.
- `onNavigate: (href, event) => void`
  Called for every link and row; prevent the default for client routing.
- `onSearch: () => void`
  Search trigger press. Omit it to hide the trigger.
- `searchLabel: string` — default `"Quick Search"`
  Pill text and the trigger's accessible name.
- `searchShortcut: string` — default `"⌘K"`
  Shortcut chip in the pill. Display only.
- `socials: SiteHeaderSocial[]` — default `[]`
  Icon links (`{ label, href, icon }`) before the GitHub pill.
- `githubHref / githubStars: string / number`
  GitHub pill target and compact-formatted star count.
- `actions: ReactNode`
  Extra controls before the theme toggle; repeated in the drawer.
- `showThemeToggle: boolean` — default `true`
  Renders the kit ThemeToggle (segmented) on the end edge and in the drawer.
- `sticky: boolean` — default `false`
  Pins the bar to the top of its scroll container.
- `brand / brandHref: ReactNode / string` — default `SiteHeaderLogo / "/"`
  Lockup on the start edge and its link.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
/** A link counts as current when it, or any row of its menu, matches the page. */
function isCurrentLink(link: SiteHeaderLink, currentHref: string | undefined) {
  if (currentHref === undefined) return false;
  return link.href === currentHref || (link.items ?? []).some((item) => item.href === currentHref);
}

/**
 * A nav link with rows: a real menu button (Enter, Space, Escape, outside
 * press all handled by the kit Dropdown) whose panel holds plain anchors, so
 * middle-click and "open in new tab" still work on every destination. The
 * chevron flips with the open state; picking a row closes the panel.
 */
function NavMenu({
  link,
  items,
  currentHref,
  isOpen,
  onOpenChange,
  onNavigate,
}: {
  link: SiteHeaderLink;
  items: SiteHeaderMenuItem[];
  currentHref: string | undefined;
  isOpen: boolean;
  onOpenChange: (open: boolean) => void;
  onNavigate: SiteHeaderProps["onNavigate"];
}) {
  return (
    <Dropdown isOpen={isOpen} onOpenChange={onOpenChange}>
      <DropdownTrigger className={cx(linkClass, "cursor-pointer", isCurrentLink(link, currentHref) && "text-text-primary")}>
        {link.label}
        <RiArrowDownSLine
          aria-hidden
          className={cx(
            "size-4 transition-transform duration-200 ease-out motion-reduce:transition-none",
            isOpen && "rotate-180",
          )}
        />
      </DropdownTrigger>
      <DropdownPopover aria-label={link.label} className="w-[320px]">
        {items.map((item) => (
          <MenuRow
            key={item.href}
            item={item}
            current={item.href === currentHref}
            onClick={(event) => {
              onNavigate?.(item.href, event);
              onOpenChange(false);
            }}
          />
        ))}
      </DropdownPopover>
    </Dropdown>
  );
}
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** Nothing of its own: no listeners, timers or effects. The Dropdown and Drawer clean up their overlays and outside-press listeners when they close or unmount.

**Reduced motion.** The menu chevron's rotation transition is removed with `motion-reduce:transition-none`; the kit Dropdown and Drawer apply their own reduced-motion fades. Colour hover transitions stay because they do not move anything.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Using `md:` / `lg:` media variants for the collapse. The header then follows the window, not its container, and shows the desktop row inside a narrow column (or the mobile row in a scaled preview).
- Binding ⌘K inside the header as well as in the search it opens. Two listeners on the same key open and immediately close the palette; keep the chip display-only.
- Rendering menu rows as buttons that set `location`. Rows are anchors on purpose, so middle-click, copy link and open-in-new-tab work.
- Forgetting `event.preventDefault()` in `onNavigate` when routing on the client: the anchor then performs a full navigation as well.

## Notes

- The ThemeToggle is the kit's own: it switches the whole document's theme and persists the choice, so two headers on one page stay in sync.
- `SiteHeaderLogo` is exported for reuse in footers; pass any node as `brand` to replace it.

## Definition of done

At 1280px the bar shows the logo, Components with a chevron, Templates, Docs, Blog, a Quick Search pill with ⌘K, two social icons, a GitHub pill reading 963, Get Pro and the theme toggle. Clicking Components opens a panel of three rows; choosing Charts closes it and marks Components current. Escape closes the panel. Clicking the search pill opens the command palette. In a 390px container only the logo, a search icon and a menu button show; the menu button opens an end drawer listing every link, and choosing one closes the drawer.

and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Skeleton

Placeholders in the shape of the content on its way: rectangles, text lines and circles tinted from the text colour at 8%, so they show on any surface in both themes. A sheen sweeps each block in three layers (a crisp 2px line, a 72px glow and a 240px bloom). Given children, a Skeleton lays the real content out invisibly to take its exact size, then cross-fades the block away while the content sharpens in from a 4px blur.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

Content-shaped placeholders with a layered light sheen that size themselves to real content and blur it in once loaded.

- Category: display
- Runtime cost: css
- Dependencies: none beyond React

## How it works

1. Paint every block with `bui-skeleton block bg-text-primary/8` plus a radius per shape: `rounded-xl` (rect), `rounded-md` (text) or `rounded-full` (circle). The 8% text-colour tint is what keeps the block visible on light and dark cards alike.
2. Draw the sheen in CSS on `.bui-skeleton::after` (in the kit theme sheet): three right-anchored `linear-gradient(90deg, transparent, <colour>)` layers sized 2px, 72px and 240px, so nothing soft runs ahead of the crisp leading line. `.bui-skeleton` sets `overflow: hidden; isolation: isolate` and leaves positioning to the component's `relative` / `absolute` classes.
3. Animate the pseudo-element with `bui-skeleton-sheen`: `translate` from -100% to 100% over the first 60% of a 2.2s `cubic-bezier(0.4, 0, 0.2, 1)` cycle, then rest off-block until the loop restarts. `:dir(rtl)` flips it with `scale: -1 1` and `animation-direction: reverse`. Dark mode lowers the three layer alphas from 0.9 / 0.55 / 0.35 to 0.2 / 0.08 / 0.04.
4. Without children, render one `<span aria-hidden>` block sized by the caller's `className` (`h-4 w-40`, `size-10`).
5. With children, render a `relative block` wrapper holding two layers: the real content in a `<span>` that is `opacity-0 motion-safe:blur-[4px]`, `inert` and `aria-hidden` until `isLoaded`, and an `absolute inset-0` skeleton block on top. When `isLoaded` flips, the content goes to `opacity-100 blur-[0px]` and the block to `opacity-0`, both via `transition-[opacity,filter] duration-300 ease-out`.
6. `SkeletonText` maps `lines` to `text`-shaped Skeletons in a `flex flex-col gap-2.5` column, each `lineClassName` tall (default `h-3.5`), with the last line at `w-3/5` when there is more than one line.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `block tint = bg-text-primary/8`
  Derived from the text colour rather than a fixed grey, so the placeholder sits at the same contrast on white and dark cards and flips with the theme for free.
- `sheen layers = 2px line, 72px glow, 240px bloom; light alpha 0.9 / 0.55 / 0.35, dark 0.2 / 0.08 / 0.04`
  A sharp leading edge with a soft tail reads as light passing over the surface. On dark surfaces the same alphas would flash, so they drop sharply.
- `sweep timing = 2.2s cycle, sweep occupies 0 to 60%, cubic-bezier(0.4, 0, 0.2, 1)`
  The rest period between sweeps is what keeps a page full of skeletons calm instead of a constant shimmer.
- `reveal = 300ms ease-out on opacity and filter; content enters from blur(4px)`
  Long enough to read as a cross-fade, short enough that loaded data is not held back. The blur hides the layout snap of text replacing a flat block.
- `SkeletonText = gap-2.5 (10px), h-3.5 lines, last line w-3/5`
  A 14px bar with 10px gaps approximates Body 1 text at a 24px rhythm; the short last line is what makes a block read as a paragraph.

## API

```ts
type SkeletonShape = "rect" | "text" | "circle"
interface SkeletonProps { shape?: SkeletonShape; isLoaded?: boolean; className?: string; style?: CSSProperties; children?: ReactNode }
function Skeleton(props: SkeletonProps): JSX.Element
interface SkeletonTextProps { lines?: number; lineClassName?: string; className?: string }
function SkeletonText(props: SkeletonTextProps): JSX.Element
```

- `shape: "rect" | "text" | "circle"` — default `"rect"`
  Corner radius: 12px, 6px or fully round.
- `isLoaded: boolean` — default `false`
  With children: fade the block out and blur the content in.
- `className: string`
  Size and placement, e.g. `h-4 w-40` or `size-10`.
- `children: ReactNode`
  Real content to size the placeholder from and reveal when loaded.
- `lines (SkeletonText): number` — default `3`
  Number of lines; the last runs 60% wide.
- `lineClassName (SkeletonText): string` — default `"h-3.5"`
  Line height, matched to the text it stands in for.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
const styles = sortCx({
  block: "bui-skeleton block bg-text-primary/8",
  shape: {
    rect: "rounded-xl",
    text: "rounded-md",
    circle: "rounded-full",
  },
});

const FADE = "transition-[opacity,filter] duration-300 ease-out motion-reduce:transition-none";

export interface SkeletonProps {
  /** `rect` (radius 12, default), `text` (radius 6), or `circle`. */
  shape?: SkeletonShape;
  /** With children: show them once true, blurring them in. */
  isLoaded?: boolean;
  /** Size and placement, e.g. `h-4 w-40` or `size-10`. */
  className?: string;
  style?: CSSProperties;
  /** Real content to measure the placeholder from and reveal when loaded. */
  children?: ReactNode;
}

export function Skeleton({ shape = "rect", isLoaded = false, className, style, children }: SkeletonProps) {
  if (children === undefined) {
    return <span aria-hidden className={cx(styles.block, "relative", styles.shape[shape], className)} style={style} />;
  }

  return (
    <span className={cx("relative block", className)} style={style}>
      <span
        aria-hidden={!isLoaded || undefined}
        inert={!isLoaded}
        className={cx("block", FADE, isLoaded ? "opacity-100 blur-[0px]" : "opacity-0 motion-safe:blur-[4px]")}
      >
        {children}
      </span>
      <span
        aria-hidden
        className={cx(styles.block, styles.shape[shape], "pointer-events-none absolute inset-0", FADE, isLoaded && "opacity-0")}
      />
    </span>
  );
}
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** Nothing to clean up. All motion is CSS animation on a pseudo-element and CSS transitions; there are no listeners, timers or effects.

**Reduced motion.** The sweep is removed (`::after { display: none }`) and each block instead breathes with `bui-skeleton-pulse`, a 2s ease-in-out opacity dip to 0.55. The reveal drops its transition and skips the blur (`motion-reduce:transition-none`, `motion-safe:blur-[4px]`), so loaded content simply appears.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Do not give the `.bui-skeleton` class its own `position` in unlayered CSS. It would beat Tailwind's layered `relative` / `absolute` utilities and break the overlay form.
- Do not render the loaded content outside the Skeleton and swap it in. The children form measures the placeholder from the real content, which is what prevents layout shift.
- Do not forget `aria-busy` on the region that is loading. Skeletons are `aria-hidden`, so without it assistive tech gets no loading signal at all.
- Do not tint the block with a fixed grey such as `bg-neutral-200`. It vanishes on dark cards; the 8% text tint does not.
- Do not leave hidden content focusable. The component sets `inert` on it until `isLoaded`; a custom version must too, or Tab lands on invisible buttons.

## Notes

- The sheen and its keyframes live in the theme sheet (`.bui-skeleton`), not in the component, so it needs the kit stylesheet to animate.
- With children, size and placement classes go on the wrapper; the overlay block inherits the wrapper's box.

## Definition of done

A card of skeletons (a 36px circle, two text bars, two text lines and a 64px rect) shows a soft sheen crossing each block left to right roughly every 2.2s, with a pause between sweeps, in both light and dark mode. Wrapping real content in `<Skeleton isLoaded={false}>` gives a block exactly the size of that content; switching to `isLoaded` cross-fades the block out over 300ms while the content un-blurs, with no layout shift. Under reduced motion the blocks pulse instead of sweeping.

and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Slab Page Transition

The outgoing page slides one screen height up and out while a solid slab rises from below to take its place. The route commits under the slab, the slab holds for a beat with the destination name on it, then the slab keeps travelling up and out while the new page follows it in from below. Nothing reverses direction at any point, which is the whole difference between a slab and a curtain: a curtain that drops and lifts reads as an interruption, a slab that passes through reads as travel.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

An opaque slab rises through the frame, the route changes under it, and it keeps going — nothing ever reverses.

- Category: transition
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: gsap@^3.15.0

## How it works

1. One paused GSAP timeline, played from zero on every navigation, covers the whole gesture. `to(content, { y: -H })` and `fromTo(slab, { y: +H }, { y: 0 })` both start at 0 and run for `duration`; a `.call()` at `duration` fires the caller's commit; `set(content, { y: +H })` on that same frame teleports the page below the frame; then `to(slab, { y: -H })` and `to(content, { y: 0 })` both start at `duration + hold`. Total length is `2 * duration + hold`.
2. The midpoint commit and the content teleport happen while the slab is exactly covering the frame, so neither is ever visible. That is the only reason the page can jump from -H to +H without a flash: there is an opaque surface in front of it for the whole of that frame.
3. Each half eases `power3.inOut` on its own rather than one tween covering the full 2H. An `inOut` across the whole travel is at its FASTEST in the middle — precisely where the slab has to look like it stopped. Two `inOut` halves meet at zero velocity, so the slab lands, holds, and leaves.
4. Travel is measured in pixels per run — `window.innerHeight` when `position="fixed"`, `root.getBoundingClientRect().height` when `"absolute"` — through GSAP function-based values. `yPercent: -100` would be 100% of the CONTENT element's own height, which on a long page is the whole document, so the page would fly thousands of pixels instead of one screen.
5. `tl.invalidate().play(0)` starts each run. `invalidate()` re-evaluates every function-based value, so a resized container or a flipped direction is picked up without rebuilding the timeline; without it the slab travels whatever height the box had when the component mounted.
6. Direction is a sign read from a ref inside those function values, and the ref is written in `run()` before `play(0)` rather than during render. `play(0)` renders the timeline synchronously, so a direction that only landed on the next React commit would be read one frame late and the two halves would disagree about which way is out.
7. The slab's parked position — `transform: translateY(100%)` — is declared in an injected stylesheet, not set from an effect. Effects run after the first paint, so a slab parked from JS is one frame of full-frame colour on mount. GSAP's inline transform outranks the rule while a transition runs, and when `useGsap` reverts it strips that inline value, which re-parks the slab with no extra code.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `SLAB_DURATION = 0.8`
  Seconds for ONE half; the full gesture is twice this plus the hold. The source ran 1 s per half and 0.8 keeps the weight while taking 0.4 s off the round trip. Under ~0.5 s the slab stops reading as a physical object and becomes a colour flash; over ~1.1 s the hold in the middle turns into a wait and people click a second nav item.
- `SLAB_HOLD = 0.12`
  Seconds the slab sits still at full cover. Two jobs: it is the beat in which the label is legible, and it is the margin in which React commits the destination — the commit fires at the start of the hold, so a page whose first layout costs two or three frames still finishes laying out before the slab moves off it. At 0 a heavy destination visibly settles while it is sliding in.
- `SLAB_EASE = 'power3.inOut'`
  Applied to each half separately. `inOut` is the only family that starts and ends at zero velocity, which is what makes the midpoint a stop rather than a peak. `power3` specifically: `power2` does not hold still long enough at the ends for the hold to read as deliberate, and `power4` spends so long near stationary that the 0.8 s feels like 1.2 s.
- `zIndex = 190`
  Above a custom cursor (150) and a scroll progress bar (120), both of which must be hidden during a transition, and below a preloader (200), which has to be able to sit over a slab on first load.

## API

```ts
function SlabPageTransition(props: { controller: SlabNavigation; children: ReactNode; duration?: number; hold?: number; direction?: "up" | "down"; color?: string; labelClassName?: string; position?: "fixed" | "absolute"; zIndex?: number; className?: string }): JSX.Element
function useSlabNavigation(): { host: RefObject<SlabRunner | null>; navigate: (commit: () => void, options?: { label?: string; direction?: "up" | "down" }) => void }
```

- `controller: SlabNavigation`
  From `useSlabNavigation()`. The component registers its runner on it.
- `children: ReactNode`
  The current page. Swapped by the `commit` you hand to `navigate`.
- `duration: number` — default `0.8`
  Seconds for ONE half. The full gesture is `2 * duration + hold`.
- `hold: number` — default `0.12`
  Seconds the slab holds at full cover, between the halves.
- `direction: "up" | "down"` — default `"up"`
  Default travel. Overridable per navigation via the options argument.
- `color: string` — default `'#000'`
  Any CSS colour. Must be opaque, or the swap shows through the slab.
- `labelClassName: string`
  Applied to the label span, so the caller owns its typography.
- `position: "fixed" | "absolute"` — default `"fixed"`
  `absolute` inside a bounded container; `fixed` for a real page transition.
- `zIndex: number` — default `190`
  Above the site and any custom cursor, below a preloader.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the root via `cn`.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
/**
 * Seconds for one half. The source ran 1 s per half; 0.8 keeps the weight and
 * takes 0.4 s off the round trip. Under ~0.5 s the slab stops reading as a
 * physical object and becomes a colour flash; over ~1.1 s the hold in the
 * middle turns into a wait, and people click a second nav item.
 */
export const SLAB_DURATION = 0.8;

/**
 * Seconds the slab sits still at full cover, between the two halves. Two jobs:
 * it is the beat in which the slab's label is legible, and it is the margin in
 * which React commits the destination. The commit fires at the start of the
 * hold, so a destination whose first layout costs two or three frames still
 * finishes laying out before the slab starts moving off it. At 0 a heavy page
 * visibly settles while it is sliding in.
 */
export const SLAB_HOLD = 0.12;

/** Both halves. `inOut` on each is what makes the midpoint a stop, not a peak. */
const SLAB_EASE = 'power3.inOut';

const SLAB_CSS = `
.kx-slab-panel {
  /* An opaque full-frame surface must never eat a click, not even while it is
     covering. Mid-transition the pointer is usually already aimed at the next
     nav item. */
  pointer-events: none;
  z-index: var(--kx-slab-z, 190);
  background: var(--kx-slab-color, #000);
  display: flex;
  align-items: center;
  justify-content: center;
  overflow: hidden;
}
/* The parked position lives in CSS, not in an inline style and not in a
   'gsap.set' inside an effect. Effects run after the first paint, so a slab
   parked from JS is one frame of full-frame colour on mount. GSAP's inline
   'transform' outranks these rules while a transition runs, and when
   'useGsap' reverts it strips that inline value — which parks the slab again
   with no extra code. */
.kx-slab-park-up { transform: translateY(100%); }
.kx-slab-park-down { transform: translateY(-100%); }
`;

export interface SlabNavigateOptions {
  /** Written into the slab, legible during the hold. */
  label?: string;
  /** Overrides the component's `direction` for this one navigation. */
  direction?: 'up' | 'down';
}

/** What the component registers on the controller. Internal. */
export interface SlabRunner {
  run: (commit: () => void, options?: SlabNavigateOptions) => void;
}

export interface SlabNavigation {
  /** Pass straight to `<SlabPageTransition controller>`. Do not read it. */
  host: RefObject<SlabRunner | null>;
  /**
   * Raise the slab, run `commit` — your navigation — under it, then lower the
   * page in behind it.
   */
  navigate: (commit: () => void, options?: SlabNavigateOptions) => void;
}

/**
 * The caller's half. `commit` is a callback rather than a router call, so
 * nothing here depends on a routing library.
 */
export function useSlabNavigation(): SlabNavigation {
  const host = useRef<SlabRunner | null>(null);

  const navigate = useCallback(
    (commit: () => void, options?: SlabNavigateOptions) => {
      const runner = host.current;
      // No mounted component — the caller wired the hook up but rendered the
      // transition conditionally, or this fired during the first commit.
      // Navigate anyway. A transition that swallows navigations is worse than
      // no transition.
      if (!runner) {
        commit();
        return;
      }
      runner.run(commit, options);
    },
    [],
  );

  return useMemo(() => ({ host, navigate }), [navigate]);
}

export interface SlabPageTransitionProps {
  /** From `useSlabNavigation()`. */
  controller: SlabNavigation;
  /** The current page. Swapped by the `commit` you hand to `navigate`. */
  children: ReactNode;
  /** Seconds for ONE half. The full gesture is `2 * duration + hold`. */
  duration?: number;
  /** Seconds the slab holds at full cover between the halves. */
  hold?: number;
  /**
   * Default travel. `up` sends everything upward; `down` mirrors it, which is
   * what a back navigation wants. Overridable per navigation.
   */
  direction?: 'up' | 'down';
  /** Any CSS colour. Must be opaque, or the swap shows through the slab. */
  color?: string;
  /** Applied to the label span so the caller owns its type. */
  labelClassName?: string;
  /** `absolute` to demo inside a bounded box; `fixed` for a real page. */
  position?: 'fixed' | 'absolute';
  /** Above the site, below a preloader. */
  zIndex?: number;
  className?: string;
}

export function SlabPageTransition({
  controller,
  children,
  duration = SLAB_DURATION,
  hold = SLAB_HOLD,
  direction = 'up',
  color = '#000',
  labelClassName,
  position = 'fixed',
  zIndex = 190,
  className,
}: SlabPageTransitionProps) {
  const root = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const content = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const slab = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const labelEl = useRef<HTMLSpanElement>(null);

  const timeline = useRef<ReturnType<typeof gsap.timeline> | null>(null);
  const pending = useRef<(() => void) | null>(null);
  const reduced = useReducedMotion();

  // Read inside the tweens' function-based values, so flipping direction
  // between navigations needs no rebuild — and therefore no `revert()`, which
  // would strip the transform GSAP is mid-way through writing. Set in `run`,
  // never during render: `play(0)` renders the timeline synchronously, so a
  // value that only lands on the next React commit would be read one frame
  // too late and the two halves would disagree about which way is out.
  const dir = useRef<'up' | 'down'>(direction);
  const defaultDir = useRef(direction);
  defaultDir.current = direction;

  // Built once and held paused. `direction` is deliberately NOT a dependency:
  // `useGsap` reverts on every dependency change, and revert removes the
  // inline transform, so a rebuild during a transition drops the slab back to
  // its CSS park mid-cover and the swap is visible.
  useGsap(
    gsap,
    () => {
      const rootEl = root.current;
      const contentEl = content.current;
      const slabEl = slab.current;
      if (!rootEl || !contentEl || !slabEl) return;

      // Travel in pixels, measured per run. `yPercent: -100` would be 100% of
      // the CONTENT's own height — on a long page that is the whole document,
      // so the page would fly thousands of pixels instead of one screen. The
      // original wrote `y: '-100vh'` for exactly this reason; measuring the
      // real box also gets the bounded case right, where one screen is the
      // container and not the viewport.
      const travel = () =>
        position === 'fixed'
          ? window.innerHeight
          : rootEl.getBoundingClientRect().height;
      const sign = () => (dir.current === 'down' ? -1 : 1);

      const tl = gsap.timeline({ paused: true });

      tl.to(contentEl, { y: () => -travel() * sign(), duration, ease: SLAB_EASE }, 0)
        .fromTo(
          slabEl,
          { y: () => travel() * sign() },
          { y: 0, duration, ease: SLAB_EASE },
          0,
        )
        // Midpoint. The slab is exactly covering the frame for the whole of
        // this and the `set` below, so neither is ever seen.
        .add(() => {
          const commit = pending.current;
          pending.current = null;
          commit?.();
        })
        .set(contentEl, { y: () => travel() * sign() })
        .to(
          slabEl,
          { y: () => -travel() * sign(), duration, ease: SLAB_EASE },
          duration + hold,
        )
        .to(contentEl, { y: 0, duration, ease: SLAB_EASE }, duration + hold)
        // Re-park the slab below the frame at the very end, so `progress(0)`
        // and `progress(1)` describe the same rest state and a second run
        // starts from a known place rather than from wherever it stopped.
        .set(slabEl, { y: () => travel() * sign() });

      timeline.current = tl;

      return () => {
        timeline.current = null;
        // A dependency change reverts and kills this timeline. If it happened
        // mid-transition the commit had not fired yet, so fire it here: the
        // visitor clicked a link and must end up on that page whatever the
        // animation did.
        const commit = pending.current;
        pending.current = null;
        commit?.();
      };
    },
    root,
    [duration, hold, position],
  );

  const run = useCallback(
    (commit: () => void, options?: SlabNavigateOptions) => {
      const tl = timeline.current;
      const span = labelEl.current;
      if (span) span.textContent = options?.label ?? '';
      dir.current = options?.direction ?? defaultDir.current;

      // Reduced motion: no slab and a synchronous commit. Not a zero-duration
      // slab — that is still one frame of full-frame colour, which is the
      // single most unpleasant thing to show someone who asked for less
      // motion. `pause(0)` suppresses callbacks, so the midpoint `.call()`
      // cannot fire a second commit.
      if (!tl || reduced) {
        tl?.pause(0);
        commit();
        return;
      }
      // A second click while the slab is in flight would queue a second commit
      // and land the visitor one page past where they aimed.
      if (tl.isActive()) return;

      pending.current = commit;
      // `invalidate()` before replaying re-evaluates every function-based
      // value: the box may have been resized, and `direction` may have
      // flipped, since the timeline was built. Without it the slab travels the
      // height the container had on mount.
      tl.invalidate().play(0);
    },
    [reduced],
  );

  useEffect(() => {
    const host = controller.host;
    host.current = { run };
    return () => {
      if (host.current?.run === run) host.current = null;
    };
  }, [controller, run]);
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** `useGsap` reverts the `gsap.context`, which kills the timeline and strips every inline transform it wrote — restoring the slab to the parked position its stylesheet rule specifies and the page to `y: 0`. The cleanup also flushes any commit that had not fired yet, so a prop change mid-transition cannot lose a navigation. The runner registration is removed from the controller on unmount, and it is removed only if it is still the current one, so a remount cannot null out the live handle.

**Reduced motion.** The timeline is never played. `navigate()` calls the commit synchronously and `tl.pause(0)` resets the slab to its rest position — deliberately not a zero-duration slab, which is still one frame of full-frame colour. `pause()` suppresses callbacks, so the midpoint `.call()` cannot fire a second commit. Navigation is a hard cut straight to the destination in both directions.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Using `yPercent: -100` on the page wrapper. Percentage transforms resolve against the element's OWN height, so on a 6000 px page the wrapper travels 6000 px in 0.8 s and the screen just goes blank a frame in. The travel has to be one screen — measured in pixels, or written as the original did with an explicit `vh` unit.
- Reversing the slab instead of driving it through. `tl.reverse()` after the commit sends the slab back down the way it came, and the eye reads the whole thing as a mistake being undone rather than as a move. The second half is a separate forward tween to `-H`.
- One `power3.inOut` across the full 2H travel. That ease is at maximum speed at its own midpoint, which is exactly the frame the route changes on, so the slab appears to accelerate straight through the cover and the label is unreadable.
- Putting the direction flag in the `useGsap` dependency list. Every dependency change reverts the context, and `revert()` strips the inline transform GSAP is mid-way through writing — so flipping direction during a transition drops the slab back to its CSS park while it is meant to be covering, and the content swap is visible. Direction is read from a ref by function-based values instead.
- Parking the slab with `gsap.set` in an effect. Effects run after the first paint, so the first frame of the page is a full-frame slab. The rest position belongs in a stylesheet; GSAP overrides it from the inline style the moment it is needed.
- Setting the slab label through state. `setLabel()` inside the navigate handler re-renders the subtree React is about to hand to GSAP on the exact frame the timeline starts. The label is one `textContent` write on a ref, and the slab is off-frame when it happens.
- Letting a second click start a second run. Without the `tl.isActive()` guard a double click queues two commits and the visitor lands one page past where they aimed.
- Dropping the commit when the timeline is destroyed. If a prop change reverts the context mid-transition, the `.call()` never fires and the route never changes — the visitor clicked a link and stayed put. The `useGsap` cleanup flushes any pending commit.
- Leaving the slab clickable. A full-frame opaque div swallows the pointer for the length of the transition, and mid-transition the pointer is usually already aimed at the next nav item. It carries `pointer-events: none` and `aria-hidden`.

## Notes

- In Next.js App Router: mount once in `app/layout.tsx` with `position="fixed"`, then replace nav `<Link>` elements with buttons calling `navigate(() => router.push(href), { label })`. Nothing in this file imports `next/navigation` — the commit is a callback, so the same component works under React Router or a plain `useState` page switch.
- The content wrapper stays in normal flow. A transform moves an element without taking it out of flow, so the page keeps its own height and the document still scrolls — which an `absolute inset-0` wrapper would break on any real page.
- The colour must be opaque. A translucent slab shows the content teleport at the midpoint, which is the single artefact this technique exists to hide.
- Browser back and forward change the route without going through `navigate()`, so they get no slab. That is correct: by the time your code hears about a history navigation it has already happened, and there is nothing left to cover.
- Set `direction: "down"` per navigation for anything that reads as going back — an up-nav click, a breadcrumb, a close button — and the site acquires a sense of which way the visitor is travelling for the cost of one ternary.

## Definition of done

Click a nav item: the page slides up out of frame while a coloured slab rises from below, the slab pauses at full cover with the destination name on it, then continues up and out while the new page follows it in from below. The slab never travels downward on a forward navigation, and there is no frame in which old and new content are both visible. Click a nav item to the left of the current one and the whole gesture mirrors — everything travels down. Click two items in quick succession and you land on the first one you clicked, not past it. Resize the preview and navigate again: the slab still travels exactly one frame height. With reduced motion the content swaps instantly with no coloured frame in either direction.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Sleep Score Card

A grey dashboard card headed "Sleep score" with a rating word ("Excellent") and a week pill with arrows. Below sits a ring split into one coloured arc per metric (Duration, Bedtime, Interruptions), each owning a share of the lap equal to its points available and filled by its score, with the total in the middle. A white panel lists the metrics with their detail and score; hovering or focusing a row (or an arc) dims the other arcs and puts that metric's score in the centre, and stepping through weeks glides the arcs to the new values.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

A segmented SVG ring that sums sleep sub-scores to a total out of 100, with a week switcher and metric rows that focus their arc.

- Category: display
- Runtime cost: css
- Dependencies: @remixicon/react@^4.9.0

## How it works

1. Each metric owns a slot of the ring sized `max / sum(max) × 100` percent (50, 30 and 20 by default, so the total reads out of 100), laid clockwise from twelve o'clock in row order. Its arc fills `score / max` of that slot.
2. Every arc is a circle with `pathLength={100}` rotated -90°, drawn with `stroke-dasharray: length 100` and `stroke-dashoffset: -start` over a full `stroke-chart-track` circle. Round caps reach half a stroke past each dash end, so the dash is trimmed by one cap on each side, `cap = (stroke / 2) / (2πr) × 100`, plus a 4% visible gap, and starts a half-gap plus a cap into its slot.
3. The dash length, offset and opacity are inline CSS properties with a 700ms expo-out `transition-[stroke-dasharray,stroke-dashoffset,opacity]`. On mount every arc has length 0 and opacity 0; two animation frames later the real values apply, so the arcs grow in. Changing week only changes the numbers, so the same transition glides each arc to its new length.
4. The week pill steps an index into `weeks` (controlled via `weekIndex` / `onWeekIndexChange`, or uncontrolled starting at the latest week); the arrows disable at either end. The rating word comes from `rate(total)` (Excellent ≥ 90, Good ≥ 75, Fair ≥ 60, else Poor) and is keyed by week so it fades in on change.
5. Focus is `preview ?? pinned`: pointer enter on a row or an arc (hit-tested on the stroke) and keyboard focus on a row set the preview; clicking a row toggles the pinned metric. Other arcs drop to 25% and other rows to 50%, and the centre swaps the total for the focused score with "of max" underneath, in a polite live region.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `SIZE / STROKE = 108px / 12px`
  A chunky band on a small ring, as in the reference; the stroke scales with `size`.
- `GAP = 4 (ring percent)`
  About 15° of track shows between arcs after the caps are trimmed, enough to read the segments as separate scores.
- `arc transition = 700ms, cubic-bezier(0.22, 1, 0.36, 1)`
  Fast start and soft landing, so a week change reads instantly but the arcs settle gently.
- `max split = 50 / 30 / 20`
  Duration matters most, so it owns half the ring; the three maxima sum to 100 so the centre total is a percentage-style score.

## API

```ts
function SleepScoreCard(props?: SleepScoreCardProps): JSX.Element
type SleepMetric = { id: string; label: string; detail: string; score: number; max: number; color: string }
type SleepWeek = { id: string; label: string; metrics: SleepMetric[] }
```

- `title: string` — default `"Sleep score"`
  Header label.
- `weeks: SleepWeek[]` — default `SLEEP_WEEKS`
  Weeks the pill steps through, oldest first.
- `weekIndex: number`
  Controlled index into `weeks`.
- `defaultWeekIndex: number` — default `weeks.length - 1`
  Uncontrolled starting week.
- `onWeekIndexChange: (index: number) => void`
  Called when an arrow changes week.
- `rate: (score: number) => string` — default `sleepRating`
  Turns the total into the headline word.
- `size: number` — default `108`
  Ring diameter in px.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the card section.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
// Every metric owns a slot of the lap sized by its `max`; its arc fills score/max of that slot.
// Round caps poke out half a stroke past each dash end, so the dash is trimmed by a cap on both
// sides plus the visible GAP. With pathLength 100 the cap length in ring percent is
// (stroke / 2) / circumference * 100.
const cap = ((stroke / 2) / (2 * Math.PI * r)) * 100;
let cursor = 0;
const segments = metrics.map((m) => {
  const slot = totalMax > 0 ? (m.max / totalMax) * 100 : 0;
  const fill = m.max > 0 ? Math.min(1, Math.max(0, m.score / m.max)) : 0;
  const start = cursor + GAP / 2 + cap;
  const length = Math.max(0, slot * fill - GAP - 2 * cap);
  cursor += slot;
  const shown = drawn || reduced;
  return { m, start, length: shown ? length : 0, visible: shown && length > 0 };
});
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** The mount effect cancels both pending animation frames on unmount. Everything else is CSS transitions and React event props.

**Reduced motion.** With `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`, `useReducedMotion` renders the arcs at their final lengths from the first frame and `motion-reduce:transition-none` removes the draw and week-change transitions, so arcs jump to new values. The rating and centre fades and the row dimming are also instant.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Forgetting the round caps. A dash of exactly the slot length overlaps its neighbour by a full stroke width; trim one cap from each end before subtracting the visible gap.
- Setting the dash values as SVG attributes and expecting a CSS transition. Put `strokeDasharray` and `strokeDashoffset` in `style` so the browser interpolates them.
- Starting from length 0 with round caps leaves a dot at each arc's start; the arcs also start at opacity 0 and fade in with the draw.

## Notes

- Exports `SLEEP_WEEKS` (six sample weeks, oldest first), `sleepRating` and the `SleepMetric` / `SleepWeek` types. A metric is `{ id, label, detail, score, max, color }`; any number of metrics works and the slots follow their maxima.

## Definition of done

The default card reads "Sleep score", "Excellent", "29 Jun - 5 Jul" and 98 in the centre, with purple, pink and blue arcs that grow in clockwise from the top over a grey track, and rows "Duration: 7h 50m 49/50", "Bedtime: 20m earlier 29/30" and "Interruptions: 5m wake up 20/20". The next arrow is disabled. Hovering the Bedtime row dims the other arcs and rows and shows 29 "of 30" in the centre. Clicking the previous arrow shows "22 Jun - 28 Jun", "Good" and 83, and the arcs shorten smoothly.

and where, so I can check them.
