# Build: Spring Lattice Field

A grid that behaves like a stretched sheet. A coarse lattice of damped springs runs on the CPU, is packed into an RGBA8 texture once per frame, and the fragment shader reads that texture with LINEAR filtering to displace its own sample coordinate. The pointer pushes cells outward and drags them along with its velocity; diffusion between neighbours turns each push into a wave that spreads and settles.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

A CPU damped-spring lattice uploaded as a texture each frame, displacing a procedural grid the cursor can push around.

- Category: webgl
- Runtime cost: webgl
- Dependencies: none beyond React

## How it works

1. The lattice is `round(width / cellSize)` by `round(height / cellSize)` cells, sized in CSS pixels rather than device pixels so the simulation is identical on a retina display instead of running four times as many cells.
2. Each step, cells within `radius` of the pointer receive two impulses: a radial one along `(cell - pointer) / |cell - pointer|` scaled by `radialStrength`, and a flow one along the pointer's own velocity scaled by `flowStrength`. Both are weighted by `t*t*(3-2t)` where `t = 1 - dist/radius` — a smoothstep falloff, C1 at both ends, so the disturbance has no visible rim.
3. Then `vel = (vel - disp * returnStiffness) * velocityDamping` and `nextDisp = disp + vel + (neighbourAverage - disp) * diffusion`. The diffusion term is what makes it a sheet rather than a field of independent springs: a local push propagates outward as a wave instead of staying put.
4. The integration writes into a scratch buffer, not in place. In place, the +x and +y neighbours would already hold the new value when a cell reads them, and the wave would visibly drift toward the lattice origin.
5. Displacement is packed into the texture as `d / DISP_MAX * 0.5 + 0.5` in RG, with cell speed in B. Speed, not displacement, drives the glow — so the field lights up while it is moving and goes dark once it settles, which is what reads as elastic rather than as a permanent dent.
6. The shader adds `disp / gridDimensions` to its uv before drawing an `fwidth`-normalised grid, so lines stay one pixel wide even where the field is stretching them, and `u_density` is set to the lattice row count so the drawn lines land on cell boundaries.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `STEP = 1 / 60`
  Fixed simulation timestep. Every other physics constant is expressed per step — `velocityDamping = 0.93` only means "keep 93% per 1/60 s" if the step is always 1/60 s. Integrating per frame instead makes the field stiffer on a 60 Hz laptop than on a 120 Hz phone.
- `MAX_SUBSTEPS = 4`
  Catch-up ceiling. Returning to a backgrounded tab otherwise tries to simulate the whole elapsed time in one frame and the page locks up for seconds. The leftover accumulator is discarded when the ceiling is hit, or the debt compounds and the simulation runs saturated forever.
- `returnStiffness = 0.018`
  Spring constant per step. Above ~0.05 the lattice snaps back before the wave can spread and it reads as rubber sheeting; below ~0.006 disturbances take several seconds to clear and the grid looks permanently dented.
- `velocityDamping = 0.93`
  Velocity retained per step. At 1.0 the lattice never loses energy and rings forever; below ~0.85 the push is absorbed within a few cells and nothing propagates.
- `diffusion = 0.22`
  Fraction of the way each cell moves toward its neighbours' average per step. This is the wave speed. Past 0.25 the explicit scheme goes unstable and the lattice fills with checkerboard noise; near 0 the cells decouple and the grid dimples pointwise.
- `radius = 5.5`
  Pointer influence, in cells. Expressed in cells rather than pixels so the physics is unchanged at any `cellSize`. Under ~3 the cursor pokes a hole; past ~10 it lifts the whole panel and the motion loses its centre.
- `radialStrength = 0.02`
  Sustained outward push per step. Equilibrium displacement is roughly `radialStrength / returnStiffness` ≈ 1.1 cells — enough for the grid to visibly part around a resting cursor without approaching the encode range.
- `flowStrength = 0.08`
  Drag along the pointer velocity. A transient impulse peaks at about `impulse / (1 - velocityDamping)` ≈ 14x, so this is roughly ten times smaller than the radial constant for a comparable displacement. Raise it and fast swipes clip the encode range.
- `MAX_POINTER_SPEED = 45`
  Cells per second. A pointer that teleports across the element — tab switch, window drag, the first event after a long pause — otherwise injects one enormous impulse and the whole lattice snaps in a single step.
- `DISP_MAX = 2.5`
  Encode range in cells. Displacement is clamped to it before packing into 8 bits; an unclamped value wraps the byte and the cell flips to the opposite sign, which reads as a hard pop exactly where the motion is strongest.
- `cellSize = 18`
  CSS pixels per cell. Cost is quadratic: at 6 a 1440x900 panel is 36,000 cells and the step stops fitting in a frame. Above ~30 the lattice is coarse enough that LINEAR interpolation between cells becomes visible as flat facets.

## API

```ts
function SpringLatticeField(props: { cellSize?: number; radius?: number; radialStrength?: number; flowStrength?: number; ink?: readonly [number, number, number]; line?: readonly [number, number, number]; glow?: readonly [number, number, number]; maxDpr?: number; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `cellSize: number` — default `18`
  CSS pixels per lattice cell. Cost is quadratic in this.
- `radius: number` — default `5.5`
  Pointer influence radius, in lattice cells.
- `radialStrength: number` — default `0.02`
  Outward push per fixed step, in cells/step².
- `flowStrength: number` — default `0.08`
  How strongly pointer velocity drags cells along with it.
- `ink: readonly [number, number, number]` — default `[0.035, 0.038, 0.048]`
  Base field colour, linear 0..1 RGB.
- `line: readonly [number, number, number]` — default `[0.16, 0.17, 0.2]`
  Grid line colour, added on top of ink.
- `glow: readonly [number, number, number]` — default `[0.35, 0.62, 0.95]`
  Colour added in proportion to cell speed.
- `maxDpr: number` — default `2`
  Upper bound on device pixel ratio.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the host element.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
const TRIANGLE = new Float32Array([-1, -1, 3, -1, -1, 3]);
const MAX_DPR = 2;

/* The simulation runs on a fixed timestep. Every constant below is tuned per
   STEP — `velocityDamping = 0.93` means "keep 93% of the velocity after 1/60 of
   a second", and it only means that if the step is always 1/60 of a second. A
   per-frame integration would make the field stiffer on a 60 Hz laptop than on
   a 120 Hz phone, which is the exact failure mode the frame-rate independence
   rule exists to prevent. Everything here is in LATTICE CELLS, not pixels, so
   the physics is identical at any cellSize. */
const STEP = 1 / 60;
/* Ceiling on catch-up steps per frame. Without it, returning to a backgrounded
   tab tries to simulate the whole elapsed time in one frame and the page hangs;
   with it, the field simply resumes from where it was. */
const MAX_SUBSTEPS = 4;

const RETURN_STIFFNESS = 0.018;
const VELOCITY_DAMPING = 0.93;
const DIFFUSION = 0.22;
/* Pointer speed cap, cells/second. A pointer teleporting across the element
   (tab switch, window drag) otherwise injects one enormous impulse and the
   lattice snaps past the encode range in a single step. */
const MAX_POINTER_SPEED = 45;
/* Encode range in cells. Displacement is packed into 8 bits as
   `d / DISP_MAX * 0.5 + 0.5`, so anything beyond this must be clamped — an
   unclamped value wraps the byte and the cell flips to the opposite sign,
   which reads as a hard pop. */
const DISP_MAX = 2.5;
/* Maps cell speed (cells/step) into the 0..1 glow channel. */
const ENERGY_SCALE = 6;

const MIN_CELLS = 8;
const MAX_CELLS = 80;

interface Lattice {
  cols: number;
  rows: number;
  /** Interleaved x,y displacement per cell, in cells. */
  disp: Float32Array;
  /** Interleaved x,y velocity per cell, in cells/step. */
  vel: Float32Array;
  /** Scratch buffer — diffusion must read the whole previous state. */
  next: Float32Array;
  /** RGBA8 upload staging. */
  pixels: Uint8Array;
}

function createLattice(cols: number, rows: number): Lattice {
  const cells = cols * rows;
  return {
    cols,
    rows,
    disp: new Float32Array(cells * 2),
    vel: new Float32Array(cells * 2),
    next: new Float32Array(cells * 2),
    pixels: new Uint8Array(cells * 4),
  };
}

/* One fixed-timestep step. Pointer position is in cell coordinates; pointer
   velocity is in cells/second and is converted here, so the caller does not
   have to know the step length. */
function stepLattice(
  lattice: Lattice,
  pointerX: number,
  pointerY: number,
  pointerVX: number,
  pointerVY: number,
  active: boolean,
  radius: number,
  radialStrength: number,
  flowStrength: number,
): void {
  const { cols, rows, disp, vel, next } = lattice;

  if (active) {
    // Only the cells inside the radius can be touched, so bound the loop
    // instead of testing every cell. At radius 5.5 that is ~120 cells out of
    // a couple of thousand.
    const minX = Math.max(0, Math.floor(pointerX - radius));
    const maxX = Math.min(cols - 1, Math.ceil(pointerX + radius));
    const minY = Math.max(0, Math.floor(pointerY - radius));
    const maxY = Math.min(rows - 1, Math.ceil(pointerY + radius));
    const flowX = pointerVX * STEP * flowStrength;
    const flowY = pointerVY * STEP * flowStrength;

    for (let y = minY; y <= maxY; y++) {
      for (let x = minX; x <= maxX; x++) {
        const dx = x - pointerX;
        const dy = y - pointerY;
        const dist = Math.sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy);
        if (dist > radius) continue;

        /* Smoothstep falloff, not linear. A linear falloff has a corner at the
           radius: cells cross the boundary with non-zero force and the edge of
           the disturbance is a visible circle. `t*t*(3-2t)` is C1 at both ends,
           so the influence dies out with zero slope and no rim appears. */
        const t = 1 - dist / radius;
        const shaped = t * t * (3 - 2 * t);

        // At dist 0 the direction is undefined; pushing nothing is correct.
        const inv = dist > 1e-4 ? 1 / dist : 0;
        const i = (y * cols + x) * 2;
        vel[i] = (vel[i] ?? 0) + dx * inv * shaped * radialStrength + flowX * shaped;
        vel[i + 1] =
          (vel[i + 1] ?? 0) + dy * inv * shaped * radialStrength + flowY * shaped;
      }
    }
  }

  // Spring toward rest, then bleed energy. Damping applied AFTER the spring
  // term keeps the system unconditionally stable at these constants.
  for (let i = 0; i < vel.length; i++) {
    vel[i] = ((vel[i] ?? 0) - (disp[i] ?? 0) * RETURN_STIFFNESS) * VELOCITY_DAMPING;
  }

  /* Integrate and diffuse in one pass into `next`. Diffusion is what makes the
     lattice behave like a sheet rather than a field of independent springs:
     each cell is pulled `DIFFUSION` of the way toward its four neighbours'
     average, so a local push propagates outward as a wave. Writing in place
     would make the result depend on iteration order — the +x and +y neighbours
     would already be updated, and the wave would drift toward the origin. */
  for (let y = 0; y < rows; y++) {
    for (let x = 0; x < cols; x++) {
      const i = (y * cols + x) * 2;
      for (let c = 0; c < 2; c++) {
        const self = disp[i + c] ?? 0;
        // Edges mirror themselves: a free boundary. Clamping them to zero
        // instead pins the border and every wave reflects off it.
        const left = x > 0 ? disp[i - 2 + c] ?? self : self;
        const right = x < cols - 1 ? disp[i + 2 + c] ?? self : self;
        const up = y > 0 ? disp[i - cols * 2 + c] ?? self : self;
        const down = y < rows - 1 ? disp[i + cols * 2 + c] ?? self : self;
        const avg = (left + right + up + down) * 0.25;
        next[i + c] = self + (vel[i + c] ?? 0) + (avg - self) * DIFFUSION;
      }
    }
  }

  disp.set(next);
}

/** Pack displacement into RG and speed into B. Returns total energy. */
function encodeLattice(lattice: Lattice): number {
  const { disp, vel, pixels } = lattice;
  const cells = lattice.cols * lattice.rows;
  let total = 0;

  for (let c = 0; c < cells; c++) {
    const i = c * 2;
    const dx = disp[i] ?? 0;
    const dy = disp[i + 1] ?? 0;
    const vx = vel[i] ?? 0;
    const vy = vel[i + 1] ?? 0;
    const speed = Math.sqrt(vx * vx + vy * vy);
    total += speed;

    const o = c * 4;
    pixels[o] = encodeSigned(dx);
    pixels[o + 1] = encodeSigned(dy);
    pixels[o + 2] = Math.min(255, Math.round(speed * ENERGY_SCALE * 255));
    pixels[o + 3] = 255;
  }

  return total;
}

function encodeSigned(value: number): number {
  const n = value / DISP_MAX;
  const clamped = n < -1 ? -1 : n > 1 ? 1 : n;
  return Math.round((clamped * 0.5 + 0.5) * 255);
}

interface Pass {
  gl: WebGL2RenderingContext;
  program: WebGLProgram;
  vao: WebGLVertexArrayObject;
  buffer: WebGLBuffer;
  texture: WebGLTexture;
  locations: Map<string, WebGLUniformLocation | null>;
  /** Allocated texture dimensions, so resize can tell reallocation from upload. */
  texCols: number;
  texRows: number;
}

function compileShader(
  gl: WebGL2RenderingContext,
  type: number,
  source: string,
): WebGLShader | null {
  const shader = gl.createShader(type);
  if (!shader) return null;
  gl.shaderSource(shader, source);
  gl.compileShader(shader);
  if (!gl.getShaderParameter(shader, gl.COMPILE_STATUS)) {
    console.error('[spring-lattice-field]', gl.getShaderInfoLog(shader));
    gl.deleteShader(shader);
    return null;
  }
  return shader;
}

function createPass(gl: WebGL2RenderingContext): Pass | null {
  const vert = compileShader(gl, gl.VERTEX_SHADER, SPRING_LATTICE_VERT);
  const frag = compileShader(gl, gl.FRAGMENT_SHADER, SPRING_LATTICE_FRAG);
  const program = gl.createProgram();
  if (!vert || !frag || !program) {
    if (vert) gl.deleteShader(vert);
    if (frag) gl.deleteShader(frag);
    if (program) gl.deleteProgram(program);
    return null;
  }

  gl.attachShader(program, vert);
  gl.attachShader(program, frag);
  gl.linkProgram(program);
  gl.deleteShader(vert);
  gl.deleteShader(frag);

  if (!gl.getProgramParameter(program, gl.LINK_STATUS)) {
    console.error('[spring-lattice-field]', gl.getProgramInfoLog(program));
    gl.deleteProgram(program);
    return null;
  }

  const vao = gl.createVertexArray();
  const buffer = gl.createBuffer();
  const texture = gl.createTexture();
  if (!vao || !buffer || !texture) {
    gl.deleteProgram(program);
    if (vao) gl.deleteVertexArray(vao);
    if (buffer) gl.deleteBuffer(buffer);
    if (texture) gl.deleteTexture(texture);
    return null;
  }

  gl.bindVertexArray(vao);
  gl.bindBuffer(gl.ARRAY_BUFFER, buffer);
  gl.bufferData(gl.ARRAY_BUFFER, TRIANGLE, gl.STATIC_DRAW);
  const attrib = gl.getAttribLocation(program, 'a_pos');
  if (attrib >= 0) {
    gl.enableVertexAttribArray(attrib);
    gl.vertexAttribPointer(attrib, 2, gl.FLOAT, false, 0, 0);
  }
  gl.bindVertexArray(null);

  gl.activeTexture(gl.TEXTURE0);
  gl.bindTexture(gl.TEXTURE_2D, texture);
  /* LINEAR is load-bearing, not a default: it is what turns a 40x24 simulation
     into a smooth field across two million fragments. CLAMP_TO_EDGE because
     REPEAT would sample the opposite edge of the lattice at the border and
     stamp a seam there. */
  gl.texParameteri(gl.TEXTURE_2D, gl.TEXTURE_MIN_FILTER, gl.LINEAR);
  gl.texParameteri(gl.TEXTURE_2D, gl.TEXTURE_MAG_FILTER, gl.LINEAR);
  gl.texParameteri(gl.TEXTURE_2D, gl.TEXTURE_WRAP_S, gl.CLAMP_TO_EDGE);
  gl.texParameteri(gl.TEXTURE_2D, gl.TEXTURE_WRAP_T, gl.CLAMP_TO_EDGE);

  return {
    gl,
    program,
    vao,
    buffer,
    texture,
    locations: new Map(),
    texCols: 0,
    texRows: 0,
  };
}

function uniformLocation(pass: Pass, name: string): WebGLUniformLocation | null {
  const cached = pass.locations.get(name);
  if (cached !== undefined) return cached;
  const found = pass.gl.getUniformLocation(pass.program, name);
  pass.locations.set(name, found);
  return found;
}

function setVec3(
  gl: WebGL2RenderingContext,
  location: WebGLUniformLocation | null,
  v: readonly [number, number, number],
): void {
  if (location === null) return;
  gl.uniform3f(location, v[0], v[1], v[2]);
}

function disposePass(pass: Pass): void {
  const { gl } = pass;
  gl.deleteVertexArray(pass.vao);
  gl.deleteBuffer(pass.buffer);
  gl.deleteTexture(pass.texture);
  gl.deleteProgram(pass.program);
  loseContext(gl);
}

export function SpringLatticeField({
  cellSize = 18,
  radius = 5.5,
  radialStrength = 0.02,
  flowStrength = 0.08,
  ink = [0.035, 0.038, 0.048],
  line = [0.16, 0.17, 0.2],
  glow = [0.35, 0.62, 0.95],
  maxDpr = MAX_DPR,
  className,
}: SpringLatticeFieldProps) {
  const host = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const canvasRef = useRef<HTMLCanvasElement>(null);
  const passRef = useRef<Pass | null>(null);
  const latticeRef = useRef<Lattice | null>(null);
  const accumulator = useRef(0);
  const prevPointer = useRef<{ x: number; y: number } | null>(null);

  const { width, height } = useResizeObserver(host);
  const reduced = useReducedMotion();
  const visible = useVisibility();
  // Light smoothing only. Heavy smoothing would blunt the velocity signal the
  // flow push is built from, and the lattice would stop reacting to flicks.
  const pointer = useSmoothPointer({ target: host, smoothing: 0.004 });
  const [supported, setSupported] = useState(true);

  const params = useRef({ radius, radialStrength, flowStrength, ink, line, glow });
  params.current = { radius, radialStrength, flowStrength, ink, line, glow };

  const drawRef = useRef<() => void>(() => {});
  drawRef.current = () => {
    const pass = passRef.current;
    const lattice = latticeRef.current;
    if (!pass || !lattice) return;
    const { gl } = pass;
    const p = params.current;

    gl.useProgram(pass.program);
    gl.activeTexture(gl.TEXTURE0);
    gl.bindTexture(gl.TEXTURE_2D, pass.texture);

    if (pass.texCols !== lattice.cols || pass.texRows !== lattice.rows) {
      gl.texImage2D(
        gl.TEXTURE_2D,
        0,
        gl.RGBA8,
        lattice.cols,
        lattice.rows,
        0,
        gl.RGBA,
        gl.UNSIGNED_BYTE,
        lattice.pixels,
      );
      pass.texCols = lattice.cols;
      pass.texRows = lattice.rows;
    } else {
      // texSubImage2D, not texImage2D: re-specifying the texture every frame
      // makes the driver re-validate and often reallocate it, which shows up as
      // a steadily climbing GPU memory graph.
      gl.texSubImage2D(
        gl.TEXTURE_2D,
        0,
        0,
        0,
        lattice.cols,
        lattice.rows,
        gl.RGBA,
        gl.UNSIGNED_BYTE,
        lattice.pixels,
      );
    }

    const uField = uniformLocation(pass, 'u_field');
    if (uField !== null) gl.uniform1i(uField, 0);

    const uRes = uniformLocation(pass, 'u_resolution');
    if (uRes !== null) {
      gl.uniform2f(uRes, gl.drawingBufferWidth, gl.drawingBufferHeight);
    }
    const uGrid = uniformLocation(pass, 'u_grid');
    if (uGrid !== null) gl.uniform2f(uGrid, lattice.cols, lattice.rows);
    const uDisp = uniformLocation(pass, 'u_dispMax');
    if (uDisp !== null) gl.uniform1f(uDisp, DISP_MAX);
    /* Grid density is tied to the lattice row count so the drawn lines land on
       cell boundaries. Decoupling them makes the displacement look like it is
       sliding underneath the grid rather than moving it. */
    const uDensity = uniformLocation(pass, 'u_density');
    if (uDensity !== null) gl.uniform1f(uDensity, lattice.rows);

    setVec3(gl, uniformLocation(pass, 'u_ink'), p.ink);
    setVec3(gl, uniformLocation(pass, 'u_line'), p.line);
    setVec3(gl, uniformLocation(pass, 'u_glow'), p.glow);

    gl.bindVertexArray(pass.vao);
    gl.drawArrays(gl.TRIANGLES, 0, 3);
    gl.bindVertexArray(null);
  };

  useEffect(() => {
    const el = host.current;
    if (!el) return;
    if (!hasWebGL()) {
      setSupported(false);
      return;
    }

    // Built here rather than rendered by React, because cleanup hands the
    // context back through `WEBGL_lose_context` and a canvas that has been
    // through that never yields another one — `getContext` returns the same
    // lost object. StrictMode's double invoke re-gave React's element to the
    // second run, whose `createPass` then compiled against a dead context and
    // demoted the component to its fallback for good.
    const canvas = document.createElement('canvas');
    canvas.className = 'block h-full w-full';

    const gl = canvas.getContext('webgl2', {
      antialias: false,
      alpha: false,
      depth: false,
      stencil: false,
      powerPreference: 'high-performance',
    });
    if (!gl) {
      setSupported(false);
      return;
    }

    const pass = createPass(gl);
    if (!pass) {
      loseContext(gl);
      setSupported(false);
      return;
    }
    el.append(canvas);
    canvasRef.current = canvas;
    passRef.current = pass;
    setSupported(true);

    // Left unhandled the lattice simply vanishes — a blank canvas that never
    // recovers and never falls back — so a loss demotes the component to its
    // static stand-in. `preventDefault` keeps a later restore possible.
    const onLost = (event: Event): void => {
      event.preventDefault();
      // Detached too: the fallback renders as a sibling in normal flow, and a
      // canvas left in place would sit on top of it.
      canvas.remove();
      setSupported(false);
    };
    canvas.addEventListener('webglcontextlost', onLost);

    return () => {
      canvas.removeEventListener('webglcontextlost', onLost);
      passRef.current = null;
      canvasRef.current = null;
      disposePass(pass);
      canvas.remove();
    };
  }, []);

  // Resize rebuilds the lattice and redraws. Under reduced motion this is the
  // only draw that ever happens, and it shows the field at rest.
  useEffect(() => {
    const canvas = canvasRef.current;
    const pass = passRef.current;
    if (!canvas || !pass || width === 0 || height === 0) return;

    const dpr = pixelRatio(maxDpr);
    const w = Math.max(1, Math.round(width * dpr));
    const h = Math.max(1, Math.round(height * dpr));
    if (canvas.width !== w || canvas.height !== h) {
      canvas.width = w;
      canvas.height = h;
    }
    pass.gl.viewport(0, 0, w, h);

    // Lattice resolution is in CSS pixels, deliberately: the simulation should
    // feel the same on a retina display, not run four times as many cells.
    const cols = Math.min(MAX_CELLS, Math.max(MIN_CELLS, Math.round(width / cellSize)));
    const rows = Math.min(MAX_CELLS, Math.max(MIN_CELLS, Math.round(height / cellSize)));
    const current = latticeRef.current;
    if (!current || current.cols !== cols || current.rows !== rows) {
      latticeRef.current = createLattice(cols, rows);
      encodeLattice(latticeRef.current);
      prevPointer.current = null;
      accumulator.current = 0;
    }

    drawRef.current();
  }, [width, height, cellSize, maxDpr, supported]);

  const running = supported && visible && !reduced && width > 0 && height > 0;

  useRaf((dt) => {
    const lattice = latticeRef.current;
    if (!lattice) return;
    const p = params.current;
    const state = pointer.current;

    const px = state.nx * lattice.cols;
    const py = state.ny * lattice.rows;

    // Velocity from the change in position, in cells/second, then capped.
    let vx = 0;
    let vy = 0;
    const prev = prevPointer.current;
    if (prev && dt > 0) {
      vx = (px - prev.x) / dt;
      vy = (py - prev.y) / dt;
      const speed = Math.sqrt(vx * vx + vy * vy);
      if (speed > MAX_POINTER_SPEED) {
        const k = MAX_POINTER_SPEED / speed;
        vx *= k;
        vy *= k;
      }
    }
    prevPointer.current = { x: px, y: py };

    accumulator.current += dt;
    let steps = 0;
    while (accumulator.current >= STEP && steps < MAX_SUBSTEPS) {
      stepLattice(
        lattice,
        px,
        py,
        vx,
        vy,
        state.active,
        p.radius,
        p.radialStrength,
        p.flowStrength,
      );
      accumulator.current -= STEP;
      steps++;
    }
    // Hit the ceiling: throw the backlog away rather than carrying a debt that
    // can never be paid off, which would leave the simulation permanently
    // saturated and running MAX_SUBSTEPS every frame.
    if (steps === MAX_SUBSTEPS) accumulator.current = 0;

    if (steps > 0) {
      encodeLattice(lattice);
      drawRef.current();
    }
  }, running);
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** Deletes the VAO, vertex buffer, field texture and program, then `loseContext(gl)`. The typed arrays are dropped with the lattice ref. The rAF subscription, resize observer and pointer listener unsubscribe with their hooks.

**Reduced motion.** No rAF subscription, so the lattice never steps and the pointer never disturbs it. One frame is drawn on mount and on resize showing the field at rest: the full grid, the vignette, no displacement and no glow. The component is a static grid, not a blank panel.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Integrating per frame instead of on a fixed accumulator. The constants above are tuned per 1/60 s; run them per frame and the same component is noticeably stiffer at 60 fps than at 120, and unstable under a frame spike. This is the one place the tuned constants and the frame-rate independence rule collide, and the accumulator is the resolution.
- Carrying the accumulator forward after hitting `MAX_SUBSTEPS`. The debt can never be repaid, so the simulation runs four substeps every frame from then on and quietly costs four times what it should.
- Diffusing in place. Cells read their +x and +y neighbours after those neighbours have already been updated, so the wave propagates faster in one diagonal than the other and visibly drifts toward the lattice origin.
- Setting the field texture to NEAREST. The lattice itself becomes visible as hard blocky steps — at `cellSize` 18 that is a grid of 18 px squares sliding under the drawn grid.
- Calling `texImage2D` every frame instead of `texSubImage2D`. Re-specifying the texture makes the driver re-validate and frequently reallocate it; the symptom is a GPU memory graph that climbs for as long as the page is open.
- Failing to clamp before encoding. Displacement past `DISP_MAX` wraps the unsigned byte, so a cell being pushed hard right suddenly reads as pushed hard left, and the field pops.
- Sizing the lattice in device pixels. A retina display quietly runs four times the cells for identical visual output, and the component drops frames only on the machines its author is least likely to be testing on.
- Heavy pointer smoothing. The flow push is built from the derivative of the pointer position, and over-smoothing flattens that derivative — the lattice stops responding to flicks while still responding to slow drags, which reads as lag rather than as smoothing.
- Leaving the context alive on unmount. Raw GL has no `dispose()`; the VAO, buffer, texture and program are deleted explicitly and `loseContext(gl)` hands the context back, or the page starts blanking its oldest canvases after roughly sixteen mounts.

## Notes

- The simulation could run on the GPU with ping-pong framebuffers, and at this lattice size it would be slower overall: two extra render targets, a readback whenever anything else needs the field state, and float-texture support to feature detect. A few thousand cells on the CPU cost under 0.2 ms and stay inspectable in a debugger.
- Resizing rebuilds the lattice from rest. Interpolating the old state into the new dimensions is possible but the disturbance is gone within a second of a resize anyway.

## Definition of done

Rest the cursor on the field and the grid parts around it by roughly one cell and holds there. Move it and a wave spreads outward through the lines and settles within about a second. Swipe fast and the lines are dragged along the swipe direction, glowing while they move and going dark once they stop. Grid lines stay one pixel wide even where they are most stretched. Throttle the CPU to 6x and the wave still travels at the same speed, just at fewer frames.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Spring To CSS linear()

A spring is a differential equation, and the usual way to run one on the web is a JavaScript loop that integrates it every frame — on the main thread, where a long task or a garbage collection makes it visibly hitch. `linear()` takes a list of output values and interpolates between them, and those values are not clamped to [0, 1], so a dense enough sample of a spring *is* the spring, overshoot included. Solve it once at author time, emit the samples, and the animation runs on the compositor where nothing on the main thread can reach it.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

Solves a spring once, samples it into a CSS linear() string, and runs the whole bounce on the compositor.

- Category: primitive
- Runtime cost: css
- Dependencies: none beyond React

## How it works

1. The motion is the second-order system `d'' + 2*zeta*w0*d' + w0^2*d = 0` on the *remaining* distance `d`, with `d(0) = 1` and `d'(0) = -velocity`. The natural frequency is `w0 = sqrt(stiffness / mass)` and the damping ratio is `zeta = damping / (2 * sqrt(stiffness * mass))`.
2. Each damping regime has its own closed form. Underdamped (`zeta < 1`) is `exp(-zeta*w0*t) * (cos(wd*t) + b*sin(wd*t))` with `wd = w0*sqrt(1 - zeta^2)` and `b = (zeta*w0 - v0) / wd`. Critically damped (`zeta = 1`) collapses to `exp(-w0*t) * (1 + (w0 - v0)*t)`. Overdamped (`zeta > 1`) is a sum of two real exponentials with roots `-zeta*w0 ± w0*sqrt(zeta^2 - 1)`. Picking the wrong branch is silent until `sqrt(1 - zeta^2)` goes imaginary and every sample is NaN.
3. `bounce` is expressed against the critical damping coefficient `2*sqrt(stiffness*mass)` rather than as an absolute damping value, which is what makes `bounce: 0` mean exactly "no overshoot" at any stiffness. Without that normalisation the same damping number is bouncy at high stiffness and sluggish at low.
4. Duration is not a parameter — it is solved. A 240 Hz scan walks the solution until the spring is both close enough (`|d| < restDelta`) and slow enough (`|d'| < restSpeed`), and the first `t` that satisfies both becomes the duration. Both tests are needed: an underdamped spring crosses the target at full speed on every oscillation, so a distance-only test declares it settled half a bounce in.
5. The solved duration is divided by `resolutionMs` to get a stop count, capped at 200, and the solution is evaluated at each stop. Samples are `1 - d(t)` — progress, not remaining distance — and are deliberately left unclamped, because values above 1 are the overshoot and clamping them is precisely how a spring degrades into an ease-out.
6. The last sample is forced to exactly 1. The scan stopped within `restDelta` of the target, so it would otherwise be ~0.999 and every transition would end with a visible sub-pixel snap as the browser jumps from the final easing output to the real end value.
7. `fallback` is a monotonic `cubic-bezier()` meant to be declared on the line *before* the `linear()` one. An engine that cannot parse `linear()` drops that declaration during parsing and the earlier one survives — the ordinary CSS cascade, with no feature query.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `MAX_STOPS = 200`
  Upper bound on samples. The compositor shows one value per frame, so stops closer together than a frame are bytes with no visible effect — 200 stops across a 1.6s spring is one every 8 ms, already finer than a 120 Hz frame. It also bounds the emitted string: a slow overdamped spring at 10 ms resolution would otherwise run past a thousand stops.
- `resolutionMs = 10`
  Milliseconds between samples. Below ~6 ms the string grows with no visual change even at 165 Hz; past ~20 ms the linear segments between stops become long enough that the interpolation reads as faceted rather than smooth, most visibly around the first peak where curvature is highest.
- `SCAN_STEP = 1 / 240`
  Integration step for the settle scan — four samples per 60 Hz frame. Coarser steps can step straight over the narrow window where an underdamped spring is simultaneously near the target and slow, which sends the duration to `maxDurationMs`.
- `MIN_RATIO = 0.05`
  Floor on the damping ratio. At zeta = 0 the spring is undamped and never satisfies the rest test, so the scan runs to `maxDurationMs` and emits a 200-stop string of a curve that oscillates forever. `bounce` is clamped to `1 - MIN_RATIO` for the same reason.
- `restDelta = 0.005`
  Distance, as a fraction of the total, that counts as arrived. At 0.005 a 400 px move stops 2 px out, under the forced final sample, so the snap is invisible. An order of magnitude tighter roughly doubles the duration of a bouncy spring for motion nobody can see.
- `restSpeed = 0.1`
  Speed, in fractions per second, that counts as stopped. Paired with `restDelta` so a fast pass through the target is not mistaken for arrival.
- `precision = 4`
  Decimal places per sample. Four is sub-pixel on any realistic distance (0.0001 of 2000 px is 0.2 px) and keeps a 200-stop string near 1.4 KB. Full float precision triples the byte count for nothing.
- `maxDurationMs = 10000`
  Hard ceiling so a pathological configuration returns a long easing rather than hanging the scan loop.

## API

```ts
function springToLinear(spring?: { stiffness?: number; damping?: number; mass?: number; bounce?: number; velocity?: number; restDelta?: number; restSpeed?: number }, options?: { resolutionMs?: number; maxDurationMs?: number; precision?: number }): { easing: string; fallback: string; durationMs: number; samples: readonly number[] }
function useSpringEasing(spring?: SpringConfig, options?: LinearEasingOptions): SpringEasing
```

- `stiffness: number` — default `100`
  Restoring force per unit displacement. Higher is faster and tighter.
- `damping: number` — default `10`
  Resistance proportional to velocity. Ignored when `bounce` is given.
- `mass: number` — default `1`
  Inertia. Raising it lowers the natural frequency and lengthens the settle.
- `bounce: number`
  Overshoot 0-1, relative to critical damping. 0 is monotonic, 0.5 is lively. Overrides `damping`.
- `velocity: number` — default `0`
  Initial velocity in fractions of the distance per second, for handing off from a gesture.
- `restDelta: number` — default `0.005`
  Remaining distance, as a fraction, that counts as arrived.
- `restSpeed: number` — default `0.1`
  Speed, in fractions per second, that counts as stopped.
- `resolutionMs: number` — default `10`
  Milliseconds between emitted stops.
- `maxDurationMs: number` — default `10000`
  Ceiling on the solved duration.
- `precision: number` — default `4`
  Decimal places per sample.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
/**
 * Upper bound on samples. The compositor can only show one value per frame, so
 * stops spaced closer than a frame are bytes with no visible effect: 200 stops
 * across a 1.6s spring is one every 8ms, already finer than a 120Hz frame.
 */
const MAX_STOPS = 200;
/** Integration step for the settle scan. 240Hz — four samples per 60Hz frame. */
const SCAN_STEP = 1 / 240;
/** A damping ratio of 0 never settles; this is the floor. */
const MIN_RATIO = 0.05;

/** Remaining distance and its derivative, at time `t` seconds. */
type Solver = (t: number) => readonly [distance: number, velocity: number];

/**
 * Closed-form solution of `d'' + 2*zeta*w0*d' + w0^2*d = 0` with `d(0) = 1`
 * and `d'(0) = -velocity`, i.e. the *remaining* distance to the target. All
 * three damping regimes have different solutions and picking the wrong branch
 * is silent: an overdamped spring evaluated with the underdamped formula
 * returns NaN the moment `sqrt(1 - zeta^2)` goes imaginary.
 */
function makeSolver(w0: number, zeta: number, v0: number): Solver {
  if (zeta < 1) {
    const wd = w0 * Math.sqrt(1 - zeta * zeta);
    const b = (zeta * w0 - v0) / wd;
    return (t) => {
      const decay = Math.exp(-zeta * w0 * t);
      const cos = Math.cos(wd * t);
      const sin = Math.sin(wd * t);
      const d = decay * (cos + b * sin);
      const dp = decay * (-zeta * w0 * (cos + b * sin) + (-wd * sin + b * wd * cos));
      return [d, dp];
    };
  }

  if (zeta === 1) {
    const a = w0 - v0;
    return (t) => {
      const decay = Math.exp(-w0 * t);
      return [decay * (1 + a * t), decay * (a - w0 * (1 + a * t))];
    };
  }

  const root = w0 * Math.sqrt(zeta * zeta - 1);
  const r1 = -zeta * w0 + root;
  const r2 = -zeta * w0 - root;
  const c1 = (-v0 - r2) / (r1 - r2);
  const c2 = 1 - c1;
  return (t) => {
    const e1 = Math.exp(r1 * t);
    const e2 = Math.exp(r2 * t);
    return [c1 * e1 + c2 * e2, c1 * r1 * e1 + c2 * r2 * e2];
  };
}

export function springToLinear(
  spring: SpringConfig = {},
  options: LinearEasingOptions = {},
): SpringEasing {
  const {
    stiffness = 100,
    mass = 1,
    velocity = 0,
    restDelta = 0.005,
    restSpeed = 0.1,
  } = spring;
  const { resolutionMs = 10, maxDurationMs = 10000, precision = 4 } = options;

  const w0 = Math.sqrt(stiffness / mass);
  // The critical damping coefficient. `bounce` is expressed against it, which
  // is what makes "bounce: 0" mean exactly "no overshoot" for any stiffness.
  const critical = 2 * Math.sqrt(stiffness * mass);
  const damping =
    spring.bounce === undefined
      ? (spring.damping ?? 10)
      : critical * (1 - clamp(spring.bounce, 0, 1 - MIN_RATIO));
  const zeta = Math.max(damping / critical, MIN_RATIO);

  const solve = makeSolver(w0, zeta, velocity);

  // Scan for the first moment the spring is both close enough and slow enough.
  // Distance alone is not sufficient: an underdamped spring passes through the
  // target at full speed on every oscillation, and a distance-only test would
  // declare it settled on the first crossing, half a bounce in.
  const maxSeconds = maxDurationMs / 1000;
  let settled = maxSeconds;
  for (let t = 0; t <= maxSeconds; t += SCAN_STEP) {
    const [d, dp] = solve(t);
    if (Math.abs(d) < restDelta && Math.abs(dp) < restSpeed) {
      settled = t;
      break;
    }
  }
  const durationMs = Math.max(Math.ceil(settled * 1000), 1);

  const stops = clamp(Math.round(durationMs / resolutionMs), 2, MAX_STOPS);
  const factor = 10 ** precision;
  const samples: number[] = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < stops; i++) {
    const t = (i / (stops - 1)) * (durationMs / 1000);
    // Progress, not remaining distance. NOT clamped: values above 1 are the
    // overshoot, and clamping them is exactly how a spring becomes an ease-out.
    samples.push(Math.round((1 - solve(t)[0]) * factor) / factor);
  }
  // The scan stops within `restDelta` of the target, so the final sample is
  // ~0.999. Left alone, every transition ends with a sub-pixel snap as the
  // browser jumps from the last easing output to the real end value.
  samples[stops - 1] = 1;

  return {
    easing: `linear(${samples.join(', ')})`,
    // Declared first so a browser without linear() support keeps it: the
    // unparseable longhand is dropped, the previous declaration survives.
    fallback: CSS_EASING.outQuart,
    durationMs,
    samples,
  };
}

/**
 * `springToLinear` with memoisation and a reduced-motion variant.
 *
 * Reduced motion does not shorten the animation to nothing — it removes the
 * oscillation. The damping ratio is forced to 1 and the initial velocity to 0,
 * which keeps the spring's stiffness and therefore its pace, and produces a
 * monotonic curve that arrives once and stays.
 */
export function useSpringEasing(
  spring: SpringConfig = {},
  options: LinearEasingOptions = {},
): SpringEasing {
  const reduced = useReducedMotion();
  const { stiffness, damping, mass, bounce, velocity, restDelta, restSpeed } = spring;
  const { resolutionMs, maxDurationMs, precision } = options;

  return useMemo(
    () =>
      springToLinear(
        reduced
          ? { stiffness, mass, bounce: 0, velocity: 0, restDelta, restSpeed }
          : { stiffness, damping, mass, bounce, velocity, restDelta, restSpeed },
        { resolutionMs, maxDurationMs, precision },
      ),
    [
      reduced,
      stiffness,
      damping,
      mass,
      bounce,
      velocity,
      restDelta,
      restSpeed,
      resolutionMs,
      maxDurationMs,
      precision,
    ],
  );
}
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** Nothing to clean up: `springToLinear` is a pure function and `useSpringEasing` only calls it inside `useMemo`. No timers, listeners, or animation frames are created. The reduced-motion subscription belongs to `useReducedMotion`, which removes its own media-query listener on unmount.

**Reduced motion.** `useSpringEasing` recomputes with `bounce: 0` and `velocity: 0`, forcing the damping ratio to exactly 1. That removes the oscillation — the trigger for vestibular discomfort — while keeping the stiffness and therefore the pace, so the motion stays the same length and simply arrives once instead of settling. It is not shortened to zero: the curve is still a real ease, just monotonic, and the demo's peak readout drops to 100% to show it.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Clamping the samples to [0, 1]. This is the one mistake that destroys the whole technique: the overshoot lives in the values above 1, and a clamped spring is an ease-out with extra bytes. It looks like the maths is wrong when the maths is fine.
- Reading the raw solution as progress. The closed form gives *remaining distance*, which starts at 1 and decays to 0; the easing needs `1 - d`. Emitting `d` directly produces an animation that runs backwards and every reviewer misdiagnoses it as an inverted easing.
- Using one formula for all damping ratios. `sqrt(1 - zeta^2)` is imaginary above zeta = 1, so an overdamped spring evaluated with the underdamped branch yields NaN, and `linear(0, NaN, NaN)` fails to parse — the transition silently reverts to `ease` with nothing in the console.
- Testing only distance for the settle time. An underdamped spring passes exactly through the target on every swing, so the scan stops on the first crossing and the emitted curve is cut off mid-bounce.
- Leaving the final sample at its solved value. It is ~0.999, and the browser jumps from there to the real end value in one frame — a visible tick at the end of every transition that reads as a rendering bug.
- Passing the `linear()` string through a CSS custom property. An unsupported value inside `var()` is invalid at computed-value time, which resolves the property to its *initial* value (`ease`) instead of falling back to the previous declaration. That silently defeats the two-declaration fallback in exactly the browsers that need it.
- Declaring the fallback after `linear()`. Later declarations win, so a supporting browser also uses the cubic-bezier and the spring never appears anywhere.
- Setting a duration by hand. Duration is an output of the spring, not an input; overriding it rescales the curve in time so a stiff spring animates slowly with a stiff shape, which looks wrong without looking obviously wrong.
- Recomputing the easing every render. The scan runs up to 2400 solver evaluations, so an unmemoised call inside a frequently-rendering component is measurable main-thread work to produce a string that never changes.
- Using this for anything interruptible. A `linear()` easing is a fixed curve of fixed length; a spring that must absorb a new target mid-flight, with its current velocity carried over, still needs a real per-frame integrator.

## Notes

- Deterministic and pure, so it is safe to precompute at build time and inline the string into a stylesheet — the runtime cost then drops to zero. `springToLinear` is exported separately from the hook for that reason.
- Works for any animatable property, including ones a JavaScript spring handles badly: `linear()` on a `background-color` transition springs the colour without touching the main thread at all.
- A `linear()` easing applies to Web Animations and CSS animations identically. Passing `easing` as the `easing` option of `element.animate()` gets the same compositor handoff.
- The overshoot means the property leaves the 0-1 range, so a spring on `scale` momentarily exceeds the target scale. Anything clipped by an `overflow: hidden` parent should be sized with that headroom in mind — the demo's peak readout is the exact multiplier.

## Definition of done

Press Run. The three squares cross their tracks and each one visibly passes its end position and settles back — Loose the most, Snap barely. The plotted curve beside each row rises above the dashed 100% line by the amount stated in the readout. Scroll or drag hard during the run and the motion does not hitch, because it is not on the main thread. Read the emitted string: it starts at 0, contains values greater than 1, and ends at exactly 1. Turn reduced motion on and re-run: every curve is monotonic, no square passes its end position, every peak reads 100%, and the durations are still hundreds of milliseconds rather than zero.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Stacked Card Fan

Cards stacked on top of each other with a slight fan: the front card sits upright in the middle and the others peek out to its left and right, each tilted, lowered, shrunk and dimmed a little more the further back it is. Hovering or keyboard-focusing the stack spreads the fan so more of each card shows; clicking the front card, or pressing an arrow key, sends it round the back and brings the next one forward, and clicking a card behind brings that card forward directly. A "See all" pill under the stack spreads the cards almost flat for a full view.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

A fanned stack of tilted cards: hover spreads the fan, clicking or arrow keys bring the next card forward, and a pill lays them all out.

- Category: display
- Runtime cost: css
- Dependencies: @remixicon/react@^4.9.0, react-aria@^3.53.1

## How it works

1. Slots: each card gets a signed circular distance `d` from the front card, `((i − active + ⌊n/2⌋) mod n) − ⌊n/2⌋`, so five cards are ordered 0, +1, +2, −2, −1 around the front. Cycling shifts every `d` by one; the card leaving one end wraps to the other end at the back of the pile, where the higher cards hide the crossing.
2. One transform per card, written once as CSS variables: `translateX(-50%) translateX(d·gap) translateY(|d|·drop) rotate(d·tilt) scale(1 − |d|·shrink)`. `--d` and `--ad` are set per card; `--spread`, `--tilt`, `--drop`, `--shrink` come from `data-state` (rest, peek, expanded) on the stage. Changing either recomputes the transform and a single 500ms `transform` transition animates it, so hover, cycle and expand share one path with no JS animation loop.
3. Fit: the wrapper is a size container. Card width is `min(cardWidth, 80cqi)` and height keeps the aspect ratio. The gap is `max(12px, min(cardW · spread, (100cqi − cardW) / (2·⌊n/2⌋)))`, so the outermost card never passes the container edge, however wide the state asks it to spread. Expanded lays the cards in a row instead, which also needs them smaller: the container width from the kit `useResizeObserver` gives `scale = width / (card · (1 + (n − 1) · 0.86))` and a gap of `0.86 · card · scale`, passed in as `--base` and `--gap`. Scale is a plain number, and CSS cannot yet divide lengths into one in every browser.
4. Depth: `z-index` is `n − |d|`, and a token-coloured veil inside each card (`bg-background-primary-default` at `0.24·|d|` opacity, capped at 0.6) dims cards behind. A veil rather than card opacity keeps cards behind from showing through each other in dark mode.
5. Input: the stage is a focusable `role="group"` with `aria-roledescription="card stack"`. Arrow keys, Enter and Space cycle; Home and End jump. react-aria `useHover` (mouse only, so touch never sticks in peek) and `useFocusRing` (keyboard focus only) drive the peek state. Cards behind are `aria-hidden`, and a polite live region announces the new front card ("Tokens, 1 of 5").

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `rest / peek spread = 0.30 / 0.46 × card width`
  Rest shows a sliver of each card; peek shows their headings.
- `expanded step = 0.86 × scaled card width`
  Cards sit in a row with 14% overlap, scaled so the whole row fits the container.
- `tilt = 5° / 8° / 1.5° per slot`
  The fan opens wider on hover; flat-ish when expanded so content reads.
- `drop, shrink = 10px / 16px / 4px per slot; 4% per slot (0 expanded)`
  Cards behind sit lower and smaller, which reads as depth without a 3D perspective.
- `transition = 500ms cubic-bezier(0.22, 1, 0.36, 1)`
  A fast start and long settle makes the cycle feel like a flick.
- `card size = 300 × 260px, 80cqi max`
  Default shown in the reference; shrinks together with the aspect ratio below about 400px.

## API

```ts
function StackedCardFan(props: { items: { id: string; label: string; content: ReactNode }[]; activeIndex?: number; defaultActiveIndex?: number; onActiveChange?: (index: number) => void; expanded?: boolean; defaultExpanded?: boolean; onExpandedChange?: (expanded: boolean) => void; showToggle?: boolean; expandLabel?: string; collapseLabel?: string; cardWidth?: number; cardHeight?: number; fade?: boolean; "aria-label"?: string; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `items: StackedCardFanItem[]`
  `{ id, label, content }`; `label` is announced when the card comes forward.
- `activeIndex: number`
  Controlled front card.
- `defaultActiveIndex: number` — default `0`
  Initial front card.
- `onActiveChange: (index: number) => void`
  Called when the front card changes.
- `expanded: boolean`
  Controlled expanded state.
- `defaultExpanded: boolean` — default `false`
  Initial expanded state.
- `showToggle: boolean` — default `true`
  Show the See all / Stack pill.
- `expandLabel: string` — default `"See all {n}"`
  Pill label while stacked.
- `collapseLabel: string` — default `"Stack cards"`
  Pill label while expanded.
- `cardWidth: number` — default `300`
  Card width in px.
- `cardHeight: number` — default `260`
  Card height in px.
- `fade: boolean` — default `false`
  Mask the bottom of the stack into the page.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
/**
 * Signed circular distance from the front card: for five cards and front 0,
 * the order is 0, 1, 2, -2, -1. The front card sits at 0, the rest alternate
 * to its right (+) and left (-), and cycling the front card makes the one
 * leaving the far end slip round behind the stack to the other end.
 */
function slotOf(index: number, active: number, count: number) {
  const half = Math.floor(count / 2);
  return ((((index - active + half) % count) + count) % count) - half;
}

/**
 * Every card has one transform made of CSS variables: `--d` (its slot) and
 * `--ad` (|slot|) are set per card, while `--spread`, `--tilt`, `--drop`,
 * `--shrink` are set by the stack state (rest, peek on hover/focus, expanded). A change of
 * either re-computes the transform and a single CSS transition animates it, so
 * hover, cycling and expanding all share one code path with no JS animation.
 * The horizontal gap is capped by the container so the outer cards never
 * leave it: half * gap + card / 2 <= 50cqi.
 */
const CARD_TRANSFORM =
  "translateX(-50%) translateX(calc(var(--d) * var(--gap))) translateY(calc(var(--ad) * var(--drop))) rotate(calc(var(--d) * var(--tilt))) scale(calc(var(--base) * (1 - var(--ad) * var(--shrink))))";

const GAP = "max(12px, min(calc(var(--card-w) * var(--spread)), calc((100cqi - var(--card-w)) / var(--span))))";

/** Each expanded card advances this fraction of a card width past the one before (14% overlap). */
const EXPANDED_STEP = 0.86;

/**
 * Expanded lays every card out in a row, so cards must also shrink: the scale
 * that makes card + (n - 1) * step * card fit the measured width. Scale is a
 * plain number, which CSS cannot derive from lengths everywhere yet, so it is
 * computed here from the container's layout width.
 */
function expandedLayout(width: number, cardWidth: number, count: number) {
  const card = Math.min(cardWidth, width * 0.8);
  const scale = Math.min(1, width / (card * (1 + (count - 1) * EXPANDED_STEP)));
  return { scale, gap: card * scale * EXPANDED_STEP };
}
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** Motion is a CSS transition with no loop to stop. The shared ResizeObserver unobserves the wrapper on unmount, and react-aria removes its hover and focus listeners itself.

**Reduced motion.** Card transforms and the dimming veil change instantly (`motion-reduce:transition-none`); hover, cycling and expanding still work. The step spinner in the sample faces stops.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Using `inert` on the cards behind: inert elements are skipped by hit testing, so clicks on them fall through and they cannot be brought forward. Use `aria-hidden` and keep the card faces non-interactive.
- Declaring `--gap` on an element above the stage: unregistered custom properties substitute their `var()` references where they are declared, so a `--gap` that reads `--spread` must sit on the element that sets `--spread`.
- Fading cards behind with `opacity` on the whole card: they become see-through and stack into a muddle in dark mode. Dim with an opaque-coloured veil instead.
- Driving peek from `onMouseEnter`: a tap on touch devices fires it and never the leave, leaving the fan open. react-aria `useHover` ignores emulated mouse events.

## Notes

- `stacked-card-fan-cards.tsx` holds five agent-dashboard card faces (tokens chart, activity calendar, requests bars, usage meters, step list) and `AGENT_DASHBOARD_CARDS`, the array the demo and the CTA Section use.
- With `fade` the lower part of the stack is masked into the page, as in a hero visual.
- Active card and expanded state are both controllable (`activeIndex`/`onActiveChange`, `expanded`/`onExpandedChange`).

## Definition of done

Five cards rest in a slight fan with the Tokens chart upright in front. Hovering spreads them and shows each heading; clicking the front card sends it round the back and brings September forward; clicking a card behind brings it forward; the arrow keys do the same with a visible focus ring. See all five lays the cards out nearly flat and Stack cards gathers them. At 360px the cards shrink and the fan stays inside the frame. Light and dark both read.

and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Stage Bars Card

A dashboard card that lists funnel stages as rounded pills over the chart track: name on the left, value and share of the top stage on the right, a 14px icon at the start of each pill. The pills grow to their shares on mount and on every period change. Hovering, focusing or tapping a stage fades the others and swaps the count-up headline to that stage with its step conversion. With `stacked`, each pill splits into its breakdown parts with a legend, and hovering a part (or arrowing through it) shows that part's value and its share of the stage.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

A funnel as rounded stage pills with value and share, optional stacked parts with a legend, stat tiles and a headline that follows hover.

- Category: display
- Runtime cost: dom
- Dependencies: @remixicon/react@^4.9.0

## How it works

1. The rows live in one CSS grid, `max-content | minmax(0,1fr) | max-content`, and every row is a `<button>` spanning it with `grid-cols-subgrid`. So the name column sizes to the longest stage name and all pills start on the same line.
2. Each pill is an absolutely positioned span inside a `bg-chart-track` track. Its width is `share * 100%`, where share is `value / top` tweened by `useTweenedValues` (520ms ease-out cubic, from 0 on mount and from the current shares on a new period). With an icon, the pill keeps a 20px minimum so the icon always sits on colour.
3. Stacked, the pill becomes a flex row with a 2px gap. Each part is `flex-basis: 0` with `flex-grow` set to its value, so the parts always fill exactly the pill. When a new period changes the mix, `flex-grow` moves through a 300ms CSS transition.
4. The legend is built from the parts' labels in first-seen order. Each series takes the next palette colour (lime, blue, purple, …) unless a part sets `color`. In mono, the series step down in opacity (1, 0.75, 0.5, floor 0.4) instead.
5. The target is `{ stage, segment | null }`. Pointer enter and focus on a row set the stage; pointer enter on a part sets the part, and leaving it goes back to the stage. On a focused stacked row, ArrowRight/ArrowLeft walk through the parts and back to the whole stage. Click toggles a pin (`aria-pressed`) that holds the stage when nothing is hovered.
6. The header shows the title, the top value and the delta chip at rest. A stage shows its name, its value and "58% of Sign-up" (step conversion) or "Top of funnel". A part shows "Sign-up · Paid", its value and "32% of Sign-up". The number counts up in a `<p>` keyed by the target, so the fade replays on every swap.
7. Inactive rows and tiles fade to 0.4 and 0.45 opacity over 200ms. Within a hovered stacked row the other parts fade to 0.35, and the active fill switches to the darker `--color-chart-N-active` tone (text-primary in mono).

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `pill = 20px tall (h-5), rounded-full, rows 28px + 4px gap`
  Matches the preview's pitch: six stages fit in about 190px, with room for a 14px icon and a hit area tall enough to hover.
- `ICON_PILL_MIN = 20px`
  A 3% stage would otherwise be a 7px sliver with its icon over the track; on the dark track the near-black icon would vanish.
- `tween = 520ms ease-out cubic, from 0 on mount`
  Shares are tweened rather than widths in px, so resizing the card never animates and a new period starts from wherever the bars are.
- `part transition = flex-grow, background-color and opacity over 300ms`
  Re-proportioning the parts at the same pace as the bar width keeps a period change reading as one motion.
- `monoOpacity = 1 − 0.25 × series index, floor 0.4`
  With one ink, stacked parts still need to read as different series; three steps stay apart on both themes.
- `tiles = 3 per row, 120px minimum`
  Six stages make two even rows, as in the preview; a 360px card wraps to two per row.

## API

```ts
function StageBarsCard(props: { title?: string; ranges?: StageRange[]; stages?: BarStage[]; delta?: number; range?: string; defaultRange?: string; onRangeChange?: (id: string) => void; stacked?: boolean; mono?: boolean; showIcons?: boolean; formatValue?: (value: number) => string; className?: string }): JSX.Element
type BarStage = { label: string; value: number; color?: ChartColor; icon?: ReactNode; segments?: StageSegment[] }
type StageSegment = { label: string; value: number; color?: ChartColor }
```

- `title: string` — default `"Pipeline"`
  Header label while nothing is active; also the card's accessible name.
- `ranges: StageRange[]` — default `PIPELINE_RANGES`
  Periods with their own stages, delta and optional headline. Two or more show the period select.
- `stages: BarStage[]`
  A single stage list, top first. Overrides `ranges` and hides the select.
- `delta: number`
  Headline chip percentage when `stages` is used.
- `range: string`
  Controlled period id.
- `defaultRange: string` — default `first range id`
  Initial period when uncontrolled.
- `onRangeChange: (id: string) => void`
  Called when the period select changes.
- `stacked: boolean` — default `false`
  Splits each pill into its stage's `segments` and shows a legend. Tile swatches are hidden, since colour then means the part.
- `mono: boolean` — default `false`
  One ink for every pill (secondary text colour, primary when active) and no tile swatches.
- `showIcons: boolean` — default `true`
  Draws each stage's `icon` at the left end inside its pill.
- `formatValue: (value: number) => string` — default `en-US integer`
  Formats the headline, row values, tiles and the accessible labels.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the card section.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
/**
 * One stage: a subgrid row of [name | pill on the track | value + share].
 * The pill's width is the tweened share of the top stage. Stacked, it is a
 * flex row of parts whose `flex-grow` is their value, so the parts always fill
 * exactly the pill and re-proportion with a CSS transition on a new period.
 */
function StageRow({
  stage,
  index,
  share,
  topLabel,
  topValue,
  series,
  mono,
  showIcons,
  active,
  pinned,
  formatValue,
  onTarget,
  onTogglePin,
}: StageRowProps) {
  const parts = series.length > 0 ? partsOf(stage) : [];
  const isActive = active?.stage === index;
  const activePart = isActive ? (active?.segment ?? null) : null;
  const color = CHART_COLORS[chartColorAt(index, stage.color)];
  const solid = mono ? (isActive ? "var(--color-text-primary)" : MONO_FILL) : isActive ? color.active : color.fill;
  const icon = showIcons && stage.icon ? stage.icon : null;
  const percent = pct(stage.value, topValue);

  const onKeyDown = (event: KeyboardEvent<HTMLButtonElement>) => {
    if (parts.length === 0 || (event.key !== "ArrowRight" && event.key !== "ArrowLeft")) return;
    event.preventDefault();
    const last = parts.length - 1;
    // Right walks 0..last then back to the whole stage; Left walks the other way.
    const next =
      event.key === "ArrowRight"
        ? activePart === null ? 0 : activePart < last ? activePart + 1 : null
        : activePart === null ? last : activePart > 0 ? activePart - 1 : null;
    onTarget({ stage: index, segment: next });
  };

  const breakdown = parts.map((p) => `${p.label} ${formatValue(p.value)}`).join(", ");

  return (
    <button
      type="button"
      aria-pressed={pinned}
      aria-label={`${stage.label}: ${formatValue(stage.value)}, ${percent}% of ${topLabel}${breakdown ? `. ${breakdown}` : ""}`}
      aria-keyshortcuts={parts.length > 0 ? "ArrowLeft ArrowRight" : undefined}
      onPointerEnter={() => onTarget({ stage: index, segment: null })}
      onFocus={() => onTarget({ stage: index, segment: null })}
      onBlur={() => onTarget(null)}
      onClick={onTogglePin}
      onKeyDown={onKeyDown}
      className={cx(
        "col-span-3 grid cursor-pointer grid-cols-subgrid items-center rounded-md py-1 text-left outline-none",
        "transition-opacity duration-200 ease-out motion-reduce:transition-none",
        "focus-visible:ring-2 focus-visible:ring-border-focus-ring",
        active !== null && !isActive && "opacity-40",
      )}
    >
      <span className="text-right text-body-regular whitespace-nowrap text-text-secondary">{stage.label}</span>
      <span className="relative h-5 min-w-0 rounded-full bg-chart-track">
        <span
          className="absolute inset-y-0 left-0 flex gap-0.5 overflow-hidden rounded-full"
          style={{
            width: `${Math.max(0, share) * 100}%`,
            minWidth: icon && stage.value > 0 ? ICON_PILL_MIN : undefined,
          }}
        >
          {parts.length > 0 ? (
            parts.map((part, partIndex) => {
              const seriesIndex = series.findIndex((s) => s.label === part.label);
              const tone = CHART_COLORS[series[seriesIndex]?.color ?? "lime"];
              const lit = activePart === partIndex;
              return (
                <span
                  key={part.label}
                  data-part={part.label}
                  onPointerEnter={() => onTarget({ stage: index, segment: partIndex })}
                  onPointerLeave={() => onTarget({ stage: index, segment: null })}
                  className="h-full min-w-0 basis-0 transition-[flex-grow,background-color,opacity] duration-300 ease-out motion-reduce:transition-none"
                  style={{
                    flexGrow: part.value,
                    backgroundColor: mono ? (lit ? "var(--color-text-primary)" : MONO_FILL) : lit ? tone.active : tone.fill,
                    opacity: activePart !== null && !lit ? 0.35 : mono ? monoOpacity(seriesIndex) : 1,
                  }}
                />
              );
            })
          ) : (
            <span
              className="h-full flex-1 transition-[background-color] duration-200 ease-out motion-reduce:transition-none"
              style={{ backgroundColor: solid }}
            />
          )}
        </span>
        {icon ? (
          <span
            aria-hidden
            className="pointer-events-none absolute top-1/2 left-[3px] flex size-3.5 -translate-y-1/2 items-center justify-center text-neutral-950"
          >
            {icon}
          </span>
        ) : null}
      </span>
      <span className="flex items-baseline justify-end gap-1.5 tabular-nums">
        <span className="text-body-medium text-text-primary">{formatValue(stage.value)}</span>
        <span className="min-w-[4ch] text-caption-1-regular text-text-tertiary">{percent}%</span>
      </span>
    </button>
  );
}
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** The width tween and `useCountUp` cancel their animation frame on every new target and on unmount. Hover, pin and keyboard targets are plain React state; there are no listeners outside React.

**Reduced motion.** `useTweenedValues` is disabled, so the pills render at their final widths on mount and jump on a period change. The parts' flex-grow/colour/opacity transitions and the row fades are removed with `motion-reduce:transition-none`. The headline count runs over 1ms, and the number fade is off.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Sizing stacked parts as percentages of the track. Their sum then drifts from the pill width as soon as the 2px gaps or the icon minimum come in. Flex-grow by value always fills the pill exactly.
- Putting the label, bar and numbers in separate flex rows. Each row then sizes its own name column and the pills start at different x positions. A shared grid with subgrid rows keeps one column for every row.
- Making stacked parts separate tab stops. Six stages × three parts is 18 stops; arrow keys on the focused stage reach the same detail with one stop per row.

## Notes

- `PIPELINE_RANGES`, `BarStage`, `StageSegment` and `StageRange` are exported. Pass `stages` (and `delta`) for one static list without the period select.
- Stages share the funnel's shape (`label`, `value`, `color`) plus `icon` and `segments`, so the same data can drive the Funnel Chart Card.
- The frame, header, period select and stat tiles come from `funnel-chart-card-shell`.

## Definition of done

The card shows "Pipeline", "1,180" and a lime "+2.4%" chip. Six rows follow: Visits 1,180 100%, Sign-up 790 67%, Active 460 39%, Pro 250 21%, Team 120 10% and Enterprise 40 3%, with lime, blue, purple, pink, yellow and emerald pills and icons. Six tiles sit three per row. Hovering Active fades the other rows and the header reads "Active", "460" and "58% of Sign-up". With "By channel", each pill splits into three parts with an Organic / Paid / Referral legend. Hovering Sign-up's second part reads "Sign-up · Paid", "253" and "32% of Sign-up". "Last 30 days" grows the pills and the headline counts to 4,820.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.
