# Build: Stat Cards

The KPI row at the top of a dashboard, driven by an array of `Stat` objects. `variant="plain"` is a compact 132px card with an icon tile, a label, the value and a delta `Chip`. `variant="footer"` adds a tinted gradient icon tile, an optional info tooltip, a display-size value and an inner footer band with a comparison caption and a delta pill. The grid reflows from one or two columns up to four, and `count` and `columns` cut it down for narrower hosts.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

A responsive row of KPI cards in two looks: a compact tile with a delta chip, or a gradient icon tile over a caption band and delta pill.

- Category: display
- Runtime cost: css
- Dependencies: @remixicon/react@^4.9.0, react-aria-components@^1.22.1

## How it works

1. `StatCards` picks `stats`, or the demo set that matches the variant (`DEFAULT_STATS` or `DEFAULT_FOOTER_STATS`), slices it to `count` and renders one card per entry keyed by `label`. The wrapper is a `grid w-full gap-4`.
2. Columns are set per variant. `columns={1}` is always `grid-cols-1`. Otherwise plain cards start at `grid-cols-2` and footer cards at `grid-cols-1 sm:grid-cols-2`, because a display-size value does not fit two-up on a phone. With `columns={4}` plain cards go four-up at `lg` and footer cards at `xl`.
3. Delta colour is data, not maths. Each stat carries `deltaColor: "lime" | "rose" | "neutral"`, and `DELTA_STYLES` maps it to a glyph (`RiArrowUpCircleFill`, `RiArrowDownCircleFill`, `RiIndeterminateCircleFill`), a text colour and a pill background. A rise that is bad news, such as refunds going up, can therefore read rose.
4. The plain card is a `section` with `h-[132px]`, `justify-between`, `rounded-2xl`, `bg-background-secondary-default` and `p-4`. The icon sits in a `bg-stat-card-icon-background` tile, the value is `text-title-1-medium`, and the delta is a `Chip variant="bold"` in the stat's colour. The value and chip row is `flex-wrap`, so a narrow card drops the chip below the number instead of overflowing.
5. The footer card is a `p-2` section in three parts. A header holds a 40px `rounded-2lg` icon tile filled with `bg-linear-to-b` from the `TILE_TONES[tone]` stops (blue by default), with a white glyph. The body holds a truncated label over a `text-display-4-medium tabular-nums` value. The band is an inner tile (`bg-background-inner-default shadow-card rounded-2lg`, `mt-auto`) holding the caption (default "From last month") and the `DeltaPill`.
6. When `hint` is set, `StatHint` renders a bare 20px info button inside React Aria's `TooltipTrigger` (200ms delay) wrapped in `Focusable`. The open state is controlled, so the tooltip opens on hover and focus as usual and the button's `onClick` also toggles it, because a glyph that small gets tapped. The button is labelled "About {label}".
7. Every subcomponent returns its JSX through `useTemplateCopy()`. With no `TemplateCopyProvider` this returns the node unchanged. With one, labels, captions and hints are translated while values and IDs are left alone.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `plain card height = h-[132px]`
  Fixed so a row of cards lines up whether or not a chip wraps. `justify-between` pins the icon to the top and the label and value to the bottom, so the row reads as one band across the dashboard.
- `footer icon tile = size-10 rounded-2lg, gradient from-*-500 to-*-600 (orange and sky use 400 to 500)`
  A top-to-bottom two-step gradient gives the tile a lit edge without an image. The tones are fixed Tailwind palette stops rather than theme tokens, so the tile reads the same on light and dark surfaces.
- `tooltip delay = 200ms`
  Long enough that sweeping the pointer across a row of cards does not flash four tooltips, short enough that a deliberate hover feels immediate. A click skips the delay altogether.
- `breakpoints = plain lg:grid-cols-4, footer sm:grid-cols-2 xl:grid-cols-4`
  The footer card's `display-4` value needs roughly a third more width than the plain card's `title-1`, so it reaches four-up one breakpoint later and stays single-column below `sm`.

## API

```ts
function StatCards(props?: { variant?: "plain" | "footer"; stats?: Stat[]; count?: number; columns?: 1 | 2 | 4; className?: string }): JSX.Element
type Stat = { icon: IconComponent; label: string; value: string; delta: string; deltaColor: "lime" | "rose" | "neutral"; tone?: StatTone; caption?: string; hint?: string }
type StatTone = "blue" | "orange" | "purple" | "pink" | "sky" | "emerald"
```

- `variant: "plain" | "footer"` — default `"plain"`
  Compact tile with a delta chip, or the gradient-tile card with a caption band and delta pill.
- `stats: Stat[]`
  Cards to render. Defaults to demo metrics that match the variant.
- `count: number`
  Render only the first `count` stats.
- `columns: 1 | 2 | 4` — default `4`
  Column count at the widest breakpoint. `2` stays two-up, `1` pins a single column at every width.
- `Stat.deltaColor: "lime" | "rose" | "neutral"`
  Picks the chip or pill colour and the up, down or flat glyph.
- `Stat.tone: StatTone` — default `"blue"`
  Footer variant only: the icon tile gradient.
- `Stat.hint: string`
  Footer variant only: adds an info button whose tooltip shows this text.
- `Stat.caption: string` — default `"From last month"`
  Footer variant only: the comparison caption in the band.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
function FooterStatCard({ stat }: { stat: Stat }) {
  const localize = useTemplateCopy();
  return localize((
    <section className="flex min-w-0 flex-col rounded-2xl bg-background-secondary-default p-2">
      {/* Icon tile + optional info glyph, both hanging from the same top inset */}
      <div className="flex w-full items-start justify-between gap-2.5 p-2">
        <span
          className={cx(
            "flex size-10 shrink-0 items-center justify-center rounded-2lg bg-linear-to-b",
            TILE_TONES[stat.tone ?? "blue"],
          )}
        >
          <stat.icon className="size-5 shrink-0 text-white" aria-hidden />
        </span>
        {stat.hint && <StatHint label={stat.label} hint={stat.hint} />}
      </div>

      {/* Label sits directly over the number, as on the plain cards */}
      <div className="flex flex-col gap-0.5 px-2 pt-2.5 pb-3.5">
        <p className="truncate text-body-medium text-text-secondary">{stat.label}</p>
        <p className="text-display-4-medium whitespace-nowrap text-text-primary tabular-nums">
          {stat.value}
        </p>
      </div>

      {/* Footer band: comparison caption + delta pill on an inner tile */}
      <div className="mt-auto flex w-full items-center justify-between gap-2 rounded-2lg bg-background-inner-default py-1.5 pe-1.5 ps-2.5 shadow-card">
        <p className="truncate text-body-regular text-text-secondary">
          {stat.caption ?? "From last month"}
        </p>
        <DeltaPill delta={stat.delta} deltaColor={stat.deltaColor} />
      </div>
    </section>
  ));
}

export function StatCards({
  variant = "plain",
  stats,
  count,
  columns = 4,
  className,
}: {
  variant?: StatCardsVariant;
  /** KPI cards to render; defaults to demo metrics matching the variant. */
  stats?: Stat[];
  /** How many KPI cards to render (from the start of the list). */
  count?: number;
  /** Columns at the widest breakpoint - 2 keeps the grid two-up for
   *  narrower hosts (docs previews, split layouts), 1 pins a single
   *  column at every width. */
  columns?: 1 | 2 | 4;
  className?: string;
} = {}) {
  const localize = useTemplateCopy();
  const items =
    stats ?? (variant === "footer" ? DEFAULT_FOOTER_STATS : DEFAULT_STATS);
  return localize((
    <div
      className={cx(
        "grid w-full gap-4",
        // The footer cards carry a display-size value, so they go one per
        // row on phones where the plain cards still fit two up.
        columns === 1
          ? "grid-cols-1"
          : variant === "footer"
            ? "grid-cols-1 sm:grid-cols-2"
            : "grid-cols-2",
        columns === 4 && (variant === "footer" ? "xl:grid-cols-4" : "lg:grid-cols-4"),
        className,
      )}
    >
      {items.slice(0, count ?? items.length).map((stat) =>
        variant === "footer" ? (
          <FooterStatCard key={stat.label} stat={stat} />
        ) : (
          <PlainStatCard key={stat.label} stat={stat} />
        ),
      )}
    </div>
  ));
}
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** Nothing to clean up in the cards. The tooltip is a React Aria overlay, and React Aria removes its portal and listeners when it closes or unmounts.

**Reduced motion.** The cards do not move. The only motion is the tooltip's 200ms blur and scale-in, a CSS transition on React Aria's `data-entering` and `data-exiting` states. It is short and does not travel, so it is kept under reduced motion.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Deriving the delta colour from the sign of the number. Whether a change is good depends on the metric. Pass `deltaColor` with the data, as the default refunds card does.
- Removing `Focusable` around the info button. React Aria's `TooltipTrigger` hands its hover and focus handlers to its child through a context, and a plain `<button>` does not read that context, so neither hover nor focus would open the tooltip.
- Making the tooltip hover-only. The info glyph is 20px and touch users tap it, which is why `onClick` toggles the controlled `open` state as well.
- Giving cards a fixed width so the values line up. The grid sizes them, and the values use `tabular-nums`. A fixed width clips "$152,313.92" at the `display-4` size.
- Keying cards by array index. They are keyed by `label`, so a reordered `stats` array keeps tooltip state with the right card. Labels must be unique.

## Notes

- `count` slices from the start of the list. Together with `columns={1}` it makes a single-card preview or sidebar summary.
- The tone palette (`blue`, `orange`, `purple`, `pink`, `sky`, `emerald`) only affects the footer variant. The plain variant always uses the neutral `stat-card-icon-background` tile.

## Definition of done

The footer variant shows a blue revenue card and an orange orders card side by side, each with a white glyph on a gradient tile, a large tabular value and a band reading "From last month" with a lime up-arrow pill. Hovering or clicking the info glyph opens a tooltip with the hint after about 200ms. The plain variant shows four 132px cards whose chips are lime, rose and neutral. Below `sm` the footer cards stack in one column while the plain cards stay two-up.

and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Status Dot

Two nested spans: a 12px round halo in a tinted status colour and a 6px solid dot centred inside it. It is the marker the kit puts in front of a purchase status ("Completed", "Waiting", "Processing") in select options and data-table cells. It is decorative by design, so the text beside it carries the meaning.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

A 12px status indicator: a solid 6px dot centred on a tinted halo, in green, yellow and indigo, for selects and table cells.

- Category: display
- Runtime cost: css
- Dependencies: none beyond React

## How it works

1. Keep the colour classes in one `sortCx` map with three keys: `base` (`inline-flex size-3 shrink-0 items-center justify-center rounded-full`), `halo` (one semantic token per colour) and `dot` (one palette class per colour).
2. Render an outer `<span>` with `base` plus `styles.halo[color]`. `size-3` makes it 12px and `shrink-0` stops a flex row (a select option, a table cell) from squeezing the circle into an oval.
3. Render an inner `<span className="size-1.5 rounded-full">` with `styles.dot[color]`: a 6px solid dot, centred by the outer flex box, painted with the plain palette steps `bg-green-500`, `bg-yellow-500` and `bg-indigo-500`.
4. Paint the halo with the semantic tokens `bg-status-dot-{green,yellow,indigo}-halo`. Light maps them to green-100, yellow-200 and indigo-100. Dark maps them to the 800 step mixed to 40% with `transparent`, so only the halo dims while the centre dot stays solid.
5. Set `aria-hidden` on the outer span and spread the remaining props after it, so the dot is skipped by screen readers unless a caller explicitly overrides it.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `sizes = halo size-3 (12px), dot size-1.5 (6px)`
  From the Figma status-dropdown dots (node 3731:3266). A 3px ring of halo around the dot is wide enough to read as a glow at body-text size without growing past the 12px icon slot of a select option.
- `light halos = green-100, yellow-200, indigo-100`
  Yellow is one step darker than the other two because yellow-100 nearly vanishes on a white surface.
- `dark halos = color-mix(in srgb, <hue>-800 40%, transparent)`
  A translucent dark halo sits on any dark surface (row hover, selected option) without a visible light disc around the dot.

## API

```ts
interface StatusDotProps extends HTMLAttributes<HTMLSpanElement> { color?: "green" | "yellow" | "indigo"; ref?: Ref<HTMLSpanElement> }
function StatusDot(props: StatusDotProps): JSX.Element
```

- `color: "green" | "yellow" | "indigo"` — default `"green"`
  Picks the halo token and the solid dot colour together.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the outer halo span through `tailwind-merge`.
- `ref: Ref<HTMLSpanElement>`
  Forwarded to the outer span (React 19 ref-as-prop).

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
const styles = sortCx({
  base: "inline-flex size-3 shrink-0 items-center justify-center rounded-full",
  halo: {
    green: "bg-status-dot-green-halo",
    yellow: "bg-status-dot-yellow-halo",
    indigo: "bg-status-dot-indigo-halo",
  },
  dot: {
    green: "bg-green-500",
    yellow: "bg-yellow-500",
    indigo: "bg-indigo-500",
  },
});

export function StatusDot({ color = "green", className, ref, ...props }: StatusDotProps) {
  return (
    <span
      ref={ref}
      aria-hidden
      className={cx(styles.base, styles.halo[color], className)}
      {...props}
    >
      <span className={cx("size-1.5 rounded-full", styles.dot[color])} />
    </span>
  );
}
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** Nothing to clean up. The component is stateless markup with no listeners, timers or effects.

**Reduced motion.** Nothing animates, so the dot renders identically under `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Do not use the dot as the only signal of a status. It is `aria-hidden`, so always render the status label next to it.
- Do not remove `shrink-0`. In a tight flex row the halo collapses into an ellipse.
- Do not paint the halo with a raw palette class such as `bg-green-100`. The semantic token is what switches to the translucent dark-mode halo.
- Do not add a colour that is not in both maps. `styles.halo[color]` and `styles.dot[color]` are indexed by the same key, and a missing key renders an invisible dot.

## Notes

- Used inside the kit by `select` (option markers) and `data-table` (the purchase-status column).
- Only three colours exist because the source design defines only three status pairs. Add a fourth by adding a halo token to both themes and a key to both maps.

## Definition of done

Each of the three colours renders a 12px circle with a 6px solid dot exactly centred in it. The halo is a pale tint of the dot in light mode and a translucent dark tint in dark mode, while the dot itself keeps the same 500-step colour. The outer span has `aria-hidden`, and the circle stays round inside a narrow flex row.

and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Status Select Cell

The coloured status badge from BoardUI table rows ("Recovering", "Under observation", "Critical") turned into its own editor. It is a React Aria Select whose trigger wears the kit Chip colours, so the cell still reads as a static pill; hovering or focusing reveals a chevron, and the list shows each status as its own pill with a check on the current one. Arrow keys, type-ahead, Enter and Escape come from the listbox.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

Table status pill in status-* colours that is also a select: hover reveals a chevron, press or Enter opens the list to change it.

- Category: form
- Runtime cost: css
- Dependencies: react-aria-components@^1.22.1, @remixicon/react@^4.9.0

## How it works

1. Value is controlled (value + onChange) or uncontrolled (defaultValue); the current option is looked up in options by id and its color picks the bg/text pair from the kit CHIP_COLORS map (status-*-background / status-*-text tokens).
2. A React Aria Select wraps an AriaButton styled as the pill (rounded-md, py-0.5, ps-1.5, text-body-medium) whose SelectValue renders only the option label, so the trigger's accessible name is "<label> <aria-label>", e.g. "Critical Status for Livia Saris".
3. A ChevronDownSmall sits at the end of the pill collapsed to width 0 and opacity 0; on data-hovered or data-focus-visible (and always on hover:none touch screens or while open) it grows to 14px wide at 0.7 opacity, 2px from the label and pulled 4px into the end padding, and rotates 180deg while open.
4. The Popover is isNonModal like the kit Select, so it never locks <html> scroll; the kit useDismissOnOutsidePress and useTriggerToggle hooks restore outside-press closing and trigger toggling with a controlled isOpen.
5. Each ListBoxItem renders the status pill and an optional description as React Aria Text slots (label / description, so the option is named by its label and described by the line), plus a RiCheckLine that is visible only when isSelected; choosing the current status is ignored, any other calls onChange(id) and the listbox returns focus to the pill.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `popover width = w-60 (240px), offset 6px`
  Fits the longest pill ("Under observation") plus a one-line description and the check column.
- `chevron = w-0 -> w-3.5 (ms-0.5, -me-1), opacity 0 -> 0.7`
  At rest the pill is as tight as a static badge; on hover the chevron signals "editable" without turning every row into a form field.
- `hover ring = ring-1 ring-current/25`
  Derived from the pill's own text colour, so the hover outline matches every status tone in light and dark.
- `focus ring = ring-2 ring-border-focus-ring ring-offset-1`
  The kit focus treatment; the offset keeps it legible against tinted pills.
- `list height = max-h-[280px]`
  Five statuses with descriptions fit without scrolling; longer workflows scroll inside the surface.

## API

```ts
export function StatusSelectCell<K extends string = string>({ options, value, defaultValue, onChange, "aria-label", size, chevron, placeholder, isDisabled, placement, className, popoverClassName }: StatusSelectCellProps<K>): JSX.Element
```

- `options: readonly StatusOption<K>[]`
  Each { id, label, color: ChipColor, description? }.
- `value / defaultValue: K`
  Selected status id, controlled or initial.
- `onChange: (value: K) => void`
  Called when a different status is picked.
- `aria-label: string` — default `'Status'`
  Accessible name; include the row, e.g. "Status for Ana Carter".
- `size: 'md' | 'sm'` — default `'md'`
  Body (14px) or caption (12px) pill text.
- `chevron: 'hover' | 'always' | 'none'` — default `'hover'`
  When the dropdown chevron is shown.
- `placeholder: ReactNode` — default `'Set status'`
  Shown in a dashed pill when nothing matches.
- `isDisabled: boolean` — default `false`
  Renders the pill at 60% opacity and blocks opening.
- `placement: 'bottom start' | 'bottom end' | 'top start' | 'top end'` — default `'bottom start'`
  Popover placement relative to the pill.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
export function StatusSelectCell<K extends string = string>({
  options,
  value,
  defaultValue,
  onChange,
  'aria-label': ariaLabel = 'Status',
  size = 'md',
  chevron = 'hover',
  placeholder = 'Set status',
  isDisabled,
  placement = 'bottom start',
  className,
  popoverClassName,
}: StatusSelectCellProps<K>) {
  const [inner, setInner] = useState<K | undefined>(defaultValue);
  const current = value ?? inner;
  const option = options.find((o) => o.id === current);

  // Same non-modal recipe as the kit Select: no scroll lock on <html>, with
  // outside-press dismissal and trigger toggling restored by the kit hooks.
  const triggerRef = useRef<HTMLButtonElement>(null);
  const popoverRef = useRef<HTMLElement>(null);
  const refs = useMemo(() => [triggerRef, popoverRef], []);
  const [isOpen, setIsOpen] = useState(false);
  const close = useCallback(() => setIsOpen(false), []);
  useDismissOnOutsidePress(isOpen, close, refs);
  const allowOpenChange = useTriggerToggle(isOpen, triggerRef);

  const select = (key: Key | null) => {
    if (key === null) return;
    const next = options.find((o) => o.id === String(key));
    if (!next || next.id === current) return;
    setInner(next.id);
    onChange?.(next.id);
  };

  const showChevron = chevron !== 'none';

  return (
    <AriaSelect
      aria-label={ariaLabel}
      selectedKey={current ?? null}
      onSelectionChange={select}
      isOpen={isOpen}
      onOpenChange={(open) => allowOpenChange(open) && setIsOpen(open)}
      isDisabled={isDisabled}
      className={cx('inline-flex max-w-full', className)}
    >
      <AriaButton
        ref={triggerRef}
        data-status={current}
        className={cx(
          'group/status inline-flex max-w-full cursor-pointer items-center whitespace-nowrap outline-none',
          'transition-[box-shadow,background-color] duration-150 ease-out motion-reduce:transition-none',
          'data-[hovered]:ring-1 data-[hovered]:ring-current/25',
          'data-[focus-visible]:ring-2 data-[focus-visible]:ring-border-focus-ring data-[focus-visible]:ring-offset-1 data-[focus-visible]:ring-offset-background-primary-default',
          'data-[disabled]:cursor-not-allowed data-[disabled]:opacity-60',
          PILL_SIZE[size],
          option ? CHIP_COLORS[option.color] : 'border border-dashed border-border-button-default text-text-tertiary',
          isOpen && 'ring-1 ring-current/25',
        )}
      >
        <AriaSelectValue className="truncate">{() => (option ? option.label : placeholder)}</AriaSelectValue>
        {showChevron ? (
          <ChevronDownSmall
            className={cx(
              'h-3.5 shrink-0 transition-[width,margin,opacity,rotate] duration-150 ease-out motion-reduce:transition-none',
              chevron === 'always' || isOpen ? CHEVRON_SHOWN : CHEVRON_ON_HOVER,
              isOpen && 'rotate-180',
            )}
          />
        ) : null}
      </AriaButton>
      <AriaPopover
        ref={popoverRef}
        isNonModal
        offset={6}
        placement={placement}
        className={cx(
          MENU_POPOVER_SURFACE,
          'w-60 p-1.5',
          'motion-reduce:transition-opacity motion-reduce:data-[entering]:scale-100 motion-reduce:data-[entering]:blur-none',
          'motion-reduce:data-[exiting]:scale-100 motion-reduce:data-[exiting]:blur-none',
          popoverClassName,
        )}
      >
        <AriaListBox items={options} className={cx(MENU_ITEMS_CONTAINER, 'max-h-[280px] overflow-auto')}>
          {(item) => (
            <AriaListBoxItem
              id={item.id}
              textValue={item.label}
              className={({ isFocused }) => cx(MENU_ITEM, 'items-start gap-2 p-1.5', isFocused && MENU_ITEM_ACTIVE)}
            >
              {({ isSelected }) => (
                <>
                  <span className="flex min-w-0 flex-1 flex-col items-start gap-1">
                    <AriaText
                      slot="label"
                      elementType="span"
                      className={cx('rounded-md px-1.5 py-0.5', size === 'sm' ? 'text-caption-1-medium' : 'text-body-medium', CHIP_COLORS[item.color])}
                    >
                      {item.label}
                    </AriaText>
                    {item.description ? (
                      <AriaText slot="description" elementType="span" className="ps-0.5 text-caption-1-regular text-text-tertiary">
                        {item.description}
                      </AriaText>
                    ) : null}
                  </span>
                  <RiCheckLine
                    aria-hidden
                    className={cx('mt-1 size-4 shrink-0 text-foreground-icon-primary', isSelected ? 'opacity-100' : 'opacity-0')}
                  />
                </>
              )}
            </AriaListBoxItem>
          )}
        </AriaListBox>
      </AriaPopover>
    </AriaSelect>
  );
}
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** Its only listeners are the kit hooks' capture-phase pointerdown handlers, added while open and removed on close or unmount; the toggle hook's 400ms safety timeout only clears a ref.

**Reduced motion.** Ring and chevron transitions are removed (motion-reduce:transition-none) and the popover drops its scale and blur entry, keeping only the opacity fade.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Do not render the label as plain children of the trigger without SelectValue: React Aria labels the button with the SelectValue id, and the value would drop out of the accessible name.
- Pass a row-specific aria-label ("Status for John Clarkson"); a column of identical "Status" names is useless to screen-reader users.
- If the popover is made modal instead, React Aria puts overflow:hidden on <html> while open, which jumps pages that scroll the root element.

## Notes

- size="sm" uses caption text for dense tables; chevron="always" suits touch-first layouts, chevron="none" a pure badge look.
- Options without a match render a dashed placeholder pill ("Set status").

## Definition of done

Tabbing to "Critical Status for Livia Saris" and pressing Enter opens a list of five status pills with a check on Critical; typing "S" moves to "Stable" and Enter closes it, the pill turns lime and reads Stable, the Critical count drops to 0 and Stable rises to 3.

and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Step-End Blinking Caret

A bar caret that blinks the way a terminal cursor does: fully on, then fully off, with nothing in between. The switch is `animation-timing-function: step-end`, which holds each keyframe value until the next one rather than interpolating toward it. The keyframe distribution is deliberately uneven so the rhythm reads as alive rather than as a metronome, and the whole thing is CSS — no JavaScript runs after mount.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

A text caret that snaps on and off instead of fading, using step-end timing and an uneven blink rhythm.

- Category: text
- Runtime cost: css
- Dependencies: none beyond React

## How it works

1. A single `@keyframes` rule sets `opacity: 1` at 0%, 70% and 100%, and `opacity: 0` at 20% and 50%. With `step-end`, each value is held until the following keyframe is reached, so opacity is only ever exactly 1 or exactly 0.
2. The shorthand `animation: var(--kx-caret-period, 1.05s) step-end infinite kinetic-caret-blink` puts the period in a custom property, so the `period` prop varies the speed through an inline `style` without generating a new class or a new keyframe rule.
3. The bar itself is an `inline-block` span with `background-color: currentColor`, so it inherits the colour of the text it sits in, and `vertical-align: -0.14em` to seat it on the baseline of the surrounding type rather than the box.
4. The `paused` state sets `animation: none; opacity: 1` rather than `animation-play-state: paused` — pausing freezes on whichever frame the clock happened to reach, which is a coin flip between a visible caret and an invisible one.
5. The stylesheet is emitted through React 19's `<style href precedence>` hoisting, so the rule is deduplicated by `href` and a hundred carets on a page produce exactly one rule in the document.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `period = 1.05`
  Seconds per full on-off-on-off cycle. Terminal defaults sit near 1s; below ~0.6s it reads as an error indicator, above ~1.6s the reader stops associating the blink with the text it follows.
- `keyframe stops = 0/20/50/70/100%`
  On 0-20, off 20-50, on 50-70, off 70-100. An even 50/50 square wave reads as a metronome. The long-on / short-off asymmetry is what makes it read as something alive rather than as a timer.
- `width = 2`
  Pixels. 1px disappears at typical body sizes on a low-DPI display; past 3px it stops being a caret and starts being a block cursor, which implies overtype mode.
- `vertical-align = -0.14em`
  Seats the bar on the text baseline. At 0 the caret floats above the descender line and looks like a stray rule; in `em` it tracks the type size, so the same caret is correct at 14px and at 72px.

## API

```ts
function StepEndCaret(props: { width?: number; height?: string; period?: number; paused?: boolean; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `width: number` — default `2`
  Bar width in pixels.
- `height: string` — default `'1em'`
  Any CSS length. `em` keeps it locked to the surrounding type size.
- `period: number` — default `1.05`
  Seconds for one full on-off-on-off cycle.
- `paused: boolean` — default `false`
  Hold the caret solid — what a terminal does while keys are down.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the bar via `cn`.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
const CARET_CSS = `
@keyframes kinetic-caret-blink {
  0%, 70%, 100% { opacity: 1; }
  20%, 50%      { opacity: 0; }
}
.kinetic-caret {
  display: inline-block;
  background-color: currentColor;
  vertical-align: -0.14em;
  animation: var(--kx-caret-period, 1.05s) step-end infinite kinetic-caret-blink;
}
/* Paused means solid, not frozen. 'animation-play-state: paused' stops on
   whatever frame it happened to be on, which is a 50% chance of an invisible
   caret. Dropping the animation entirely re-exposes the base opacity. */
.kinetic-caret[data-paused='true'] {
  animation: none;
  opacity: 1;
}
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  .kinetic-caret {
    animation: none;
    opacity: 1;
  }
}
`;

export interface StepEndCaretProps {
  /** Bar width in px. */
  width?: number;
  /** Any CSS length. `em` keeps it locked to the type size around it. */
  height?: string;
  /** Seconds for one on-off-on-off cycle. */
  period?: number;
  /** Hold the caret solid — what a real terminal does while keys are down. */
  paused?: boolean;
  className?: string;
}

export function StepEndCaret({
  width = 2,
  height = '1em',
  period = 1.05,
  paused = false,
  className,
}: StepEndCaretProps) {
  return (
    <>
      <style href="kinetic-step-end-caret" precedence="medium">
        {CARET_CSS}
      </style>
      <span
        aria-hidden
        data-paused={paused ? 'true' : 'false'}
        className={cn('kinetic-caret', className)}
        style={
          {
            width,
            height,
            '--kx-caret-period': `${period}s`,
          } as CSSProperties
        }
      />
    </>
  );
}
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** Nothing to clean up. There is no effect, no timer and no listener; unmounting removes the span, and React's stylesheet hoisting handles the shared rule.

**Reduced motion.** A `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` block inside the component stylesheet sets `animation: none; opacity: 1`. The caret remains fully visible and correctly positioned — it simply stops blinking. It is never left in the off state.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Leaving the default `ease` timing function. The opacity interpolates and the caret pulses like a glow, which reads as decoration; a cursor must be unambiguously present or absent.
- Using `animation-play-state: paused` for the held state. It stops on an arbitrary frame, so roughly half the time the "solid" caret is invisible and the user thinks the field lost focus.
- A symmetric 50/50 blink. It reads as mechanical timekeeping rather than as a cursor waiting for input.
- Hardcoding the caret colour. `background-color: currentColor` is what lets the same component sit inside inverted, accented or muted text without a variant per context.
- Emitting the keyframes per instance in a styled-component or inline `<style>` without a precedence key. Ten carets means ten identical rule sets the style engine has to resolve.
- Exposing the caret to assistive technology. It is `aria-hidden` — a screen reader announcing a decorative bar between every phrase is noise.

## Notes

- No JavaScript executes after mount: no rAF loop, no timer, no listener, nothing to clean up. The component is a span and a stylesheet.
- Designed to be composed — `asymmetric-typewriter` renders this component and drives its `paused` prop from its own typing state.

## Definition of done

The bar is either fully opaque or fully invisible at every moment — screenshot it repeatedly and no intermediate opacity appears. Set `paused` and it goes solid immediately rather than freezing wherever it was. Render ten carets and inspect the document: one `kinetic-step-end-caret` stylesheet. Enable reduced motion and the caret is present and solid.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Stepped Film Grain

A full-screen transparent grain layer for stacking over hero art, video, or flat colour. The pixels are an ordinary hash, and everything that makes it look like film rather than television snow is in the clock: the noise offset is quantised to twelve changes per second, and the frames in between are not drawn at all. Grain cells are sized in CSS pixels, so the overlay weighs the same on a laptop and on a 3x phone.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

A transparent grain overlay whose pattern jumps twelve times a second instead of every frame, so it reads as film.

- Category: webgl
- Runtime cost: webgl
- Dependencies: three@^0.185.1

## How it works

1. A `PlaneGeometry(2, 2)` is written straight to clip space — `gl_Position = vec4(position.xy, 0.0, 1.0)` — so there are no matrices and no camera transform, only a fragment shader over the whole canvas.
2. Each fragment picks a lattice cell with `cell = floor(gl_FragCoord.xy / uPixelRatio / uCellSize) + uOffset`, dividing by the pixel ratio so a cell is a fixed number of CSS pixels rather than of device pixels.
3. `cell = mod(cell, uTile)` wraps the lattice at 170 cells, which keeps the hash argument small enough for float precision and turns the offset into a jump anywhere inside a finite, tiling field.
4. The value is `fract(sin(dot(cell, vec2(12.9898, 78.233))) * 43758.5453)`, shaped into signed grain by `g = (n - 0.5) * uContrast + uLift`. The lift is film base fog: it raises the mean so the layer opens crushed blacks instead of only speckling them.
5. One normal-blended draw carries both directions: the colour is `vec3(step(0.0, g))` — white above the lift, black below — and the alpha is `abs(g) * uOpacity`, with anything under 0.0035 discarded.
6. The rAF callback computes `index = floor(elapsed * stepsPerSecond) % steps` and returns immediately if the index is unchanged, so the GPU sees twelve draws a second regardless of display refresh rate. On a step it reads `uOffset` from a seeded table of integer jumps and renders once.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `stepsPerSecond = 12`
  The filmic/snow dial. Below about 8 the pattern visibly ticks and reads as a stutter; past about 18 the eye fuses the steps into continuous shimmer and it is television snow again. 12 is 24 fps film with each pattern held for two frames.
- `steps = 24`
  Table length. At 12 steps a second this is a 2-second cycle before the sequence repeats — long enough that nothing breathes on a one-second beat, and the whole table is 48 floats.
- `tile = 170`
  Cells before the lattice wraps. Large enough that the repeat is imperceptible in unstructured noise; small enough that `dot(cell, vec2(12.9898, 78.233))` stays around 15 000, where `fract(sin(x) * 43758)` still has usable precision.
- `contrast = 0.24`
  Peak-to-peak swing before opacity, giving a signed range of ±0.12. Past ~0.4 the grain competes with the image it sits on; below ~0.1 it disappears once the browser composites it at 8 bits.
- `lift = 0.095`
  Just under half the contrast, so roughly 80% of samples land above zero. That asymmetry is what makes it read as an emulsion over the image rather than as symmetric static in front of it.
- `opacity = 0.4`
  Peak alpha works out at 0.4 x 0.215 ≈ 0.086. Above ~0.6 the layer stops being texture and starts being a visible veil over type.
- `cellSize = 1 CSS pixel`
  One cell per CSS pixel is the finest grain that is still DPR-invariant. Larger values give coarser, pushed-film grain; smaller values ask for detail below a CSS pixel that the backing store cannot hold.
- `maxDpr = 1`
  A grain cell is a whole CSS pixel, so a 2x backing store draws four device pixels of identical value per cell — four times the fill rate for a bit-identical image. This is the one full-screen shader that should not be rendered at device resolution.
- `ALPHA_EPSILON = 0.0035`
  Just under 1/255. Below it an 8-bit compositor shows nothing, but blending still costs a framebuffer read-modify-write — and on a lifted, low-contrast field a large share of pixels land there.

## API

```ts
function SteppedFilmGrain(props: { opacity?: number; contrast?: number; lift?: number; cellSize?: number; tile?: number; stepsPerSecond?: number; steps?: number; maxDpr?: number; seed?: number | string; className?: string }): JSX.Element
```

- `opacity: number` — default `0.4`
  Overall strength, multiplied onto the grain magnitude.
- `contrast: number` — default `0.24`
  Peak-to-peak swing of the noise before opacity.
- `lift: number` — default `0.095`
  Mean added to the noise — base fog, which biases the layer toward lightening.
- `cellSize: number` — default `1`
  Size of one grain cell in CSS pixels. Clamped to a 0.25 floor.
- `tile: number` — default `170`
  Cells before the lattice repeats. Clamped to a floor of 8.
- `stepsPerSecond: number` — default `12`
  How many times a second the pattern changes. Also the draw rate.
- `steps: number` — default `24`
  Entries in the seeded offset table; the cycle length is steps / stepsPerSecond seconds.
- `maxDpr: number` — default `1`
  Backing-store cap. 1 is deliberate; see the constant.
- `seed: number | string` — default `'stepped-film-grain'`
  Seeds the offset table so the sequence is stable across reloads and matches the server.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the host element via `cn`.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
export function SteppedFilmGrain({
  opacity = 0.4,
  contrast = 0.24,
  lift = 0.095,
  cellSize = 1,
  tile = 170,
  stepsPerSecond = 12,
  steps = 24,
  maxDpr = 1,
  seed = 'stepped-film-grain',
  className,
}: SteppedFilmGrainProps) {
  const host = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const stage = useRef<Stage | null>(null);
  const [unsupported, setUnsupported] = useState(false);

  const { width, height } = useResizeObserver(host);
  const size = useRef({ width, height });
  size.current = { width, height };

  const reduced = useReducedMotion();
  const visible = useVisibility();
  const ready = width > 0 && height > 0;

  const stepCount = Math.max(1, Math.round(steps));

  useEffect(() => {
    const el = host.current;
    if (!el || !ready) return;

    if (!hasWebGL()) {
      setUnsupported(true);
      return;
    }

    let renderer: THREE.WebGLRenderer;
    try {
      renderer = new THREE.WebGLRenderer({
        // Nothing here has a geometric edge, so MSAA would allocate a
        // multisample buffer the size of the canvas and resolve it every draw
        // for no visible difference.
        antialias: false,
        alpha: true,
        depth: false,
        stencil: false,
        powerPreference: 'low-power',
      });
    } catch {
      // A context can still be refused between the probe and the construction —
      // the tab may have hit the browser's live-context ceiling in between. three
      // throws rather than returning null, and an uncaught throw here takes the
      // page with it.
      setUnsupported(true);
      return;
    }
    renderer.setPixelRatio(pixelRatio(maxDpr));
    renderer.setClearAlpha(0);

    const scene = new THREE.Scene();
    // The quad is authored in clip space, so the camera exists only because
    // three's render signature requires one.
    const camera = new THREE.Camera();

    const geometry = new THREE.PlaneGeometry(2, 2);

    const uniforms: Uniforms = {
      uPixelRatio: { value: renderer.getPixelRatio() },
      uOffset: { value: new THREE.Vector2() },
      uCellSize: { value: Math.max(cellSize, 0.25) },
      uTile: { value: Math.max(tile, 8) },
      uContrast: { value: contrast },
      uLift: { value: lift },
      uOpacity: { value: opacity },
    };

    const material = new THREE.ShaderMaterial({
      vertexShader: STEPPED_FILM_GRAIN_VERT,
      fragmentShader: STEPPED_FILM_GRAIN_FRAG,
      uniforms,
      transparent: true,
      depthTest: false,
      depthWrite: false,
      // Normal blending, not additive: the shader emits black as well as white
      // and additive could only lighten, which turns grain into haze.
      blending: THREE.NormalBlending,
    });

    const quad = new THREE.Mesh(geometry, material);
    quad.frustumCulled = false;
    scene.add(quad);

    /* The offset table. Seeded, not `Math.random`, so the sequence is identical
       on the server, on the client, and on every reload — and integer, so each
       jump lands exactly on the cell lattice. A non-integer offset resamples
       cell boundaries and the grain appears to slide a fraction of a cell,
       which is the crawl this component exists to avoid. */
    const rng = createRng(seed);
    const wrap = uniforms.uTile.value;
    const offsets: Array<[number, number]> = [];
    for (let i = 0; i < stepCount; i += 1) {
      offsets.push([Math.floor(rng() * wrap), Math.floor(rng() * wrap)]);
    }

    el.appendChild(renderer.domElement);
    renderer.domElement.style.display = 'block';
    renderer.domElement.style.width = '100%';
    renderer.domElement.style.height = '100%';

    let lastIndex = -1;

    const resize = (w: number, h: number) => {
      if (w <= 0 || h <= 0) return;
      renderer.setPixelRatio(pixelRatio(maxDpr));
      renderer.setSize(w, h, false);
      // Re-read rather than assume: dragging the window between a retina and a
      // non-retina display changes devicePixelRatio without changing the CSS
      // size, and a stale value rescales every grain cell.
      uniforms.uPixelRatio.value = renderer.getPixelRatio();
      // Resizing a canvas clears its drawing buffer, and this component only
      // draws on a step change — without a redraw here the overlay would be
      // blank until the next step, up to 1/stepsPerSecond later.
      renderer.render(scene, camera);
    };

    const step = (index: number) => {
      if (index === lastIndex) return;
      lastIndex = index;
      const pair = offsets[index] ?? offsets[0];
      if (pair) uniforms.uOffset.value.set(pair[0], pair[1]);
      renderer.render(scene, camera);
    };

    resize(size.current.width, size.current.height);
    stage.current = { resize, step };
    step(0);

    return () => {
      stage.current = null;
      geometry.dispose();
      material.dispose();
      disposeRenderer(renderer);
      renderer.domElement.remove();
    };
  }, [ready, opacity, contrast, lift, cellSize, tile, stepCount, maxDpr, seed]);

  useEffect(() => {
    stage.current?.resize(width, height);
  }, [width, height]);

  useRaf((_dt, elapsed) => {
    // Quantised time, not time. Everything filmic about this component is the
    // fact that this number changes twelve times a second and the draw call
    // is skipped in between.
    const index = Math.floor(elapsed * stepsPerSecond) % stepCount;
    stage.current?.step(index);
  }, ready && visible && !reduced && !unsupported);
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** Nulls the stage ref, disposes the quad geometry and the ShaderMaterial, calls `disposeRenderer` for `dispose` + `forceContextLoss` + a zeroed drawing buffer, then removes the canvas from the DOM. `useRaf` releases its own frame subscription, and there are no listeners of the component's own — sizing comes from the shared ResizeObserver and visibility from the shared document listener.

**Reduced motion.** The component reads `useReducedMotion` itself. No rAF subscription is opened, and the grain is drawn once at table entry 0 — the texture is fully present and correct, it simply never advances. That is the right degradation for grain: it is a surface quality, not a motion, and removing it entirely would change how the artwork beneath it reads.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Advancing the noise every frame. It is the single thing that separates film grain from TV static, and it also makes the effect frame-rate dependent — the same overlay churns twice as fast on a 120 Hz display. Quantising the offset fixes both at once.
- Sliding the offset by a constant per step instead of jumping to table entries. A constant increment makes the whole field crawl in one direction, and the eye locks onto and tracks that direction; uncorrelated jumps have nowhere to track.
- Using a fractional offset. Non-integer values move the lattice off the pixel grid, so cell boundaries resample and the grain shimmers within each step — the artefact the stepping was supposed to remove.
- Declaring `precision mediump float` out of habit. The hash argument reaches ~15 000, which a 16-bit float holds to three digits, so adjacent cells return the same value and the grain becomes flat blocks tens of pixels wide. This shader needs highp.
- Sizing grain in device pixels. `gl_FragCoord` is a device-pixel coordinate, so grain authored without dividing by the pixel ratio is three times finer and effectively invisible on the phone, while looking correct on the machine it was tuned on.
- Rendering the overlay at the device pixel ratio. A cell is one CSS pixel of constant value; a 2x buffer costs four times the fragments and produces the identical image.
- Forgetting that resizing a canvas clears its drawing buffer. A component that only draws on a step change goes blank for up to 1/stepsPerSecond after every resize, which during a window drag is a visible flicker — the resize path redraws explicitly.
- Using additive blending so the grain can only lighten. The result is haze rather than grain; emitting black or white with the magnitude in alpha gets both directions out of one normal-blended draw.

## Notes

- The host is `pointer-events-none` and `aria-hidden`. It is a decorative layer that must never intercept a click on the content underneath it.
- If WebGL is unavailable the component renders an empty box. A missing grain layer is a correct degradation — the content beneath is untouched.
- Stack it as the last child of a relatively-positioned container with `absolute inset-0`. It composites through the browser, so no blend mode is required, though `mix-blend-mode: overlay` is a reasonable variation over photography.

## Definition of done

A fine speckle over the content that visibly holds still for a beat and then changes, roughly twelve times a second — count it by eye and it should read as a flicker, not a fizz. Zoom the browser from 100% to 200% and the grain gets larger with the layout rather than staying pinned to device pixels. Resize the window and the overlay never blanks. With reduced motion the grain is still there and completely static.

and where, so I can check them.

# Build: Steps Card

A grey dashboard card headed "Steps" with the week total ("31,600 total steps") and a week pill with arrows. Below are seven rounded grey tracks, Monday to Sunday, each filled from the bottom with a teal bar for that day's steps. The bars grow in on mount and glide to new heights when the week changes, while the total counts to the new figure. Hovering or focusing a bar outlines it, deepens its teal and rolls the headline to that day's steps ("6,340 steps on Thu").

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

Seven daily step bars with a week switcher, a total that counts up, and an outline on the hovered bar that rolls the headline to that day.

- Category: display
- Runtime cost: css
- Dependencies: @remixicon/react@^4.9.0

## How it works

1. All weeks share one scale: `max`, or by default the busiest day across every week rounded up to the next 1,000 (8,000 for the sample data). A fill's height is `steps / scale` as a percentage of its track, so switching weeks compares like with like instead of re-stretching each week to its own peak.
2. Each fill is an absolutely positioned span at the bottom of its track with an inline `height` percentage and a 600ms expo-out `height` transition, delayed 40ms per bar from Monday so the row grows left to right. On mount every height is 0; two animation frames later the real heights apply, so the transition draws them in. A week change only changes the heights, so the same transition moves them.
3. The headline number is `useCountUp(target, 600)` from the shared hooks. The target is 0 until the bars are drawn, then the hovered day's steps or else the week total; the hook eases from whatever is on screen to the new target, so hovering across bars or changing week mid-roll never jumps. The unit ("total steps" or "steps on Thu") is a keyed span, so `.animate-number-fade` replays when it changes.
4. Bars are buttons in a group with a roving tabindex: Arrow Left and Right move focus, Home and End jump to Monday and Sunday. Pointer enter and focus set the active bar and pointer leave of the row or blur clears it. The active track gets a 2px teal outline, offset 2px and faded in over 150ms, and its fill switches to `chart-1-active`; keyboard focus uses the focus-ring colour instead.
5. The card is a container (`@container`). Under 420px the unit drops below the number so the header never collides with the week pill, and from 480px the bar gap opens from 8px to 30px.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `chartHeight = 200px`
  Tall enough that a 1,000-step difference is 25px, which the eye reads at a glance.
- `GROW_MS / STAGGER = 600ms / 40ms`
  The whole row settles in under a second, and a short stagger reads as a sweep without making Sunday wait.
- `scale rounding = up to the next 1,000`
  The busiest day nearly fills its track but never touches the top, so no bar looks clipped.
- `count-up = 600ms ease-out cubic`
  Same length as the bar growth, so the number and the bars land together.

## API

```ts
function StepsCard(props?: StepsCardProps): JSX.Element
type StepsWeek = { id: string; label: string; days: number[] }
```

- `title: string` — default `"Steps"`
  Header label.
- `totalLabel: string` — default `"total steps"`
  Unit after the week total.
- `weeks: StepsWeek[]` — default `STEPS_WEEKS`
  Weeks the pill steps through, oldest first.
- `weekIndex: number`
  Controlled index into `weeks`.
- `defaultWeekIndex: number` — default `weeks.length - 1`
  Uncontrolled starting week.
- `onWeekIndexChange: (index: number) => void`
  Called when an arrow changes week.
- `max: number` — default `busiest day rounded up to 1,000`
  Top of the shared bar scale.
- `chartHeight: number` — default `200`
  Height of the bar tracks in px.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the card section.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
// One fixed scale for every week, so switching weeks compares like with like.
const scale = useMemo(() => {
  if (maxProp && maxProp > 0) return maxProp;
  const peak = Math.max(0, ...weeks.flatMap((w) => w.days));
  return Math.max(1000, Math.ceil(peak / 1000) * 1000);
}, [weeks, maxProp]);
const live = drawn || reduced;
const total = days.reduce((sum, n) => sum + n, 0);
const activeSteps = active !== null ? days[active] : undefined;
// The headline rolls to the hovered day's steps, back to the week total, or up from 0 on mount.
const target = live ? (activeSteps ?? total) : 0;
const counted = useCountUp(target, 600);
const shown = reduced ? target : counted;
const pct = (n: number) => (live ? Math.min(100, Math.max(0, (n / scale) * 100)) : 0);
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** The mount effect cancels both pending animation frames on unmount, and `useCountUp` cancels its frame whenever the target changes or the card unmounts. Pointer, focus and key handling are React event props.

**Reduced motion.** With `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`, the bars render at their final heights from the first frame and `motion-reduce:transition-none` makes week changes and hover outlines instant. The headline shows the target value directly instead of counting, and the unit no longer fades.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Scaling each week to its own peak. Every week then looks equally busy; a shared scale is what makes the switcher useful.
- Animating the bars with `scaleY`. It squashes the rounded corners while it grows; transitioning `height` keeps the 10px radius intact, and seven elements are cheap to lay out.
- Rolling the number with a fresh tween that starts from the old target. If the pointer crosses bars mid-roll the number jumps; easing from the value on screen keeps it continuous.

## Notes

- Exports `STEPS_WEEKS` (six sample weeks, oldest first) and the `StepsWeek` type `{ id, label, days }`, where `days` holds seven counts starting on Monday.

## Definition of done

The default card reads "Steps", "31,600 total steps" (counting up from 0 on load) and "29 Jun - 5 Jul", with the next arrow disabled. Seven teal bars grow left to right in grey tracks: Friday is the tallest at about nine tenths of its track and Wednesday the shortest. Hovering Thursday outlines its track in teal and the headline rolls to "6,340 steps on Thu"; leaving the row rolls it back to 31,600. Clicking the previous arrow shows "22 Jun - 28 Jun", the bars move to their new heights and the total counts to 32,010.

# Build: Stroke-To-Fill Hover Rows

A list of large type where every row is an outline with a ghost of fill, and the hovered row materialises: the stroke drops to zero width, the fill goes to full `currentColor`, and the row steps 12px to the right while its siblings recede. The row does not light up, it becomes solid. Everything is CSS, so nothing but the compositor runs on hover.

Build this as a React component in my project. Match my existing conventions —
file layout, styling system, and naming — rather than the ones implied below.
Everything after this line is specification, not code to copy verbatim.

## What it does

An index of outlined type where the hovered row fills in solid, drops its stroke, and steps sideways.

- Category: text
- Runtime cost: css
- Dependencies: none beyond React

## How it works

1. Two properties carry the effect, and they are separate on purpose: `-webkit-text-stroke-width` goes 1px to 0, and `-webkit-text-fill-color` goes from a ghost of `currentColor` to `currentColor` itself.
2. `-webkit-text-fill-color` overrides `color` for the glyph interior only, which is what lets the outline stay at `currentColor` while the inside is nearly transparent. Doing this with `color` alone is impossible — `color` is also what `currentColor` resolves to, so fading the fill fades the stroke with it and the row just dims.
3. The ghost is `color-mix(in oklch, currentColor var(--kx-sf-ghost, 16%), transparent)` rather than a literal `rgba`. It inherits the surrounding text colour, so one component is correct on a dark page and a light one, and mixing in oklch keeps the 16% step perceptually even instead of clumping toward black the way sRGB alpha does.
4. The three tunables are custom properties set on the `<ul>` from props (`--kx-sf-stroke`, `--kx-sf-ghost`, `--kx-sf-nudge`), so per-instance configuration needs no extra class and no extra rule.
5. Sibling dimming is scoped to the list's own hover: `.kinetic-sf-list:hover .kinetic-sf-row:not(:hover) { opacity: 0.45 }`. Scoping to the list is what makes the resting state "all rows equal" rather than "all rows dimmed".
6. Every hover rule is duplicated for `:focus-visible`. Each row is a real `<a>` or `<button>` inside an `<li>`, so keyboard traversal produces the same state change — without it a keyboard user tabbing ten identical outlines has no idea where they are.
7. The stylesheet is emitted once through React 19's `<style href precedence>` hoisting, so any number of lists on a page share one rule set.

## Constants — use these values

These are tuned. Each one has a reason; do not round them off or replace them
with values that "look cleaner".

- `STROKE_WIDTH = 1`
  Pixels of outline at rest. At the 28-72px type this component targets, 1px is a hairline that still reads as a complete letterform; 2px starts to close up counters in tighter faces and the row looks bold rather than outlined.
- `GHOST = 16`
  Percent of `currentColor` mixed into the resting fill. At 0 the glyph interiors are fully transparent and the type dissolves into whatever is behind it; past ~30% the resting and hovered states are too close for the transition to register.
- `NUDGE = 12`
  Pixels the hovered row steps right. Enough to be unmistakable next to a static neighbour; past ~24px the row visibly leaves the left margin of the list and the alignment looks broken.
- `transition duration / curve = 380ms cubic-bezier(0.16, 1, 0.3, 1)`
  A strong ease-out. The row arrives quickly and settles, which matches the pointer having already stopped. A symmetric ease at this duration lags the cursor noticeably on a fast pass down a ten-row list.
- `sibling opacity = 0.45`
  Enough separation that the hovered row is unambiguous, while the others stay legible — dimming to 0.2 turns a browsable index into a spotlight and hides the thing the user is scanning for.

## API

```ts
function StrokeToFillRows(props: { items: StrokeToFillItem[]; strokeWidth?: number; ghost?: number; nudge?: number; className?: string; onSelect?: (item: StrokeToFillItem, index: number) => void }): JSX.Element
```

- `items: StrokeToFillItem[]`
  Rows. Each has a `label`, an optional `meta` node for right-hand metadata, and an optional `href`.
- `strokeWidth: number` — default `1`
  Outline thickness in px at rest.
- `ghost: number` — default `16`
  Resting fill as a percentage of `currentColor`.
- `nudge: number` — default `12`
  Pixels the hovered row steps right.
- `className: string`
  Merged onto the `<ul>` via `cn`.
- `onSelect: (item: StrokeToFillItem, index: number) => void`
  Called when a row without an `href` is activated.

## Reference implementation of the core

This is the part that is hard to get right. Adapt it; do not treat the rest of
the component as fixed.

```tsx
const ROWS_CSS = `
.kinetic-sf-title {
  -webkit-text-stroke: var(--kx-sf-stroke, 1px) currentColor;
  -webkit-text-fill-color: color-mix(in oklch, currentColor var(--kx-sf-ghost, 16%), transparent);
  transition:
    -webkit-text-fill-color 380ms cubic-bezier(0.16, 1, 0.3, 1),
    -webkit-text-stroke-width 380ms cubic-bezier(0.16, 1, 0.3, 1),
    transform 380ms cubic-bezier(0.16, 1, 0.3, 1);
  transform: translate3d(0, 0, 0);
}
/* :focus-visible alongside :hover, always. A keyboard user tabbing an index
   of ten rows otherwise sees ten identical outlines and no current position. */
.kinetic-sf-row:hover .kinetic-sf-title,
.kinetic-sf-row:focus-visible .kinetic-sf-title {
  -webkit-text-fill-color: currentColor;
  -webkit-text-stroke-width: 0px;
  transform: translate3d(var(--kx-sf-nudge, 12px), 0, 0);
}
/* Everything that is not the hovered row recedes. Scoped to the list's own
   hover so the resting state is all rows equal, not all rows dimmed. */
.kinetic-sf-list:hover .kinetic-sf-row:not(:hover) {
  opacity: 0.45;
}
.kinetic-sf-row {
  transition: opacity 380ms cubic-bezier(0.16, 1, 0.3, 1);
}
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  /* The stroke-to-fill swap is a state change, not motion, and it stays. The
     12 px lateral travel is motion, and it goes. */
  .kinetic-sf-row:hover .kinetic-sf-title,
  .kinetic-sf-row:focus-visible .kinetic-sf-title {
    transform: none;
  }
}
`;

export interface StrokeToFillItem {
  label: string;
  /** Right-hand metadata: a year, a category, a count. */
  meta?: ReactNode;
  href?: string;
}

export interface StrokeToFillRowsProps {
  items: StrokeToFillItem[];
  /** Outline thickness in px at rest. */
  strokeWidth?: number;
  /** Resting fill, as a percentage of `currentColor`. */
  ghost?: number;
  /** Pixels the hovered row steps right. */
  nudge?: number;
  className?: string;
  onSelect?: (item: StrokeToFillItem, index: number) => void;
}

const STROKE_WIDTH = 1;
const GHOST = 16;
const NUDGE = 12;

export function StrokeToFillRows({
  items,
  strokeWidth = STROKE_WIDTH,
  ghost = GHOST,
  nudge = NUDGE,
  className,
  onSelect,
}: StrokeToFillRowsProps) {
  return (
    <>
      <style href="kinetic-stroke-to-fill" precedence="medium">
        {ROWS_CSS}
      </style>
      <ul
        className={cn('kinetic-sf-list w-full', className)}
        style={
          {
            '--kx-sf-stroke': `${strokeWidth}px`,
            '--kx-sf-ghost': `${ghost}%`,
            '--kx-sf-nudge': `${nudge}px`,
          } as CSSProperties
        }
      >
        {items.map((item, i) => {
          const inner = (
            <>
              <span className="kinetic-sf-title block text-[clamp(28px,5.5vw,72px)] leading-[1.06] tracking-[-0.03em]">
                {item.label}
              </span>
              {item.meta ? (
                <span className="meta shrink-0 pt-[0.35em]">{item.meta}</span>
              ) : null}
            </>
          );

          return (
            <li key={`${item.label}-${i}`} className="border-b border-line">
              {item.href ? (
                <a
                  href={item.href}
                  className="kinetic-sf-row flex w-full items-start justify-between gap-6 py-[0.35em] text-left outline-none"
                >
                  {inner}
                </a>
              ) : (
                <button
                  type="button"
                  onClick={() => onSelect?.(item, i)}
                  className="kinetic-sf-row flex w-full items-start justify-between gap-6 py-[0.35em] text-left outline-none"
                >
                  {inner}
                </button>
              )}
            </li>
          );
        })}
      </ul>
    </>
  );
}
```

## Requirements

These are not optional. A version of this component that skips any of them is
not finished.

**Cleanup.** Nothing to clean up: no effect, no listener, no timer. Unmounting removes the list; React's `<style precedence>` hoisting owns the shared rule set.

**Reduced motion.** The stroke-to-fill swap is a state change, not motion, so it is kept in full — the hovered row still fills solid and its siblings still recede. Only the 12px lateral travel is removed, via `transform: none` in a `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` block. The rows are never left unreadable.

**Frame-rate independence.** Any smoothing must be a function of delta time.
`x += (target - x) * 0.1` converges twice as fast at 120 Hz as at 60 Hz; use
`x = target + (x - target) * Math.pow(smoothing, dt)` instead, where
`smoothing` is the fraction of the gap remaining after one second.

**Strict mode.** Assume effects run twice in development. Setup must be
idempotent and teardown must fully undo it.

## Known pitfalls — avoid these specifically

- Trying to build this with `color` alone. Fading the fill fades the stroke with it because `currentColor` resolves to the same value, so the row dims instead of filling.
- Transitioning the `-webkit-text-stroke` shorthand. Shorthands are not independently interpolable here; transition `-webkit-text-stroke-width` explicitly or the stroke snaps off in one frame while the fill glides.
- Hardcoding the resting fill as `rgba(255,255,255,0.16)`. The component is then wrong the moment it lands on a light background, and wrong again in an inverted section of the same page.
- Mixing the ghost in sRGB. The intermediate steps clump toward black, so the resting fill on a mid-tone accent looks muddy rather than faint.
- Dimming siblings without scoping to `.kinetic-sf-list:hover`. Every row is then permanently at 0.45 and the "recede" has nothing to recede from.
- Styling `:hover` and forgetting `:focus-visible`. Keyboard users get ten identical outlines and no indication of the current row, which is a genuine accessibility failure and not just a polish gap.
- Animating `left` or `margin-left` for the nudge. Both trigger layout on every row of a large-type index; `translate3d` stays on the compositor.

## Notes

- No text splitting and no motion library: this is a state change on a whole row, so imposing a splitter or GSAP on the consumer for a CSS-cost effect would be pure overhead.
- `-webkit-text-stroke` is unprefixed-less by history but supported in every current engine including Firefox and Safari. There is no standards-track alternative that composites the same way.
- Rows render as `<a>` when `href` is given and as `<button>` otherwise, so the list is keyboard-traversable either way without a `tabIndex` hack.

## Definition of done

Hover a row: the outline thins to nothing as the glyph interiors fill to full colour, and the row slides 12px right while the others fade back. Tab through with a keyboard and the same state appears on the focused row. Flip the page between light and dark themes and the resting ghost fill is still faintly visible in both, without editing the component. With reduced motion enabled the fill still happens and the row does not move.

When you are finished, tell me which of the requirements above you implemented
and where, so I can check them.
